#5507. Pending Sales Down Over 16% as 2026 Market Craters

Pending home sales have slowed significantly according to the latest data from the National Association of Realtors® (NAR), sparking questions about the long-term health of the housing market as activity falls to levels seen three decades ago.

NAR’s Pending Home Sales report for October reveals that sales dropped by 4.7% month-over-month, and fell 16.7% on an annual basis. The monthly decrease is not as severe as September’s drop of 7.3%, but pendings are now far below the same point in the housing cycle last year as economists expect an even slower fall and winter market.

“October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said.

Prior to the report’s release, Realtor.com® Senior Economist Hannah Jones expected pending sales to fall, attributing high mortgage rates as the cause.

“Mortgage rates climbed nearly 75 basis points from late August to mid-October, adding roughly $200 a month to the typical mortgage payment on a median-priced home, assuming a 10% down payment. That is more than many already-strained buyers can easily absorb,” she stated.

The latest data from Freddie Mac showed the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 7.11%, down from mid-October’s high around 7.40%. Despite rates reducing, Jones noted that she expects affordability problems to persist.

“Markets now expect that a Fed rate hike is coming in December,” she added. “Until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a downward path, affordability problems are likely to persist, keeping contract signings and home sales subdued.”

Although Jones predicts one final rate hike before the end of the year, Federal Reserve Open Market Committee Chairman Kevin Warsh did not allude to housing or rate hikes in his Nov. 16 remarks. Rather, he honed in on the impact of “superintelligence”—an alternative term for AI preferred by President Donald Trump—on the economy at large.

In line with September’s data, October saw all four regions decline in pending home sales, both monthly and annually.

Western states experienced the greatest drop month-over-month, with a 6.9% decrease. Following the West was the South, Midwest and Northeast at declines of 6.3%, 2.7% and 0.8%, respectively.

Annually, the rankings are the same. The West’s pending home sales fell by 20.3%, South by 18.7%, Midwest by 14% and the Northeast at 11.1%.

On a local level, the report notes that pending home sales fell annually even in the strongest markets. Using data from Realtor.com, NAR highlighted the top 10 strongest markets for pending home sales, and found that they still experienced declines.

The slowing in pending home sales coupled with lackluster homebuilder confidence—which was last reported at a new 14-year low—leaves many questioning whether 2027 will see a turn-around for the housing market, as 2026 will likely end on a low note.

“It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million,” Yun concluded. “Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.”

Desirae Sin is an assistant editor for RISMedia. She graduated from the University of Connecticut in 2025 with a double major in Journalism and Political Science. Prior to joining RISMedia, Desirae wrote stories geared toward policy issues for the Connecticut Mirror. She also worked as a staff writer for The Daily Campus, UConn's student-run newspaper.

#5506. 3 Housing Questions That Might Come Up at Your Next Family Dinner

This time of year usually means more time spent with family and friends. And in recent years, when everyone gets together, the conversation has a way of drifting to housing.

Your uncle is sure home prices are about to crash. Your cousin heard foreclosures are surging. And someone across the table brings up the word “recession.”

If you’ve wondered about any of this yourself, that makes sense. There’s a lot of noise out there. So let’s look at what the data actually shows, so you’ll have real answers the next time it comes up.

Let’s start with your uncle’s crash prediction. The short answer is no. Experts project home prices will keep climbing nationally in 2027.

On average, forecasters expect prices to rise about 1.4% next year (see graph below). That’s slower than the big jumps of a few years ago, but it’s still growth, not a crash.

Prices are dipping in some markets, though. It just depends on where you live. Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), explains why:

“Price declines are occurring mainly in southern states, where there has been robust new home construction in recent years. Given the region’s faster job growth, these price drops should be viewed as temporary and as a second-chance opportunity for those previously priced out of the market.”

So, the dips that are fueling all the social media chatter are limited to select areas, and experts think they’ll be short-lived. It doesn’t mean a crash is looming.

If you’re thinking about moving, look at the numbers for your area.

Then your cousin chimes in about foreclosures. They’ve ticked up lately, but here’s some important context. That’s compared to very low levels. They’re still below where they were before the pandemic, according to ATTOM.

So, why doesn’t today look like 2008? Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . we have had many recessions post-WWII but only one foreclosure crisis. That foreclosure crisis started with a massive credit boom from 2002-2005, and then a credit bust. . . none of that is happening now . . .“

Today’s homeowners also have something a lot of people didn’t have back then – equity. In every state, the average homeowner with a mortgage has more than $100,000 of it, according to Cotality (see map below):

If a homeowner hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house instead of facing foreclosure.

While someone in your family may be convinced a recession is coming, experts don’t agree. The average forecast from The Wall Street Journal’s survey of economists puts the odds at about 24%, so most experts aren’t expecting one. And that’s a good thing.

But even if one hits, history shows a recession doesn’t mean home prices will automatically fall. In 5 of the last 6 recessions, prices actually went up, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) (see graph below):

The one exception was 2008, the only one of these recessions that started in the housing market itself.

So, the next time your uncle predicts a crash or your cousin brings up 2008, you’ll know prices aren’t crashing, foreclosures are still low, and a recession doesn’t automatically spell trouble for housing. If a move in 2027 is on your mind, connect with a local real estate agent to look at what prices are doing in your neighborhood so you can plan with real local numbers, not scary headlines.

#5505. Matt Damon Reveals the One Strict Rule He Makes His Kids Follow on Movie Nights at Home

Movie star Matt Damon has revealed he doesn't fool around when it comes time for his family to watch movies at their sprawling property.

While speaking to People, the actor, 56, opened up about their at-home rules he ensures his wife, Luciana Damon, and their daughters Alexia, Isabella, Gia, and Stella follow.

“I tell my kids, it’s the same rules as when we go to the theater: no phones, no talking. I try to create the movie experience as much as I can in my house. That’s not easy to do. ... In our living room, behind us is a dining room and a kitchen. It’s an open floor plan. So there’s a lot of light. So it’s like, you get all the lights off, and you get it dark," he told the outlet.

The Hollywood icon revealed his kids adore films just as much as he does.

"This generation is really coming back to theaters, which is wonderful," he said. "So I just try to instill in them that it can be like that at home, too. If you give it that same kind of reverence, it can be just as fun.

"Because being on this side of it and knowing what it takes to make every shot and how much love and care and work is put into every single shot that you’re seeing, you want to give the director and the team your complete attention as much as you can."

He also opened up about how fans should stream his hit film "The Odyssey," telling moviegoers that they should re-create the experience at home.

Damon's co-star John Leguizamo told the outlet, “You want to immerse yourself because it’s a community experience you hope to have at home as well as going to the theater. You want to see people’s reactions, and you want them to feel the things you felt.”

Leguizamo admitted that he and his wife, Justine Maurer, sobbed during their first viewing of the film, adding, "You live vicariously through her experience, and it means something different.”

Meanwhile, producer Emma Thomas told the outlet about how she and her husband, writer-director Christopher Nolan, transformed their garage into a home movie room.

“It’s actually also where Chris and our editor edit the film. We have a very large collection of physical media, and we watch films that way a great deal. ... It is nice because you can have a cup of tea and the dog can be sitting at your feet," Thomas told People.

“I’m a big fan of darkening a room and getting a projector up on a wall. You know, I might try to twist their arms into doing that. I think they’ll probably watch the behind-the-scenes [features] to see if they made it in," Nolan added.

#5504. Dell bets liquid-cooled, software-defined storage can keep AI factories fed

AI factories are growing so dense that storage, not just compute, now decides how quickly they turn data into tokens. For Dell Technologies Inc., the answer starts with turning its PowerEdge servers into flexible, software-defined storage nodes that can change roles as workloads shift.

The move from training toward inference and agents has put new pressure on time to value. Dell has spent the year extending its AI Data Platform with a semantic layer for agentic workloads. Its AI factory pitch now reaches well beyond compute and graphics processing units, according to George Papadopoulos (pictured), senior vice president of product and engineering at Dell.

“We look at our AI factory not just as a set of CPUs and GPUs, but networking becoming more and more important, particularly around speed, reliability of storage and the ability to take your raw data and generate context and knowledge from it,” he said.

Papadopoulos spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Dell is adapting its storage and cooling to keep AI factories running at scale. (* Disclosure below.)

Customers want storage they can buy for today’s needs and repurpose later. For instance, a customer might start with file and move to object or parallel file as workloads evolve. Agentic workloads lean on small input/output operations rather than streaming, so the right storage type can shift quickly, Papadopoulos explained. Dell’s answer is Dell Exascale Storage, which runs as licensed software on Dell servers.

“It’s our really purpose-built software-defined solution for allowing us to take a PowerEdge-based node and … with flexible licensing, allow you to deploy a file persona, a block persona, an object persona or a parallel file persona, and allow that flexibility to change over time as your needs change,” he said.

Density is also forcing a rethink of cooling. The power envelope of today’s AI systems is so large that customers are planning for 100% liquid-cooled data centers, according to Papadopoulos. That requirement now extends to storage.

“The conversations have really gotten down to how can we most effectively provide a direct liquid-cooled solution — and the storage, that means even liquid cooling the drives, which is something that hasn’t been done as of yet,” he said.

At SC26, Dell unveiled a 2U, 32-drive node with 100% liquid cooling, which it bills as the first direct liquid-cooled storage for rack-scale AI. The node deploys as an Exascale system with any persona. Separating the software from an appliance also lets Dell bring new PowerEdge generations to market faster. That flexibility matters for neocloud operators, who need an off-ramp for every purchase, Papadopoulos noted.

“That allows them to make an upfront purchase and know that they won’t be locked into one particular storage type,” he said, “or have a set of data silos that they can’t leverage as they go forward.”

#5503. The Thanksgiving Hosting Stress Test: Is Your Place Ready for the Big Day?

Hosting Thanksgiving in your first home is exciting, but it can also feel overwhelming.

“You likely want everything to look and feel ‘put together’ as soon as possible despite the fact that a fresh move-in is typically anything but,” says Kate Pechinka, founder and principal designer of Kate Kelly Interiors in Chester Springs, PA.

The pressures of living up to the warm environment you’ve either experienced growing up or seen in movies or advertisements combined with the added demands on your home’s systems don’t make things any easier.

“Suddenly, multiple people are using the bathrooms, the dishwasher and garbage disposal are running frequently, the oven is working for hours, and guests are moving through spaces that may not have been arranged for entertaining,” explains Kevin Vander Hyde, vice president of Vander Hyde Services in Grand Rapids, MI.

Here’s the good news: With a little preparation and planning, you can ensure your home is Thanksgiving-ready and alleviate a great deal of stress long before your guests arrive.

These expert tips can help you address safety concerns, secure your belongings, and prevent common hosting mishaps this Turkey Day—all while keeping your sanity and budget in check as a new homeowner.

Ensure keepsakes, special family heirlooms, and other high-value items are either put away, well protected, or displayed in a place that invites appreciation, but not direct interaction like a high mantel or glass-front china cabinet.

“Anticipate that curious guests of all ages might not be able to fight the urge to touch,” Pechinka explains.

Chances are guests will set drinks or food items down on your tables, couches, and other furniture. That’s why it’s important to shield them from accidental spills, stains, and scratches.

For pieces with inviting tabletop surfaces you don’t intend to move, Pechinka recommends  having a piece of glass cut at your local glass shop to place on the surface.

“This option can create a polished look and provide a high level of protection. It’s also cost-effective when you consider the cost to refinish or replace a piece of furniture,” says Pechinka.

No matter where you live, your home is likely filled with trip hazards like step-downs into family rooms, or area rugs that change the height of flooring surfaces. These potential hazards can create unique challenges for guests of all ages.

“To reduce their risk, improve lighting in these areas. You can also use rug tape to keep rug corners down,” Pechinka explains.

Children or nosy adults may walk into bedrooms and other rooms you might not want them to venture into.

Make sure you know how many dishes, coffee cups, and utensils you need.

“This simple check keeps you from washing dishes midparty and lets you remain fully engaged with your guests,” Pechinka adds.

Make sure the oven heats properly, the stovetop burners work, and the dishwasher completes a cycle without leaking.

“If you're preparing several dishes, plan out cooking times and oven space in advance. Avoid plugging multiple high-wattage countertop appliances into the same overloaded circuit,” says Vander Hyde.

Run the kitchen and bathroom faucets, flush the toilets, and check that sinks and tubs drain properly.

“Slow drains, low water pressure, dripping faucets, or unusual odors can be signs of a plumbing issue you should address before guests arrive,” Vander Hyde explains.

Remember that catching and resolving a small problem early on is always easier and less expensive than dealing with an unexpected and much larger repair once the holiday is over.

Resist the temptation to treat the garbage disposal like a trash can.

Avoid putting grease, cooking oil, large amounts of food, or fibrous scraps down the drain. Run cold water while operating the disposal, and feed food scraps gradually rather than trying to grind everything at once.

“Grease and food buildup are common contributors to holiday drain clogs,” says Vandrer Hyde.

With multiple guests showering, washing dishes, and using hot water, demand can increase significantly. That’s why it’s vital to ensure the water heater is operating normally.

“Watch for signs of trouble, such as inconsistent hot water, leaks, or unusual noises. If you notice any of them, it’s time to call a plumber,” Vander Hyde explains.

Before guests arrive, test the thermostat, replace a dirty air filter, and make sure vents aren't blocked by furniture or rugs.

“If the furnace is making unusual noises or struggling to maintain the temperature, arrange an inspection before the holiday,” adds Vander Hyde.

#5502. Builder Sentiment Falls to 14-Year Low in November

Builder confidence fell sharply in November as higher mortgage rates, persistent affordability challenges, and rising construction costs continued to weigh on the new-home market, according to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB).

The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index fell four points to 25 in November, its lowest reading since April 2012. The index stood at 29 in October. Any reading below 50 indicates more builders view market conditions as poor than good.

“Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today’s economy,” says Bill Owens, chairman of the NAHB. “Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction.”

All three components of the HMI declined during the month. The index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, while the component measuring sales expectations over the next six months declined two points to 30. Prospective buyer traffic dropped two points to 16, its lowest level in 15 years excluding the onset of the pandemic in 2020.

In response to weaker demand, builders continued to rely heavily on incentives and price reductions to attract buyers. The share of builders cutting home prices increased to 46% in November, the highest level of the post-Covid period. The average price reduction remained at 6% for the eighth consecutive month.

Meanwhile, 68% of builders offered sales incentives, also a post-Covid high. November marked the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders reported using incentives. That represents a further deterioration from October, when 43% of builders reported cutting prices and 65% used incentives.

“The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges, including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability,” says Robert Dietz, NAHB chief economist. “Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence, and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back.”

On a three-month moving-average basis, builder confidence declined in every region. The Northeast fell four points to 34, the Midwest declined five points to 35, the South dropped three points to 27, and the West fell three points to 23.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5501. OpenAI rolls out GPT-6.2 Astra for professional work and GPT-6.2 Sol for everyday work

OpenAI Group PBC today announced the launch of GPT-6.2 Astra, a new frontier artificial intelligence model for complex professional work that is claimed to outperform its predecessor at less than a third of the cost, along with an updated version of its everyday model, GPT-6.2 Sol.

The new models are aimed at businesses and developers looking for frontier performance at a cost that works at scale, with both said to deliver better results on demanding tasks while using fewer output tokens.

According to OpenAI, GPT-6.2 Astra sets a new high on Agents’ Last Exam, a benchmark that tests multistep professional work, scoring 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra while costing under a third as much. It is claimed to have finished 5.5 points ahead of Anthropic PBC’s Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost.

OpenAI is positioning GPT-6.2 Astra as the best model in the world for scientists, with the model scoring 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, a benchmark for scientific work carried out in a terminal. On Harvey LAB-AA, a test of legal assignments, the model more than doubled the pass rate of Fable 5.2 at about one-sixth of the cost.

Along with improved benchmark scores, GPT-6.2 Astra was trained to create slides, spreadsheets and documents that more closely follow the conventions used by professionals in fields such as law, sales, finance and accounting. The model can match a slide template from an original file or a screenshot, including layout, colors and typography down to the exact font size.

Early testers of the model include accounting AI startup Basis, which said that its average time for long-horizon accounting work fell by 50%, with the time for its most complex work falling by up to 73%.

Described by OpenAI as its go-to model for everyday work, GPT-6.2 Sol is claimed to let users complete more tasks on the same paid plan than GPT-6.1 Sol did. According to OpenAI, the model came within 0.5 points of GPT-6.2 Astra on Cognition AI Inc.’s FrontierCode 2.0 coding benchmark at about one-fifth of the cost.

GPT-6.2 Astra comes less than two months after OpenAI called off the planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra, after internal testing found the model fell short on staying within scope and authorization. The decision was announced the day before the company’s DevDay event in September, where GPT-6.1 Sol launched on its own.

Like GPT-6 Astra, both GPT-6.2 models meet the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework, and their increased capabilities have led the company to launch them with tighter safeguards for higher-risk cybersecurity assistance that are also said to restrict some legitimate vulnerability research. The company said it will work to bring the GPT-6.2 models to Daybreak, its program for vetted cyber defenders.

GPT-6.2 Astra is also the first externally released OpenAI model to meet the High threshold for AI self-improvement, a measure of a model’s ability to accelerate AI research. OpenAI tracks the capability because models that help build future AI systems could outpace safeguards and human oversight, and earlier this month it disclosed Control Room, a system already deployed across its research infrastructure that can halt model output when intervention is needed.

The company noted that in two of its alignment tests, the new models were more likely than GPT-6 Astra to omit mentioning obstacles that blocked their work, such as a missing file. OpenAI said it has added instructions in Codex that substantially reduce the omissions and is continuing to investigate the behavior.

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are available starting today to Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex, with Enterprise and Edu access requiring a workspace admin to enable it. Developers can also access both models through the OpenAI API. API pricing for GPT-6.2 Astra is $8 per million input tokens, 40 cents for cached input and $40 per million output tokens, a 20% discount on input and output tokens compared with GPT-6 Astra. GPT-6.2 Sol carries forward GPT-6.1 Sol’s rates of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

Czar brings more than 25 years of new-home sales leadership experience to the role. He will oversee sales strategy, leadership development, and execution across Ashton Woods’ 16 markets, working with local sales leaders throughout the organization.

#5499. Consumer Groups Request California Officials Investigate Zillow

Several consumer groups have penned a letter to California state officials, requesting an investigation into Zillow’s partnership with Redfin, as well as its referral and mortgage practices.

“We write because the California housing market is broken in ways that leave families suffering dire economic harm—and one of the most aggressive actors in distorting the market, to its own profit and to the detriment of the public, has been Zillow,” the letter reads.

Signed by five consumer-focused advocacy organizations—namely, the Consumer Federation of America, Demand Progress Education Fund, Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, Children’s Advocacy Alliance and Revolving Door Project—the the letter requested officials to investigate Zillow’s agreement with Redfin, and business practices the organization described as “steering.”

This is not the first letter of its kind made calling out the portal, as several consumer groups—also including the Consumer Federation of America—sent a letter to the National Association of Attorneys General back in September requesting investigations into Zillow for similar reasons.

In a statement on the letter, Zillow said its position is “unchanged” from previous challenges, denying any wrongdoing alleged.

The FTC had previously sued both Zillow and Redfin over the two portal’s rental-focused partnership, alleging Zillow effectively paid $100 million (and other benefits) to Redfin to end its advertising customers’ contracts, stop competing in the multifamily advertising market for up to nine years and serve as an “exclusive syndicator” of Zillow listings. That suit, however, has since been settled after the portals agreed to “unwind” some aspects of their partnership, with Redfin set to once again offer its own separate service.

The consumer groups’ Nov. 17 letter described said settlement as “far less than California consumers deserve,” as Zillow said it would maintain some level of partnership with Redfin “through at least 2030.”

“It (Zillow) retains the customer relationships the illegal arrangement produced and continues to benefit from the market consolidation it achieved during its term,” the letter reads. “And Redfin is left to rebuild its competitive position from scratch, in a market where Zillow remains the 800-pound gorilla.”

Zillow said in its statement that its partnership with Redfin “is pro-consumer and procompetitive.”

In terms of the allegations of steering, the letter referred to Zillow’s practice of having its “Contact Agent” buttons direct consumers to Zillow-affiliated agents rather than the listing agent as “deliberate consumer deception.”

“The Zillow Preferred Agent is essentially an interloper paying Zillow to execute a man-in-the-middle attack,” the letter read. “This has triggered class-action litigation that includes RICO claims, alleging that Zillow and the participating brokerages meet the definition of a criminal enterprise.”

This has also been the point of a lawsuit against Zillow, which was later combined with another suit against the portal over its alleged steering to Zillow Home loans through its preferred agents. The combined suit was dismissed back in July, with a judge saying that a “reasonable consumer” would not be deceived by Zillow’s “lead diversion” practices, but the plaintiffs have refiled with hopes to once again reopen the case.

On this suit, Zillow said in a statement that “The court dismissed all of plaintiffs’ claims in July, and the amended complaint simply repackages the same already-rejected theory related to free Zillow Home Loans pre-approval letters.”

The portal also noted that for its premarketed Zillow Preview listings, the “Contact Agent” button leads “directly to the listing agent, free,” and that “any listing agent revenue share is paid by Zillow at no additional cost to consumers or agents.”

“Zillow’s tools are free and optional, and our business relationships are clearly disclosed,” the statement continued.

Also in terms of alleged mortgage business steering, the letter referred to a previous suit from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) against Rocket Homes for similar allegations as are laid against Zillow.

However, this suit was later dropped by the CFPB in 2025 after what the letter described as the Trump administration’s “illegal effort to dismantle the CFPB in 2025.”

The letter also cited several academic studies as evidence for its allegations against Zillow, including a study from Georgetown University Law Center Professor Steven Salop that claimed to show Zillow Home Loan borrowers pay higher rates (that study, notably, was funded by CoStar, one of Zillow’s main competitors).

Zillow previously disputed these findings and alleged Salop relied on “selectively chosen data and inadequate controls to produce a distorted view of Zillow Home Loans.”

The letter requested that the California Department of Real Estate enact its “disciplinary and rulemaking authority” to investigate the alleged instances of steering.

Additionally, the letter requests the officials to bring “enforcement actions for the deceptive ‘Contact Agent’ and ‘Request a Tour’ interfaces, undisclosed Flex commissions, and the failure to disclose that agent recommendations reflect Zillow’s financial interests, not the consumer’s,” and potentially file an antitrust lawsuit.

Lastly, the groups asked that the officials “coordinate with the multistate coalition that brought the Redfin action so that Zillow cannot exploit jurisdictional gaps between state enforcers.”

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5496. Token sticker shock pushes enterprises from frontier labs toward open-weight AI factories

Enterprises have spent the AI boom racing to secure graphics processing units, or GPUs, but the harder decisions now sit above the hardware. Token bills, data sovereignty and model choice increasingly decide which AI pilots reach production, a shift on display at the SC26 supercomputing conference.

Dell Technologies Inc. has spent the past year pushing its AI Factory beyond servers and storage. Customers now want a full-stack outcome that covers software, open-source tools, models and operations, according to Brad Maltz (pictured), senior director of AI solutions at Dell.

“The hardware’s key because that drives the tokens,” he said. “You really, truly need a full-stack AI factory view above and beyond just the hardware stack.”

Maltz spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how token bills and data sovereignty are steering enterprises toward open-weight models and a full-stack AI Factory. The interview came as Dell rolled out AI Factory updates at the conference. (* Disclosure below.)

Many enterprises are still stuck in pilot mode, and coding assistants are often the easiest place to start. Employees have already tried tools from Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC, so teams want to apply that experience to business use cases. Once those pilots grow, the bill arrives, Maltz explained.

“The token spend right now in the frontier labs and the hyperscalers — that’s a little more than we expected,” he said. “We didn’t expect to spend $10,000, $20,000 per person per month.”

Cost is only one trigger. Data sovereignty, intellectual property leakage, security and governance all have to be addressed before a pilot goes live. Those requirements are steering many enterprises toward open-weight models they can fine-tune and run on-premises, including U.S. options such as Nvidia Corp.’s Nemotron, according to Maltz.

“There will always be frontier labs. There will always be open-weight models,” he said. “The question is going to be: do we have enough diversity with the open weights to meet the enterprise use cases?”

To keep pace, Dell launched its AI Ecosystem Program to validate software partners on its AI Factory. About 60 more partners have applied or are under evaluation, and each addition lets Dell solve 10 to 30 more customer problems, Maltz noted. For sovereign deployments, that often means disconnected, on-premises systems that keep models next to the GPUs and data enterprises already control.

“People understand data is the lifeblood of AI,” he said. “It’s the thing that trains the models. It’s the thing the models operate against. It comes from your enterprise business applications.”

#5495. Ryan Adams Is Engaged to 20-Year-Old Musician Kate Farr and Planning To Ditch L.A. for the Midwest After 6 Months of Dating

Musician Ryan Adams is engaged to Kate Farr, a writer and producer.

The couple shared the news with TMZ, explaining that they got engaged in early October after meeting through mutual friends six months prior.

“I’ve never been happier in my life,” the former Whiskeytown front man, 52, said. “Kate is the most fascinating, kindest nerd I’ve ever met. She’s my best friend, and I’ve never been happier. Here’s to love.”

According to the publication, Farr, 22, recently “moved to Los Angeles to be with Ryan,” and the pair are currently living together.

However, they seem to have plans to leave the West Coast soon, with Adams noting they’re house-hunting in the Midwest so they can be closer to Farr’s family in Ohio.

Adams made headlines over the summer when he canceled his European tour in July. At the time, he said he had fallen on “tough times” and had “been sick.”

In a previous Instagram Story, he had revealed that he was selling some personal belongings—including guitars, musical equipment, and a vehicle—because he was “broke and sick and tired and defeated.”

In 2019, seven women—including Adams’ ex-wife, actress Mandy Moore, 42, and singer Phoebe Bridgers, 32—publicly accused the singer of abuse.

In a New York Times piece, they alleged a “pattern of manipulative behavior,” in which he “dangled career opportunities while simultaneously pursuing female artists for sex.”

Bridgers reported “obsessive” behavior from Adams during the pair’s “whirlwind romance” in 2014, when she was 20 and he was nearly 40. She has claimed that he floated the idea of marriage in the first week of the relationship, and told Bridgers’ mother that his looking out for her daughter was a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.”

In the aftermath, the singer-songwriter’s album release was canceled amid an FBI investigation surrounding sexually explicit communications with an underage fan. The bureau closed its investigation without charges that fall, according to Page Six.

Adams’ lawyer, Andrew B. Brettler, denied the claims, stating the musician never “engaged in inappropriate online sexual communications with someone he knew was underage.”

“As someone who has always tried to spread joy through my music and my life, hearing that some people believe I caused them pain saddens me greatly,” Adams wrote in a social media post at the time of the reports, according to People magazine.

“I am resolved to work to be the best man I can be. And I wish everyone compassion, understanding and healing.”

A year later, in a lengthy letter published in the Daily Mail, Adams made an additional statement.

“All I can say is that I’m sorry. It’s that simple. This period of isolation and reflection made me realize that I needed to make significant changes in my life,” he wrote. “I’ve gotten past the point where I would be apologizing just for the sake of being let off the hook and I know full well that any apology from me probably won’t be accepted by those I’ve hurt.”

Noting that he understood that “there’s no going back,” Adams claimed he was “fully accountable” for his “harmful behavior” and will continue to be for “actions moving forward.”

Adams and Moore ended their six-year marriage in 2016. They were married in 2009 and separated in 2015. The former couple had previously lived in a Los Feliz home Moore purchased in 2002 for $1.7 million, splitting the mortgage. However, they offloaded the property for $3.2 million amid their split.

The “This Is Us” star has since married Dawes front man Taylor Goldsmith. After their 2018 wedding, the couple welcomed three children—August “Gus” Harrison, 5, Oscar “Ozzie” Bennett Goldsmith, 4, and Louise “Lou” Everett Goldsmith, 2.

Moore reflected on her first marriage in a 2024 episode of “Dinner’s on Me with Jesse Tyler Ferguson.”

“It’s so weird because I think back to that chapter, and it almost feels like it was someone else entirely that it happened to, because I’m in such a different place in my life, and I’m married and I have children,” she explained. “It’s almost like, how did I ever do that? How did I ever find myself in that place where I allowed myself to be treated that way, that I viewed myself that way?”

#5492. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.

#5491. Business as usual for Nvidia as it beats expectations in first earnings call after Huang’s resignation

Nvidia Corp. delivered earnings and revenue that surpassed Wall Street’s expectations and offered strong guidance for the current quarter in its first earnings call since the shocking resignation of its iconic co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang.

The results were so impressive that they slammed the brakes on a weeklong slide, as Nvidia’s stock rose more than 4% in late trading today.

The chipmaker reported third-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.68 per share, surpassing Wall Street’s target of $2.48 per share by a comfortable margin. Revenue for the period came to $115.84 billion, more than double a year earlier and above the $109.1 billion consensus estimate.

The vast majority of those sales stemmed from Nvidia’s core data center business, which delivered revenue of $107.6 billion, higher than the Street’s $101.87 billion forecast. For the current quarter, Nvidia said it’s expecting its revenue to grow by about 90%, to $130 billion. Though that suggests a slowdown sequentially from the prior quarter, it’s still nicely above Wall Street’s target of $125.1 billion.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress (pictured, with Huang in the background) has become a familiar face to analysts on Nvidia’s conference calls, but today she found herself in a very different position. For the first time, she was fielding questions as the company’s interim CEO, which means her responsibilities now go well beyond the numbers. She was joined on the call by Nvidia’s Chairman of the Board Harvey Jones, who insisted that the board has no intention of bringing Huang back as CEO.

Nvidia has been under a cloud all week following the abrupt resignation of Huang, which came days after he admitted to having an affair with a businesswoman who’s alleged to be a Chinese spy. In the days that followed that scandal, which included rumors of a second affair with an Nvidia executive and also a potential third fling with yet another company employee, the chipmaker’s stock had been in a downward spiral. But that trend was finally reversed following the company’s strong guidance today.

One of the central questions investors had going into the call was if Nvidia would scrap its previous forecast for 70% revenue growth in the fiscal year ending January 2028. However, Kress did the opposite and raised the company’s full-year guidance to 75% growth.

In raising the company’s outlook, Kress told analysts on the call that “it’s business as usual at Nvidia,” despite all that has happened. And indeed, throughout much of her commentary, she focused strictly to the numbers that revealed a business still in good health. With regard to the guidance, Kress stressed that this forecast “considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of customer demand and our customers’ access to capital.”

“Our leadership has stood up so strongly over the last week to support both what we are doing here at earnings, but also supporting all of our different employees around the world,” Kress said. “Remember, we have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class, multiyear roadmap. And I think that’s important from a business perspective.”

Kress said Nvidia expects frontier labs such as OpenAI Group PBC, Anthropic Group PBC and others to account for about 15% of its data center revenue this year, in a sign that they’re increasingly standing up their own data center infrastructure rather than renting from cloud providers.

“As frontier models become more capable, adoption and revenue are scaling rapidly, with Anthropic annualized revenue reaching $181 billion at the end of October,” Kress said.

Another big chunk of Nvidia’s revenue comes from so-called neocloud infrastructure providers. Much of the money those customers spend on its chips stems from a complex web of financing, with much of it being traceable back to Nvidia itself. Kress told analysts that the company is continuing to help neoclouds and frontier labs to secure the land, power and data center capacity they need to grow, and that it may be willing to share revenue from neoclouds together with the upfront sales of its products, if they meet certain conditions.

Kress said Nvidia currently has more than $32 billion in total commitments to neoclouds through 2032, but insisted that these take effect only if those customers are able to “secure the funding they need to purchase the data center infrastructure products they require, and if the related compute capacity is deployed and made operational.”

Another closely watched number is Nvidia’s gross margin, which has narrowed in recent quarters as its supply commitments have slowly piled up. Investors will have been pleased to see that Nvidia beat Wall Street’s expectations on that metric, with its nonstandard gross margin ending the quarter at 74.9%, above the forecast of 74%. Its margins still declined compared to the previous quarter, though, blamed on the ramping up of production of its latest generation Rubin graphics processing units.

The results prove that AI demand remains as strong as ever. But the bigger question for the market now is not how long Nvidia can sustain its growth, rather whether or not it can sustain its current level of profitability, Forrester analyst Naveen Chhabra told SiliconANGLE.

“The next battle is not against competitors. Nvidia must navigate export controls, sovereign AI initiatives, supply chain expansion and rising capital intensity, all while trying to protect its industry-leading margins,” Chhabra said. “Nvidia continues to defy gravity with triple-digit growth, software-like margins and a strong outlook despite trade restrictions. The next test is whether it can preserve its economic dominance as geopolitics and AI infrastructure costs rise.”

Despite the after-hours gain, Nvidia’s stock is still down 24% this month, and last Friday it completed its sixth successive weekly decline. That’s the company’s longest losing streak since 2012, and its shares are now trading at their lowest level since July 2025.

The decline began several weeks before news of Huang’s extramarital escapades became public knowledge. The company has also faced rising concerns about a possible slowdown in the artificial intelligence industry and a political shift in Washington D.C. as a result of the Republicans’ stunning losses during the midterm elections earlier this month.

Despite Jones’ insistence that Huang will not be returning to the CEO role, the prospect of his doing so cannot be ruled out. In his first public comments since his ousting, Huang said in a post on X that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

There are plenty of people who would like to see Huang return, including U.S. President Donald Trump and various luminaries from the technology world. Last Thursday, someone created an online petition calling for the reinstatement of Huang, and it has been signed by names including Elon Musk, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games Inc. CEO Tim Sweeney.

It could be possible that Huang ends up returning to the company in a different capacity than CEO. Susquehanna analyst Chris Rolland told CNBC that the chipmaker could end up taking him back under a new role, such as a consultant or a strategic adviser.

“I think that helps bridge the gap here, he can give technical and strategic advisory services that I think would be incredibly important to the company,” the analyst said.

#5489. HomeServices of America Names Maria Latushkin Chief Technology Officer

HomeServices of America has announced the appointment of Maria Latushkin as chief technology officer, a newly created role with enterprise-wide responsibility for technology strategy, development, engineering, infrastructure and IT operations. Latushkin brings more than 20 years of technology leadership at some of the nation’s best-known consumer-facing businesses.

According to a release, Latushkin will report to Chris Kelly, president and CEO of HomeServices of America, and will oversee all technology initiatives and IT functions across HomeServices, HSF Affiliates, Prosperity Home Mortgage, HomeServices Insurance and HomeServices Title. The structure brings greater alignment, coordination, and accountability to how the company invests in, builds, deploys and supports technology.

“Technology is central to how real estate professionals win business and serve their clients, and our agents deserve the strongest tools in the industry,” said Kelly. “Maria has a track record of delivering. She has built and scaled technology for major consumer brands, and she knows how to turn investment into results people can see. Her leadership will help us implement a robust technology package that serves both consumers and our agents and keep improving it long after launch.”

The release notes most recently, Latushkin served as group vice president of Technology and Engineering at Albertsons Companies. As part of the senior leadership team, she helped guide technology and product strategy across retail, payments, customer service and supply chain operations. She led a global technology organization of approximately 1,000 people and oversaw more than $400 million in annual operating expenditures. Her work included advancing artificial intelligence and modernizing digital platforms to improve operational performance and better connect the business with its customers.

Earlier in her career, Latushkin served as chief technology officer at Omada Health, Narvar and One Kings Lane, and held technology leadership roles at Peet’s Coffee and Walmart.com. She has built and scaled consumer-facing technology, modernized e-commerce platforms and improved digital customer experiences, with a focus on measurable business results, the company stated.

For HomeServices operating companies, agents and employees, HomeServices says the new structure means a more coordinated approach to technology and faster delivery of new capabilities. Platforms will be enhanced more quickly with a strong focus on adoption and giving agents and consumers a more complete real estate experience.  As the company continues the rollout of Maestro, OnePoint Digital and its broader technology ecosystem, beginning November 30, Latushkin will focus on continuously improving those tools and expanding what they can do.

For more information, visit www.homeservices.com.

#5487. Fed Officials Expect Further Interest Rate Hikes After Pausing Last Month

Leaders at the Federal Reserve held firm on interest rates in October, but also felt a future rate hike "would likely be appropriate" as some mulled a larger hike in December, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday.

At the Oct. 27-28 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), policymakers voted 10-2 to keep the overnight rate at its previous 3.75%-4% range. The decision came days before the 2026 midterms, even as FOMC members agreed inflation was a persistent concern,

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh joined the majority, while Fed Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, both voted in favor of a quarter-point increase. One month before, the FOMC voted to raise rates for the first time in three years in an effort to clamp down on inflation.

The minutes—which don't name FOMC members specifically while discussing their deliberations—show that some of the FOMC members considered that, while the impact of tariffs on the economy was waning, high energy costs continue to pressure Americans.

Indeed, some participants even noted that, if the inflation numbers got too unfavorable, they would consider a rate hike of more than a quarter-percent in December. Bond markets still view that as unlikely, with the probability of a larger half-point hike next month at just 5%, according to CME FedWatch.

Still, Federal Reserve Gov. Christopher Waller told CNBC Wednesday it may be necessary to "shock people" with a larger rate hike. He said in a speech this month that a half-percent point hike might be necessary next month.

"Inflation's been above our target for over five years, so if you really want to get it down you have to start taking more aggressive actions," Waller told CNBC.

FOMC members also said the rapid artificial intelligence buildout was contributing to inflation. But more scrutiny of the industry could slow spending and reduce inflation pressures.

Those members later determined holding rates steady at the October meeting would allow for time to "assess the durability of AI-related investment demand, the evolution of financing conditions, the transmission of the September rate increase to the economy, or geopolitical developments."

"A couple of participants noted that, at the current juncture, a gradual approach to policy firming wouldgive businesses and households time to adjust to higher interest rates," the minutes state.

Inflation remained hot in October. Overall prices rose 0.4% from September, according to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) last week.

Some numbers look better. After a disappointing September, U.S. payrolls came roaring back in October as employers added 165,000 new jobs, pushing the unemployment rate down to 4.1%.

CME FedWatch currently prices a roughly 95% chance of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raising the federal funds to a 4%-4.25% range in December, followed by a 69% probability of 4.25%-4.5% in January.

The meeting minutes show that Fed leaders are aware that public sentiment broadly expects the December rate hike. "Some participants," the minutes state, judge those estimates to be "broadly consistent with their assessments of the appropriate policy rate path."

Several of the meeting members also said it was a "close call." In the meantime, Cook and Hammack said that inflation remained too high and they didn't see enough signs that it was letting up. They worried that delaying the rate hike any further could risk higher inflation becoming entrenched. That, in turn, could mean more drastic rate hikes in the future.

Waller isn't the only Fed leader saying that the market needs more than one quarter-point rate hike.

"The economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027 to achieve 2% inflation in a timely manner," St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said this week at a conference in Argentina.

Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale said the market ultimately anticipates two or three hikes over the next 6 to 8 months. The Market has reacted. Pending home sales in September dropped to their lowest level on record.

"While the market and the Fed both seem to agree that some monetary policy restriction is warranted, most investors currently expect more restriction than the Fed has projected," Hale said last month.

But there is still an opportunity for homebuyers in this environment. Hale recommended homebuyers set themselves up for a better mortgage rate by boosting credit, making a higher down payment, and shopping around for a mortgage.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5486. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. #5485. Alphabet’s Isomorphic Labs raises $5B to accelerate drug discovery with AI

Isomorphic Labs Ltd. today announced that it has closed a $5 billion investment led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital.

The venture capital firms were joined by more than a half-dozen other backers. The group included Isomorphic parent Alphabet Inc., which made a “significant investment.” The search giant provided the capital through its GV and CapitalG startup funds.

Isomorphic offers a software platform called the Isomorphic Labs Drug Design Engine, or IsoDDE for short. It uses artificial intelligence to speed up several of the tasks involved in developing new medicines. The Alphabet unit says that multiple pharmaceutical companies are already using IsoDDE to power drug discovery programs.

Pathogens such as viruses comprise numerous proteins that each power a different biological process. Drugs work by neutralizing a single, particularly important protein without which the pathogen can’t function. Developing a new drug requires researchers to find a vulnerable protein within a pathogen and then develop a compound that can effectively target it.

The first step of the workflow is mapping out the shape of a target protein. Researchers look for so-called binding pockets, recesses on the protein’s surface to which a drug can be attached. The task is highly complicated because proteins don’t have fixed shapes. Their configuration changes when they interact with other molecules or encounter new environmental conditions, which happens often.

Isomorphic says that IsoDDE speeds up the task of finding binding pockets. When there are no such pockets, it helps researchers develop compounds that cause a target protein to form them.

Once scientists identify a binding pocket, they have to find a way of attaching a drug molecule to it. The pharmaceutical industry searches for such binding mechanisms using a method called FEP. FEP algorithms can be highly hardware-intensive, which makes them costly. Moreover, they often require a detailed, three-dimensional model of a target protein.

The process of creating 3D protein models for FEP algorithms is itself a highly complex task. It requires scientists to freeze a target protein in a crystal and scan it using specialized X-ray equipment.

IsoDDE skips that step of the research workflow. Furthermore, Isomorphic says that the software can generate higher-quality output than FEP algorithms.

“Our drug design engine is generating molecules with unprecedented precision and speed,” said Isomorphic Chief Executive Demis Hassabis. “This round enables us to accelerate our progress: building foundational biology models, deepening our systemic disease understanding, and driving our first therapeutic programs towards clinical trials.”

Isomorphic added that it plans to build new bioengineering infrastructure and grow its partner ecosystem.

#5483. Lot Supply Rises for Ninth Consecutive Quarter

The supply of vacant developed lots continued to loosen in the third quarter as slower construction activity brought the national lot market further into balance, according to Zonda.

Zonda’s New Home Lot Supply Index rose to 88.5 in the third quarter, up 20.8% from a year earlier and 3.9% from the second quarter. It marked the ninth consecutive quarterly increase in the index.

The index measures the supply of single-family vacant developed lots relative to the rate at which builders absorb those lots through housing starts. Zonda rated the national market “appropriately supplied” in the third quarter.

In the second quarter, the index sat at the boundary between “slightly undersupplied” and “appropriately supplied.” The third-quarter increase placed the national market in the latter category.

“The national lot market is moving more firmly into balance,” says Sean Fergus, vice president of economic research for Zonda. “But that balance needs to be viewed in the context of today’s housing market.”

Fergus noted that affordability pressures and widespread incentives continue to challenge builders’ ability to convert demand into sales. An appropriately supplied lot market indicates that lot availability is better aligned with the current pace of construction, he said, but does not mean the industry’s longer-term land constraints and cost pressures have disappeared.

Lot supply increased year over year in every major metropolitan area tracked by Zonda except Boise, Idaho. Among the markets where supply increased, the average annual gain was 32%.

Baltimore, Portland, and Seattle posted the largest year-over-year increases in lot supply. Boise was the only market where supply tightened, with its index falling from 65.7 in the third quarter of 2025 to 51.9.

Despite the broader improvement in availability, 12 of the 30 markets tracked by Zonda remained “significantly undersupplied.” Eight markets changed supply ratings during the quarter, Zonda points out.

Zonda also reported a modest increase in the future lot pipeline. Total upcoming lots increased 1% year over year and 1.6% from the second quarter.

Upcoming lots include properties in the later stages of development that are typically expected to become vacant developed lots within 12 to 18 months.

The increase suggests additional lots are moving toward delivery, although the pipeline is expanding much more slowly than the current supply index. The divergence reflects the role of softer starts in loosening lot conditions: available lots are lasting longer as builders respond to weaker demand and elevated mortgage rates.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5482. Nick Cannon Pulls Back the Curtain on the Drama of Raising 12 Kids Across Multiple Homes in Netflix’s ‘Raising the Cannons’

Nick Cannon is lifting the lid on what it takes to raise a family across multiple homes—and his kids have a few things to say about it, too.

In “Raising the Cannons,” premiering on Dec. 18 on Netflix, the father of 12 gives viewers a glimpse of home life with his blended family.

Among those offering their own take are Moroccan and Monroe, the 15-year-old twins he shares with ex-wife Mariah Carey, who have some candid thoughts about their dad’s choices.

For a family spread across several households, the Cannons live surprisingly close together. According to Netflix’s Tudum, the six mothers of his children—Carey, “Selling Sunset” star Bre Tiesi, Abby De La Rosa, Alyssa Scott, Brittany Bell, and LaNisha Cole—all live within a 5-mile radius of one another.

That proximity comes in handy for school pickups. For Cannon, it also makes something more personal possible. He wants the time his children spend with him to give them a chance to grow up together, even when they go home to different houses.

“I want my children to have relationships with one another,” he says in the trailer.

Cannon credits the mothers with helping him bring the kids together. De La Rosa, who shares twins Zion and Zillion and daughter Beautiful Zeppelin with him, wants that for her children, too.

The radio personality and DJ is also open to getting to know the other mothers better.

She and Cannon first met through morning radio, where they bonded over music and entertainment. As parents, Cannon says, they’ve found they also share many of the same values about how they want to raise their three children.

Cole offers a different perspective in the trailer. The photographer, who shares daughter Onyx with Cannon, says she feels little need to present the entire group as one big, happy family.

Cannon tells Tudum it took him time to find his footing with Cole after their romantic relationship ended in 2022. When she moved on with a new partner, he says, he had to put his ego aside, respect her boundaries, and focus on what worked best for Onyx.

For “Selling Sunset” fans, one of the bigger surprises may be what Tiesi gets up to in her own home.

Viewers know the luxury real estate agent for showing palatial properties. Cannon, who shares son Legendary Love with her, knows her as someone who’s just as happy taking on a project around the house.

He tells Tudum that “at home she’s always decorating and baking—DIY projects all around the house, building chicken coops.”

The series also follows Cannon as he balances fatherhood and work while managing lupus nephritis, a condition that affects the kidneys. The trailer shows him in a hospital bed as a voice expresses concern about the toll stress is taking on him.

Elsewhere in the preview, Moroccan questions whether his father can sustain the way he’s living.

Moroccan and his sister were just 5 when Cannon and Carey divorced in 2016. The twins are now in high school, and Cannon says he and Carey still speak regularly about parenting and what comes next for their children. Of all his co-parenting relationships, he points to theirs as the model he hopes to follow with his younger kids.

These days, the twins have advice of their own for their father, particularly when it comes to his love life.

“They’re the parents, I’m the kid,” Cannon jokes to Tudum.

Monroe gives viewers a sense of just how frank those conversations can be. In one exchange in the trailer, she tells her father that if he hadn’t gone on to have more children, she thinks he and her mother would have found their way back to each other.

#5479. General-purpose robot maker Genesis AI reels in $500M at $3.5B valuation

Genesis AI SAS today announced that it has raised $500 million in funding from a group of prominent investors.

Premji Invest, Khosla Ventures and Eclipse led the Series A round. They were joined by the venture capital arms of Nvidia Corp., Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Zoom Communications Inc., Samsung Electronics Co. and Ericsson. Former Google Chief Executive Eric Schmidt contributed as well along with other tech executives.

Paris-based Genesis develops a general-purpose robot called Eno (pictured). Unlike humanoid robots, it moves using a wheeled base rather than legs. The wheeled base can adjust Eno’s height using a mechanism that consists of two large panels connected by a hinge. The module enables the robot to adapt its configuration to each task.

Eno is powered by a custom artificial intelligence model called GENE. Genesis says that the algorithm is easier to train than traditional robotics-optimized neural networks, which can translate to higher output quality.

The dataset on which an AI model is trained must be tailored to the robot it’s intended to control. If a company is building an AI model for a four-legged robot, the training dataset must include footage of four-legged robots. The more specialized the robot, the more difficult it is to collect the necessary training data.

Genesis has come up with a workaround to that challenge. Eno’s palms and fingers are based on a custom design closely modeled after the human hand. As a result, the robot can be trained on demonstrations in which humans perform tasks with their hands. That kind of training data is much easier to produce than footage of robots performing work.

Eno’s robotic hands have 20 degrees of freedom, which means they can perform that many motions. The human hand has 27 degrees of freedom. Additionally, Genesis covered the hands with a soft material designed to mimic skin.

The GENE foundation model that powers Emo can perform tasks comprising dozens of steps. Genesis has released demo videos that show the system playing the piano, cooking and solving a Rubik’s Cube. According the company, that versatility enables Eno to operate in not only industrial environments but also homes.

“We’re working to build the world’s best general-purpose robot,” said Genesis co-founder and CEO Zhou Xian. “By building it all ourselves, we can obsess over every detail and improve the entire robot faster in one closed loop. This funding will accelerate our efforts to deploy our robots in the real world at scale.”

The company will use the capital to hire more AI researchers and roboticists. Additionally, Genesis will step up its training data collection efforts in a bid to expand its AI model’s capabilities.
