#5464. We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

Here’s the usual scenario: You sign up for a coaching program. You’re excited, and you should be. Everybody wants to feel a little less alone in a job you mostly do by yourself, in your car.

You didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

The reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

Nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

This isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

The veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

We do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

What would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

That work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

We haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

If you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

We’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

You aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.

#5463. Scripts can’t run AI factories: Dell moves cluster management from the server to the rack

As artificial intelligence clusters grow to supercomputing scale, the hard part of the AI factory is no longer buying hardware. It is keeping racks, switches, GPUs and cooling running once they are switched on.

That operational burden is reshaping what infrastructure providers sell. Dell Technologies Inc. has spent the past year pushing its AI Factory beyond servers and storage, and customers are now asking for best practices and better tools to stand up and run what they buy, according to Andrew Vaz (pictured, left), vice president of product management for the Telecom Systems Business at Dell.

“What we are seeing is a fundamental shift from procuring supply to actually standing up and running these very complicated AI clusters and data centers,” Vaz said. “One of the interesting things that we’ve seen is it’s actually now impossible to manage these things with just a few scripts, manually, in an old world manner. The toolsets are becoming more important.”

Vaz and Saurabh Kapoor (right), director of product management and strategy for AI compute and networking solutions at Dell, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed supercomputing, rack-scale management, AI observability and why networking sits on the critical path for AI clusters. (* Disclosure below.)

Dell used the conference to introduce Dell OpenManage Rack Scale and Dell Fabric Manager, two tools for running AI infrastructure from deployment through daily operations. OpenManage Rack Scale manages 100,000 devices in its first release, up from 8,000 servers for its predecessor, OpenManage Enterprise, Kapoor explained. Systems such as Nvidia Corp.’s NVL72 racks bundle compute, power shelves, switches and coolant distribution units into one unit.

“OpenManage Enterprise, the previous product we had, was perfect for servers. Server was the unit of compute,” Kapoor said. “But you have seen in the last 18 months, the world has moved very quickly to larger ecosystems and infrastructures. Rack is the new unit of play.”

Visibility is the other half of that equation. Dell’s iDRAC controller pulls more than 320 metrics from every server, and an AI-assist chatbot can query that telemetry through local large language models, according to Kapoor. A single cooling leak can damage millions of dollars of gear, so every layer has to report in, Vaz noted.

“It could be something as simple as, ‘Hey, this transceiver’s about to die that you can’t diagnose with metrics you have today,'” Vaz said. “You need to use AI to go look at it. You need telemetry off the system to go collect all of that, correlate it, run your algorithms on them, train it and understand what’s happening.”

The network is where those pressures concentrate. Dell Fabric Manager turns validated designs built with Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. into deployable blueprints across different network operating systems and silicon. Agentic AI is also reshaping traffic, and enterprise bandwidth is outrunning a projected 3.5-fold increase, Vaz noted.

“We’re getting blown away by it. It’s more like nine to 10x,” Vaz said. “It’s going everywhere: east, west, north, south.”

#5462. Tech Roundup: Zillow Preview listings go live in RealScout

Can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s new monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

“Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

The time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

For real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

The money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

Debt was a big part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and said the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on new real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and new ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb plans to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the company said in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

Instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment issues, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

“Travel is aspirational,” Chesky said. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”

The announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the company’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first announced in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

Preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

“Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner said in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”

For agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.

#5461. Exclusive: Wherobots AI agents automate complex spatial data engineering

Cloud-native spatial analytics and artificial intelligence startup Wherobots Inc. today introduced an artificial intelligence agent that enables users to build and deploy spatial data pipelines using natural-language instructions, reducing the need for specialized programming expertise.

Called Waldo, the agent can discover data sources, generate queries, perform analysis, visualize results and schedule recurring operations. It’s designed for applications involving location-based information such as satellite imagery, road networks, GPS tracking data and geographic features.

Spatial data presents unusual processing challenges because it combines multiple data types, including geographic coordinates, imagery and geometric shapes. Analyzing this information at scale often requires specialized tools and scarce technical expertise.

A recent survey by Global Marketing Insights Inc. concluded that the global geospatial workforce is 10 to 15 years behind in building the skill levels employers need.

Wherobots, which was founded in 2022 by the creators of the open-source Apache Sedona spatial analytics engine, said Waldo can compress development projects that traditionally take weeks into days.

“Waldo is our new agentic interface,” said Damian Wylie, Wherobots’ head of product. Unlike general-purpose AI coding assistants, he said, Waldo can invoke specialized computational engines that can process enormous geographic datasets.

“We’re not deploying some net-new [large language model] under the hood,” Wylie said. “We’re connecting existing LLMs to our product and also giving it the context it needs to speed up that spatial data workflow.”

The agent orchestrates several components of Wherobots’ platform. Its Havasu spatial data and knowledge catalog discovers and prepares public geographic datasets alongside customers’ private information. RasterFlow, Wherobots’ serverless Earth intelligence and inference engine,  processes satellite and aerial imagery using computer vision models to identify features such as buildings, roads and land-use changes.

WherobotsDB executes the resulting analysis using more than 300 spatial functions, while Wherobots Maps visualizes the results. Completed pipelines can be scheduled to refresh automatically as new data arrives.

The distributed processing platform uses existing cloud storage and enterprise data catalogs, including Amazon Web Services Inc.’s Glue and Databricks Unity Catalog, eliminating the need for customers to migrate their data, Wylie said.

In a demonstration, he showed how Waldo could identify the drainage area surrounding Montana’s West Boulder River using geographic and elevation data. The agent located relevant datasets, constructed a geographic representation of the watershed and displayed the results on a map.

The resulting geometry could support subsequent analysis of snowfall, water runoff or changing environmental conditions, Wylie said. Waldo can also process satellite imagery using specialized machine learning models, including Meta Platforms Inc.’s Segment Anything Model 3.

Potential commercial applications include identifying delivery vehicles that deviate from planned routes, assessing weather-related transportation disruptions and analyzing advertising impressions based on billboard locations and mobility patterns.

Wherobots said customer Action Engine Inc. is using the technology to build recurring fleet analytics pipelines and reports that it can deliver new spatial analyses two to three times faster that was possible with manual processes. Another customer used the platform’s distributed computing architecture to reduce a large-scale data-joining operation from approximately a week to less than an hour, said Benjamin Pruden, Wherobots’ go-to-market executive.

Waldo isn’t intended to eliminate human oversight, executives said. Users can inspect generated queries, review geographic visualizations and create Jupyter notebooks to examine individual processing steps. Wylie acknowledged that the technology can’t guarantee accurate results from every prompt.

“That’s an area we’ll invest,” Wylie said. “We’re not at the stage where we’re going to say every prompt is the best quality you’ll ever get.”

Waldo is available in public preview, with agent tokens currently included at no additional charge in Wherobots Professional Edition. Customers pay primarily for the computational resources they consume, with controls to select processing capacity and monitor costs.

#5460. Existing-home sales sink to a 16-year low as mortgage rates bite

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

Existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

“Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun said in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant said in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”

Yun and Sturtevant said mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant said. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”

Added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

As a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun said, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

“Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he said. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

“If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun said in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale said existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

“Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she said. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”

Hale said jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

“[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she said. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”

Yun said rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

“One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he said. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the big change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”

However, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she said. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on new pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”

#5459. In Portland, OR, Entry-Level Buyers Suddenly Have More Options

A new metro-by-metro analysis from Realtor.com® reveals where buyers can still find a starter home. These options have felt increasingly scarce as rising prices and climbing mortgage rates create challenges for many would-be buyers.

According to research, the national share of starter homes in active inventory fell from 38.1% in August 2019 to 36.2% in August 2026. During that same period, starter home prices rose 30.8%, from about $260,000 to $340,000.

However, some cities are bucking this trend, and Portland, OR, has seen an encouraging uptick in starter homes in recent years.

A starter home is defined as a property priced at roughly 80% of a metro's median list price, capturing the relative affordability of an area's lower-end market. These homes are typically smaller and less expensive, making them accessible to a first-time buyer or a household with an Income at or below the local median.

In the Portland-Vancouver, OR-WA, metro area, the share of starter homes has shown positive growth. The share was 28.0% in 2019 and dipped slightly to 27.8% in 2022 before rising to 32.0% in 2026.

This represents a total increase of +4.0 percentage points since 2019, signaling growing opportunity for buyers in the market.

For those deciding between renting or buying, current data suggests renting is the more affordable path for now. A July Rent Report found that the cost of buying a starter home in the 50 largest metros was $858 higher per month than renting one. This financial advantage to renting holds true across all 50 of the largest metros.

In the Portland-Vancouver, OR-WA, market, the median rent cost was $1,606 as of July 2026.

This figure represents a 1.60% decrease year-over-year, making an apartment an even more financially sound choice while saving for a down payment. Prospective buyers can use a rent vs. buy calculator to weigh their options.

#5458. He sold Bibles door to door. Now he runs a 35,000-home luxury exchange club in 103 countries

What do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

On this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

He explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel important.

They also get into handling rejection, taking big risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

Shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy says many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

For agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

His advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.

#5457. From store outlets to methane leaks: AI’s hunt for power

AI factories are outgrowing traditional data centers as models grow and distributed inference moves from concept to deployment. The infrastructure behind those models now has to span racks, sites and even scattered pockets of power.

Dell Technologies Inc. is betting that the answer lies in building complete systems rather than components, from rack-scale management to fully liquid-cooled designs. The size of modern AI clusters dwarfs anything high-performance computing has handled before, according to Ihab Tarazi (pictured), senior vice president and chief technology officer of AI, compute and networking at Dell.

“The difference with AI is the scale is massive: tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of GPUs that are all on a single fabric. It may be multiple clusters, but they end up being a single fabric at the end of the day,” he said.

Tarazi spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and host Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed Dell’s 100% liquid-cooled networking system, distributed inference and turning stranded energy into AI capacity. (* Disclosure below.)

Dell’s latest move takes liquid cooling beyond the graphics processing unit. The company is shipping what it calls the first 100% liquid-cooled networking system, with switches, optics and cabling pretested in its factory and delivered as a single rack, Tarazi explained.

“The fact that it’s pretested as a single-rack system means [that] instead of having to assemble hundreds of pieces on-site and take maybe two weeks or three weeks to find the bugs, it all comes in, you install it [and] we turn it up in hours,” he said.

The networking launch follows Dell’s debut of liquid-cooled storage for AI racks. Compute, networking and storage can now operate within a common cooling and power architecture.

“Instead of building two data centers — one for GPU, one [for] network — being able to do one is a massive reduction in time and cost for us,” he said.

Software is the next lever for distributed inference. Customers want a single control plane that can work across different GPUs and CPUs and link as many as 1,000 small sites, each with some spare power, Tarazi noted. That approach turns stranded energy into AI capacity for companies that can’t quickly build a massive data center.

“You’ll be surprised what power availability means,” he said. “It doesn’t mean just that you have power in your store. It could also mean methane coming out — every source of power possible. People are going backwards to say, ‘How do I leverage that power for compute and enable inferencing in a distributed manner?'”

#5455. Kris Jenner Turns Her $20 Million California Mansion Into a Holiday Spectacle With a ‘Magical’ Christmas Light Display

Kris Jenner is welcoming the holiday season with a glowing display at her California mansion, where warm white lights outline the gates, hedges, roofline, and doorways.

The reality TV star, 71, shared a look at the decorations in a video posted to Instagram on Nov. 13, giving followers a view of the home’s exterior as the entrance gates opened.

The clip is set to “Somewhere in My Memory,” the instrumental piece associated with the film "Home Alone."

As the gates move apart, the lights come into view across the landscaping and around the house, creating a bright welcome along the property’s entrance.

“It’s my favorite time of the year!” Jenner wrote in the caption. She described the setup as “the chicest Christmas lights in all the land” and “just magical! I could stare at them all night.”

The display extends beyond the immediate entrance. Trees, bushes, and other landscaping are also illuminated, making the lights visible throughout the grounds.

The video focuses on the home’s exterior, where the warm white lighting brings attention to the landscaping and the architectural outlines of the mansion.

Jenner’s post arrives as her family begins sharing its holiday decorating for the year.

Her daughter Khloé Kardashian showed off the lights at her own Los Angeles home earlier in November.

Thousands of white lights were arranged around the trees, windows, and doors, giving the exterior a gingerbread house-inspired look. Kardashian credited lighting installation company The Christmas Brothers with the work.

The holiday displays have become a recurring part of the Kardashian-Jenner family’s seasonal social media posts.

Last year, Jenner’s daughters Kim and Kourtney Kardashian gave followers a peek at another festive detail at their mother’s home: a bunk room prepared for the grandchildren.

The sleeping area featured several sets of bunk beds dressed with red checked bedspreads, Christmas wreaths, and twinkling lights.

Kourtney described the setup as “magical” in an Instagram Stories post, while Kim shared her own reaction to the room, asking how cute her mother’s bunk bed room was for the children.

Jenner also shared glimpses of the family’s interior holiday decorations in photos from their Christmas Eve celebration in 2025.

The images showed a fireplace dressed with garland and lights, with stockings hanging from the mantel.

A collection of Christmas trees stood beneath the staircase, each dripping in ornaments. The dining table was arranged with red linens, plaid dishes, greenery, and reindeer-inspired candleholders.

This year’s video turns the attention back outside, offering a quick look at the lights welcoming guests to Jenner’s home.

With the gates opening onto illuminated landscaping and the house outlined in white lights, the display gives the family’s holiday season a festive start.

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. #5454. The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

Wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients. Here’s how the multi-market real estate agent combines local expertise with a connected brokerage network.

Ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place. A primary home in Los Angeles, a ski house in Aspen, a pied-à-terre in New York, a winter retreat in Miami or the Caribbean.

Wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it. The agents who serve these clients best are evolving alongside them, building expertise across markets and cultivating relationships that extend well beyond their own backyards.

That shift is changing what it means to be a local expert. For brokerage leaders, it also raises an important question: Are we building networks that reflect how our clients actually live?

Remote work, flexible schedules and a generation of buyers who think of themselves as global citizens have loosened the link between where someone earns, where they live and where they invest.

Today’s luxury buyers are driven by lifestyle, whether that means access to mountains, water, a particular school system or a city’s cultural calendar, and they are comfortable buying in places where they spend only part of the year. What has not changed is their expectation of personalized service.

For these clients, a traditional handoff creates friction. Each time they are passed from one agent to another, they repeat their goals, rebuild trust and wonder whether anyone sees the full picture. A client’s real estate portfolio is one story. Their advisor should be able to tell it across markets.

Going global does not mean going generic. A Manhattan co-op board, a Florida insurance requirement, a Colorado water right and a California disclosure obligation each carry real consequences, and clients need professionals who understand the market in which they are buying or selling.

The mistake is confusing geographic reach with geographic expertise. The strongest multi-market agents know where their knowledge is deepest and where collaboration adds value. The future of the multi-market real estate agent isn’t about being an expert everywhere. It’s about knowing where your expertise ends, who to bring into the conversation and how to make that collaboration seamless for the client.

When a client has a positive experience with an agent in one city, that relationship shouldn’t end at the city limits. But there is a meaningful difference between providing a referral and extending a trusted relationship. If an agent simply passes along a name, the client starts over. If that introduction comes with shared context and a clear understanding of the client’s priorities, the experience feels seamless.

Trust is portable, but only when it is supported by consistent service and relationships built before a client needs them.

A global footprint alone does not create a global client experience. Offices in multiple markets mean little if they operate independently. Brokerages need to provide the infrastructure that makes cross-market relationships work, including introductions between offices, shared market intelligence, consistent training and clear expectations around communication and referrals.

At The Agency, we encourage agents to bring colleagues from other offices into client relationships early, so clients experience a connected team rather than a series of separate introductions. Technology helps agents share insights, access inventory and present properties remotely, but the real advantage comes from the relationships behind it.

Start by looking at the markets that consistently appear in your referral activity and client conversations. Those patterns show where to build stronger partnerships between offices.

Invest in cross-market education so agents recognize regional nuances and regulatory considerations and know when to bring in specialized expertise. Set clear collaboration standards for how clients are introduced, who takes the lead and how agents stay involved. Then measure success beyond the transaction: Did the client feel supported, and was communication consistent?

As brokerage leaders, we should be asking whether our networks are simply growing in size or becoming more connected. Those are very different measures of success.

Local expertise has never been more valuable. What is changing is its reach. The brokerages that treat their agents’ knowledge as a connected network, rather than a set of separate territories, will be better positioned to serve today’s clients and the next generation of buyers who increasingly see the world, not one city, as their real estate market.

Rainy Hake Austin is president of The Agency in Los Angeles. Get connected on Instagram.

#5453. Mortgage Applications Dip as Rates Hit Three-Week High

House keys with a house shaped keychain resting on a mortgage application form

Mortgage applications dipped slightly this week, in keeping with the average 30-year mortgage rate rising to a three-week high.

The latest Market Composite Index from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA)—its measure of mortgage loan activity volume and includes purchases and refinances—shows mortgage application activity decreasing 2.3% on a seasonally adjusted basis after last week’s 6.2% increase. On an unadjusted basis, the Index decreased 5% compared with the previous week.

This week’s decline follows weeks of fluctuations as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate still solidly remains over 7%–last week decreasing to 7.11% according to Freddie Mac but currently sitting at 7.46%, according to Mortgage News Daily. Freddie Mac’s next rate report will be released Thursday.

“Mortgage applications dipped as mortgage rates moved higher, with the 30-year fixed mortgage rate up to its highest level in three weeks at 7.35 percent,” said Joel Kan, CMB, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist. “Purchase applications were down 18 percent from a year ago, as renewed affordability challenges from elevated mortgage rates have pushed prospective homebuyers to the sidelines.”

MBA’s Refinance Index decreased 2% from the previous week and was 54% lower than the same week one year ago. MBA’s seasonally adjusted Purchase Index–its weekly measurement of nationwide home loan applications based on a sample of about 75% of U.S. mortgage activity–decreased 3% from one week earlier. The unadjusted Purchase Index decreased 7% compared with the previous week and was 18% lower than the same week one year ago, according to the report.

The refinance share of mortgage activity saw an increase this week–to 41.1% from 39.8% the previous week, with Kan pointing to a rise in FHA refinances as most notable.

“Overall refinance activity was down over the week, but FHA refinances increased almost 7 percent,” Kan stated. “The FHA rate was around 30 basis points below the conforming rate, which supported refinance opportunities for some homeowners.”

The FHA share of total applications increased to 16.1% from 15.5% the week prior, with MBA listing the VA share of total applications increasing to 12.8% from 12.4% the week prior. The USDA share of total applications remained unchanged at 0.5 percent from the week prior.

Kan also pointed to additional macroeconomic indicators as potentially weighing on home-purchase application activity into the new year.

“Treasury yields rose last week amid data showing inflation accelerated in October and Fed officials acknowledging that additional rate hikes may be needed in the coming months,” he said.

#5452. Stalled data center buildouts send inference chips hunting for space in telco and colo sites

Demand for inference is outrunning the construction of new AI data centers, as power, capital and permitting delays push fresh capacity further out. That gap is sending chipmakers to hunt for room in existing facilities.

Many older telco and colocation sites have the space and power. But most can’t take today’s dense, liquid-cooled GPU racks without costly retrofits, which opens the door for air-cooled inference systems, according to Anton McGonnell (pictured), vice president of core product at SambaNova Systems Inc.

“We as an industry are just encumbered by the velocity of data center buildouts, and that’s been slowed down by just the physics of how long this takes, by the access to capital, and more and more by legislative hurdles — particularly in the U.S.,” McGonnell said.

McGonnell spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI data centers and the demand for air-cooled inference racks. (* Disclosure below.)

SambaNova’s fifth-generation chip, the SN50, targets the decode phase of inference, where output tokens are generated and data movement becomes the bottleneck. Its racks stay air-cooled and light enough to fit existing facilities, McGonnell explained. Newer GPU racks, by contrast, can demand reinforced flooring and 120 to 250 kilowatts of power per rack, he noted.

“On all of this stuff — the power and the cooling gear — there’s 18- to 24-month lead times to get this equipment into the data centers. Never mind all of the construction costs,” McGonnell said.

SambaNova, which investors valued at $11 billion in July, pairs its decode chips with partners that handle prefill, the compute-heavy first phase of inference. At SC26, it is demonstrating Intel’s D-Series GPUs for prefill alongside its SambaRack SN50 for decode in an air-cooled heterogeneous setup.

“They have developed a chip that has much, much better cost performance for the prefill phase of inference,” McGonnell said. “They’ve sacrificed HBM, which isn’t needed for prefill because it’s a compute-bound problem.”

#5451. Florida Homes Are Flooding in the Dry Season—and Too Many Owners Are Unprepared

The Sunshine State is facing an unusual bout of heavy rain and flooding in the middle of its dry season, which usually begins in November.

The unexpected weather has put pressure on drainage systems and left standing water in many communities, particularly those in South Florida’s Broward County and along Central Florida’s Atlantic Coast in places like Daytona Beach and Cape Canaveral.

On Nov. 18, the western part of Broward County faced what meteorologists refer to as a “rain bomb.” In just 24 hours, West Hollywood received over 15 inches of rain, while surrounding neighborhoods saw about 10 inches.

Due to the severity of the situation, which has led to issues such as stranded cars and out-of-service traffic signals, Broward County and Hollywood declared states of emergency, with Hollywood officials encouraging residents to shelter in place and avoid unnecessary travel.

Forecasters expect additional rainfall through the end of this week as well as 2 to 4 inches across Eastern Florida, with about 4 to 8 inches from Miami to Jacksonville between Tuesday and Friday. Some areas may even get hit with up to 12 inches.

While the wet and windy conditions are expected to improve, the Southeast may see a cooler, rainier Thanksgiving this year. The rain could linger from the upper coast of Texas toward the southern Atlantic Coast throughout the holiday weekend.

“The dry season doesn’t mean your house is in the clear. Florida is currently showing us that heavy rain can flood homes miles from the beach,” says John Espenschied, owner at InsuranceBrokers.com in O'Fallon, MO.

If you’re a Florida homeowner, these unexpected weather conditions are a reminder that flooding may occur year-round—even outside of the traditional summer, hurricane season.

They can also give you a nudge to review your home insurance policy as it relates to flooding and take precautionary steps to protect your property and loved ones.

Florida’s current flooding is drawing attention to the fact that many homeowners do not have enough insurance coverage to recover from the damage.

The Realtor.com® 2026 Housing and Climate Risk Report highlights the financial consequences. It found that over 6% of U.S. homes face severe flood risk, representing almost $3.4 trillion in property value.

At the same time, the number of active flood insurance policies from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) fell by 4.5% between May 2025 and May 2026, decreasing from 3.62 million to 3.45 million.

And the issue goes beyond coastal communities.

Moody's U.S. flood risk analysis, which accounts for flooding from heavy rain and overflowing rivers rather than just coastal storms, found that potential uninsured residential flood losses could exceed $375 billion in a modeled 1-in-100-year flood scenario. This may result in a national insurance protection gap of 65%.

According to Chris Bacon, chief operating officer of Openly in Boston, there are four primary factors that explain why many homeowners are lacking adequate flood protection.

First, most homeowners do not live in the highest-risk flood zones, so they don’t consider it a significant peril. Second, the cost of flood insurance can be high, especially for homeowners in higher-risk flood zones.

“The additional cost can be a constraint of homeowners’ budgets, and thus they choose to not purchase the coverage,” explains Bacon.

Third, mortgage companies do not require flood coverage unless the home is located in a high flood risk zone, so homeowners simply skip it to save money. Finally, the coverage from the NFIP, which goes up to only $250,000, is often lower than what a consumer needs should there be a major loss.

While there are private flood providers that can cover higher limits, premiums can be significantly higher because pricing reflects each property’s individual flood risk.

“That’s why working with an independent insurance agent is so critical. They can provide the right coverage advice and show multiple options so you can make an informed decision for your unique situation,” Bacon adds.

If you own a home in Florida (or any other state where flooding may occur), take a close look at your home insurance coverage. Determine whether it covers water that rises from the street or yard. Unfortunately, most policies don’t.

In the event you don’t have flooding insurance, get quotes from both the NFIP and private insurers.

“The federal program caps building coverage at $250,000. You can buy up to $100,000 in separate coverage for your belongings. If your home would cost $400,000 to rebuild, ask what it would cost to insure the extra $150,000,” adds Espenschied

Don’t forget to compare deductibles and start dates, and remember that federal coverage usually takes 30 days to kick in.

John Dickson, president and CEO at Aon Edge, a private flood insurance provider based in Kalispell, MT, points out that deciding whether to purchase flood insurance is a question of values.

“When you get a picture of how much you can lose, choosing to purchase flood insurance becomes an easy decision,” Dickson explains.

Fortunately, there are a number of precautions you can take to reduce the risk of serious flood damage on your property.

“Keep gutters clear of debris, and remove or clear debris blocking nearby storm drains and install a sewer backflow check valve,” says Bacon.

If you have a basement, elevate HVAC equipment, electrical panels, and water heaters above expected flood levels where possible.

Outside of your home, grade soil away from the foundation and extend downspouts to improve drainage. Finally, keep sandbags or flood barriers on hand, and know your evacuation routes.

If you have a swimming pool, proper pool preparation is key. Avoid draining the pool completely, as hydrostatic pressure from waterlogged soil can cause the pool shell to pop out of the ground.

“Instead, lower the water level slightly (no more than 1 to 2 feet) to allow room for heavy rainfall, turn off power to the pool equipment at the breaker, and secure or store loose pool furniture and equipment inside to prevent severe damage,” Bacon explains.

To protect personal property, particularly high-value, irreplaceable, and sentimental items, move them off ground-level floors and store them on upper levels or high shelves. Keep important documents, family heirlooms, and electronics in sealed, waterproof containers, and create digital backups of critical financial and personal records.

For furniture or heavier items that must remain on the ground level, use blocks or risers to elevate them above potential floodwater lines before severe weather arrives.

“None of these steps eliminates risk, but together they reduce damage and help lead to faster recovery,” adds Bacon.

#5450. Paychecks are growing, but buyers are still falling behind

Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year. Average hourly pay rose 3.1 percent.

The October jobs report showed employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace. Over the past year, the monthly payment on a median-priced home has climbed about three times as fast as average pay.

The gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov. 6. The rate has remained within a narrow band of 4.1% to 4.3% since March, according to the BLS. The bureau also revised August and September up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38, a 3.1 percent gain over the year.

At October’s national median existing-home price of $416,700, a buyer putting 20 percent down would pay about $2,243 a month in principal and interest at this week’s average 30-year fixed rate of 7.11 percent, according to an Inman calculation. The same loan at the year-earlier rate of 6.24 percent would cost about $2,050. The difference is about $192 a month, or about 9 percent, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent.

The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 0.6 percent in September, BLS reported Nov. 10. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as did shelter.

The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point hike, according to the Fed’s statement. “But inflation is too high,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said in his press conference opening statement. The Fed meets again in December.

Adjusted for inflation, average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October, according to the BLS Real Earnings report. BLS said a 12-month comparison for October is not available because BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent from September 2025 to September 2026, according to the agency’s September report.

The number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October, according to BLS. These workers wanted full-time jobs but had their hours cut or could not find full-time work.

The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11 percent for the week ending Nov. 12, up from 6.24 percent a year earlier, according to Freddie Mac.

Existing-home sales fell 5.5 percent from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October, down 8.8 percent from a year earlier and the lowest pace since August 2010, Inman reported. Annual sales fell in all four regions, and the Northeast was the only region with a monthly decline.

The median price rose 0.4 percent to $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7 from 107.3 a year earlier, and inventory reached 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.4 months in October 2025.

Forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share NAHB has reported since 2020, and 65 percent used sales incentives, according to the National Association of Home Builders. NAHB’s builder confidence index fell three points to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012.

The October data overall shows an economy adding jobs at more than three times its 12-month average pace, while rates and prices keep pressure on buyer budgets. Agents can work from monthly payment figures and available concessions as tools to help keep transactions moving while the Fed weighs its December decision.

#5449. Humyn Labs raises $47M to bridge the gap between AI training and real-world robotics

Humyn Labs, a company turning human experience into training for robots and artificial intelligence, today announced it has raised $47 million in early-stage funding to accelerate intelligent robotic deployment readiness in real-world environments across Brazil, South Korea and India.

Accel led the $26 million equity portion of the round, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Finserv Intelligence through Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton and Jump Trading LLC. Lighthouse Canton led the remaining $21 million in venture debt, with participation from Trifecta Capital.

Founded in early 2026, Humyn’s proposal is that AI models for humanoid robots don’t learn dexterity from staged demonstrations; they must learn by observing how humans move in real environments. This provides actual behaviors showing how hands work on objects, reach, touch, handle and recover without explicit instructions.

Unlike generative AI models that learn from vast amounts of text, images and video, physical AI models must learn how to interact with the world around them. That means understanding not only what objects look like and where they are, but also how to manipulate them, how much force to apply and how to respond when something goes wrong.

“The results can be very, very, very dramatic and catastrophic,” co-founder and Chief Executive Manish Agarwal (pictured) told SiliconANGLE in an interview.

Agarwal pointed out how mistakes that might be inconsequential for a chatbot can have serious consequences for a robot operating alongside people. That makes access to diverse, high-quality data about how humans physically interact with their environments critical for training robots to work safely and reliably in the real world.

To address this, the company built a video corpus captured from head-mounted cameras as participants performed everyday household tasks, comprising up to 200,000 hours of intentional human motion. The company also shipped a dataset of 120,000 faces across five regions for facial recognition, including adjustments in lighting, pose, expression, glasses, hairstyle, facial hair, accessories, age and locale.

That’s combined with more than 50,000 hours of representative speech data for underserved language markets, including Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Odia, Assamese, Korean, Tagalog, Arabic, Vietnamese and Portuguese. Voice AI models that understand natural language already have vast amounts of data for widely spoken languages such as English, Mandarin or Spanish, but real-world customer support within South and Southeast Asian markets lacks routine coverage.

Humyn’s engine uses sound, sight, motion and touch as data inputs, which it curates, normalizes and labels so that AI models can understand the kinematics of motion, force and environmental factors. Together, this provides training patterns for physical AI models, world models, general foundation models, and audio and voice AI.

Geographic diversity is also important because robots must understand the environments and cultural practices where they will operate. “Diversity gets you in the room. The quality ensures that you stay in the room,” Agarwal said.

To make this point, Agarwal emphasized the importance of geographic and cultural diversity in collecting training data. A household robot trained in the United States may struggle with tasks in an Indian home, where everything from cooking utensils and kitchen appliances to laundry practices and room layouts can differ. These regional differences mean that robots need experience with the specific environments and practices of the people they will eventually serve.

By collecting data across more than 20 countries, Humyn can train models on data that more closely resembles their intended deployments, potentially accelerating readiness for real-world work.

Agarwal added that the company is seeing interest from customers building household robots for domestic tasks and elder care, alongside industrial applications involving object manipulation and movement through factories, warehouses and commercial environments.

“The next phase in the deployment cycle is about how well these models perform in the wild,” Agarwal said.

In the end, data is only the beginning. Humyn wants to measure where robots fail in real-world conditions and use that to feed the AI flywheel and build better models. That means using virtual simulations, physical replicas and partnering with the enterprise and researchers to have field deployment labs to identify the differences between expected and actual performance.

The company said it intends to use the new funding to build deployment-readiness infrastructure in Brazil, South Korea and India, develop its hardware and enrichment engine, and expand its on-the-ground presence in San Francisco, London and Seoul. Agarwal said this will also involve testing robots in real-world environments to identify gaps between their expected performance and actual behavior, feeding those results back into model development.

#5448. Resident of Collapsed Brooklyn Building Sues for Negligence After Losing $100K Record Collection

The first of what is likely to be several lawsuits was filed in Kings County Superior Court on Monday, alleging widespread negligence by a host of landlords, construction companies and contractors in last week's deadly Brooklyn building collapse.

Dengane Omari Jack lived at 1321 Flatbush Ave., which collapsed last Wednesday, tragically killing eight and wounding 18 others. Jack was at work at the time of the collapse, but rushed home to see if his extensive reggae vinyl record collection, valued at $100,000, might be salvaged. It was a total loss.

"He was one of the lucky ones," a friend wrote on a GoFundMe campaign to support Jack. "But surviving came at an unimaginable cost: in a matter of seconds, he lost his home, everything he owned, and a lifetime's worth of memories and work."

Now, Jack is suing his landlord and management company, as well as half a dozen companies affiliated with 2625 Bedford Ave., the lot adjacent to his Flatbush building. None of those entities have filed a response to the complaint yet in court.

The suit alleges the building's owner, Isolag Realty Group, and the property manager, Olufemi Falade, failed to take action after he pointed out cracks in the facade of 1321 Flatbush Ave earlier this year.

According to the lawsuit: “During October 2026, Plaintiff observed cracks at or near the Building's entrance, photographed those cracks, and reported the condition to the landlord or management responsible for the Building.”

The suit goes on to allege that Falade “personally received or responded to the report of the cracks on behalf of the Building's ownership or management. Plaintiff was falsely told, in substance, that the condition was not the landlord's fault or could not be fixed.”

Falade has appeared on the city's "Worst Landlord" watch list, put out by the city's Public Advocate office, six times in the last decade.

Jack’s suit also names several entities tied to 2625 Bedford Ave., the adjacent lot where excavation work was taking place at the time of the building collapse.

Those defendants include general contractor Townhouse Builders, d/b/a Promont; New Jersey-based LMW Engineering Group and its president, Jieming Wang; W6 Facility X, an LLC affiliated with Robert Fischman; and LLCs affiliated with lot owners Faigy Fischman and Judy Swimer.

The suit points to a pre-construction survey commissioned by the builders which documented that the facade of 1321 Flatbush Ave. was in "poor" condition prior to the excavation.

"The Defendants, who were responsible for excavation, design, supervision, inspections and monitoring received, or in the exercise of reasonable care, should have obtained and considered, the Pre-Construction Survey to evaluate all relevant Pre-Construction Site Conditions and, in particular, the Building's condition and its need for support and protection before proceeding with work at the Construction Site," the suit alleges.

Further, the suit says the defendants "had actual notice through the surveys, reports, observations or complaints applicable to their respective work, or constructive notice because the conditions were discoverable through the inspections and monitoring they were required to perform."

Further, the suit claims that "the excavation, inadequate structural protection, negligent engineering orinspection services, and failure to address the Building's developing dangerous conditionproximately and/or substantially caused the Building to collapse, causing Plaintiff's losses."

The 2625 Bedford construction project had a history of safety violations noted by the Department of Buildings. The demolition of a building that had previously been on the site was halted in March of this year after demolition contractor N Tech Design of America had failed to take proper safety precautions, including installing netting and putting up sidewalk shields, records show.

A month later, inspectors returned to the site and found that the demolition had gone ahead anyway, in defiance of the stop-work order, according to city records. A $10,000 fine was issued.

In May, a city inspector issued additional citations and another stop-work order against the contractors for allegedly failing to ensure adequate protections of neighboring buildings and for deviating from approved construction plans. Within a week, the city lifted that stop-work order.

Jack is suing for compensatory damages, rent relief, and punitive and exemplary damages.

In an interview with Gothamist, he valued his lost record collection at more than $100,000.

“ Nobody has contacted me from the city for, like, ‘We found some stuff that is still usable.’ I didn't hear anything like that,” Jack told the outlet. “And I don't know who to reach out to either.”

Thankfully, he'd been transferring many of his vinyl treasures into digital files prior to the collapse and had his hard drive with him at work when the building fell.

“ Every single day I was just backing up stuff. I don't know if it's intuition was telling me to do this. But I was doing it every day for the past week,” he added.

The GoFundMe to support Jack, who DJs under the name Roots Outernational, has raised more than $12,000 so far.

Last Wednesday, hours after the collapse, Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez opened a criminal inquiry into the collapse. No charges have been filed yet.

Realtor.com has reached out to Townhouse Builders, LMW Engineering, Jack, and Jack's lawfirm, Antin, Ehrlich, & Epstein, LLP, for comment.

She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. #5447. 5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

Real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

Access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely shows you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

This fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

One had stopped going to the program’s update calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the company can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

How to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same company that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

Real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

In real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

If the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

How to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

Say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

Now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

How to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

Many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The company running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

How to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the company itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

Many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”

The lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”

How to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

Commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your plan, not the floor under it.

The average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

Amanda Neely is a Certified Financial Planner and the CEO of Counterflow. Connect with her on LinkedIn and Substack.
