#5420. AI’s hidden energy tax: More than 80% of scale-up traffic is just memory moving around

Memory bottlenecks are emerging as one of the costliest problems in AI infrastructure as inference overtakes training. GPUs sit idle waiting on data, while high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, stays bolted to processors that cannot share it.

Photonics is shaping up as one way out. Marvell Technology Inc. has been pairing optics with photonic memory to stretch memory beyond the edge of a chip. The payoff is better efficiency in data centers enterprises have already paid for, according to Preet Virk (pictured, left), senior vice president and general manager of the Photonic Fabric Business Unit at Marvell.

“In the data center today, we have a lot of room for improvement of efficiency,” Virk said. “And when I say efficiency, I’m alluding to the wasted flops because we have GPU utilization that’s very low.”

Virk and Andy Mills (right), vice president of advanced product development at Penguin Solutions Inc., spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how photonics and shared memory pools can ease memory bottlenecks in AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.)

Penguin’s MemoryAI Photonic Appliance moves HBM into a separate box tens of meters from the GPU, linked by Marvell’s Photonic Fabric. Each appliance holds 16 terabytes of HBM and DDR5 memory that servers across multiple racks can share, Mills explained.

“The challenge there is making sure your LLM doesn’t forget what you started talking to it about 10 minutes ago,” Mills said. “To do that, you need a large amount of memory, large token lengths.”

Optics also changes the energy math. Copper still works inside a rack, but crossing a pod of thousands of GPUs requires optics, according to Virk. More than 80 percent of scale-up network traffic is memory transactions, and a shared pool means much of that data never moves at all, he noted.

“Within data movement, the memory transactions are a place to focus on,” Virk said. “So with this solution versus a copper-based data movement, we could immediately get to a quarter of the energy, picojoules per bit, of data movement.”

Agents raise the stakes, generating far more token requests than human users ever did. As inference spreads across more racks and sites, Mills sees shared pools as the practical answer to memory bottlenecks.

“If anything, distributed encourages shared because you don’t want to recompute,” Mills said. “The whole thing about KV cache was a huge success because it stops recomputation of the same data. And when you can share that data on a broader base and wider across more racks, your efficiencies go up as well.”

#5419. Officials blame aging FAA telecom gear as U.S. airspace reopens, see no link to Microsoft or AI

by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 3:04 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 7:58 pm

Updated with officials’ explanation of the cause and the reopening of U.S. airspace.

The nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. commercial air travel Friday was not caused by the Microsoft 365 outage that began a day earlier, federal officials said at an evening news conference, blaming aging FAA telecom equipment that was overloaded with data.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened the news conference by raising the Microsoft outage himself. “I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft,” he said. “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy likewise ruled out a role for SMART, the FAA’s new AI traffic-planning tool, saying it isn’t connected to the core systems controllers use to track flights.

“There was no possible way SMART would have impacted what happened today,” he said.

The FAA reopened U.S. airspace at 5:15 p.m. Pacific, more than four hours after the problems began, Duffy said. He said flights would resume slowly, depending on whether airlines had crews available, and some may not depart until Saturday morning.

Microsoft confirmed in a statement that it had no indication the FAA ground stop was related to its service disruption.

Asked whether a cyberattack or “rogue AI” could be ruled out, Mullin said there was “nothing completely certain right now,” but “it appears that this was mechanically driven.” He said he could not rule out the possibility of a cyberattack but said there was “zero evidence” of one so far.

What happened: Duffy said the FAA began seeing unstable radar and communications data at air traffic control facilities across the country at 12:36 p.m. Pacific. Aging switches and routers in the agency’s telecom network “got overloaded with data” and began producing inconsistent information, he said, adding that the FAA still relies on “1980s little copper lines.”

“Our new IP switches did not go down. It’s the old hardware that went down,” he said. The FAA restored service after deploying fixes to reduce the overloading on its switches, he said.

Mullin said the overload appeared to have been triggered by new equipment the FAA was installing. As the agency put “patches into the system” and added “new equipment and new technology,” he said, it “was overwhelming the older system.” Neither official said exactly what that equipment was.

The FAA is in the middle of replacing its legacy telecom network with a modern internet-protocol network. AT&T took over the lead role on that project in August with an initial $74.3 million award, as the FAA works toward a goal of finishing by the end of 2028.

Duffy and Mullin used the briefing to press Congress for money to finish rebuilding the air traffic control system. Mullin said President Trump has declared the situation a national emergency.

The administration has asked Congress for an additional $30.1 billion for aviation infrastructure, AeroTime reported. Duffy said at the evening news conference that he wants $50 billion.

Earlier in the day, Mullin had said officials were looking into a possible link to SMART, including through DHS’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The FAA said Tuesday it was expanding the system to the airspace managed by all 22 of its en route air traffic control centers.

The agency describes SMART as a cloud-based system that pulls in about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths and controller staffing, to recommend flight schedules and routes. FAA specialists review its recommendations, and local facilities decide whether to act on them.

SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million FAA contract with Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which denied any connection to the issue. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

The FAA halted departures nationwide shortly before 1 p.m. Pacific. More than 3,500 planes were in the air at the time, Duffy said. It’s the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks, after a January 2023 failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system.

FlightAware counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled as of Friday afternoon.

#5417. Gov. Ferguson seeks $10M to help develop Eastern Wash. clean-energy hub

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 4:32 pmNovember 16, 2026 at 10:09 am

Gov. Bob Ferguson is proposing $10 million to fund basic infrastructure needed for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, a master-planned industrial area in Eastern Washington that will foster development of large-scale clean energy, advanced manufacturing and supply chains. The proposal will be included in his 2027–29 capital budget.

If approved by lawmakers, the funding would support sewer, water, electrical and road infrastructure at the park.

“This investment will support thousands of good-paying jobs in the trades and advanced industries, and unlock billions in private investment,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The 1,641-acre site was formerly part of the Hanford Nuclear Reservation, a sprawling federal property along the Columbia River near the Tri-Cities that is undergoing a massive environmental cleanup. Hanford was established during World War II to produce plutonium for the Manhattan Project.

Mel Clark, president and CEO of the CleanTech Alliance, an industry trade group, welcomed the news as the state struggles to get clean power plugged into the grid.

“Washington needs more energy generation, more clean energy, and more manufacturing,” Clark told GeekWire via email. “We’re excited to see the Governor take action to change our last-place ranking in building new clean energy projects.”

According to the governor’s office, two projects have committed to locating at the park once infrastructure construction is complete: Atlas Agro’s low-carbon fertilizer production plant and the utility-scale Ruby Flats Solar Farm.

State officials said General Matter is also considering the location for producing advanced nuclear fuel for small reactors. That siting could potentially be beneficial for another project planned for the same area: Amazon, X-energy and Energy Northwest are developing plans for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility, a nuclear plant comprised of clustered, small reactors.

In 2024, the Norwegian company Cenate expressed interest in building a factory at the park to produce lithium-ion battery components, according to the Tri-Cities Area Journal of Business, ultimately withdrew its plans.

The Tri-Cities is also attracting fusion-energy investment. Last year, Seattle startup Avalanche Energy landed a $10 million grant from the Washington State Department of Commerce’s Green Jobs Grant Program to develop FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies. The project is being developed in an existing Port of Benton building in Richland.

Washington is heading into its 2027–29 biennial budget with a multibillion-dollar shortfall, but officials have not yet settled on a definitive public estimate.

Ferguson has acknowledged the scale of the gap but has not publicly specified an amount. The shortfall concerns the state’s operating budget, which is separate from the capital budget funding proposed for the energy park.

Editor’s note: Comment from CleanTech Alliance President and CEO Mel Clark added 11/16.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5416. Unsiloed nabs $7.5M to turn scanned documents into structured data for AI agents

Document-scanning firm Unsiloed Inc. today announced it has raised $7.5 million in seed funding to turn PDFs and other complex documents into structured, readable data for artificial intelligence agents.

Participants in the round, led by Felicis, included Y Combinator, Orange Collective, Uncorrelated Ventures, Aarthi Ramamurthy and Beth Turner.

A variety of documents arrive in formats that are not straight data or text. Financial statements, insurance claims, contracts, clinical records, and operational forms make up the constellation of critical information for everyday business and operations. This information could be stored as images, PDFs or other formats and include charts, layouts and other elements that don’t translate directly into text.

Determining which column or axis of a chart belongs to which row, which heading leads which clause, or whether a pull quote interrupts the flow of the text or appears at the end of the document becomes a question of how to store the information.

Unsiloed parses documents such as PDFs using intelligent visual-first scanning to understand structured tables, sections and parent-child relationships between text. The company, which describes itself as intelligence-directed and vision-first, technology can scan forms, presentations, Word files and images into Markdown or JSON, a JavaScript Object Notation standard format readily readable by large language models.

“We believe AI agents will eventually read and write more documents than humans,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Aman Mishra. “Those agents do not just need better OCR. They need a dynamic interface to read, update and act on unstructured data.”

OCR, or optical character recognition, is the standard technology that is used to convert physical or image-based text, such as scanned paper documents or PDFs, into digital text. However, OCR doesn’t recognize tables, graphics or layouts; it only pre-processes the document to identify text, recognizes text and then outputs a contextual stream based on what it sees.

Unsiloed goes a step further by accounting for the page’s layout and format and providing a structured, machine-readable document that inherits the document’s original features. This means that if the presentation included headings, charts or other parts that relate to one another, those relationships are included in the data.

OCR is the most common way companies digitize documents today; Unsiloed believes it can do it better.

The company’s parser rated an 88.0 score on the olmOCR-Bench benchmark, a benchmark published by the Allen Institute for AI that is a rigorous, reproducible evaluation of how well modern AI models handle real-world OCR challenges. Compared with other services, Unsiloed said, it stacks up extremely well; for example, Anthropic PBC’s Claude Opus 4.7 ranks at 81.9, OpenAI Group PBC’s GPT 5.5 ranks at 84.6 and Google LLC’s Gemini 3 Pro ranks at 77.7.

“We combine deterministic computer vision algorithms with dual-stream vision models to build the interface that ranked first among 19 systems on olmOCR-Bench for AI agents to interact with unstructured data,” said co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Adnan Abbas.

The company said its dual-stream vision architecture allows it to process content and visual layouts at the same time. Developers can upload custom schemas to extract fields, classify and split documents, and update text and images while preserving document formatting.

It said it has processed millions of pages of documents for organizations across industries, from early-stage AI startups to banks, publicly traded insurance companies and law firms. The platform supports private-cloud, on-premises and fully air-gapped machines, allowing enterprise organizations to build Unsiloed into their document pipeline and do processing on their own infrastructure.

“We’ve significantly enhanced accuracy, context understanding, and response quality across all knowledge-base-powered conversations,” said Prateek Sachan, founder and CTO of Bolna AI, a company that builds voice agents for languages spoken across India.

#5412. Another record low for pending home sales, NAR index drops to 63

NAR reported the Pending Home Sales Index fell to 63 in October, down 4.7% from September and 16.7% from a year ago. All 4 regions declined, led by the West, while economists see limited near-term rebound with rates elevated.  AI Summary

Pending home sales fell to yet another record low in October, according to data published by the National Association of Realtors (NAR) on Wednesday.

According to the report, NAR’s Pending Home Sales Index fell to a reading of 63 in October, down 4.7% from a month ago and 16.7% a year ago. An index value of 100 is equivalent to the level of contract signings in 2001.

Despite the new record low, NAR’s chief economist is optimistic that things may turn around in November.

“October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” Yun said in a statement. “Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s. It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million. Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.”

HousingWire Data, which is more up to date, shows that for the week ending Nov. 13, 2026, 295,621 single family homes were pending in the U.S., down 14.1% from a year ago.

Pending home sales declined in all four major regions on both a year-over-year and month-over-month basis in October, according to NAR data. The West posted both the largest annual and monthly declines, dropping 20.3% from a year ago and 6.9% a month ago to an index value of 45.8. The Northeast (58.5) posted the smallest monthly and annual declines at 0.8% and 11.1%, respectively. Despite falling 18.7% annually and 6.3% from a month ago, pending home sales in the South remained the closest to 2001 levels, with an index reading of 74.5. Meanwhile, pending sales in the Midwest (65.5) fell 2.7% month-over-month and 14.0% from a year ago.

Locally, pending home sells fell annually in all 50 of the largest metro areas analyzed, with the smallest declines occurring inCincinnati, OH-KY-IN (-4.7%), Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos, TX (-9.7%) and Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, CT (-10.0%) according to data from Realtor.com Economics.

Looking ahead, with the Federal Reserve expected to raise interest rates at their meeting in December, economists believe a near-term rebound in contract signings is unlikely.

“A meaningful rebound looks unlikely any time soon, with further rate hikes by the Federal Reserve likely to keep a floor under rates as it keeps up its fight against inflation,” Sam Williamson, First American’s senior economist, said in a statement. “While those hikes could eventually open the door to lower rates, but it will take convincing evidence that inflation is retreating toward the Fed’s target. In the meantime, life events will keep some households moving, even as high rates discourage move-up and other discretionary moves and give some first-time buyers a little more reason to wait. Higher incomes and slower price growth may restore some buying power, but rates will limit how much of it turns into sales.”

#5410. Agents want the crown jewels: HPE and Daxa push governance down to the data layer

Enterprises are handing AI agents their most sensitive data, and governance is struggling to keep pace. Techniques such as semantic caching are emerging as a way to enforce controls inline without slowing agents down.

Moving agents from pilot to production means letting them read, change and even delete the records that matter most. That shift makes data access the central security question for agentic AI, according to Huseni Saboowala (pictured, right), co-founder and chief executive officer at Daxa Inc.

“For agents to really get to value, they need to be able to interact with your real enterprise data, and that includes your crown jewels, your intellectual property, your customer data in your [customer relationship management] and your proprietary trading algorithms,” he said. “That creates an unprecedented level of risk for enterprises because the agents are not just reading data; they’re also able to now go manipulate data at scale.”

Saboowala and Robin Braun (left), vice president of AI business development at Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., spoke with theCUBE’s Enterprise Editor, Paul Gillin, during coverage of SC26 on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. Daxa is a partner in HPE’s Unleash AI program, which offers pre-validated software on HPE Private Cloud AI. (* Disclosure below.)

Firewalls, data loss prevention and identity management still have a job to do. But they were built for users and applications, not software that reasons over data, Saboowala explained.

“Those agents are operating, though, at layer 8, what we call the cognitive layer,” he said. “This is where you have the prompts, the responses, the retrievals and the tool calls happening. Traditional tools really are not operating at this layer.”

Saboowala’s answer is reasoning-based access controls, backed by agents that flag abnormal behavior. HPE builds governance into its Private Cloud AI stack from the start, according to Braun.

“Being able to build in that governance from day one allows you to understand what is it going to look like so that … you’re not bolting it on later,” she said. “Instead, it’s a part of the workflow.”

Timing matters as much as policy. Offline governance arrives too late for agents working at machine speed, so enforcement must happen inline through semantic caching, specialized small language models and a distributed data plane, Saboowala explained. A regional bank that deployed Daxa with HPE has since connected its agents to source code and regulated customer data.

“I believe that the winners in this agent era are not just the ones who have the most [graphics processing units],” Saboowala said. “But they will be enterprises who have agents they can trust with their data.”

#5409. ‘I hope this email finds you’: Microsoft declares outage over as the world digs out of its inbox

by Todd Bishop on Nov 14, 2026 at 10:35 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:28 am

Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted.

“Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.

Later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote.

Microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The company says the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details.

The company said late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log. Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal.

A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user, he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five.

In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one company’s cloud.

Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth.

Among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto, a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health said patient care continued without disruption.

In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported, citing Nikkei.

In New York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems, including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email.

About the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”

Microsoft itself looked to preempt the speculation a few hours earlier, posting on X that it had “no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.”

The Microsoft 365 outage was at least the fourth significant one this year. A January outage lasted nearly 10 hours, and in July a bug in Microsoft’s automated network maintenance system disrupted Azure and Microsoft 365 services for hours. On Aug. 31, an Exchange Online outage also hit Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint.

Instead of “I hope this email finds you well,” many people joked, it should just be “I hope this email finds you.” (Consider this our nomination for the “Overworked Twitter Joke of the Week” on The Ringer’s Press Box podcast.)

Microsoft said Friday afternoon that it was watching the backlog of delayed email “to ensure all process successfully before considering the issue resolved.” The University of Washington’s IT department told its users that email delayed during the outage would be delivered as mail queues continued to be processed.

Many people coped with the flood of returning email with a bit of levity.

As the mail started flowing again, CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter said he was getting “a deluge of emails from PR people pitching their clients to talk about the Outlook outage.” Most were sent during the outage, he noted, “which, fittingly, prevented the pitches from reaching me.”

The security company Malwarebytes captured the paradox in a message to its followers: “We regret to inform you that Teams and Outlook are coming back online after a global outage.”

#5408. The mortgage industry was built to help Americans buy homes. An aging America needs more from it.

Survey of 2,000 homeowners 55 plus shows 88% prioritize staying home and 90% prioritize independence

For decades, the mortgage industry has helped Americans achieve one of their biggest financial goals: buying a home and building equity over time.

It’s a model we know well. Homeowners purchase properties, make mortgage payments, refinance when it makes financial sense and gradually accumulate wealth. Much of the mortgage industry is structured around supporting that journey.

But what happens after decades of building that wealth?

As homeowners approach retirement, the financial equation shifts. Instead of focusing primarily on acquiring a home and paying down debt, the question becomes how to use the wealth they’ve accumulated to support the years ahead. Housing presents a unique opportunity but also a challenge because, for many Americans, their largest financial asset is also the place they call home.

You can sell a stock without moving. Selling a home is another matter. Trading down and moving to a less expensive home to tap home equity is both expensive and difficult. This might be why our recent research shows that the desire to remain at home continues to grow stronger with age.

In a recent Longbridge Financial, LLC (NMLS #957935) study of more than 2,000 U.S. homeowners ages 55 and older, 90% said maintaining their independence was extremely or very important to their ideal retirement. Nearly as many (88%) said the same about remaining in their homes. Both priorities ranked above paying for health care, paying off debt, long-term care and providing financial support to family members.

The desire to age in place isn’t surprising. What’s particularly revealing is how strongly that sentiment differs across age groups.

Among homeowners ages 55 to 64, 85% rated remaining in their homes as extremely or very important. That figure rose to 88% among those ages 65 to 74 and 93% among homeowners 75 and older. The importance of maintaining independence followed a similar pattern, climbing from 87% in the youngest group to 96% in the oldest.

These are differences between age groups at one point in time, rather than a measure of how individual preferences change over time. Still, the pattern points to an important finding in understanding how homeowners think about retirement.

Over decades, homeowners accumulate substantial equity through mortgage payments and increases in property values. Yet the very home that holds the wealth is also where many want to spend their later years. Its financial value tells only part of the story. Giving a homeowner a choice to move to a less expensive, and thus less attractive, home to use their home equity may not be much of a choice at all.

Consider two retired households with the same net worth. One holds most of its wealth in savings and investments. The other holds much of it in home equity.

Their balance sheets might look similar, but their financial flexibility is different. The first household may be able to draw from liquid accounts to cover an unexpected expense. The second has wealth, too, but accessing it may involve borrowing against the home or selling it altogether. Both options come with trade-offs, particularly when remaining in the home is a priority.

For an industry accustomed to measuring property values, loan balances and equity, this is an important distinction. These figures describe a homeowner’s financial position, but not necessarily how easily they can access that wealth — or what they might have to give up in the process.

The same survey reinforces why this distinction matters. Among homeowners ages 55 to 64, 73% rated paying for health care as extremely or very important to their ideal retirement. That figure climbed to 85% among those 75 and older. While these findings don’t tell us how much homeowners will spend or whether they’ll tap into their home equity, they do highlight how financial priorities can shift across different stages of life.

Mortgage finance has traditionally centered on transactions: purchasing, refinancing, servicing and eventually paying off a loan. Those functions remain essential. But paying off a mortgage doesn’t end a homeowner’s financial relationship with their home.

For some older homeowners, selling or downsizing may be the right choice. Others may have sufficient income and savings to remain in place. Still others may consider home equity loans, lines of credit or reverse mortgages, depending on their financial circumstances, eligibility and the associated costs and risks.

The opportunity for our industry extends beyond any single product. It’s about understanding the role home equity can play in supporting homeowners through retirement, while recognizing the personal value they place on remaining in their homes.

It also requires recognizing that homeowners’ priorities differ. In our study, 93% of women rated independence as extremely or very important, compared with 88% of men. Similar five-point gaps appeared for remaining at home and paying for health care. While the research doesn’t explain why these differences exist, it underscores the importance of understanding homeowners as individuals rather than treating homeowners 55 and over as a single market with identical needs and priorities.

Housing has always been both an investment and a place to live. As homeowners age, the balance between those roles deserves greater attention from the industry that helped them achieve homeownership in the first place.

We’ve spent decades helping Americans build wealth through homeownership. The next opportunity is helping them understand how that wealth can support the years ahead, without losing sight of what they value most: independence, financial flexibility and, for many, the ability to remain at home.

#5407. /C O R R E C T I O N - Aimbient/

In the news release, Aimbient AI Automates OR Documentation Across Specialties With Human-Level Accuracy, Study in JAMA Surgery Finds, issued 18-Nov-2026 by Aimbient over PR Newswire, we are advised by the company that changes have been made. The complete, corrected release follows, with additional details at the end:

Research shows Aimbient can automatically capture the reliable OR data health systems need to improve efficiency at scale

NEW YORK, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The first large-scale, multispecialty validation of automated operating room documentation, led by Stanford Medicine researchers and published in JAMA Surgery, found that ambient surgical and procedural AI from Aimbient (formerly Surgical Safety Technologies) matches human accuracy on key OR timestamps.

The findings show Aimbient can automatically generate reliable OR documentation at scale, a foundation for health systems looking to improve OR utilization and efficiency.

Running continuously across 14 operating rooms and one procedure room at Stanford Health Care during the eight-month study, Aimbient used real-time computer vision to automatically detect when patients entered and exited the operating room. Researchers compared those automated timestamps with manually entered timestamps, using blinded human video review as the ground truth. They found no statistically significant difference in accuracy between Aimbient's automated timestamps and manual documentation across seven surgical service types.

And while human accuracy degraded during overnight shifts and long transplant cases, Aimbient remained resilient to documentation fatigue.

"Every OR metric a health system cares about, from first-case on-time starts to turnover time, is based on the accuracy of the timestamp underneath it," said Teodor Grantcharov, MD, PhD, founder and CEO of Aimbient. "Stanford Medicine researchers showed Aimbient can capture those timestamps automatically, around the clock, with the same accuracy as a human at the keyboard. Our AI systems are resistant to fatigue, stress, and furthermore free up cognitive bandwidth for the operative team to focus on patient care. Logging accurate timestamps, 24/7-365, gives health systems reliable data to see how their ORs are actually running and get more capacity from the ORs they already have."

Previous validations of computer-vision OR timestamps were limited to a single procedure type. The Stanford Medicine study in JAMA Surgery was conducted independently and included every surgery performed in the study rooms, spanning general, vascular, transplant, urologic, gynecologic and orthopedic surgery.

Manually entered timestamps lag the actual event by an average of five to six minutes, as the circulator is busy caring for the patient the minute they roll in.

In use, Aimbient documents these timestamps as events occur, giving perioperative teams a more current view of room activity without waiting for manual entry. More reliable, timely timestamps could also strengthen the data used for scheduling, operational reporting and capacity decisions.

"To our knowledge, this is the first study of its kind that examines the accuracy of automated OR documentation at scale, across multiple surgery types in a major academic hospital," said Chloe Nobuhara, MD, general surgery resident at Stanford Medicine and lead author of the study. "These timestamps are a relatively small milestone in the entire patient's journey, but now there is the ability for computer vision to parse data out of a highly chaotic OR environment."

The stakes are significant. According to published estimates, operating rooms generate up to 70% of hospital revenue and can cost as much as $100 per minute to run. Improving operational efficiency by even a few minutes can yield substantial annual operating margin, and health systems are increasingly turning to data-driven technologies to improve performance.

Automated timestamps are one application of Aimbient's broader intelligence platform, which is designed to work before, during and after every surgical case or procedure. Aimbient runs across the day: forecasting the schedule before the first case, tracking and documenting in real time during it, and turning every completed procedure into data that improves the next. By showing what is actually happening in the room, Aimbient gives health systems a reliable basis for scheduling and capacity decisions, moving procedural AI beyond documenting what happened and toward improving what happens next. Read the full study here.

About Aimbient: Aimbient (formerly Surgical Safety Technologies) is an ambient AI platform that helps health systems improve efficiency and safety across surgical and procedural care. Founded by surgeons and trained on more than 15 million hours of real procedural data, Aimbient brings together real-time room visibility, predictive planning, safety insights and performance benchmarking on one platform. It gives clinical and operational leaders a shared source of intelligence to coordinate daily operations, improve scheduling and staffing, and continuously improve care across rooms and specialties. Aimbient's platform is deployed in 650 surgical and procedural rooms. Learn more at www.aimbient.com and follow Aimbient on LinkedIn.

#5406. Who should run Nvidia? Our picks for Jensen Huang’s successor, whether the board likes it or not

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 14, 2026 at 2:10 pmNovember 14, 2026 at 2:10 pm

Nvidia’s board says it’s too early to speculate about who will succeed Jensen Huang. Sorry, we’re having too much fun coming up with names.

The board said in a statement Friday that it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates. That came after the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas — a name John had presciently floated when we recorded this week’s GeekWire Podcast on Thursday.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Colette Kress, the company’s longtime CFO, is serving as interim CEO. She spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to run a deliberate search that leaves open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Elon Musk said on X that he was signing a petition to reinstate Huang.

The organizers of one, called “Stand with Jensen,” say it has more than 108,000 names, including more than 5,600 people who identify themselves as current Nvidia employees.

The case for Haas: The Arm CEO spent about seven years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in February 2022, when Nvidia’s $40 billion deal to acquire Arm collapsed amid regulatory opposition. SoftBank, Arm’s majority owner, kept Nvidia’s $1.25 billion prepayment.

Arm, based in Cambridge, England, designs processor technology that’s ubiquitous in smartphones, and licenses it to other chipmakers. That includes Nvidia, whose Grace data center CPU, paired with its GPUs in AI systems, is built on Arm cores. Amazon’s Graviton and Microsoft’s Cobalt server chips also use Arm designs.

Haas is one of several candidates, and there’s no guarantee he’ll be offered the job or take it, the FT reported.

He also has a link to Harvey Jones, the longtime Nvidia director named the company’s first board chair this week. Haas was vice president of sales at Tensilica, a chip-design company, from 1999 to 2004, according to his LinkedIn profile. Jones co-founded Tensilica and chaired its board until chip-design software maker Cadence acquired it in 2013.

Haas has also seen Huang’s resistance to succession planning firsthand. “He didn’t like the idea,” Haas said in a 2024 interview, as quoted by the New York Times this week. “He felt it would create competition among executives and be divisive.”

One complication: SoftBank named Haas CEO of SoftBank Group International in April, helping coordinate chip and AI companies in its international portfolio while he continues to run Arm. The FT reported that the appointment was aimed at pushing forward Project Izanagi, SoftBank’s AI chip effort launched to compete with Nvidia.

He knows Nvidia from the inside, but he also knows what it’s like to run a public company — which matters for a board searching in the middle of a crisis.

John’s argument on the podcast: Nvidia needs someone who can shepherd a company through turmoil, not just a great technologist. Think Alan Mulally going from Boeing to Ford, or Dara Khosrowshahi moving from Expedia to Uber after Travis Kalanick’s ouster.

What the betting markets say: On Kalshi, Ian Buck, the Nvidia vice president who created the CUDA software platform, was the favorite at midday Friday. By midday Saturday, Haas had overtaken him, at 25% to Buck’s 18%. Kress was at 10%.

The Axios list of 11 names also includes Apple Executive Chair Tim Cook, for whom President Trump lobbied on Truth Social (“A Legend replaces a Legend!”), along with AMD CEO Lisa Su and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian.

A Northwest wildcard: Analysts have also floated Sanjay Mehrotra, CEO of Boise, Idaho-based Micron Technology, whose memory chips power Nvidia’s AI servers. Mehrotra co-founded SanDisk in 1988 and has run Micron since 2017.

The AWS chief: Matt Garman has run Amazon Web Services since June 2024, overseeing a business with a $142 billion annual revenue run rate at the end of last year. He started at Amazon as an MBA intern in 2005, joined AWS full time in 2006 as one of its first product managers, and later led its compute business and then its sales and marketing organization.

Another Amazon pick: We’d also look at Peter DeSantis, who now leads a new organization that includes Amazon’s AI models, custom chips and quantum computing, reporting directly to CEO Andy Jassy.

DeSantis joined Amazon as a software developer in 1998. He led the EC2 team from Cape Town, South Africa, through its 2006 launch, and spearheaded Amazon’s 2015 acquisition of Annapurna Labs, the Israeli chip designer behind its custom silicon.

In 2018, DeSantis unveiled Graviton. In June, he told Bloomberg that AWS was in talks to sell its Trainium AI chips to other companies for their own data centers.

He knows chips, data centers and AI infrastructure at enormous scale. The catch, as John noted: he’s never been a CEO, and the board may want that experience given the circumstances.

The other Amazon name: Dave Treadwell took over AWS compute and machine learning services in August. Treadwell spent 27 years at Microsoft, where he worked on Windows NT, .NET and Xbox and rose to corporate vice president, before joining Amazon in 2016.

The Microsoft bench: On the podcast, Todd ran through a few Microsoft executives who would bring relevant experience:

The insider with Microsoft roots: Nick Parker, a 26-year Microsoft sales veteran, joined Nvidia in August as executive vice president of worldwide field operations, with a pay package worth more than $40 million. He’s new, but he already runs the team that sells Nvidia’s chips to the world’s largest companies.

One more angle: Whoever gets the job will face a growing list of customers trying to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, including Amazon. In his annual shareholder letter in April, Jassy wrote that Amazon’s chips business would have an annual run rate of about $50 billion if it sold chips to AWS and other third parties the way other chipmakers do.

Jassy said it’s “quite possible” Amazon will sell racks of them to third parties in the future.

In a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14, Huang said he hoped his successor was already inside the company. The board has said it will consider both internal and external candidates.

Listen to our full discussion on this week’s GeekWire Podcast.

#5405. How far can brokerages go when clawing back commissions from departing agents?

The Q2 2026 Agent Migration Report found external brokerage switches essentially unchanged year over year. In Massachusetts, Lamacchia Realty alleges Chinatti Realty imposed 75%-85% referral fees tied to database leads, and the court cited missing CRM records during discovery.  AI Summary

The number of real estate agents moving from one brokerage brand to another essentially remained flat year-over-year during the second quarter of 2026, according to the Q2 2026 Agent Migration Report, published by Recruiting Insight and Lone Wolf Technologies in late July.

Of the 113,372 records and four MLS corridors the report analyzed, just 3,390 agents made an external move during the quarter, a difference of just six moves from Q2 2025.

At the same time, the report found that name-brand internal transfers grew from 526 in Q4 2024 to 800 in Q2 2026, a 52% increase over 18 months.

While agents may choose to change firms for access to better technology and educational opportunities or to be working in a company culture that better aligns with their values, these moves do not happen in a vacuum and can have real financial consequences for agents.

Some firms have been known to employ “clawbacks,” where the brokerage firm may withhold a percentage of pending commissions on listings nearing contract, charge transfer or cancellation fees if clients follow the agent, or “claw back” signing bonuses or incentives the agents have received upon changing firms.

A lawsuit in Massachusetts, however, claims that one brokerage has taken things a step further, charging referral fees as high as 85% when an agent who left the company closed a transaction with a lead that exists in their former brokerage’s database.

In a suit originally filed in August 2024 and amended in late February 2025, Lamacchia Realty, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, eight of its agents and its former sales manager Jason Posnick, claim that Chinatti Realty Group and its broker-owner Lisa Chinatti has been unjustly enriched through her referral fee practices.

The lawsuit, first reported by Inman, is pending in Massachusetts Superior Court for Middlesex County. It claims that the agent plaintiffs’ independent contractor agreements were unconscionable because they imposed referral fees as high as 85% when they closed transactions with leads in the Chinatti Realty Group’s database after joining Lamacchia Realty.

The agent plaintiffs allege that this allowed Chinatti and her firm to continually make claims for referral fees on many of the agents’ sales since they have left the company and that this has prevented them from earning a living in real estate. Lamacchia Realty claims that, to date, it has paid Chinatti Realty Group in excess of $350,000 in 75% to 85% referral fees on behalf of former Chinatti agents.

In addition to this, the agents claim that they were not paid anything on transactions that were pending when they transitioned from Chinatti to Lamacchia. Lamacchia Realty has said it has paid agents $113,443 to make them whole on commissions not paid to them from Chinatti for pending transactions that closed after they departed Chinatti Realty Group.

The agents also claim Chinatti and her firm misclassified them as independent contractors despite exercising controls beyond the normal supervisory obligations of a broker.

Lamacchia Realty first contacted Chinatti and her firm regarding these alleged issues in November of 2022 via letter.

This past summer, during the discovery process, the court and Judge Lynn Rooney, who is overseeing the suit, said they learned that Chinatti Realty Group had swapped consumer relationship management software providers from Real Geeks to Zillow’s Follow Up Boss in December 2024. To move the data over, Chinatti said Zillow paid a vendor to handle the migration, but that the vendor found certain records were unable to be transferred.

According to a mid-September ruling from the court, Chinatti knew the allegedly lost records were relevant to the dispute between the firms thanks to the November 2022 letter she and her firm received from Lamacchia.

“I find that Lisa Chinatti knew when she received the demand letter in November 2022 that the information contained in Real Geeks was highly relevant to the plaintiffs’ causes of action. I find that Lisa Chinatti did nothing to preserve that documentation and instead, deliberately and intentionally caused the Real Geeks CRM to be destroyed,” Judge Rooney wrote in her ruling. “I find that the Plaintiffs have demonstrated that they have suffered unfair prejudice as a result of Ms. Chinatti’s actions. Plaintiffs likely would have retained the services of a forensic expert to review the data contained in Real Geeks. As stated at the hearing, the Real Geeks data would have included information concerning the daily work and activity of each of the plaintiff agents, statements by Ms. Chinatti, and the nature of the interactions/communications between Ms. Chinatti and the plaintiff agents.”

If the lawsuit proceeds to trial, the judge has said that at a minimum, the plaintiffs were entitled to “very clear and forceful instruction [to the jury] that the evidence, had it been available, would have been unfavorable to the Defendants.”

In addition to this, the court said it discovered that agents’ CRM activity and phone conversations were monitored and recorded, without the permission of call participants. The judge said she had forwarded the ruling and these concerns to the Massachusetts Attorney General’s Criminal Bureau for review of potential wiretap violations.

Earlier this month, the plaintiffs filed a motion for the denial of the summary judgement motions the defendants have filed since the start of the year. They argue that the unresolved factual disputes that have surfaced during discovery warrant a trial and have requested that the court schedule a final pretrial conference.

The court has yet to rule on this motion or Chinatti’s motions for summary judgement.

Chinatti did not respond to HousingWire’s request for comment regarding the allegations in the lawsuit nor the court’s ruling.

#5404. AI factories push liquid cooling beyond CPUs and GPUs to nearly every rack component

The liquid cooling supply chain is under mounting pressure as AI factories pack more heat into every rack.

To meet demand, operators have invested heavily in denser racks and liquid cooling, as well as the hoses and couplings that move the fluid must arrive faster and in larger volumes than ever. But for component makers, keeping up takes more than extra shifts. With liquid cooling reaching more of the rack, equipment makers need connections suited to a wider range of components, according to Tyler Glenn (pictured, right), engineer, product applications and data centers, at Danfoss Power Solutions, a division of Danfoss A/S.

“We went from air cooling to hybrid cooling and we’re moving a lot now towards full liquid cooling,” Glenn said. “Traditionally, it was just the CPUs and GPUs that were being liquid cooled. But as more components are starting to have to get integrated, there’s a lot more opportunity for us to have different types of connections to solve specific challenges that this industry faces.”

Glenn and Lauren Witter (left), vice president of sales at Omni Services Inc., spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the liquid cooling supply chain, the universal quick disconnect and designing systems for rising heat density. (* Disclosure below.)

When a rush order comes in for a large data center build, suppliers need parts on hand to assemble hoses quickly, Glenn explained. Danfoss works with distributors that carry its hoses and couplings to keep a minimum stock available as part of a strategy to stay ahead of projections

“A lot of times our customers will provide us forecasts, but we like to shoot above that and look ahead and make sure that in case that the demand increases beyond that, that we’re prepared for that,” Glenn said. “When it comes to our component suppliers, we’re making sure to order additional materials, but also keeping track of making sure we have enough stock.”

But when a data center builder needs parts for denser AI racks on short notice, having stock on hand gives distributors a head start. Omni’s CoolFlow division works directly with Danfoss’s data center team to handle those requests, according to Witter. Both teams focus on liquid cooling, so Omni can take a rush order straight to the engineers it already works with.

“No one gets frustrated when we’re calling Tyler saying we need these parts yesterday,” Witter said. “They get it. They’re playing the same game we are.”

#5401. Real REMAX Group confirms additional layoffs after merger

Real REMAX Group confirmed additional organizational changes after its REMAX acquisition. Executives previously disclosed a 14% headcount reduction and more than $40 million in annualized gross cost savings tied to integration efforts.  AI Summary

After a merger or acquisition closes, companies almost always look for cost synergies. These efforts frequently result in layoffs, which they did at the recently formed Real REMAX Group, a RealTrends Verified firm.

During the company’s third-quarter 2026 earnings call with investors and analysts, which occurred a little over two months after The Real Brokerage closed its acquisition of REMAX, executives said the company reduced its combined headcount by more than 14%, eliminating 150-plus positions across the combined organization.

This came as the company said it found more than $40 million in annualized gross cost savings and expects to realize more than $30 million in adjusted EBITDA savings in 2027, which could increase to more than $40 million in 2028.

At the time of the earnings call, executives said the initial phase of headcount restructuring was largely complete but that they were still looking for ways to simplify operations and improve efficiencies.

But based on a recent slew of posts on LinkedIn, it appears that headcount reductions are not over just yet. Over the past week, several individuals who claim to be former REMAX employees shared posts stating that they’d been impacted by a recent round of layoffs at the company.

A spokesperson for Real REMAX Group told HousingWire via email that following the acquisition, “Real REMAX Group is continuing to evaluate opportunities that streamline operations, create efficiencies and better integrate the two organizations.”

“As part of this ongoing process, we can confirm that additional organizational changes have taken place at the company,” the spokesperson wrote. “We will continue to assess our business needs to ensure we have the right structure and resources in place to support our long-term strategic priorities and better serve real estate professionals.”

The spokesperson declined to share details regarding the size of the layoffs, which departments were impacted or if the layoffs were performance related.

Real REMAX Group is not alone in laying off employees as part of an attempt to rightsize after a merger.

Earlier this year, Compass International Holdings announced it was laying off 110 employees after it closed its acquisition of Anywhere Real Estate. Compass has estimated $500 million in total net cost synergies over the next three years.

#5400. Guild’s Nora Guerra on helping baby boomers buy and rehab homes with reverse mortgages

Guild Mortgage’s Nora Guerra said lenders underserve older, equity-rich buyers despite NAR data showing boomers are 42% of buyers and 55% of sellers. She pointed to $15.34 trillion in 62-plus housing wealth and rising use cases for reverse mortgage for purchase transactions.  AI Summary

Baby boomers represent 42% of homebuyers and 55% of sellers, according to the most recent data from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), yet the mortgage industry has yet to fully account for their presence.

That was the message shared last week by Nora Guerra, senior vice president of community lending solutions at Guild Mortgage, during the National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA)’s Annual Meeting & Expo in San Antonio.

Guerra — who previously worked at Freddie Mac, where she studied how homebuyers change by age group — told the audience that lenders have spent years chasing younger consumers while overlooking older, equity-rich groups who are moving frequently and are in need of help.

“This 55-plus buyer, it’s a main demographic buyer. Everybody has been so focused on the millennial — the older millennial, the younger millennial — and now the Gen Zer,” she said.

Before the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, boomers were largely staying put and had few incentives to move, Guerra said. But that changed quickly as single-family home price appreciation skyrocketed from 3.2% in 2019 to 11.3% in 2021 and 11.9% in 2022, according to HousingWire Data.

That contributed heavily to home equity accumulation, with homeowners 62 and older now holding $15.34 trillion in housing wealth, according to NRMLA and RiskSpan. Additionally, the pandemic caused a rupture in many families’ living situations. “They were sheltered in place. They couldn’t see their loved ones, their grandchildren and their children, and it shook them very hard,” Guerra said.

Across years of research, Guerra has uncovered four distinct groups of older homebuyers:

Each of these groups are likely to need financing to accomplish their goals, she said. Reverse mortgages may offer a more cost-effective solution since they don’t require a monthly payment, and they’re often a fit for applicants who’ve been turned down for other types of mortgage credit.

Reverse mortgage for purchase programs, in particular, can fulfill their needs. These products allow seniors to sell their current home and use the equity to buy a similar or more expensive property without monthly payments or the need to pay in cash. “They really don’t know what options are out there, so they feel no one wants to finance me,” Guerra remarked.

According to NAR research cited by Guerra, senior homebuyers frequently utilize mortgages, but the trend wanes as the buyer grows older. The data shows that among 61- to 70-year-olds, 61% financed their purchase during the year ending in June 2025. The percentage dropped to 54% among 71- to 79-year-olds, and to 48% among those 80 and older.

Guerra said mortgage professionals spend too much time discussing problems and not enough time on finding or developing solutions. This can be particularly unhelpful when working with house-rich, cash-poor clients who have significant equity but little in the way of savings or retirement funds.

With these types of needs-based borrowers, reverse mortgage professionals should be asking about the cash they’re looking to access for both everyday living expenses and unexpected expenses. Develop a cash-flow plan based on what they have in their retirement accounts and other investments.

Whether a client is considering a federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgage or a proprietary reverse mortgage, counselors certified by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) are a key resource to tap into. Guerra said she works with more than 200 counselors nationwide who “help educate and hold the hand of your parent, and tell them all about this program and how it works.”

Originators should ask direct questions about the client’s preferences to pay for their next home, identify any assets they don’t want to touch for that purpose, and offer comparisons of what the financial results will look like with a reverse mortgage versus a cash deal.

Family members often fear there will be nothing left for them when their parent or grandparent dies. But planning ahead of time can help heirs to sell the home and keep any proceeds, or to repay the reverse mortgage and continue living there. Some lenders offer private-label solutions for these exact situations.

Guerra also pointed to NAR data showing that 14% of recent home purchases were tied to multigenerational living situations. These clients often need their family involved when making decisions about reverse mortgages. Adult children want to protect their parents’ assets, so originators should include relatives early in the process.

“Mom and dad haven’t bought a home in the last 10 or 15 years due to lack of inventory. Grandma and grandpa haven’t bought a home in the last 15 to 20 years due to the same reason,” Guerra told the audience. “Multigenerational living is what we’re seeing on these 1003 (loan applications) — lots of grandparents cosigning for their millennial and Gen Z grandchildren if they can afford it, but also lots of gift letters.”

#5398. Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am

The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.

A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.

Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

The window is closing. Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

Competitors are everywhere. AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”

The data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each new model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

The data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

Momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.

Learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

Jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its big commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

At AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”

Finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook says Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”

Prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick important problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”

Swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

Farecast, the airfare prediction company I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments company whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.

Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, said it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”

So pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one big shot once you have it.

Chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

To repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one says, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.

In AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.

#5397. AI’s GPU focus meets a CPU reality check at Dell and AMD

Agentic AI is rewriting the business development playbook for chipmakers and server builders. Graphics processing units still grab the headlines, but as supercomputing and AI converge, the next wave of demand is landing on central processing units that must fit within data centers’ existing power budgets.

The shift has been building for years. Customers that hung more GPUs off a single CPU found they were starving expensive accelerators of data, leaving them idle, according to Scott Tease (pictured, left), vice president of business development for high-performance computing and sovereign AI at Advanced Micro Devices Inc.

“People have realized how important that CPU is in a GPU architecture. But beyond that, agentic is not necessarily just a GPU thing,” Tease said. “Agentic is going to be very CPU heavy because with agentic, what you’re looking at, you want to go very fast, but you also want concurrency.”

Tease and David Schmidt (right), vice president of PowerEdge product management at Dell Technologies Inc., spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the growing role of CPUs in agentic workloads and the challenges of balancing compute performance with data center power constraints. (* Disclosure below.)

Dell and AMD have been building rack-scale AI platforms together, but power remains the binding constraint. When Dell began planning its portfolio 2.5 years ago, enterprise customers expected rack power requirements to remain at 15 to 20 kilowatts and said they often ran out of power before filling a rack, according to Schmidt. Dell responded with the PowerEdge R9825, a 3U server built on AMD’s sixth-generation EPYC 9006 processors.

“It’s been optimized for power efficiency and cooling efficiency,” Schmidt said. “That means we’re using less power to cool the system overall, and that’s power that we can return to our customers.”

That efficiency compounds at refresh time. A single EPYC 9006 server can take 13 legacy machines out of production while cutting the system power needed for cooling by 80 percent, Schmidt noted. Tease sees reclaimed power feeding agentic workloads, where agents could turn one researcher’s ideas into thousands of compute jobs.

“Same number of researchers, massive increase in the amount of compute. Agentic is going to continue to drive more and more IT, and we’ve got to find a way to power it,” Tease said.
