#5396. Why 2027 may turn into a land negotiation year for homebuilders

Scott Cox says 2027 could become a negotiation-driven year in land, with re-trades and real price resets. He argues builders should focus on counterparties’ incentive structures to understand likely outcomes.  AI Summary

In the early ’90s, I worked in Wells Fargo Bank’s real estate workout group in Southern California. The aerospace collapse was crushing the local economy; Los Angeles County alone lost 400,000 jobs. Roughly 25% of WFB’s assets were in commercial real estate (including homebuilding), and another 25% in home mortgages, mostly in California. That was half the bank. Writing off loans and walking away to clean up the books wasn’t an option; we lacked the capital. So we fought for every penny.

We asked for re-margins early on, short-term extensions and collected from borrowers before they ran out of money. We pursued personal guarantees and were willing to fight for them. I realize it is not what an audience of builders wants to hear, but everyone fights to survive.

Bank of America was in a different position. It had less real estate concentration and wanted to expand by buying distressed banks, but it couldn’t until regulators were convinced it had moved past its own problems. So BofA cut deals or foreclosed, cleaning house. Its real estate recovery rate was far lower than ours. That doesn’t mean BofA was wrong. It simply had different incentives.

Everyone knows Charlie Munger’s line, “Show me the incentive and I’ll show you the outcome.”

We tend to apply it to individuals. But the coming year will be driven largely by company incentives. If you’re a builder, understanding the incentives of the companies across the table may be the most valuable market intelligence you can gather.

Why the coming year? As I’ve said before, I’m not a big fan of short-term market projections. Over longer time spans, demographics, the fundamental balance of supply and demand, and affordability play out; they’re directionally predictable, if not precise. The short term has so many unforeseeable temporary factors that it can, paradoxically, be harder to call. Strategy is for the long term; in the short run, it’s mostly tactics, adapting to what’s in front of you. But caution about predicting short-term conditions is different from dismissing contingency planning.

Housing market conditions have clearly deteriorated. Whatever the cause (war, politics, rising rates or all of the above), I suspect we never had the correction we should have after rates spiked in ’22. A frozen-in-place resale market and the effectiveness of rate buydowns made the following years difficult, but less so than many of us expected.

One of the most intriguing aspects is that I can’t recall a more difficult period in homebuilding (to be clear, I’ve been through far worse, twice) that had so little impact on the land market. The reason was the belief that land was in such short supply that builders couldn’t afford to give up what they had and would need to buy more. Builders weren’t staying in current deals because they necessarily made sense, nor were they buying new ones because they liked the prices.

The attitude was: what’s the alternative?

That belief rested on two assumptions. First, that today’s weakness is a short-term problem: the rate shock would wear off, and buying would pick up. Second, that long-term fundamentals hadn’t changed, so demand would rebound and buoy prices. Either could prove true, but I’m skeptical. As I’ve written over the past year, future demand looks weak relative to the past, not a temporary dip but the start of a regime change. Once that becomes conventional wisdom, why would builders feel the need to control six to seven years of lots? Remember when three to four was considered plenty? Why won’t that be the case again?

I think 2027 is the year land prices will correct, not just terms but real prices. It’s current economics meeting a dawning recognition that the future will need fewer lots. Beyond a few year-end closings, not much will happen in the rest of 2026, and some will wait to see whether a magic spring rebound arrives. But over the last few months, we’ve seen a sharp downgrade in builder expectations for next year. Few expect things to improve soon.

The public builders reinforce this. Many are eliminating forecasts or revising unit counts downward. Much like the difference between making a dollar and losing a dollar, which is much bigger than two dollars, once a builder admits it won’t be growing, it becomes much easier to walk from some positions. Once that threshold is crossed, Wall Street cares far less whether a builder shrinks 2% or 6%.

Reasonable people can differ on this; there are multiple paths forward. But I think the odds are high enough to warrant contingency planning. If I’m right, what happens?

To start, many land bankers (not the old vets, but the newcomers) will learn they weren’t offering a credit product. Like it or not, they’re in real estate and have taken real estate risk. Too many fundamentals in that business were stretched on the belief that big builders wouldn’t walk en masse.

Expect meaningful re-trades, not just extensions. Meanwhile, land sellers will hear builders say they have options and don’t need to rush: “We’ll pay less and take them down on a rolling schedule with a 3% annual escalator. We can’t pay a land banker 10% to hold them; the margin’s too thin.”

That’s where incentives come in. How each negotiation goes will depend heavily on the incentives of the companies involved, and each company has multiple layers. Using land bankers as an example, here are a few questions worth addressing.

How are their asset management fees calculated and collected? As a percentage of revenue, assets (write-downs matter), or cost? Are they amortized over the deal’s life, or literally eat-what-you-kill, paid at closing? Last cycle, it wasn’t uncommon for equity funds to earn asset management fees based on revenue, with half taken up front and the rest amortized over the deal’s projected life.

When deals stretched out, and total revenue fell, the fee shrank and had to last longer. Once it was used up, it was used up, and a manager could be left without enough fee income to run the business but still obligated to manage the assets. That argues for resolving deals. But many of those structures also triggered a true-up at close-out, which argues for delaying resolution. Which pressure drives a given manager? It depends, and that’s exactly why you need to know.

Is their profit from fees or from promotes? A manager who relies on asset management fees will protect them. A manager focused on promotes, with good profits already built up in a tranche, may prefer to resolve an asset quickly, even at a loss, rather than let the overall IRR erode further.

Millrose Properties is an interesting case. Its external manager, Kennedy Lewis (KL), is paid a fee based on the vehicle’s tangible assets rather than on performance, and Millrose is permanent capital with no fund life to force a resolution. That structure rewards keeping the asset base intact; a sale shrinks it, and so does a write-down. I can’t know how KL will respond, and there are counterweights, since Millrose is a public REIT with a dividend and a stock price to consider.

But if I were betting, I’d expect the fee base to weigh heavily. If conditions worsen, few builders will be seeking new land banking, so raising more capital matters less until a recovery brings new deals. One way to keep assets on the books would be to lower option fees and ease takedown terms to keep builders in contract, even at weak returns. A more classic fund structure, by contrast, might push a manager toward resolution rather than managing assets for little or no fee.

Similar dynamics will play out among land sellers. Traditionally, well-capitalized sellers are reluctant to cut prices at first. Doing so immediately crushes expected returns, and the weakness might prove temporary. But at some point, it becomes clear it isn’t temporary, and the concern shifts from return on capital to return of capital.

For fund-backed sellers, the next fundraising effort makes the difference between “we’ve never lost money on a deal” and “we’ve never lost more than 5% on a deal” stark. They don’t read the same in a pitch book. So structures that aren’t ideal from a return perspective get more attention: a lower lot price in exchange for a meaningful true-up or profit participation, with little to no deposit and very soft takedowns. These structures keep open the possibility of at least recovering capital.

How do you learn all this? Ask. Some won’t tell you, but more will than you’d expect. Your counterpart has their own pressures and concerns, and a gentle question can yield a lot of information. Ask before you’re in a workout. If you’re buying, ask what their key motivations are and listen carefully to their answers. In effect, you’re trying to determine whether you’re dealing with a Wells Fargo or a Bank of America.

So, what’s the point of these speculations? Just a reminder that we stand a decent chance of 2027 being the year of negotiations. Understanding the incentive structures of those on the other side of the table may be your most important piece of market intelligence.

#5395. Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Update, Tuesday Nov. 17: ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests Vulcan’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff. Read our follow-up story for details. This story has been updated with ULA’s preliminary findings.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit Sunday, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased.

ULA said Sunday that it didn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it would work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as quickly as possible.

Amazon Leo said in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to reach orbit. The Centaur, powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris, appears to have started normally and couldn’t make up for the shortfall. ULA appears to have lost telemetry and the mission about 10 minutes into the flight.

Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t said what caused the shortfall.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

In June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security launches after February.

ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the New Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight, CBS News reported.

ULA is also under new leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

#5394. Bitcoin Price Holds $64K Ahead of Nvidia Earnings: AI Bubble Finally Pops?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price is struggling to find direction just below $65,000 as we brace for Nvidia earnings report. BTC USD has recovered from its weekend low near $62,000, but remains down 13% over seven days. Its modest rebound comes as technology stocks face yet another selling pressure.

This timing puts the Bitcoin price in an uncomfortable position. Nvidia’s results could determine if investors return to risk assets or abandon another crowded trade. With market sentiment still deep in extreme fear, we still have little conviction that the worst is over.

Meanwhile, Michael Burry is increasing his bearish bets against technology stocks. The investor made famous by The Big Short is targeting the Nasdaq-100 and semiconductor sector. His positioning raises an ugly question: Is the AI boom approaching its own dot-com moment?

Burry doubled his Nasdaq-100 put position on November 12, targeting early 2027 options 20% below the index’s market level. He also bought back part of his previously reduced bearish position in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF.

His argument goes beyond stretched stock valuations. Burry believes conventional accounting earnings can exaggerate technology companies’ underlying profitability. Depreciation schedules, particularly across expensive data-center infrastructure, sit at the center of his concerns.

Consider a hyperscaler investing billions in GPUs and AI infrastructure. Those purchases become capital assets rather than immediate operating expenses. Companies subsequently recognize depreciation across their estimated useful lives.

This accounting treatment can make current earnings look stronger than the underlying cash economics. If hardware becomes obsolete faster than expected, reported profitability could overstate actual investment returns.

The concern becomes significant when companies must continuously replace expensive accelerators. Their infrastructure spending needs to generate sufficient revenue before the equipment loses economic value.

Burry isn’t alone in questioning the investment cycle. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman previously acknowledged excessive enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence.

“Are we in a phase where investors as a whole are overexcited about AI? My opinion is yes,” Altman said.

Jeff Bezos offered another interpretation, describing the spending cycle as an “industrial bubble.” He argued that excessive investment could still produce valuable infrastructure, even when individual investors lose money.

Nvidia’s own Jensen Huang previously defended the industry’s economics. According to him, the AI infrastructure was already generating productive revenue, rather than merely attracting speculative capital.

The disagreement exposes the central tension surrounding the AI bubble. Demand can be genuine while valuations and infrastructure commitments become unsustainable.

The dot-com crash offers an important historical comparison. The Nasdaq Composite lost 78% between March 2000 and October 2002. Internet technology survived, but countless businesses and investors did not.

Today’s AI infrastructure market has similarities, particularly aggressive capital expenditure and expectations of exponential demand. However, established hyperscalers now finance much of the expansion through enormous operating businesses.

Now, can future AI revenue justify today’s investment?

Bitcoin once traded with relatively little correlation to traditional equities. That relationship changed dramatically as institutional participation expanded.

CME Group’s historical correlation research illustrates the shift. Between 2014 and 2016, Bitcoin’s correlation with the S&P 500 stood near -0.01. Its correlation with the Nasdaq-100 was effectively zero. Between 2020 and 2022, those correlations climbed to 0.40 and 0.42, respectively. They remained positive through April 2025, reaching 0.30 against both indices.

The shift matters because institutional investors increasingly treat Bitcoin as another liquid risk asset. Portfolio rebalancing, leveraged positions, and macroeconomic conditions can influence its price alongside technology stocks.

An AI sell-off could create another liquidity shock across crypto. Investors facing losses elsewhere might sell Bitcoin to raise cash or reduce overall exposure. But an AI correction doesn’t automatically invalidate Bitcoin’s monetary thesis. A technology valuation reset could eventually redirect capital toward alternative assets.

The gap lies between an isolated technology correction and a financial liquidity crisis. Bitcoin could eventually decouple from semiconductor stocks under the first scenario. The second could pressure both markets simultaneously. For now, Bitcoin price remains exposed to the same risk appetite driving technology shares.

Nvidia’s third-quarter fiscal 2027 results arrive at a particularly sensitive moment. Wall Street expects $109 billion in revenue and $2.47 in adjusted earnings per share.

Investors will focus heavily on Data Center revenue, gross margins, and forward guidance. The company’s Vera Rubin platform also faces scrutiny as customers expand their AI infrastructure commitments.

A headline earnings beat might not satisfy investors demanding another acceleration in growth. Strong revenue accompanied by cautious guidance could trigger another sell-the-news reaction.

The opposite scenario could restore confidence across technology stocks. Strong guidance would reinforce expectations that hyperscaler spending remains sustainable. Bitcoin could benefit if investors regain their appetite for speculative assets.

Technically, Bitcoin needs to stabilize above its recent $62,000 weekend low. A break below that level would expose the psychologically important $60,000 threshold.

A stronger recovery would put $68,000 back into view as an important technical resistance area. Reclaiming that level could help establish if buyers are returning.

Bitcoin price now faces a test extending beyond crypto markets. Nvidia must demonstrate that AI infrastructure spending can translate into durable earnings growth.

Burry is betting that expectations have run too far ahead. Huang’s former company built the infrastructure powering the AI revolution, but investors now need proof of its economic returns.

If the AI bubble starts deflating, Bitcoin must answer another question: Can it survive without Wall Street’s appetite for technology risk?

#5392. Newrez settles Washington state servicing case with $3 million payout

Newrez reached a consent order with the Washington Department of Financial Institutions resolving allegations of unfair or deceptive mortgage servicing practices from 2021 to 2026. The company will pay just over $3 million, including a $2.5 million payment to DFI, at least $500,000 for consumer remediation and technology upgrades, and an investigation fee.   AI Summary

Newrez agreed to pay roughly $3 million and implement broad mortgage servicing changes to resolve allegations by the Washington Department of Financial Institutions (DFI) that the company engaged in unfair or deceptive acts or practices.

The consent order, which stems from a multiyear servicing investigation, lands below the $4.175 million civil penalty sought earlier this year by DFI in a statement of charges, but it still represents a significant financial and operational hit for the nonbank servicer.

Newrez does not admit or deny any wrongdoing under the agreement. A company spokesperson told HousingWire the company is “pleased to have resolved this matter.”

“The underlying examination resulted in limited findings, most of which had already been addressed by Newrez. The agreement, which includes no admission of wrongdoing, credits Newrez for several investments made to enhance its operations. We remain committed to supporting homeowners and meeting the high standards they expect,” the spokesperson said.

Under the order, Newrez must pay $2.5 million to DFI, plus at least $500,000 earmarked for consumer remediation and technology and system upgrades. The company also owes an investigation fee of $14,888.90 to cover the agency’s staff time.

The case grew out of more than 125 consumer complaints to DFI, including allegations of unfair or deceptive acts or practices affecting at least 29 borrowers. Regulators also cited failures to maintain and service escrow accounts for at least 71 loans to Washington residents.

Earlier charges alleged servicing breakdowns in Washington from 2021 to 2026. These included loan boarding errors that caused private mortgage insurance and escrow problems, misapplied payments, issues with escrow and force‑placed insurance, inaccurate information during foreclosure mediation, faulty statements, and overdue responses to both borrowers and the regulator.

In addition to the monetary obligations, the consent order requires Newrez to undertake affirmative actions across its servicing platform. The company must tighten loan onboarding processes, overhaul core servicing functions, and improve controls over escrow and insurance handling, among other changes. Newrez has to demonstrate to DFI that these corrective actions are complete within 30 days of the order’s effective date.

“Washington state mortgage servicing laws exist to ensure homeowners are treated fairly and that their loans are serviced properly,” DFI Director Charlie Clark said in a statement. “DFI will take action to hold mortgage servicers accountable and will order affirmative action needed to protect Washington homeowners.”

#5391. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of monday.com’s Elevate event

AI workflow automation is changing how businesses build applications and manage everyday work, raising questions about the role of established software platforms. As organizations experiment with AI-generated applications and autonomous agents, they must also determine how to maintain access controls, integrate existing systems and manage increasingly complex workflows.

The growing accessibility of AI development tools has prompted speculation that businesses could replace traditional software-as-a-service platforms with applications built for specific needs. But building an application and operating it securely across an enterprise present different challenges, according to Casey George, chief revenue officer of monday.com Ltd.

“We are seeing customers come back to a platform that’s integrated — that’s governed, that’s permissioned with their infrastructure, that is secure — like monday.com,” he told theCUBE. “I joke and say it was an expensive funeral, but we learned a lot. Customers learned a lot.”

George, along with executives and practitioners, spoke with host Rebecca Knight at monday.com’s Elevate event during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The discussions examined enterprise AI deployment, governance requirements and the challenges of scaling AI workflow automation across organizations. (* Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Casey George:

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of monday.com’s Elevate event:

Making autonomous agents available to employees does not guarantee business returns. After an internal initiative produced more than 3,600 agents, monday.com established monday Frontier, an organization combining managed services and deployment engineers to help customers identify workflow bottlenecks and implement AI projects. The initiative addresses the implementation challenges involved in moving agents into productive use, according to Eran Zinman (pictured), co-founder and co-chief executive officer of monday.com.

“Adopting AI really requires expertise. I know how hard it is because we experienced ourselves that you have this amazing technology, but how do you actually use it?” he said during the event.

As organizations deploy AI agents, security teams must account for how access rights change across users, applications and environments. Incremental rollouts offer a way to test capabilities before expanding their reach, while permission management remains an ongoing responsibility, according to Ryan Nigro, security trust and enablement team lead at monday.com.

“It just comes to making sure that your users are properly being given just enough to do their roles but not too much to cause harm,” Nigro told theCUBE. “There’s no reason why a sales rep should have the ability to change your production environment.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Ryan Nigro:

At Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., employees are using monday vibe, monday.com’s no-code application builder, to create custom tools. One executive dashboard replaces the manual process of copying charts into presentation slides while retaining the ability to export to PowerPoint, according to Kate Kenner, capability and community lead for strategic sourcing and planning at HPE.

“[Executives] knocked a whole bunch of the meetings off the calendar,” she told theCUBE. “Instead of weekly, now they’re monthly.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Kate Kenner:

At Lowe’s Cos. Inc., coordinating store setups and remodels once required tracking information across Microsoft Excel, emails and other communications. The retailer now uses monday.com to monitor individual store bays and dozens of simultaneous projects, according to Lanny Finley, director of remerch and new stores at Lowe’s.

“I can take the dashboard and see which projects are on track, which ones are at risk, and then make the appropriate actions and get the right partners in place to make the corrections to get everything back on track and completed,” he said during the event.

Lowe’s also developed an internal Green Dot Board to track issues such as missing components during store projects. The company is exploring additional automation that could initiate vendor orders when components are needed and close issues once replacements are installed, according to Brian Olms, senior business partner manager at Lowe’s, who joined Finley during the discussion.

“We needed a way to automate the process, make it more user-friendly [and] make it simpler. That’s what we started the Green Dot Board for,” he told theCUBE. “Here at Elevate, we’re seeing ways that we could even take it a step further and start to use agents and more automation and [the] vibe app.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Lanny Finley and Brian Olms:

For nonprofits facing growing demand, AI workflow automation offers a way to expand organizational capacity without placing additional administrative burdens on employees. At Feed the Children Inc., a two-person team oversees relationships with more than 500 community partners, according to Colleen Finn Ridenhour, chief growth and strategy officer at Feed the Children.

“Things from [memorandums of understanding] and legal contracts, annual renewals and compliance and reporting — it’s quite a lot. It’s been a very manual process, historically, for them to keep track of that all the time. We really want them focused on the human element of that job, which is bringing in new partners to help us scale our impact,” she told theCUBE.

The nonprofit uses monday.com’s forms, boards, automations and agents to coordinate partner activities and manage information. Employees can also build dashboards for specific needs, including budget tracking, while retaining human oversight of compliance-related work, according to Ridenhour.

“We’re not going to be able to scale our impact by just always asking people to work harder. [We need to find] ways to repeat a lot of these repetitive actions in a much easier way and [share] information so [that] people’s jobs get easier and it frees up their time to do the things that only they can do,” she said during the event.

#5390. Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am

It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).

Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows users are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS.”

Instead, the Copilot as “a new OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

Microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

Many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.

The high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

Operating systems like Windows provide users with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the new Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

The New OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

Currently, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the new Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as New OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

If you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business plan and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, users don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

“We increasingly think of all our apps together as a new operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” said Nadella in his letter to shareholders, published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.

The end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella said.

The Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race: In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.

Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.

#5388. Single-family permits telegraph a weakened 2027 building pipeline

U.S. housing starts rose in October, largely from a 23.6% jump in multifamily starts. Single-family permits fell to 772,000, down 12.9% from a year ago, pointing to slower single-family production ahead.  AI Summary

While October saw a blip in housing starts, the latest residential construction data from the U.S. Census Bureau shows a single-family construction market seeking rock bottom, with single-family permits hitting a nearly four-year low.

National housing starts rose to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.309 million in October, up 9.9% from the revised September figure of 1.191 million and 2.8% above the same month last year (1.273 million). Most of that increase came from multifamily, where starts climbed 23.6% from September to an annualized rate of 445,000.

Single-family starts came in at an annual rate of 864,000 in October, up 4.0% from September but down 3.2% from a year earlier, suggesting single-family construction lacks momentum.

“Given monthly volatility, the three-month moving average provides a clearer signal, which fell to 859,000 units,” according to a note by National Association of Home Builders Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington

The future construction pipeline also looks soft. Single-family permits, a forward-looking indicator of where new home construction levels are headed, dropped 8.7% in October to an annual rate of 772,000, down from a revised 846,000 in September and 12.9% lower than a year ago. That marks the lowest level for single-family permits since January 2023.

Total housing permits, including both multifamily and single-family, were 8.7% below the October 2025 rate of 1.418 million.

“Permits point to a slowdown in single-family production ahead,” First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming said in a provided statement. “Since permits lead construction, the decline suggests builders are moving ahead with projects already in the pipeline, while authorizing fewer single-family homes for future construction.”

The new data comes as homebuilder confidence fell to its lowest level in nearly 15 years in November, with affordability constraints and hesitant buyers weighing on the market. That buyer hesitancy is reflected in the latest new home sales figures, which show sales down 5.3% year over year in September and sales prices down roughly 4.0% to $400,400.

Fleming pointed to weakening demand, higher costs and elevated mortgage rates as catalysts for a softening residential construction pipeline.

“Prospective buyer traffic fell to its weakest level in 15 years, outside the start of the pandemic. Builders are using price cuts and incentives to reach buyers, while labor shortages and higher fuel costs are adding to the cost of building. That combination leaves builders cautious about adding production when affordability is already keeping many buyers on the sidelines,” he said.

The stock of homes under construction continues to move down from recent highs. Housing units under construction totaled 1.27 million in October, 3.0% below a year earlier. Single-family units under construction came to 581,000, down 2.5% year over year, while multifamily units in progress fell to 691,000, 3.5% lower than a year ago and well off the peak of more than 1 million reached in December 2023.

Meanwhile, housing completions improved from September but remained negative year on year. Total completions reached an annual rate of 1.272 million in October, up 6.5% from September’s revised 1.194 million but 10.4% below the 1.419 million recorded in October 2025.

Single-family completions came in at 900,000, down 10.7% compared to a year earlier, while multifamily completions in buildings with five or more units ran at 362,000, down 9.0% on the year.

Year to date, combined single-family and multifamily starts rose 3.8% in the Northeast and 0.2% in the South, while falling 0.7% in the Midwest and 6.7% in the West. Single-family construction declined across all four regions, signaling the strain high construction costs and affordability constraints are putting on homebuilders and prospective buyers.

The permit data points in the same direction. Total permits are up 8.7% in the Northeast and 2.0% in the Midwest this year, but down 4.4% in the South and 2.5% in the West. With single-family permits lower in all four regions, the outlook for a slowing national construction pipeline looks even more likely.

Zillow Senior Economist Kenny Lee noted that the slowdown in single-family starts and permits indicates that homebuilders may be preparing for a relatively weak spring selling season.

“While homebuilders have been adapting to the softer market by offering concessions and building smaller homes, the 2027 spring home-shopping season could see a slow start as buyer demand continues to wane,” Lee explained.

#5387. What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am

Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.

That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.

According to the report, the attempts to recover were further complicated by a second problem: servers that engineers restarted were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again, a phenomenon known as a “thundering herd.”

Microsoft says active service disruptions lasted nearly 24 hours. Delayed email continued to be delivered after service returned Friday morning, and the company posted its public all-clear on X late Friday night, nearly 38 hours after the outage began.

The underlying flaw dates to July, when Microsoft began rolling out a fix to the software that handles incoming connections on its networking gateway, the servers that sit in front of Outlook and many other Microsoft 365 services.

Microsoft hasn’t said what the fix was meant to address. It ran worldwide for more than three months without problems, according to the report.

Under heavy load, however, parts of that software could get stuck waiting on one another, using up the servers’ processing power and memory until they froze.

That’s what happened last week. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved Teams traffic onto the same servers that handle Outlook email, adding to their load, according to the report. Microsoft called the switch part of normal operations but didn’t say what prompted it.

Complicating matters, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already out of service because of an unrelated problem, which also isn’t detailed in the report.

When traffic peaked during the U.S. workday, that was enough to trigger the outage.

Two things stand out as likely areas of scrutiny:

Microsoft’s testing didn’t catch the bug. Its labs mostly used less powerful machines with fewer processing cores, running a different mix of traffic, while the problem was worst on the newer servers handling real customer load.

The fix also passed through Microsoft’s standard staged rollout, spreading worldwide over several weeks without any sign of trouble, according to the report.

The company certainly has the means to test on the hardware it actually runs. It spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its most recent quarter, much of it on AI infrastructure.

The safeguards meant to contain the damage didn’t hold. Walls between regions failed because of what the report calls “a separate issue,” which it doesn’t explain, so the outage went global.

The gateway is made up of thousands of “capacity units” grouped into regions, with walls between them meant to keep a failure in one place. Microsoft also runs a second, independent gateway so services can switch over during a disruption.

Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps made that switch, which is why Teams chats and meetings mostly kept working. Exchange couldn’t, “for scale reasons,” as the company put it, so email stayed down.

Microsoft’s own tools added to the problem. Its automated recovery “was not designed” for a fleet that was almost entirely unresponsive, according to the report, and its usual ways of rolling back a bad change couldn’t quickly undo one that was months old.

The company’s systems automatically shifted traffic from unresponsive servers to healthy ones, and the extra load triggered the same bug on those servers, too. About 10 hours in, engineers turned off some of that automatic rerouting.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, posted an abridged version of the report on X late Sunday. “We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” he wrote.

Lamanna had previewed the findings Friday afternoon, blaming “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” for the slow recovery, as GeekWire reported when Microsoft declared the outage over.

Microsoft says it has rolled back the defective code, added server capacity and monitoring, and put new limits on how traffic is redistributed to avoid another cascade. A final report with a full list of repairs is due Nov. 20.

It may also answer the biggest question the preliminary report leaves open: why the walls between regions didn’t stop the outage from spreading worldwide. Microsoft blames that on “a separate issue,” apart from the July bug, but hasn’t said what it was.

#5386. Global Times: From blueprints to the Asia-Pacific stage: How Shenzhen's innovators turn ideas into reality

BEIJING, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- In the high-tech industrial parks of Nanshan District and the bustling aisles of the Huaqiangbei electronics market in Futian District, tech veteran Xie Tiandi and young entrepreneur Chen Haotian have both witnessed and participated in the city's leap from traditional contract manufacturing to the frontiers of drones, LiDAR, and robotics. Through their firsthand accounts, we gain a close-up view of Shenzhen's dynamic innovation pulse - and see how China's complete industrial supply chains are deeply intertwined with the everyday needs of partners across the Asia-Pacific.

A 'pole vault' for Shenzhen's high-tech industries

Step into a cafÃ© in Yuehai Subdistrictin Shenzhen's Nanshan District, and the city's innovation pulse is immediately palpable: rather than exchanging everyday small talk, young professionals at neighboring tables are far more likely to be heard debating "multimodal large models," "LiDAR point-cloud algorithms," and "degrees of flexibility in robotic hands."

Covering roughly 20 square kilometers, Yuehai Subdistrict holds unique weight in the Chinese tech community. Having nurtured a roster of globally influential Chinese tech giants - including Tencent, DJI, ZTE, and Huawei - and home to more than 100 listed companies, the neighborhood has been dubbed "China's most powerful street" and serves as a bellwether for Shenzhen's transition from traditional processing and manufacturing to original, ground-up innovation.

"When I first arrived in Yuehai in 2012, there were hardly any cafÃ©s around. The roads were built to factory-zone standards to accommodate heavy freight trucks, and it wasn't even easy to grab lunch near the office buildings," Xie Tiandi, former public relations director at drone maker DJI who now works in the LiDAR and robotics sector, told the Global Times at the cafÃ©.

Back then, Shenzhen stood at a crossroads between original equipment manufacturing (OEM) and independent innovation. "More than a decade ago, foreign buyers came to Shenzhen looking for 'cheaper alternatives.' And then, by around 2015, as the commercial network and industrial ecosystem matured, the wind shifted completely - global buyers began eagerly asking, 'What original new products has Shenzhen come up with this time?'" Xie recalled.

Xie has lived through three remarkable "pole vaults" in Shenzhen's tech sector.

First, young talent from across the country flocked to the city, and connected smartphones, wristbands, and novel hardware to the internet. DJI's consumer drones - initially dismissed by outsiders as "flying smart gadgets" - soon defined global industry standards through breakthroughs in flight control and gimbal stabilization. Next came the explosion of autonomous driving and new-energy vehicles (NEVs), which put robotic perception and control technologies on wheels. Today, more than a decade of accumulated momentum in mechatronics, algorithms, and sensors is spilling over into embodied AI and robotics.

"Shenzhen's industrial leaps have always been anchored in its deep hardware foundation," Xie said. "Developing AI here has never been just about writing code online or floating concepts in the cloud; it naturally gravitates toward hardware integration - making machines actually move and get real work done in the physical world. That runs in the same vein as the manufacturing DNA Shenzhen has built up over decades."

With the APEC meeting underway, the Honghualing industrial park in Nanshan District, where Xie works, has become a hot spot for international visitors exploring Shenzhen's smart manufacturing, packing his schedule to capacity. Park administrators and resident companies have been busy hosting government delegations, business groups, and foreign media outlets from around the world - all eager to see firsthand how Shenzhen's automated production lines and robotics supply chains operate.

Staging the 2026 APEC gathering in Shenzhen, with its focus on the three priorities of "openness, innovation, and cooperation," offers the world a prime window to examine the city's innovation DNA up close.

"We should forge science, technology and innovation partnerships, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and AI, and promote green and low-carbon transition. By doing so, we can turn strengths in innovation into drivers of growth, and provide strong impetus for economic growth in the Asia-Pacific," Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Wednesday when delivering a keynote speech at the APEC CEO Summit 2026 in Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province.

Shenzhen's transformation from a contract-manufacturing workshop into a bustling global tech hub attracting a steady stream of international buyers is a vivid illustration of how human talent, technological foundations, and market scale can be forged into an engine of innovation.

Heavy trucks driving up to the ninth floor

The Honghualing base in Nanshan, where Xie is currently based, is China's first demonstration project for "vertical manufacturing" -or "factories in the sky."

Stepping into the complex, visitors are greeted by a striking architectural sight: in land-scarce Nanshan District, where listed firms are densely clustered, modern factories have been stacked vertically into high-rises to keep high-end production lines right next to R&D engineers. Up close, fully loaded heavy-duty trucks can be seen rumbling up a spiral ramp wrapped around the exterior of the ultra-high-load-bearing building, climbing 60 meters above the ground to the ninth-floor platform to unload batches of LiDAR components directly into sky-high workshops.

Following the opening of its first phase this year, the Honghualing base has already brought in 14 supply-chain anchor firms - including RoboSense, Dobot, and EngineAI - and "little giant" enterprises, seamlessly integrating the R&D and manufacturing of core perception components and complete robots within a single compound.

Xie's company has set up a fully automated production line here: algorithms are developed upstairs while LiDAR units and robotic sensors are mass-produced downstairs. Meanwhile, downstream robotics clients conduct tests in the adjacent building, allowing engineers to simply walk downstairs for on-the-spot debugging alongside the assembly line whenever an issue arises.

This vertical "spatial folding" packs upstream and downstream players tightly together, pushing collaborative R&D and manufacturing efficiency to the extreme. And in Shenzhen, efficiency is the very lifeline of tech enterprises.

"On average, we roll out a new robotic arm roughly every three months. From finalizing a product concept to molding and completing the first delivery, the entire cycle takes just six to nine months - we are iterating complex robotic hardware at nearly the speed of smartphones," Chen Haotian, chief marketing officer of Elephant Robotics, a firm rooted in Huaqiangbei, dubbed "China's No. 1 Electronics Street," told the Global Times.

Founded in 2016, the company has been anchored in Huaqiangbei from day one. Looking out the window of its fourth-floor office, the 1.45-square-kilometer neighborhood below is densely packed with over 1 million types of electronic components and more than 115,000 business entities.

In many overseas cities, developing hardware and validating a new idea often entails weeks of waiting for cross-border parcels. In Huaqiangbei, however, trial-and-error and prototyping are measured in hours.

Around 2020, the Elephant Robotics team decided to develop a lightweight desktop six-axis robotic arm tailored for education, research, and the global maker community. As soon as an engineer came up with a new design concept, Chen recalled, there was no need to order parts online and wait for days. Instead, they could simply take the elevator downstairs, stroll through the stalls of the electronics market to see which development boards were trending among global makers, buy all the necessary chips, servo motors, and sensors on the spot, and assemble a working demo upstairs that very day. If testing revealed flaws in the design, they could head back downstairs for replacement parts and start over the next morning.

Once a prototype passes validation, supporting manufacturers in Shenzhen's Bao'an and Longhua districts, as well as neighboring Dongguan, quickly take over mass production. The assembled units are then trucked back to the fourth floor of the Zhifangzhou Building in Huaqiangbei for firmware flashing and quality inspection, while packaging suppliers downstairs promptly deliver custom shockproof inserts. Every week, boxed robotic arms and bionic robotic pets are shipped by air and sea to more than 70 countries and regions across North America, Europe, Japan, South Korea, and Southeast Asia.

Sharing an open innovation foundation with the Asia-Pacific

In the eyes of local tech practitioners, Shenzhen's strength lies in a distinctive system and ecosystem of innovation.

"In Shenzhen, no single link can be singled out to take all the credit - if you look at any one element in isolation, it may not necessarily outshine other global industrial hubs. The real secret is the chemical reaction generated when every link meshes tightly together," Xie said.

This interlocking "systemic innovation," he noted, combines pragmatic goals geared toward mass production, a vast pool of multidisciplinary engineering talent, a hyper-responsive supply chain within a one-hour drive, fierce competition driving extreme performance at lower costs, and -crucially -a safety net at the bottom that tolerates failure.

In a late night in 2013, walking along an empty street after working overtime, Xie spotted an illuminated lightbox poster at a bus stop bearing an encouraging message for entrepreneurs: "In Shenzhen, there is no shame in failure." More than a decade later, having witnessed several waves of industrial rise and fall, those words resonate with him more deeply than ever.

"The cost of trial and error is relatively low in Shenzhen. Here, a startup or a product may fail, but the technical talent it brought together, the manufacturing processes it honed, and the production capacity it built do not vanish. They are quickly absorbed, reintegrated, and reused by the next, stronger enterprise. This self-regenerating systemic capacity is what allowed us to move from 'manufacturing according to others' blueprints' to 'drawing the blueprints ourselves,'" he explained.

And once a city acquires the original capability to "draw its own blueprints," the fruits of its innovation are no longer confined within its borders, but flow across the Asia-Pacific through networks of open cooperation. From product trade to joint technological R&D, pragmatic financial cooperation, and green development, Shenzhen continues to share its innovation dividends with regional partners.

Chen told the Global Times that APEC member economies currently account for over 60 percent of Elephant Robotics' overseas business, maintaining rapid annual growth of more than 25 percent in recent years, with close partners spanning the US, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand, and ASEAN nations.

China's development has benefited from an open and interconnected Asia-Pacific, and is deeply rooted in innovative ecosystems like Shenzhen's. Championing universally beneficial and inclusive globalization, China consistently creates new opportunities for the world through its own continuous development.

In Volume V of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China, President Xi pointed out that "innovation is the source of productivity. We should make full use of artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies to boost the world economy and stimulate growth through the current scientific and technological revolution." "Advances in science and technology should benefit all of humanity. We should help developing countries with their capacity building in science and technology and promote global flows of knowledge and technology," Xi noted.

To address the shared challenge of population aging across APEC economies, Chen's team has established a dedicated working group to advance eldercare-tech exchanges with regional partners, accelerating the deployment of companion robotic pets across member economies and exploring how AI can support the mental health and special needs of seniors with cognitive impairments.

Meanwhile, in developing APEC economies undergoing critical manufacturing upgrades and digital transformation - such as Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand - lightweight, user-friendly collaborative robotic arms and maker kits developed by Chinese firms are entering university classrooms, research labs, and small workshops, helping local young engineers and SMEs master automation and programming at a fraction of the traditional cost.

In Xie's view, the greatest takeaway Shenzhen's experience offers to Asia-Pacific partners lies in how to cultivate genuine, self-sustaining industrial capacity on their own soil by supplementing and strengthening supply chains.

"Today, every country aspires to build its own original brands. And the innovation and supply-chain capabilities accumulated in Shenzhen are not meant solely for exporting Chinese goods; more importantly, they can serve as an open foundation that empowers partners across the Asia-Pacific to grow their own domestic industries - making local markets more prosperous and regional economies more vibrant," Xie said.

#5385. Why housing construction is sliding back toward COVID-era lows

U.S. building permits fell to a 1,295,000 annual rate in October, with single-family permits at 772,000. With mortgage rates above 7% and builder margins pressured, construction momentum is tracking back toward COVID-era levels.  AI Summary

The great housing construction boom that people have been cheering about for four years now looks to be on the cusp of falling to COVID-era lows. How is this possible when people have been saying for the past five years that we need to build more homes and Congress just passed the giant ROAD to Housing Act this summer — which was designed to help spur more construction.

The old laws of economics still play out here; there simply isn’t enough housing demand to build more homes. This is something I wrote about back in June 2021: when mortgage rates eventually rise this whole thing will reverse. Now, in November 2026, we are not that far away from the COVID-19 recession lows, as housing permits are already at COVID-19 recession levels and mortgage rates are above 7%.

From Census: Building Permits: Privately-owned housing units authorized by building permits in October were at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1,295,000. This is 7.4 percent below the revised September rate of 1,398,000 and is 8.7 percent below the October 2025 rate of 1,418,000. Single-family authorizations in October were at a rate of 772,000; this is 8.7 percent below the revised September figure of 846,000. Authorizations of units in buildings with five units or more were at a rate of 475,000 in October.As we can see in the chart below, housing permits have been slowly falling for years and we are not only at levels last seen during the COVID-19 recession, but we’re on pace to hit the lows of that time period if this trend continues. And all this is happening when mortgage rates are close to 7.5% and the Fed is starting a new rate hike cycle.

Single-family permits are not only close to the lows of 2022, but not that far from the COVID-19 recession lows either. Builders have done an admirable job keeping new home sales elevated enough to keep housing starts from falling further, but that has limits as profit margins fall. As you can see here, the single-family permits have taken a noticeable dive.

One question I got recently, which has merit: Why is builder confidence at multiyear lows, but new home sales have grown over the last few months? Just remember that the builder confidence index is tilted toward smaller homebuilders, not the big publicly traded homebuilders that are still buying down rates to move product.

New home sales are still at 2019 levels, and so are housing starts and permits. If the big builders lose their ability to buy down rates, this sales data should eventually break below 2019 levels, but for now sales have operated within a small range for the past 10 years.

Since mortgage rates shot toward 7.60%, we have seen housing data turn very negative. Compare that to last year at this time, when mortgage rates were heading toward 6% and existing home sales hit a nine-month high. The big builders can only do so much to keep starts from falling more. For now, it doesn’t look good for housing construction in 2027, given where mortgage rates are at and the builders profit margins falling more and more.

#5384. Recent spate of outages attributed to technical issues amid accelerated AI bug discovery

U.S. authorities don’t believe that the recent outages at federal agencies and top tech firms were caused by cyberattacks.

The Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines, Apple Inc. and Microsoft Corp. were among the affected organizations. All four said that their systems were disrupted by technical issues rather than hackers. Experts noted that artificial intelligence models’ ability to find software bugs has made patching more complicated, which may increase the risk of outages.

The first major service disruption hit Exchange Online on Thursday. The Microsoft-operated email service went offline for nearly a day, which left 450 million users without access to their inboxes. The company attributed the downtime to two separate bugs in the software that powers its network. The first one went undetected for three months, while the other cropped up a day before the outage.

The FAA experienced a network disruption of its own on Friday. An issue with a router at the agency’s El Dorado, Arkansas campus disrupted aircraft communications and radar data feeds. The outage led to more than 12,000 flight cancellations.

United Airlines reported a fairly extensive, but brief infrastructure disruption a few days later. The issue took several of the carrier’s pilot-facing applications offline for 30 minutes. Fewer than 150 flights were affected.

Yet another high-profile network outage occurred on Tuesday, this time at the U.S. National Security Agency. A technical problem cropped up in NSANet, an internal network that agency staff use to exchange classified information. The cause of the outage and its duration were not specified. However, officials did tell NBC the disruption wasn’t caused by a cyberattack.

U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton reiterated that point in a Tuesday interview. He added that officials have “looked very closely” into the other outages that occurred over the past week and ruled out cyberattacks as the cause. According to Clayton, authorities believe that the disruptions occurred because companies are patching vulnerabilities “on much larger scale” than before.

Frontier AI models have found thousands of software vulnerabilities over the past few months. That accelerated pace of discovery is creating more work for administrators, who have to roll out patches more frequently than before. The less time there is to prepare a patch, the greater the risk of human error.

“As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and development cycles, pressure is mounting on companies to deploy fixes quickly, often without fully understanding how those changes will affect interconnected systems, “ said Prince Kohli, the chief executive officer of software testing provider Sauce Labs Inc. “The only way to prevent these issues is continuous testing and release validation in their development processes, even more so for critical software updates.”

Apple and Workday Inc. are also among the companies that have experienced outages in recent days. Separately, several financial services temporarily became unavailable because of an issue with one of JPMorgan Chase’s on-premises systems. All the incidents have been resolved.

#5383. Amazon picks its Bond: Robert Pattinson to play 007, ending years of speculation over coveted role

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 16, 2026 at 8:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 8:32 am

Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media, “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson.

The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series. He takes over from Daniel Craig, whose fifth and last Bond film, “No Time to Die,” came out in 2021.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond films when it bought MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, and it took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Fans and bookmakers had been guessing about Craig’s successor since he said in 2019 he was leaving the role.

Over the years, the rumored contenders included Idris Elba, Tom Hardy, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Holland and Henry Cavill. By the end, there were five finalists. Pattinson beat out Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner after screen tests in London in late October, according to The New York Times. Casting director Nina Gold ran the tests, which covered stunts, dialogue and camera presence.

Bond is one of the most valuable properties Amazon got in the MGM deal, its second-largest acquisition ever behind Whole Foods. The franchise has earned nearly $7 billion at the domestic box office, adjusted for inflation, since “Dr. No” in 1962. Now Amazon is running it without the Broccoli family, whose stewardship over six decades built it into one of Hollywood’s biggest moneymakers.

Pattinson’s casting is the most visible move yet in Amazon’s plans for Bond. As the Times noted, the 2025 deal followed years of behind-the-scenes friction over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe beyond the films. The Times also pointed out that Amazon has to win over a generation of moviegoers who grew up during the franchise’s long hiatus and gravitated toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Amazon is already putting the back catalog to work. Alongside Monday’s announcement, it published a guide to streaming the 007 films on Prime Video.

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk

To lead the next film, Amazon brought in producers Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman, and David Heyman, who produced all eight “Harry Potter” movies. Denis Villeneuve (“Dune”) is directing from an original screenplay by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight. No release date has been set, and the Times reports that a theatrical release before 2028 is unlikely.

“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond,” Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said in a statement. Hopkins said Pattinson’s “remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice” to carry on the 007 legacy.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

Some longtime fans have worried that under Amazon, Bond will lose his distinctly British character and become more corporate and American, the Times reported. Pascal and Heyman, in a joint statement, called the English actor “the perfect Bond for our times.”

Bezos had yet to weigh back in on social media about Amazon’s pick, but Amazon CEO Andy Jassy did in a LinkedIn post, writing that he was “excited” to have Pattinson in the role, calling him “one of the most versatile actors of his generation, who consistently makes fearless choices, and keeps surprising people with his performances.”

Fans online were split. Some posted images of Elba or Cavill, calling Pattinson as 007 a “huge miss.” Others said the actor was on a “generational run” right now with the roles he’s landing. Others shared GIFs of Sean Connery, saying there will only ever be one Bond.

I checked in with my mom, a longtime Bond lover and the biggest movie fan I know. She quickly responded via text.

“No way … not sexy enough for me,” she wrote of Pattinson. “I really liked Daniel Craig, but Sean Connery has always been a favorite.”

#5382. Star Catcher Partners With Common Space To Power Humanitarian Satellite Constellation

The first power grid in space will contribute in-kind on-orbit power so that energy is never the limiting factor for Earth observation

ST. LOUIS, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Common Space, the nonprofit building the world's first independent, community-governed high-resolution satellite constellation for the public good, today announced Star Catcher Industries, Inc. ("Star Catcher") as its first technology partner. Star Catcher, which is building the first power grid in space, will contribute in-kind on-demand orbital power to Common Space's humanitarian missions. The partnership gives the Common Space constellation flexibility to respond to the impacts of climate and conflict, and to benefit local communities when they need it.

The world does not lack satellite imagery. More than 1,000 Earth observation satellites image the planet every day. Yet, the people who respond to disasters, document human rights abuses, and protect ecosystems still cannot reliably get high-resolution data or task a satellite when and where the need is greatest. This is because commercial satellite companies are optimized for government and commercial customers, which naturally shapes pricing, access models, and tasking priorities.

Common Space aims to establish a new model for Earth observation

Common Space is working to fill this gap. Co-founded by Bill Greer (Esri, Albedo, Maxar) and Rhiannan Price (NASA Lifelines, Maxar), Common Space is moving satellite imagery away from commercial and military incentives to reliable public infrastructure for humanitarians, climate advocates, researchers, journalists and civil society. Common Space's community designed how imagery is tasked, prioritized, shared and protected from misuse through rigorous governance that puts humanitarian needs first

"Earth observation satellites have been used for everything from tracking climate change to disaster preparedness and response, stopping illegal fishing and documenting genocide," says Bill Greer, co-founder of Common Space. "We have proven this technology is super important to protect our planet, but the access has been limited, expensive and restricted by governments. We're building a transparent and independent system to serve the community of people that are trying to make the world better."

Common Space aims to establish a new model for Earth observation in which critical satellite data functions as shared public infrastructure rather than a narrowly controlled source of visual evidence. Star Catcher is building shared infrastructure for powering space: the Star Catcher Network uses optical power beaming to deliver concentrated solar energy to a satellite's existing solar arrays, which can increase available power by up to 10x with no retrofit required.

For humanitarian missions, more available power means more flexibility when something urgent is happening on Earth such as an active war or climate disaster: whether that is imaging, onboard processing, communications or other spacecraft operations. Under this partnership, Star Catcher will:

"I am a firm believer that a company can simultaneously be commercially viable and make the world a better place," says Andrew Rush, co-founder and CEO of Star Catcher. "With Common Space, we have an opportunity to scale our technology with an incredible humanitarian use case built in; we hope other leaders in our industry will choose to do the same."

Common Space launches with broad backing: more than 50 letters of support from academia and from global for-profit and nonprofit impact organizations. Humanitarian groups including MapAction, the Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team and Justice Rapid Response have voiced support for the mission.

The Star Catcher partnership is the first of what Common Space hopes to be a model for others in the space industry. Both organizations are inviting satellite operators and data providers, across SAR, InSAR, EO and other modalities, to join them in showing what's possible when space companies share their services for the public good. "Together, we're showing what's possible when space infrastructure is built for the public good," says Rhiannan Price, co-founder of Common Space. "When space companies share what they've built, everyone working to make the world better gets to see it more clearly."

For more information, visit www.commonspace.world and www.star-catcher.com.

For press inquiries, contact Daniel Sherman: [email protected]

Common Space is a nonprofit building an independent, community-governed humanitarian satellite constellation for open, public-benefit Earth observation. Its high resolution imagery is openly licensed, tasked by humanitarian need, with governance designed by and for the people and organizations it serves. Organizations interested in membership, partnership, or funding can learn more at commonspace.world.

Star Catcher is an energy company building a power grid in space, providing the infrastructure to enable the next generation of spacecraft and advanced missions. Star Catcher removes power as a limiting factor for spacecraft, allowing continuous mission execution, increased operational endurance, and the ability to support higher power payloads without redesigning existing platforms. Founded in 2024 by Andrew Rush and Michael Snyder (Made In Space, Redwire), alongside Bryan Lyandvert (T-Bird Capital, Amazon), the company has raised $88M to date from B Capital, Shield Capital, Cerberus Ventures, Initialized Capital, among others. Based in Jacksonville, FL, the company currently holds the world record for optical power beaming.
