#5381. Study: 403 U.S. data centers rival Denmark’s carbon emissions; Oregon ranked No. 2 in power use

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 17, 2026 at 3:48 pm

A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

The research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, said in a statement.

Guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

The research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability and explored in an associated website, comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions.

In the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.

Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

The researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

Nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

The study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group.

All three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for new clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.

“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July.

Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the company to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

“So that is a real challenge,” Hurst said in September, “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”

At the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. Amazon has agreed to become the anchor tenant of a massive planned data center campus with proposed natural gas and nuclear power generation, according to the Financial Times.

“Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers” published in Nature Sustainability and researchers from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, University of Pisa, IMT School of Advanced Studies, Aurora Energy Research, Environmental Systems Research Institute, Baxtel and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

#5380. Fix-and-flip margins tighten in Q3 as prices dip and costs rise

The Burns + Kiavi Fix and Flip Market Index dropped to 53 in Q3 2026, the lowest reading in nearly 4 years. Investors cited mortgage rates above 7%, softer prices and labor constraints that pressured margins.  AI Summary

The U.S. fix-and-flip market weakened in the third quarter as mortgage rates above 7% slowed buyer demand, while falling home prices and higher labor costs squeezed investors’ margins, according to a survey from Kiavi and John Burns Research and Consulting.

The Burns + Kiavi Fix and Flip Market Index fell to a reading of 53 in the third quarter, down from 59 in the second quarter and 56 a year earlier. The index, which measures market conditions on a scale of 0 to 100, reached its lowest level in nearly four years.

Readings below 50 indicate market contraction, while readings above 50 indicate expansion. The November 2026 report is based on a proprietary quarterly survey of approximately 280 fix-and-flip investors.

Only 23% of flippers expect good sales over the next six months, the lowest share in four years. Meanwhile, 19% anticipate poor sales, the highest share since Q4 2022.

The slowdown is affecting investors of different sizes. Large flippers, defined as those who bought or sold at least eight homes over the previous 18 months, reported worse market conditions than smaller operators for the first time since Q3 2022.

Higher mortgage rates have also reduced pricing power for investors. Forty percent of flippers said home sale prices in their markets were lower than a year earlier, compared with 16% who reported higher prices. Another 36% said prices were largely unchanged.

The Southwest reported the greatest share of flippers experiencing lower prices, at 67%, followed by Southern California at 50%. In Texas and the Southeast, 47% reported lower prices, while 44% of Florida respondents said the same.

About one in five flippers said they were selling homes mostly below their initial after-repair value estimates, approaching the highest level recorded by the survey since 2021.

The survey also found that immigration enforcement is affecting renovation labor availability and costs. Forty-one percent of flippers said increased immigration enforcement had negatively affected their labor force, up from 33% when the question was asked in Q2 2025.

Respondents reported difficulties finding workers, higher labor costs and longer project timelines. The impact was particularly pronounced in Florida and the Southeast, although flippers in other regions also reported challenges.

More available inventory is creating additional acquisition opportunities for investors. Twenty-four percent of flippers said competition for deals was lower than usual, the highest share in the survey’s history.

Despite the increased availability, investors remain cautious about how much they’re willing to pay. The average flipper targeted a maximum purchase price of 67% of a property’s after-repair value, down slightly from the previous quarter.

Renovation costs also varied significantly by region. The national average cost per flipped home was $72,000 in the third quarter, with costs reaching $133,000 in Southern California and $86,000 in the Northeast. Costs were lower in the Southeast and Texas, at $47,000 and $46,000, respectively.

The survey’s findings point to continued pressure on investors as higher financing costs, weaker buyer demand and labor constraints complicate project economics. As a result, John Burns recommended that flippers remain disciplined when acquiring properties and build in sufficient margins to account for potential price declines and higher labor expenses.

The firm also advised lenders to underwrite properties based on expected sale prices at the time of disposition rather than relying solely on recently closed comparable sales, which can lag in a declining market.

#5379. LNG Trading Profits could Turn Negative in Next Supply Glut

SINGAPORE, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Global liquefied natural gas (LNG) trading profits could turn negative during the next supply glut, expected to last from 2030 to 2034, according to new analysis by Bain & Company. This is a sharp reversal from the $20 billion or more in annual gross trading profits earned during recent supply disruptions, as a growing number of LNG buyers become traders themselves and compete for a shrinking pool of margins.

Bain forecasts that annual gross LNG trading profits could fall to approximately $5.5 billion during the next glut, compared with an estimated $20 billion in 2026. However, holders of Henry Hub-linked free-on-board (FOB) volumes must still pay liquefaction fees on cargoes they cannot place. If sanctioned production capacity arrives on time, approximately one in six US cargoes could go unlifted, resulting in around $5.8 billion in annual cancellation fees. These losses could push the aggregate trading profit pool below breakeven, even before accounting for additional losses on cargoes lifted and sold below cost.

"The LNG market is getting crowded in the middle. After every shock, buyers did the sensible thing and locked in flexibility. Many became traders without meaning to, and this set up the next glut. Japanese companies now resell about 40% of the LNG they handle; importers in China, India and Turkey are following, and midsize European utilities are building portfolios of their own. Today's LNG crunch may be traders' last windfall before the glut," said Chung Yen Wong, partner in Bain & Company's Energy & Natural Resources practice.

The shift follows successive supply shocks that prompted LNG buyers to secure more flexible supply. Between 2022 and 2025, buyers signed long-term contracts of 15 years or more worth a combined 211 million tonnes per year of LNG, more than half from US projects and many on FOB terms. Meanwhile, spot and short-term deals rose from 34% of global LNG trade in 2019 to 43% in 2025, according to GIIGNL data. In addition, Bain's Intersectsm model estimates liquefaction capacity utilization could fall from 90% in 2026 to below 75% between 2030 and 2034, even counting only plants already operating or under construction. That would be about as deep as the 2020 glut, but last five years rather than one. Additional planned capacity would further increase the risk of oversupply.

As more participants compete in LNG trading, Bain expects margins on flexibility, logistics and credit services to shrink first. During the 2030â34 glut, each traded cargo may earn only about $1 million in gross profit, compared with roughly $6 million during the 2022â23 supply shock. The remaining margins will increasingly depend on managing mismatches in contract length and pricing indices, which can generate profits during supply shocks but losses during a glut.

The eventual outcome will vary significantly across market participants. Books matched or hedged in timing and price could retain much of their margins, while portfolio holders with US volumes they cannot place, or buyers contracted beyond their own needs, would bear the costs.

"In a crowded middle, copying the competition is the one strategy guaranteed to fail. The winners will start from what they bring that others cannot: assets, customers, balance sheet and information," said Wong.

Bain's analysis also points to the potential emergence of a new service model, where established merchant traders take on smaller players' surplus for a fee or a share of the upside, rather than buying cargoes outright. Consolidation is also likely through the glut.

Bain underscores the need for LNG companies to reassess their business models, risk appetite, and trading capabilities in the current supply crunch. This includes setting limits on uncontracted cargoes, separating industrial portfolio management from short-term optimization, and strengthening the systems and analytics needed to monitor exposures and manage increasingly complex trading portfolios. Investors looking at LNG trading books, portfolios and projects should test who really carries the volume and price risk when the glut arrives.

#5378. Palo Alto Networks bets $4.5B on AI startup Applied Compute as earnings top forecasts

Cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks Inc. today announced that it has agreed to acquire artificial intelligence model training and inference startup Applied Compute Inc. in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion.

The news came alongside fiscal first-quarter earnings and revenue that were well ahead of Wall Street expectations. Shares of Palo Alto Networks rose more than 8% in late trading, adding to a gain of nearly 10% during the regular session.

The acquisition, subject to regulatory clearance, is expected to close in Palo Alto Networks’ fiscal third quarter. Once the deal closes, Applied Compute co-founder and Chief Executive Yash Patil will become co-chief AI officer at Palo Alto Networks, with the startup’s research team also joining the company.

Founded in 2025 by former OpenAI Group PBC researchers Patil, Rhythm Garg and Linden Li, Applied Compute offers a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight models. The platform is designed to make it easier for companies to train, serve and improve their own models, with an autoscaling inference engine and a model router called Shift-1 also included.

Applied Compute raised $350 million at a $3.25 billion valuation earlier this month in a round led by Elad Gil, with Nvidia Corp., Shopify Ventures and HubSpot Ventures also participating. At the time, the company said that its annualized recurring revenue had topped $100 million. Notable customers include Microsoft Corp. and DoorDash Inc. Coming into its acquisition, Applied Compute had raised more than $500 million in total.

Palo Alto Networks is pitching the deal as a bet that enterprise AI will be hybrid, as a large share of companies run open-weight models tuned to their own data. According to the company, no large provider is currently delivering those models securely. With Applied Compute, enterprises will be able to train and deploy open-weight models with security built in, either in the public cloud or in sovereign environments.

“Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” Chairman and Chief Executive Nikesh Arora said. “Applied Compute has built the best post-training and inference platform we’ve seen, and its research team is exceptional.”

The deal came on the same day Palo Alto Networks reported what Arora called a record first quarter. For the quarter that ended on Oct. 31, the company reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.05, up from 93 cents in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $3.44 billion, up 39% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 97 cents per share on revenue of $3.31 billion.

Next-generation security annual recurring revenue grew 66% from a year earlier, to $9.73 billion. Remaining performance obligations rose 35%, to $21 billion. Helped by a tax benefit of $457 million, net income on an unadjusted basis came to $482 million, up from $334 million in the same quarter a year ago.

Chief Financial Officer Dipak Golechha said that given the current threat environment and the demand ahead, the company is “materially raising” its full-year guidance.

For its fiscal second quarter, Palo Alto Networks expects adjusted earnings per share of $1.01 to $1.03 on revenue of $3.53 billion to $3.55 billion. Full-year revenue is now forecast at $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion, up from the $14.10 billion to $14.20 billion guided in September, with adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 per share ahead of the $4.18 expected by analysts polled by FactSet.

#5377. Former UW AI researchers Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin raise $110M for AI startup Noeri

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:37 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:14 pm

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a company’s own work.

Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Noeri’s software studies a company’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company said.

It works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the company said.

The pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin said at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”

Noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

Choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

Noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

#5375. Hackers Hijack 178 Major Websites, Including BBC, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, and Ledger

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Hackers have turned some of the world’s most recognizable websites into potential crypto theft traps after compromising a third-party platform used by 178 major organizations. The attack injected malicious JavaScript through Optimizely, a website experimentation platform trusted by companies including BBC, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, Salesforce, IKEA, and crypto hardware wallet maker Ledger.

Visitors could unknowingly load malware simply by opening an affected webpage, and the consequences go far beyond stolen browsing data. The malicious code can replace crypto wallet addresses copied to the clipboard, redirecting payments straight into attackers’ wallets. Security researchers have already identified $7,040 in crypto received by wallets linked to the campaign.

🚨 BREAKING: Ledger and 177 other major organizations, including Zoom, CNN, and Salesforce, were affected by a massive JavaScript attack.The malware stole cryptocurrency, payment card details, and user data, while also targeting iPhones with exploit kits.

The investigation by cybersecurity firm Report URI identified 188 infected JavaScript snippets belonging to 178 organizations after examining 1,611 Optimizely scripts. The malware operated through trusted website infrastructure, making the attack particularly dangerous. Rather than breaking into every company’s servers individually, attackers injected malicious code into Optimizely customer projects.

Affected websites continued loading JavaScript through Optimizely’s legitimate content delivery network. Visitors had little reason to suspect that a familiar website was serving malicious instructions. This is a dangerous clipboard hijacking mechanism.

The malware searched webpages for crypto wallet addresses and replaced legitimate destinations with addresses controlled by attackers. It could also intercept copied addresses, meaning someone browsing an affected website could potentially paste a fraudulent wallet address elsewhere.

The attack targeted several major crypto networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, TRON, and Litecoin.

A victim could believe they were sending funds to an exchange, another wallet, or a friend. Instead, the transaction could land directly in an attacker’s wallet.

Report URI identified $7,040 in receipts across attacker-controlled wallets by November 16. The funds included Bitcoin, Litecoin, Ethereum, TRON, and stablecoins.

The scale of the incident raises questions about how much trust businesses place in third-party website services. The affected organizations span several industries, including banking, technology, media, retail, and crypto.

HSBC was among the financial institutions affected, alongside Equifax and other major organizations. BBC, CNN, Fox News, Zoom, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, and Air France-KLM also appeared in Report URI’s investigation.

Ledger’s inclusion makes the incident particularly concerning for crypto users. The company is known for its hardware wallets, which help customers store private keys away from internet-connected devices. However, the incident demonstrates how threats can reach users through ordinary browsing activity, outside the hardware wallet itself.

The malicious campaign also contained capabilities targeting Apple devices. Researchers identified exploit infrastructure associated with Coruna and DarkSword, two iOS exploit kits designed to target vulnerabilities in iPhones and iPads.

This means the operation was not limited to stealing crypto or payment information. It also carried tools capable of targeting mobile devices through malicious webpage content.

Optimizely confirmed that attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects. The company said it blocked access to the vulnerable pathway, deployed a fix, removed injected code, revoked active tokens, and reset access for affected accounts.

Earlier today, Optimizely identified and contained a security incident affecting some Optimizely Web Experimentation customers. The vulnerable path is blocked, the injected code was removed, and customers have been contacted directly. Updates: https://t.co/ptZHZviIeC

However, the incident raises serious questions about third-party website security. Report URI’s investigation found that even Optimizely’s own websites carried the malicious code. Researchers also observed the attacker rebuilding the malware 26 times during the campaign, adding capabilities and additional cryptocurrency wallets.

Most infected snippets were subsequently cleaned up, with Report URI finding only one remaining infected snippet in its final November 16 sweep.

But the financial damage and potential exposure remain difficult to measure. Researchers have identified crypto receipts, but the number of affected visitors, compromised payment cards, and exposed browser sessions remains unknown.

The bigger problem is that website visitors rarely know which third-party scripts are running behind the pages they trust. A familiar banking website, news outlet, or crypto platform can become an unexpected entry point for malicious code without its visitors noticing anything unusual.

#5374. Portland startup Fairly raises $22M to pair local caretakers with AI for vacation rentals

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:58 pm

Fairly, a Portland, Ore.-based vacation rental startup led by Vacasa founder Eric Breon, raised a $22.4 million Series A round, the company announced Tuesday.

Oregon Venture Fund led the round, with participation from Elevate Capital and Breon.

Fairly pairs vacation rental owners with local caretakers who look after the homes. Its software handles pricing, bookings and scheduling, and uses AI to draft routine guest messages and flag maintenance problems.

Guests booked more than $66 million in reservations through Fairly over the past year, up from about $5 million the year before, the company said. Nearly 900 caretakers now manage about 2,000 homes across 47 states, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Owners pay a single 20% fee, which Fairly splits with the caretaker, compared with the 25% to 40% the company says other managers typically charge. Fairly also says it doesn’t tack extra fees onto guest bills, so guests pay less overall.

“At Vacasa, I led a 7,000-person team, and delivering quality, individualized care at that scale is not an easy task,” Breon said in a statement. “At Fairly, we take a completely different approach: we empower dedicated, hyperlocal caretakers to care for homes, and our systems do the heavy lifting around them.”

Breon founded Vacasa in Portland in 2009 and spent more than a decade there. The company went public via a SPAC deal in 2021 and was acquired in May 2025 by Phoenix-based Casago, a vacation rental manager.

Fairly, founded in 2023, emerged from stealth in December 2024 with $10.1 million in pre-seed funding. The company has now raised $32.5 million in total.

Fairly now employs 106 people, up from 25 at its launch in 2024. Co-founder Subechya Person remains chief product officer; co-founder and former CTO Jeff Flitton left the company in February.

#5373. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO priced at $83 per share, higher than expected

Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic PBC today priced one of the most eagerly anticipated initial public offerings in history at a price of $83 per share, setting the stage for the biggest stock market listing ever.

The pricing, which has been reported by multiple news outlets including Bloomberg, Reuters and the Financial Times, is even higher than the company’s expected range of $70 to $78 per share.

If that price is correct, and if Anthropic sells all of its shares, it would raise in excess of $68 billion from the sale. Including the $26 billion in private placements, that puts Anthropic’s offering at more than $94 billion, surpassing even Space Exploration Technologies Corp. blockbuster $86 billion listing back in June.

In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission last week, Anthropic had said its expected price range would give it a valuation of $1.4 trillion, but its market capitalization could well be even higher than that. The company’s shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq exchange on Thursday under the ticker symbol “ANT.” Its debut might help the AI industry to push back against growing concerns that it’s entering into unsustainable bubble territory after years of breathtaking technological advances that has seen investors pour billions of dollars into almost any AI bet they can.

The listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has recently been beset by numerous setbacks, including the U.S. population’s backlash against data center building that was evident during the midterm elections, and then the ousting of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Jensen Huang last week. Those events raised concerns even higher in a market that was already jittery about the prospect of rising interest rates that could put debt financing out of the reach of many smaller AI infrastructure companies.

Some of the technology industry’s biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as customers, partners and shareholders. For instance, both Amazon.com Inc. and Google LLC have sizable stakes in the company, and others including Microsoft Corp., Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. have invested billions into its IPO. Meanwhile, the company is one of the biggest buyers of AI chips from those firms.

“If we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia,” said Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei (pictured) in a roadshow video last week. “We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time.”

Anthropic has been surrounded by immense hype and equally sizable controversy, generating billions of dollars in revenue while raising even more, and sparking serious concerns over the safety of the technology it has pioneered. Amodei has emerged as one of the biggest sources of the numerous doomsday stories surrounding AI, writing essays and repeatedly warning anyone who will listen of the dangers of humans losing control. In addition, he has attracted the ire of U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after refusing to let the Pentagon do as it pleases with the company’s tools.

“If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian,” Amodei wrote in a viral essay in September.

Industry analyst Dan Ives told the New York Post that most investors view Amodei’s comments as “background noise” relative to the growth opportunity Anthropic has as one of the perceived leaders in frontier model development. “It’s a white-knuckle period and it’s a vote of confidence that Anthropic could have a successful IPO with the black cloud around Nvidia, Jensen and the AI trade,” he said.

Going forward, Amodei and his team will try to defy a stock market that has looked increasingly volatile this year. But even if they fail, they will walk away from this as incredibly rich men, with some reports suggesting that he and his six co-founders could each earn around $18 billion from today’s sale.

“Anthropic’s IPO will test just how much value frontier AI companies can capture as the industry moves from building increasingly capable models to putting them to work,” DatologyAI Inc. CEO Ari Morcos told SiliconANGLE.

Wall Street anticipates massive growth for the company in the coming years. Anthropic has been engaged in a titanic struggle with OpenAI Group PBC and Google LLC to develop the best AI models and recruit enterprise customers, and it appears to be winning. It has enjoyed a meteoric rise this year driven by the success of its popular AI coding tool Claude Code.

According to its IPO prospectus, it generated revenue of $33.24 billion in the nine month period ending Sept. 30, up around 1,200% from the same period one year earlier. During that period, it recorded a staggering $104 billion net loss, though most of that was due to a change in the value of convertible notes issues to investors and its derivative liabilities, the Financial Times said. Over the same stretch in 2025, Anthropic’s total losses came to $25.1 billion.

In a recent amendment to its IPO filing, the company said it had achieved a revenue run-rate of $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the prior month.

Regarding projections, some analysts have forecast Anthropic’s revenue to hit $53 billion by the end of its fiscal year, rising to between $135 billion and $137 billion in fiscal 2027 and between $270 billion and $280 billion by 2028.

Anthropic’s rival OpenAI had originally hoped to beat it to the public markets, but its founder and CEO Sam Altman later delayed its listing. While it has confidentially filed paperwork for an IPO, it’s not expected to make its market debut until sometime next year.

#5371. Radian Aerospace plans to make its own composite materials for space plane (and for other companies, too)

by Alan Boyle on Nov 17, 2026 at 4:00 amNovember 17, 2026 at 4:11 am

On the way to building a space plane, Seattle-based Radian Aerospace is planning a factory to make the advanced materials it’ll need — and it plans to sell those materials to other companies as well.

Radian CEO Richard Humphrey said he envisions the factory, known as Foundry 1, as a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility with a footprint spanning “just under 100,000 square feet.” Six to 12 sites around the country — including sites in the Pacific Northwest — are currently under consideration, with late 2027 as the target for starting production, he said.

Foundry 1 is meant to produce ceramic matrix composites, or CMCs — not only for Radian’s space plane, but also for other applications ranging from gas-turbine components to high-performance braking systems.

“Each of these industries has a bottleneck that’s being driven by a lack of an industrial base to really build these next-gen materials,” Humphrey told GeekWire.

Humphrey and his teammates ran into that bottleneck while developing Radian One, a reusable rocket-powered plane that’s meant to transport cargo and crew to and from low Earth orbit. Securing a reliable supply chain for the required materials proved so challenging that Radian decided to produce its own.

“Defense and space programs need these materials at costs and production rates that today’s supply base cannot deliver,” Humphrey said today in a news release. “Foundry 1 unlocks a substantial commercial opportunity for Radian and a more direct path to revenue. It positions us to supply customers across these industries while advancing the technology that will make Radian One possible.”

Ceramic matrix composites embed reinforcing fibers, such as carbon or silicon carbide, within a lightweight ceramic material. The ceramic provides resistance to extreme heat, while the fibers help the material carry loads and resist damage from cracking.

Carbon-fiber composites have been around for decades, but turning them into products is typically labor-intensive and expensive. To drive down the cost while improving quality, Radian is developing an automated system for producing CMCs. The company says it’s targeting a 50% reduction in CMC manufacturing costs by cutting manual labor, shortening processing cycles and minimizing waste.

Artificial intelligence will play a role as well, Humphrey said. “We see an AI-native base where we can actually learn from each individual piece while digital-twinning them, so each piece ends up with a digital passport,” he said. “We know exactly where every fiber is, the angle of each fiber to the fiber next to it, and then we do in-process CT screening.”

Greg Scofield, an adviser to Radian and former director of the Purdue Hypersonics Laboratory, said Radian is taking an integrated approach to the challenges surrounding CMC production. “Designing fiber placement, thermal processing and inspection together creates an opportunity to improve cost and quality throughout the production line, with benefits for customers across defense and space,” he said.

The payoff could be huge: A report from Polaris Market Research suggests the global market for advanced composites could rise to $126 billion by 2034.

In partnership with NASA’s Glenn Research Center, Radian has already tested a patent-pending composite material called Dur-E-Therm at temperatures exceeding 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit (1,480 degrees Celsius) under conditions that simulate hypersonic flight.

Radian’s next steps are to select the site for Foundry 1 and begin construction while continuing CMC development at partner facilities. That’s a tall order for a small company.

Humphrey said the company currently has about 20 employees working at locations including the University of Washington’s Advanced Composites Center. Back in 2022, Radian announced a $27.5 million funding round that brought total investment to $32 million at the time. Humphrey said Radian has raised additional funding since then, but he wasn’t ready to share updated figures.

So, how much will Foundry 1 cost? “We’re not quite ready to put a pin in the number,” Humphrey said. “It’s fair to say it’s sub — not a lot less, but it’s sub $100 million in terms of total capital to stand this up for what we’re doing.”

He acknowledged that following through on the plan for Foundry 1 will require raising more capital. “It is part of what we do, and we have a really super group of investors that have been behind us for a long time,” he said.

Humphrey said the Radian One space plane remains the focus of the company’s long-term vision — but for now, the company is devoting all of its resources and capital to Foundry 1.

“It’s the bottleneck to Radian One being successful,” he said. “We think that by applying all of our attention to that, it serves the broader market but also serves advancing Radian One. Both of those are hard things, so we’re going to focus on one hard thing at a time.”

Is Radian becoming an advanced materials and aerospace company? Humphrey said that’s “a good way to think about it,” but he emphasized that aerospace still gets top billing.

“I’d rather be launching today than just be building CMCs,” he said. “But building CMCs is what gets us to flying tomorrow. By advancing materials, it’s our single best way to be ready for Space 3.0, if you want to call it that. … At times we have to be adaptable to really move the project forward, and sometimes it goes a little sideways before you go forward. It’s just the way I’ve come to accept it.”

#5369. Booking Holdings’ travel startup Vayo starts booking trips with AI agents, even on rival Expedia

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:20 amNovember 17, 2026 at 6:21 am

Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup launched by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel plans — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of users in its invite-only beta.

That includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group. Vayo confirmed that its AI agents book there by navigating Expedia’s website, without a direct integration or partnership for those bookings.

The company says Vayo recommends the best option for the traveler, wherever that option is booked, not just through its parent company’s brands.

Vayo is led by Mike Fridgen, a longtime Seattle entrepreneur with deep roots in travel. Booking Holdings, the parent of Booking.com, Priceline, Kayak and OpenTable, said last month that it plans to invest $100 million in Vayo, depending on its progress and market conditions.

Companies are still working out how to handle AI agents that use their sites on behalf of customers. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com, saying the agent didn’t identify itself.

When Vayo launched last month, Fridgen said it was relying on APIs and direct partnerships with travel companies, in part to avoid the risk of being blocked. Vayo says no site has blocked its bookings so far.

How the bookings work: Vayo’s new booking features work in two ways. It can book hotels, rental cars and activities through a direct connection with sister company Booking.com, and it has similar links to OpenTable for restaurants and SeatGeek for event tickets.

For flights and other bookings, its AI agents navigate the booking websites, signing in to the traveler’s existing accounts where needed and completing the purchase. Every booking requires the traveler’s approval, the company says.

If a site doesn’t allow AI agents, Vayo leaves that booking to the traveler.

Vayo uses 1Password to sign in to travelers’ accounts and, on sites other than Booking.com, Stripe’s Link agent wallet to pay, without seeing their passwords or card details, the company says. It reports a reservation as confirmed only after the supplier confirms it.

Payments and pricing: Travelers pay whichever company they book with, and Vayo is not the merchant of record. The company declined to share details on commissions, saying its partner arrangements are still taking shape and won’t factor into its recommendations.

When Booking.com has the best option, Vayo users get Genius Level 3 pricing, Booking.com’s top loyalty tier, with discounts of up to 20% on select stays.

The service is free to use during the invite-only beta. Responding to GeekWire’s questions, Vayo didn’t say how many people are using it or how many have completed a booking.

Who’s behind Vayo: Fridgen, the Vayo co-founder and CEO, was on the founding team of Expedia’s vacation-package business, led Alaska Airlines’ digital business and was founding head of product at airfare-prediction startup Farecast, before leading Decide.com and Madrona Venture Labs.

His co-founder and CTO is Allen Chen, the former CTO of Fanatics Collectibles, who previously co-founded Seattle software startups CloudPress and DataBlade. Ian Fliflet, OfferUp’s former chief growth officer, is head of growth. Vayo had about 20 employees, all working in downtown Seattle, when it launched last month.

Next on its product roadmap, the company says it plans to work inside the messaging apps people already use, and to let groups of travelers plan trips together.

#5368. Google upgrades Gemini’s agentic Task mode with new model, e-commerce features

Google LLC is releasing a new version of its Gemini artificial intelligence assistant that is better at performing multi-step tasks.

Josh Woodward, the vice president responsible for the Gemini app, detailed the update in a Thursday blog post.

The AI assistant has two modes that are accessible through separate interface tabs. The first, Chat, generates quick, relatively simple responses to prompts. The second mode, which is called Task, enables Gemini to perform complex tasks such as booking appointments and comparing online product listings. Task is the focus of this week’s update.

Google is switching the feature to Gemini 4 Hydrogen, its newest large language model. It’s somewhat less capable than Gemini 4 Carbon, the search giant’s most advanced LLM, and significantly more cost-efficient. Hydrogen is also fast: Google says that it can process some tasks 2.8 times faster than its previous entry-level model.

One way Hydrogen reduces wait times is by parallelizing project steps that are usually performed one after another. According to Woodward, users of Gemini’s Task mode can give the model feedback after each step to guide its work. The model proactively asks users for instructions before performing a sensitive task such as making an online purchase.

Today, Gemini’s Task mode uses Google Wallet to process transactions. Woodward said that the search giant is working with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa to add support for a technology called payment tokenization. It replaces the user’s card number with a placeholder value called a token. That token is shared with merchants instead of the card number to reduce the risk of data leaks.

Google also plans to add support for a second technology called the Universal Commerce Protocol, or UCP. It makes it easier for AI agents such as Gemini to interact with online stores and thereby lowers the risk of errors.

Gemini’s Task mode can use data in other Google services such as Gmail to inform its decisions. For example, the agent might take the user’s past purchases into account when generating shopping suggestions. One of Gemini’s main selling points is that it can use such data without moving it off Google infrastructure, which is often not the case with competing agents.

“When you assign Gemini a task, it uses Google Cloud’s Agent Compute Engine to work in a hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users,” Woodward wrote. “Each virtual machine is sandboxed, so Gemini works in a separate, isolated environment that’s regularly tested by our security red teams.”

Google has made Gemini’s Task mode free in the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India as part of the update. That’s notable because Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC charge for the comparable features they offer as part of their chatbot services. Google’s move may prompt them to revise their pricing.

#5367. Seattle fleet tracking company Zonar names Atlanta-based CEO, who says HQ is staying put

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am

Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking company, has a new CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.

Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no plans to change that.” He said he visits the company’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.

Consoli succeeds Charles Kriete, who led GPS Trackit when the Florida-based company acquired Zonar from German auto supplier Continental in late 2024. Kriete ran the combined company, which is backed by private equity firm Inverness Graham, until September and is now a board advisor.

Consoli previously held revenue chief roles at legal software company Assembly Software, Skuid and Liaison Technologies, which OpenText acquired for $310 million in 2018. He also led North American sales at asset-tracking company I.D. Systems, and started his career as an aerospace engineer at General Dynamics.

Zonar sells GPS tracking hardware, cameras and software that fleet operators use to monitor vehicle location, fuel use and driver behavior, and says it has more than 400,000 active units installed.

Its biggest market is student transportation. Consoli said Zonar serves about half of the school bus market, and its customers also include trucking and delivery fleets such as US Foods, utilities and small businesses.

Zonar’s Seattle-area customers include the Kirkland Police Department, which in 2024 became the first agency to roll out Zonar’s mobile inspection app and GPS asset trackers in its patrol fleet after a pilot program. Officers use the app to complete a digital inspection of their patrol car before each shift, checking tire pressure, emergency equipment such as defibrillators and the rear enclosure used to transport suspects. Each inspection takes two to four minutes, according to the company.

Zonar has 409 employees after combining with GPS Trackit, including 70 in Seattle, more than in any other state. Consoli declined to share revenue figures but said Zonar has “more than doubled our profitability in the last 10 months,” helped by new pricing, a reorganized sales team, renegotiated hardware contracts and cost cuts.

Zonar has added 1,000 new customers so far this year, a spokesperson said. Sales to existing customers are running at 118% of the company’s 2026 plan, while new customer wins are at 97%.

“We’re a very attractive asset in this market right now,” Consoli said.

Zonar competes with larger players including Samsara, Motive and Geotab. Consoli said Zonar sets itself apart through customer service and flexibility. It offers Zonar One, a turnkey system that customers can install the day after ordering, and Zonar Flex, which is customized for large enterprise fleets.

He said those customers are “not going to get that level of tailoring and customization from any of the big players.”

Consoli also wants to lean further into AI. The goal is to send customers proactive alerts instead of making fleet managers dig through dashboards after the fact: a driver running stop signs, a truck off its route, or a school bus running late. Zonar already lets school districts notify parents through an app when a bus is delayed.

“Fleet operators today are really focused on outcomes,” Consoli said. “They want to know that compliance is handled, safety is improved.”

Founded in Seattle in 2001, Zonar was majority-owned by Continental from 2016 until the 2024 sale. The company cut 57 jobs in August 2024, when it had more than 300 employees, and made more layoffs after the acquisition.

PAYETTE, Idaho, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Valley Family Health Care, Inc. ("VFHC") is providing notice of a data security incident that may have involved personal and/or protected health information belonging to certain individuals.

On or about March 13, 2026, VFHC experienced a network disruption and immediately initiated an investigation of the matter. In doing so, VFHC engaged cybersecurity experts to assist with the investigatory process. As a result of the investigation, VFHC determined that an unauthorized actor accessed and acquired certain files. Upon making this determination, VFHC undertook a comprehensive review of the files and learned that personal information and/or protected health information was involved. VFHC then worked with a third-party vendor to obtain the necessary information to effectuate formal notification. This process was completed on October 9, 2026.

The accessible information varied by individual and may have included individuals' names in combination with a Social Security number, driver's license or state identification number, date of birth, financial account information, medical information, and health insurance information. Not all data elements were affected for all individuals. Please note that there is no evidence of any misuse, or attempted misuse, of the potentially impacted information.

#5365. 13 Friday the 13th facts, from Jason's burlap sack to the calendar math

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Friday the 13th trivia covering Jason's hockey mask, his mother's killing spree, Tom Savini's effects, Kane Hodder and why the date itself is considered unlucky

The most recognizable part of Jason Voorhees is something he did not have at the start. The white hockey mask now tied to the whole Friday the 13th series first appears in the third film. By then, the franchise had already gone through two movies, a different killer and a different disguise.

That gap between the image and its origin runs through much of the series. The first Friday the 13th opened on May 9, 1980, and Jason was not the one doing the killing. When an adult Jason finally arrived in the sequel, he hid his face behind something other than a hockey mask. The look most people picture took shape gradually, one film at a time.

The franchise grew to 12 films between 1980 and 2009. Across those releases, Jason drowned as a boy, returned as a grown man, was killed and came back again. He eventually shared the screen with another horror villain. More than one actor played him. One sequel opened in 3D, and more than one release landed on a Friday the 13th.

The title also stretched beyond the films. Friday the 13th: The Series ran on television from 1987 to 1990. Despite the shared name, it does not feature Jason. The show used the brand without the character.

This collection of Friday the 13th trivia covers 13 points. It runs from the burlap sack Jason wore before the mask to the sound cue built from a few repeated syllables. It also covers the effects artist behind the original film's deaths, the actor who played Jason in four films and a sequel twist that put a copycat behind the killings.

The final slide steps away from the movies and looks at the date itself. Fear of Friday the 13th has a formal name. The calendar math behind how often the date comes around is more exact than the folklore about why it is unlucky. Each slide stands on its own. Readers can start with the mask or skip ahead to the superstition.

Jason Voorhees first wears his hockey mask in Friday the 13th Part III, the 1982 sequel directed by Steve Miner. Before that film, Jason did not wear a hockey mask.

After Part III, the mask stayed. It became Jason's permanent look, and the character kept it in the sequels that followed Miner's film.

How the mask came to be used is less settled. Accounts of the production disagree on who chose it. They also disagree on how it reached the set. With no agreed version, no single person can be credited with the choice.

Jason Voorhees first appears as an adult in Friday the 13th Part 2, released in 1981. In that film, he wears a burlap sack over his head rather than a hockey mask.

Part 2 is the starting point for the grown-up version of the character. The original 1980 Friday the 13th never shows an adult Jason.

The burlap sack is the first face covering an adult Jason wears on screen in the series. Its 1981 release came one year after the original film.

The original Friday the 13th was filmed at Camp No-Be-Bo-Sco, a real camp in Hardwick Township, New Jersey. On screen, those grounds stand in for Camp Crystal Lake, the fictional summer camp at the center of the 1980 film.

The movie uses two names for one place. Camp Crystal Lake is the name viewers hear in the story. Camp No-Be-Bo-Sco is where the production shot its scenes.

Camp Crystal Lake is an invented name. A search for it on a map will not turn up the place seen in the film. The real location behind the fictional camp is Camp No-Be-Bo-Sco, in Hardwick Township, New Jersey.

The "ki ki ki, ma ma ma" sound in Friday the 13th is the work of composer Harry Manfredini. He built it from syllables drawn from the phrase "kill her, mommy."

Manfredini wrote the score for the original 1980 film. This cue is not a melody. It is a short string of clipped syllables.

Each half of the cue comes from one word. The "ki" is taken from "kill." The "ma" is taken from "mommy." Each syllable appears three times as the cue is written.

Not every word of the phrase survives in the sound. The "her" in "kill her, mommy" drops out entirely. What remains is the opening sound of the two words at either end of the phrase.

The phrase behind the sound points to the film's killer, Pamela Voorhees. Its final word, "mommy," fits a story in which a mother is the one committing the murders.

Corey Feldman plays Tommy Jarvis in Friday the 13th: The Final Chapter, released in 1984. Tommy is the character who kills Jason Voorhees in the film.

The Final Chapter reached theaters two years after Friday the 13th Part III. Counting from the original 1980 film, it is the fourth entry in the series.

The title presented the film as the end of the franchise. It was not. Friday the 13th: A New Beginning followed in 1985.

The ending puts Feldman's character at the center of the climax. Tommy, not Jason, is the one who ends the film's run of killings.

A lightning strike brings Jason Voorhees back from the dead in Jason Lives, the 1986 Friday the 13th sequel. Tom McLoughlin directed the film.

Jason had already died on screen before this film. The lightning bolt is the device that returns him, and it puts the series' central villain back at the center of the story.

The title spells out that premise. In Jason Lives, Jason is alive again.

Counting from the original 1980 release, Jason Lives is the sixth Friday the 13th film. It arrived one year after Friday the 13th: A New Beginning.

Jason Goes to Hell, released in 1993, ends with Freddy Krueger's glove pulling Jason's mask underground. Freddy vs. Jason followed in 2003. A reboot that reused the title Friday the 13th arrived in 2009.

The final image of Jason Goes to Hell puts Freddy's glove and Jason's mask in the same frame. It does not show the two characters fighting. The mask is pulled below ground, and the film ends there.

The scene points toward a meeting between the two villains without staging one. It leaves that matchup for a later film.

Freddy vs. Jason reached theaters 10 years after that ending. Ronny Yu directed the film. The crossover put on screen the pairing that the glove scene had only hinted at.

The casting marked a change. Ken Kirzinger played Jason in Freddy vs. Jason. Kane Hodder, who had played Jason in the films just before it, did not take the role for the crossover.

Jason Voorhees is not the killer in the original Friday the 13th. The murderer in the 1980 film is his mother, Pamela Voorhees, played by Betsy Palmer.

Sean S. Cunningham directed the film, and Victor Miller wrote the script. Their story is set at Camp Crystal Lake, the summer camp where the killings take place.

Jason's part in this first installment is small. In the story, he drowned as a boy at Camp Crystal Lake. His death belongs to the film's backstory, not to its run of murders.

He appears on screen only in a shock scene late in the film. That brief moment is the full extent of his role in the original.

The later sequels made Jason the franchise's central figure. In the 1980 film, the character whose name now defines the series is a drowned child, not the attacker.

The answer to "who is the killer in Friday the 13th?" depends on which film the question refers to. For the 1980 original, it is his mother.

Tom Savini created the special effects for the original 1980 Friday the 13th. His work includes the death of Kevin Bacon's character, who is killed by an arrow through the neck.

Bacon is part of the first film's cast. His character does not survive the story.

The arrow scene is one of the killings Savini's effects put on screen in the 1980 film.

Friday the 13th Part III opened in 3D on Aug. 13, 1982. That date fell on a Friday.

The timing put the third film in theaters on the exact day its title names. A series named for an unlucky date had one of its entries premiere on that date.

The 3D format was part of the release itself, not a later reissue. The film arrived in theaters in 3D on its opening date.

Jason Voorhees is not the killer in Friday the 13th: A New Beginning. The 1985 film reveals that a copycat, not Jason, committed its murders.

A New Beginning is the fifth film in the Friday the 13th series. It arrived one year after Friday the 13th: The Final Chapter.

The twist makes it the second film in the series in which Jason does not commit the killings. The first was the 1980 original.

The copycat setup did not carry into the next entry. Jason Lives, the sixth film, returned the real Jason to the center of the series.

Kane Hodder played Jason Voorhees in four Friday the 13th films, released between 1988 and 2001. His run covers The New Blood, Jason Takes Manhattan, Jason Goes to Hell and Jason X $TWTR.

Hodder first took on the role in The New Blood, released in 1988. He returned the following year for Jason Takes Manhattan, released in 1989. Those were his only back-to-back appearances as the character.

The gaps between his films then grew longer. Jason Goes to Hell followed in 1993, four years after Jason Takes Manhattan.

Hodder's final film as the character was Jason X, released in 2001. It arrived eight years after Jason Goes to Hell, the longest break in his run.

From The New Blood to Jason X, Hodder's tenure as Jason spans 13 years.

The 2009 reboot came six years after Freddy vs. Jason. Marcus Nispel directed it. The film carried no subtitle and no number.

It took its name directly from the original 1980 movie, Friday the 13th. The plain title marked it as a reboot rather than another numbered sequel.

The reboot opened on Feb. 13, 2009. That day was a Friday. The film's release date matched its own title.

No one knows for certain why Friday the 13th is considered unlucky. The calendar is more precise: every year has at least one Friday the 13th and no more than three.

The fear of the date has a formal name: paraskevidekatriaphobia. The superstition's origin is unclear. Several historical events are regularly tied to the date. None of them has been shown to be the source of the belief.

The Last Supper is one of the most frequently cited links. It turns up in many retellings of where the superstition began. That connection belongs to folklore, not to established history.

The arrests of the Knights Templar are another. They took place on Friday, Oct. 13, 1307. Popular accounts often point to that day as a starting point. That link is also folklore rather than an established cause.

A later event also shows up in the record. The composer Gioachino Rossini died on Friday, Nov. 13, 1868. His death is often cited in early printed references to the date. A date of death fixes when something happened. It does not explain why a belief began.

The Gregorian calendar repeats its pattern of dates and weekdays every 400 years. Across that cycle, the 13th of a month lands on a Friday 688 times. No other weekday reaches that total.

Friday's lead is slight. A 400-year cycle holds 4,800 months, which means 4,800 13ths. An even split across all seven weekdays would give each day about 686. Friday's 688 sits about two dates above that mark.

Spread over the full cycle, those 688 dates average 1.72 Friday the 13ths per year. No single year can match that average, because each year's count is a whole number. In practice, a given year has one, two or three.

The two halves of this story differ in certainty. The folklore has no confirmed starting point, while the calendar count can be checked to the exact date.

#5364. Glenn Kelman’s next act: Former Redfin CEO takes on health care with stealthy startup Sojourn

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 8:37 am

Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.

The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.

“Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software company, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site.

His co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen, an internist who co-founded digital health company Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation.

This is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the company filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health plans that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management.

Kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words, confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their plans “after we’ve built our product.”

But after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health.

Searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.”

From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com, which sketches out the plan.

Why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story.

“Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care.

“The choices were all terrible,” it says.

Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost.

As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site says, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.”

Kelman, by his own account, is new to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now.

“I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote.

The team: In a LinkedIn post last week, Kelman said the founding team also includes Jennifer Chao and Ben Baker, with Sasha Aickin “adding some part-time magic.” He promised that “the mission is good and the ambition is vast.”

The lineup draws on Kelman’s past and the health insurance world:

Chao and Aickin both worked with Kelman at Plumtree Software, the enterprise software company he co-founded in 1996, before following him to Redfin. Sojourn’s recruiting page nods to the pattern: “We’re honored by the old friends who have worked with us from company to company, but we’re also eager to bring in new blood.”

The Sojourn site says the company is likely to have engineering hubs in Seattle for the member experience, San Francisco for the clinical platform, and Austin for the claims system.

AI all the way down: Sojourn is hiring software engineers and product managers “at every level of the organization.” The first thing on its list of qualifications: experience using frontier AI tools “to generate reliable, high-scale production code.”

That fits with his guest column. A recruiter told him Seattle’s startup scene was “dead,” he wrote, and a friend described CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at companies with old code. Kelman wrote that “the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.”

What we don’t know: The website doesn’t say when Sojourn plans to launch or where it will offer coverage first, although Chen’s bio suggests employers will be key customers, describing a care model “designed around the member and the employer who pays for it.”

A new health plan typically requires state insurance licenses and significant capital reserves, and the company hasn’t disclosed any funding. Kelman wrote in his column that he “met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea,” but he didn’t name them, and a search of SEC filings for Sojourn Health and Silica Health found no record of a fundraise.

In June, he joined venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence, saying at the time that he was still looking to start a new mission-driven enterprise, a process that involved “exploring ideas that are never going to work and howling at the moon.” It’s not clear whether Greylock is among his backers.

Kelman stepped down as Redfin CEO in January, six months after Rocket Companies completed its $1.75 billion acquisition of the Seattle brokerage. He said at the time that he wanted to find “another mission-driven enterprise outside of real estate.”

He appears to have found one. Whether health care is more or less screwed up than real estate is a question that will have to wait until he’s ready to chat.
