#5363. 5 recalls and a federal rule that show how ingredient problems spread

Free daily briefing on global business news.

An ingredient recall can spread across many brands when manufacturers share one supplier, as four past recalls and an FDA tracing rule help explain

A single batch of an ingredient can leave one supplier's plant and end up inside products sold under many different brand names. Each of those products carries its own label and its own lot code. When that batch turns out to be contaminated, the recall cannot stop at the supplier's door. It has to follow the ingredient to every company that bought it.

That tracing problem explains why one ingredient recall can reach so far. Manufacturers often buy shared inputs such as flavorings, proteins, pastes and active drug ingredients from a small number of suppliers. A processor may mix one supplier's batch into many finished foods or medicines. Each buyer then has to work out which of its own products used the affected material. It also has to find which batches of those products reached customers.

The basic chain is short. A supplier sells to manufacturers. Manufacturers sell under brand names, and retailers stock those brands side by side. A shopper sees separate products. The supply chain behind them may trace back to one shared source.

Lot codes are the tool meant to make that work possible. A lot code lets a company say exactly which production batches are affected. The company can then pull those batches and leave the rest on sale. The system only holds together if every buyer in the chain keeps records linking incoming ingredient lots to the finished products that used them. A missing record at any step makes it harder to say which finished products are affected.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration sorts recalls into classes based on health risk. Class I is the most serious category. It applies where there is a reasonable probability that using the product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death. Class II and Class III cover lesser risks.

The five examples below show the pattern in different settings. They include a pet food recall, two food ingredient recalls tied to Salmonella, a generic blood pressure drug recall and a federal rule written to speed up tracing. They are a selection, not a complete or ranked list. Each one shows a different part of the tracing problem.

The 2007 Menu Foods recall showed how one tainted input can surface under several pet food brands at once. Wheat gluten contaminated with melamine came from a supplier in China. It went into food that Menu Foods produced for a range of labels.

Menu Foods, based in Ontario, Canada, announced its recall in March 2007. The company worked largely as a contract manufacturer. It made wet foods, such as chunks in gravy, that other companies sold under their own names. Those customers included national brands and store brands.

That business model explains why the problem crossed brand lines. A pet owner reading a can saw a familiar label, not the name of the plant that made it. Nothing on the packaging linked one brand to another. A single contaminated ingredient at one manufacturer still reached shelves under more than one brand name.

Wheat gluten is a concentrated protein extracted from wheat. In wet pet food it helps bind ingredients and form chunks with a meat-like texture. It also contributes to the protein content printed on the label.

Melamine is an industrial chemical used to make plastics and resins. It is rich in nitrogen. Common protein tests estimate protein by measuring nitrogen. Melamine can therefore make a diluted ingredient look more protein-rich than it is.

Investigators also found cyanuric acid, a related compound, in the contaminated material. Melamine and cyanuric acid can combine to form crystals in the kidneys. Affected cats and dogs suffered kidney failure.

The gluten passed through more than one company before it reached pet food. ChemNutra, a Las Vegas importer, brought it into the U.S. from Xuzhou Anying Biologic Technology Development in China. In 2008, a federal grand jury indicted both companies and ChemNutra's owners.

Each handoff added distance between the source of the contamination and the pet owner. Investigators had to work backward from sick animals to finished food, then to the plant and the gluten shipments. They then had to work forward again to every product made with those shipments.

The recall did not stop at Menu Foods. Some other pet food makers that had used wheat gluten from the same importer also recalled their own products. The trail from one importer's shipments led into several separate companies' production lines.

Peanut Corporation of America was not a household brand. It worked as a processor, turning raw peanuts into products that other companies bought in bulk. Investigators focused on its plant in Blakely, Georgia. A second company plant, in Plainview, Texas, also came under scrutiny and was shut down in 2009. The outbreak strain was Salmonella Typhimurium.

That structure shaped the recall. Once investigators identified the Georgia plant as the source, the recall moved outward through the processor's list of buyers. A peanut butter sandwich cracker, a peanut ice cream and a candy bar could all trace back to that one plant.

The case also carried legal consequences. Peanut Corporation of America filed for bankruptcy in February 2009. Its former chief executive, Stewart Parnell, was later convicted on federal charges connected to the outbreak, including conspiracy and fraud. In 2015 he was sentenced to 28 years in prison.

In 2010, a Salmonella problem was tied to hydrolyzed vegetable protein made by Basic Food Flavors of Las Vegas. Food companies that used the ingredient recalled products containing it. The case showed that a minor flavoring, present in small amounts, can still set off many recalls.

Hydrolyzed vegetable protein, often shortened to HVP, is a flavor enhancer. It is made by breaking down protein from plant sources such as soy, corn or wheat into its amino acids. The result has a savory, brothlike taste that deepens the flavor of processed foods.

Manufacturers add it to soups, sauces, dips, snack seasonings and similar products. They use it in small quantities. U.S. ingredient lists run in descending order by weight. HVP therefore tends to sit near the end of a label.

That small dose helps explain how one supplier's output can reach so many products. A modest batch of a flavor enhancer can season a large volume of finished food. The same ingredient can also travel inside a seasoning blend or flavor base that another company mixes before selling it on.

Each of those steps adds a layer to the trace. A food maker that bought a seasoning blend may need records from its blender to learn whether HVP from the affected supplier was inside. Only then can it check its own production records for affected products.

Dry ingredients pose a particular challenge with Salmonella. The bacteria cannot multiply without moisture. They can, however, survive for long periods in low-moisture foods such as powders and seasonings. A dry ingredient does not become safe simply by sitting on a shelf.

How a product is eaten also matters. Thorough cooking can kill Salmonella in a soup simmered at home. Seasoned chips and dips served straight from the container are often eaten with no further cooking.

U.S. rules require a protein hydrolysate's label name to identify its food source, as in "hydrolyzed soy protein." That naming tells consumers what plant the protein came from. It does not tell them which company made it. That is the detail a recall depends on.

The 2018 valsartan recall showed that medicines can follow the same supply pattern as food. Several generic versions of the blood pressure drug were recalled because they contained an impurity called N-nitrosodimethylamine, or NDMA. Their active ingredient came from Zhejiang Huahai Pharmaceutical in China.

Valsartan belongs to a drug class called angiotensin II receptor blockers, often shortened to ARBs. Doctors prescribe it for high blood pressure and heart failure. Many patients take it daily for years. A recall therefore created practical work for pharmacies and prescribers, on top of the safety question.

NDMA is a nitrosamine, a type of chemical that can form during some industrial and food processes. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies NDMA as probably carcinogenic to humans. Its presence in valsartan tablets led to regulatory action in the U.S. and Europe.

The route from one supplier to many labels runs through the active pharmaceutical ingredient, or API. That is the compound that produces a drug's effect. Generic drug companies often buy their API from specialist chemical manufacturers instead of making it themselves.

Those companies then turn the API into finished tablets. They add inactive ingredients, press and package the product, and sell it under their own names. The chemistry happens at one company, while the label belongs to another.

That division of labor meant one API maker could sit behind several finished drugs. Once the impurity was traced to valsartan from Zhejiang Huahai Pharmaceutical, each buyer of that ingredient had to check its own batches. Bottles with different company names on them shared the same upstream source.

The check also had to cover combination pills. Valsartan is sold alone and in single tablets paired with other blood pressure drugs. Any of those products made with the affected ingredient fell into the same review.

Generic substitution made the problem harder for patients to see. A pharmacy can fill a valsartan prescription with any approved generic version. The maker can change from one refill to the next. A patient may not know which company made the tablets in a given bottle.

Pharmacists had to match the manufacturer name and lot number on each container against recall notices. The FDA advised patients on recalled valsartan to keep taking it until a doctor or pharmacist provided a replacement or another treatment. Stopping a blood pressure drug abruptly carries its own risks.

The concern later widened beyond valsartan. Nitrosamine impurities were found in some versions of other ARBs, including losartan and irbesartan, and those products were recalled too. The FDA later issued guidance asking drug makers to assess and control nitrosamine risks in their medicines.

The FDA food traceability rule requires companies that handle foods on the agency's Food Traceability List to keep extra records. Those records are meant to help investigators follow a food and its ingredients through the supply chain faster during an outbreak or recall.

The rule comes from Section 204 of the FDA Food Safety Modernization Act, the food safety law signed in January 2011. The FDA finalized the traceability requirements in November 2022. Compliance was originally due on January 20, 2026. The agency has since extended that date by 30 months, to July 20, 2028.

The rule is built around specific points in a food's journey. The FDA calls these points critical tracking events. They include harvesting, cooling, initial packing, shipping, receiving and transformation. At each event, a company must record key data elements, such as quantities, locations, dates and a traceability lot code.

The traceability lot code ties those records together. A code is assigned when a food is first packed, first received on land after harvest at sea, or transformed into a new product. Transformation covers steps such as cutting, mixing or cooking a food into something else.

When a firm transforms a listed food, it assigns a new lot code to the result. It also records which incoming lots went into it. That link lets an investigator move from a finished product back to a specific ingredient batch.

The rule also sets a deadline for producing records. When the FDA asks, a covered company must hand over the information within 24 hours or within a reasonable time the agency agrees to. In some situations, such as an outbreak investigation, the firm must provide it as an electronic sortable spreadsheet.

The list itself is limited. It names foods including leafy greens, fresh herbs, tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, melons and sprouts. It also covers shell eggs, nut butters, cheeses other than hard cheeses, finfish, crustaceans, molluscan shellfish and ready-to-eat deli salads. Foods that contain a listed item as an ingredient can also be covered. That generally applies only while the listed ingredient stays in the same form, such as fresh.

This scope means the rule does not reach every ingredient. Dry flavorings, flours and many other shared inputs fall outside it. For those, tracing still rests on the one-step-forward, one-step-back records required under the Bioterrorism Act of 2002. Those records show where a company got an ingredient and where it sent its products. They do not carry the Section 204 rule's critical tracking events, key data elements or 24-hour spreadsheet requirement.

#5362. Early data points to Vulcan’s first stage in launch failure that cost Amazon 40 Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA said Tuesday.

In its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit.

That stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA said it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete.

The Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA said. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally.

The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes.

What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn.

ULA said Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based company hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning.

“It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and New Glenn for our return to flight.”

Impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on New Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight.

Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites.

Amazon has said it plans to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

#5361. What Is Backpack Crypto? BP Explodes 30% After CFTC Approval

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

First, what is Backpack crypto? Why is it exploding? Backpack is suddenly becoming one of the market’s hottest stories after securing a major regulatory breakthrough in the United States. Its native BP token surged 30% in 24 hours as traders rushed to price in the exchange’s latest expansion. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has effectively opened the door for Backpack to challenge established crypto derivatives platforms on American soil.

The approval gives Backpack the regulatory foundation to operate a US derivatives exchange and clearinghouse. Its ambitions extend beyond simply offering another place to trade Bitcoin and Ethereum. The company wants to combine leveraged crypto trading, collateral management, and global liquidity under one regulated platform.

The development also arrives as competition heats up over who can deliver the next generation of crypto trading infrastructure.

Founded by Armani Ferrante, Backpack started as a Solana-focused crypto wallet and exchange. It has since expanded into securities, tokenization, and derivatives. The company then reports more than $450 billion in cumulative trading volume and customers across over 150 countries.

Its latest breakthrough involves two separate approvals from the CFTC. The Designated Contract Market (DCM) registration allows Backpack to operate a regulated derivatives exchange.

Backpack is coming home to the USA. 🇺🇸We’ve received landmark CFTC approval to establish the first-ever derivatives exchange powered by one order book with unified global liquidity.Leveraged perpetuals. Crypto collateral. Cross-margin. 24/7 trading.Join the waitlist:…

Meanwhile, its Derivatives Clearing Organization (DCO) registration provides the infrastructure needed to manage collateral, margin, and settlement obligations. Together, these approvals establish the foundation for Backpack to offer leveraged crypto perpetual futures in the United States.

The proposed platform will support 24/7 trading, crypto and fiat collateral, cross-margining, and access to Backpack’s global order book.

That last feature could prove particularly important. Rather than isolating American traders inside a separate liquidity pool, Backpack wants to connect US customers with its international trading ecosystem.

BP responded immediately. The token climbed by more than 30% over 24 hours to $1.10, pushing its market cap higher as trading activity accelerated. The rally ties to growing expectations that Backpack could become a serious competitor in the American derivatives market.

The regulatory breakthrough also strengthens its position against offshore platforms that have dominated leveraged crypto trading for years.

Backpack’s approval exposes an interesting opportunity across the wider crypto market. Bitcoin remains the industry’s largest liquidity pool, yet its base layer was never designed for sophisticated smart contracts, high-speed decentralized trading or complex margin products.

That creates an infrastructure gap developers are racing to fill. Solana demonstrated how quickly decentralized applications can execute transactions. Bitcoin, meanwhile, offers a much deeper pool of established capital.

Bringing those strengths together could unlock an entirely different market for Bitcoin-denominated trading.

Projects exploring this direction, Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER), which combines Bitcoin Layer 2 infrastructure with Solana Virtual Machine technology. Its architecture aims to let users bridge BTC into a faster environment supporting smart contracts and decentralized applications.

The potential goes beyond faster transfers. Bitcoin liquidity could eventually support decentralized spot markets, margin trading, and perpetual futures without forcing traders to abandon Bitcoin for another blockchain ecosystem.

Bitcoin Hyper has already attracted more than $33.2 million through its presale, exceeding Backpack’s previously disclosed $17 million Series A funding round. Its token currently sells for just $0.0137, while its staking program advertises rewards of up to 35% APY.

With its November 26 launch target approaching, the presale is entering its final stretch. The combination of Bitcoin liquidity and Solana-style execution is attracting attention as developers look for ways to bring more sophisticated financial applications to Bitcoin.

Backpack now has something many offshore competitors cannot easily replicate: a regulatory pathway into the American derivatives market. The company still needs to turn its approvals into actual trading activity, but the potential market is enormous.

American traders represent an important source of institutional and retail liquidity. Bringing them into a unified order book could strengthen Backpack’s competitive position while attracting market makers and professional trading firms.

BP’s 30% rally shows investors are already anticipating that expansion, and Backpack’s regulatory breakthrough could mark the beginning of a much larger shift in crypto trading.

The race is no longer just about building another exchange. It is about connecting deeper liquidity, faster execution, and increasingly sophisticated financial products. Bitcoin’s enormous capital base makes that opportunity particularly difficult to ignore.

#5360. Who calls NFL plays? How a play-caller differs from a coordinator

Free daily briefing on global business news.

NFL play-caller vs. coordinator roles explained, from helmet radios and booth versus sideline setups to why head coaches keep or hand over the play sheet

The coach with "offensive coordinator" as a job title is not always the coach deciding what happens on third down. In the NFL, the title and the decision can belong to two different people. One is a job title. The other is a game-day task. The NFL play-caller vs. coordinator split explains much of how a coaching staff divides its work on game day.

A coordinator is an assistant coach who runs one of a team's three units: offense, defense or special teams. The coordinator reports to the head coach and oversees the position coaches in that unit. During the week, the coordinator usually builds the game plan, runs meetings and teaches the scheme to players.

A play-caller does something narrower. That coach picks the specific play, formation or defensive call for each snap while the game is underway. On offense, the call travels by radio to the quarterback. On defense, it goes to one designated player wearing a radio helmet.

In many cases, the coordinator does both jobs. The play sheet can still sit with someone else. Some head coaches keep play-calling for themselves while a coordinator holds the title. Andy Reid, Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan have each been known for calling their own offense. In those setups, the coordinator's role leans toward planning and teaching rather than snap-by-snap decisions.

The difference shapes how credit and blame get handed out. Fans and media often judge an offense or defense by the coordinator's title, even when another coach chose the plays. It also affects how a head coach spends a game. A head coach who calls plays is managing the clock, challenges and personnel at the same time.

The 10 slides that follow break the distinction into its working parts. They cover what each role includes and why the two are separate responsibilities. They explain how the helmet radio and its green dot work, including the cutoff at 15 seconds on the play clock. They compare calling plays from the press box with calling them from the sideline. They also walk through what a defensive call contains and who decides fourth downs. The last slides cover how teams settle who gets the play sheet when they hire a coordinator.

An NFL play-caller is the coach who chooses the specific play, formation or defensive call for each snap of a game. The role is defined by that in-game decision, not by a job title.

On offense, the play-caller picks what the unit runs next. The choice can cover the play itself or the formation the offense lines up in. The call reaches the quarterback through a radio in his helmet.

On defense, the task means selecting the defensive call for the snap. That call does not go to the quarterback. It travels by radio to one designated defensive player instead.

The work repeats throughout the game. A play-caller does not make one choice before kickoff and then step back. Every snap requires a fresh decision, and that decision has to be made before the ball is snapped again.

Who holds the task varies from team to team. The coordinator for that unit usually calls the plays. A head coach can keep the task instead. That is why the play-caller and the coordinator are not always the same person.

Whichever coach holds the play sheet on game day is the one choosing, snap by snap, what the offense or defense runs.

An NFL coordinator is an assistant coach who runs one of a team's three units: the offense, the defense or special teams. The title describes a position in the staff hierarchy, not a single game-day task.

Each unit has its own coordinator. The offensive coordinator oversees the side of the ball trying to score. The defensive coordinator oversees the side trying to stop the opponent. The special teams coordinator oversees the groups that take the field for kicks, punts and returns.

The title sits in the middle of the coaching staff. A coordinator answers to the head coach, who holds authority over the whole team. Below the coordinator are the position coaches assigned to that unit.

That supervisory line is the core of the role. On offense, position coaches typically work with specific groups such as quarterbacks, running backs, wide receivers, tight ends and the offensive line. On defense, they typically handle the defensive line, linebackers and defensive backs. The coordinator directs those coaches so each position group fits the unit's overall approach.

Special teams is built differently from the other two units. Its coordinator does not oversee a fixed group of starters. Kick, punt and return units draw many of their players from the offense and the defense. They play alongside specialists such as the kicker, punter and long snapper. Many of those players also work under position coaches on offense or defense during the week.

The reporting line also limits a coordinator's independence. The head coach sets the direction for the team. The coordinator runs one unit within that direction and answers to the head coach for how it performs.

A coordinator title, on its own, does not settle who selects plays during a game. That task is assigned separately and is not automatically part of the job. An offensive coordinator may or may not be the coach sending in each call on a given Sunday.

Play-calling is one task inside a coordinator's job, not the whole job, and it can belong to someone else. A coordinator usually builds the weekly game plan, leads meetings and teaches the scheme. Choosing plays during the game is a distinct duty.

The two responsibilities sit at different points in the week. Coordinating happens mostly before kickoff. The game plan, the meetings and the teaching all shape what a unit is prepared to run on game day.

Play-calling starts once the game does. It is the choice of a specific play, formation or defensive call for each snap. That choice draws from the plan, but it is made in real time.

The tasks can be separated. One coach does not have to hold both. The coordinator title describes the assistant who runs the offense, the defense or the special teams unit. Nothing in that title requires the same person to pick each play.

A team can have a coordinator who designs and teaches the scheme while another coach makes the in-game calls. In that setup, the coordinator's work shows up in how the unit is prepared. The play-caller's work shows up in which part of that preparation gets used, and when.

The split can happen on either side of the ball. A head coach may keep the offensive calls. A head coach with a defensive background can take over the defensive calls instead. In either case, the coordinator keeps the title and the weekly preparation duties. Whoever holds the play sheet, the coordinator still reports to the head coach and oversees the unit's position coaches.

The overlap also explains why the two roles are easy to confuse. The coordinator usually holds both tasks. That makes the title and the task look like the same thing. They are not. One is a position on the staff chart. The other is a responsibility the staff assigns.

Andy Reid, Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan have each been known for calling their own offense as NFL head coaches. In that arrangement, the head coach picks the offensive plays on game day while an assistant holds the offensive coordinator title.

The setup separates a title from a task. The offensive coordinator keeps the title and still reports to the head coach. The head coach keeps the play sheet and makes the snap-by-snap offensive calls.

All three examples come from the offensive side of the ball. Each coach is associated with choosing the plays himself rather than passing that job to the assistant whose title suggests it.

A play-calling reputation describes what a coach has been known for. It does not show who holds the play sheet for a particular team in a particular season. A head coach can keep the duty or give it to a coordinator, and that choice can change.

The coordinator title alone cannot tell a viewer who chose a given play. In staffs run the way these three coaches have been known to run them, the answer sits with the head coach, not the coordinator.

The NFL lets a play-caller speak directly to the quarterback through a radio receiver inside his helmet. That helmet is marked with a green dot. The link cuts off when 15 seconds remain on the play clock.

Only one quarterback helmet carries the receiver, and the green dot shows which one it is. The coach choosing the play talks into a headset. The call travels from there to that single receiver, and no other offensive player hears it by radio.

The play has to reach the quarterback before the cutoff. After that point, the radio goes silent and he runs the snap without coaching input. Any adjustment from there has to come from the players on the field.

The cutoff makes timing part of the play-caller's job. Choosing the right call is not enough on its own. The call also has to arrive with enough time left for the quarterback to hear it before the link drops. A slow decision on the sideline or in the press box shrinks that window.

The defense uses its own version of the setup. One designated defensive player wears a helmet with a radio. That player is the defense's link to the coaching staff. The defensive call reaches the rest of the unit through him.

The two sides gained this tool at different times. League rules have allowed quarterback radios since 1994. Defensive radios followed in 2008, 14 years later. Through that stretch, only the offense could receive a call by helmet radio.

The 2008 change put both units on matching terms. Each side now works with the same basic arrangement: one connected helmet and one shared cutoff point on the play clock.

Those two limits shape how a coach uses the link. One helmet per unit means a single player carries each call to the rest of his teammates. The fixed cutoff sets how much a coach can say before a snap. It also marks the moment the players take over.

An NFL play-caller works from one of two places on game day: the press box or the sideline. The press box offers a higher view of formations, while the sideline offers direct contact with players.

The choice applies to offense and defense alike. Any coach who holds the play sheet, whether a coordinator or a head coach, works from one of these two spots.

From the press box, the play-caller looks down on the field from above. That elevated angle makes it easier to see how an opponent lines up before the snap. Formations are harder to read from ground level, where players block one another from view.

The sideline trades that overhead view for proximity. A caller standing on the field can talk with players in person between series. Those conversations happen face to face instead of being passed along by another coach.

Neither location cuts the play-caller off from the rest of the staff. Coaches in both spots wear headsets that link them during the game. A caller upstairs can stay in contact with coaches on the field. A caller on the sideline can hear from staff in the box.

The location shapes which kind of information reaches the play-caller most directly. Upstairs, it is the wider picture of the opponent's setup. On the field, it is the players who carry out each call.

A defensive play-call tells 11 players three things before the snap: the front, the coverage and whether to blitz.

The front describes how the defense lines up near the line of scrimmage. It sets where the defensive linemen and linebackers stand before the ball is snapped. A front choice shapes which gaps each player is responsible for against the run.

Fronts are often named by their personnel. A 4-3 front uses four down linemen and three linebackers. A 3-4 front uses three down linemen and four linebackers.

The coverage governs the players farther from the ball. It tells cornerbacks, safeties and linebackers how to handle receivers once the play begins. In man-to-man coverage, a defender follows one assigned player. In zone coverage, defenders guard areas of the field instead of specific opponents. Coverages are also named by structure. Cover 2, for example, splits the deep part of the field between two safeties.

The blitz is the optional part of the call. A blitz sends extra defenders after the quarterback, beyond the players who rush on a standard down. A linebacker or a defensive back can be the added rusher. An extra rusher usually leaves one fewer defender in coverage. That trade-off means the blitz and the coverage have to fit together.

Those three pieces travel as one call, not as separate instructions. The play-caller sends the full call to the one defender wearing a radio helmet. That player then passes it to teammates, either in the huddle or at the line of scrimmage.

The relay makes the radio-helmet player the link between the coaching staff and the rest of the unit. Every teammate depends on him to repeat the call accurately before the snap.

The defensive coordinator is the usual caller. A head coach with a defensive background can take that role instead. When that happens, the coordinator keeps the title. The head coach, not the coordinator, chooses the front, coverage and blitz on each snap.

The head coach generally has final say on fourth down, choosing whether to punt, kick a field goal or go for it. The special teams coordinator advises on that choice, and the head coach makes it.

Fourth down is a decision that sits above any single unit. It does not belong to the offense, the defense or special teams alone. It falls to the coach in charge of the whole team.

Each option sends a different group onto the field. A punt brings out the punting unit. A field goal try brings out the kicking unit. Going for it keeps the offense on the field.

The question on fourth down is not only which play to run. It is which unit takes the next snap.

The special teams coordinator manages the kicking, punting and return units. Two of the three fourth-down options use those units. That places the coordinator's advice inside two of the three choices a head coach weighs.

The return unit covers the other side of the kicking game. It takes the field when the opponent punts or kicks. That group also falls under the special teams coordinator.

The division matches how authority runs on a coaching staff. A coordinator runs a unit and gives input. The head coach decides questions that cross from one unit to another.

A coordinator calls plays only when the head coach hands over that duty. The decision often gets made when a team hires a coordinator. At that point, the head coach chooses whether to delegate the play sheet or keep it.

The authority to decide follows the reporting line. A coordinator answers to the head coach. The head coach therefore sets the terms of the job, including who picks the call for each snap.

The title alone does not settle the question. Two coaches can both be offensive coordinators on different staffs and still do different work on game day. One chooses the call for every snap. The other leaves that choice to the head coach once the game starts.

That split changes how much control one coach has over a unit. A coordinator who calls plays has more direct influence over the unit during games. The order of calls and the response to what the opponent shows run through that coach's headset.

A coordinator who does not call plays fills a different role. That coach works mainly as a planner and a teacher. The coordinator still builds the weekly game plan and teaches the scheme in meetings. That influence shows up in how the unit is prepared, not in the choice of each snap.

Game-day workload is one reason the duty gets delegated. A head coach who calls plays has to handle other game-day decisions at the same time. Many head coaches hand over the play sheet for that reason.

The same choice exists on defense. The defensive coordinator is the usual caller there. A head coach with a defensive background can take that role instead. In that case, the defensive coordinator moves into the planning role.

For a coaching candidate, the assignment shapes the job. Two openings with the same title can carry different authority on game day. One includes control of the play sheet, and the other does not.

Fans and media often give credit or blame for an NFL offense or defense to the coordinator, based on the title. That habit can miss the coach who actually chose each play during the game.

The title is the public label attached to a unit. Who holds the play sheet is harder to see from the stands or on a broadcast. A head coach can keep play-calling while an assistant carries the offensive coordinator title.

The same split can happen on defense. The defensive coordinator usually calls that side of the ball. A head coach with a defensive background can take over that role. The coordinator's name then stays attached to calls made by someone else.

When the roles sit with different coaches, the coordinator's name still tends to absorb the reaction. A stalled drive can be pinned on the coordinator even when the head coach made the call. The reverse also happens. A strong performance can be credited to the coordinator even when the in-game choices came from someone else.

The split is not all-or-nothing. A coordinator who does not call plays usually still builds the weekly game plan and teaches the scheme. That coordinator can shape the plan the calls come from without choosing a single snap.

The head coach's game-day load adds another layer. A head coach who calls plays is also managing the clock. That coach is deciding on challenges and handling personnel at the same time. Each of those duties competes for attention with the next call.

The gap between title and task shapes how a unit's results are judged. The coordinator title names who runs the unit. The play-calling assignment names who chose its plays in a given game. Those can be the same coach or two different ones. Knowing which coach holds the play sheet, not just the title, shows who made those calls.

#5359. ‘Dillon Brooks? On Kalshi? Hell nah’: LeBron James sues the sports betting app whose AI version of him said it

In an ad, LeBron James sits in an NBA locker room in a No. 23 jersey with “Bron” printed across the back, scrolling through bets on his phone. He stops on a photo of Phoenix Suns forward Dillon Brooks, one of his best-known on-court rivals. “Dillon Brooks? On Kalshi? Hell nah,” he says, in James’ voice.

Except it isn’t James. It’s an AI-generated version of him, made by a two-person startup to sell a sports betting app called Bron. And James, who has an exclusive endorsement deal with Kalshi-rival Polymarket, is now suing.

King James has been at the center of many notable brand deals—spanning massive contracts with Nike, Sprite, and of course, Polymarket. But the NBA’s oldest active player, and his company LBJ Trademarks LLC, is accusing the app’s creator PlayVision Inc. of exploiting his likeness in an AI-generated ad—and using an alleged affiliation with the star to promote itself.

The suit, filed on Nov. 17 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York against the app’s parent company and its cofounders Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby alleges trademark infringement, false endorsement and false advertising. According to the complaint, the founders are PlayVision’s only employees, and it includes  an argument that the company deliberately chose the name Bron and used an AI version of James in its marketing to capitalize on his global recognition.

“The word ‘Bron’ has no dictionary definition and no special meaning in the context of sports analytics, wagering, or artificial intelligence,” the filing read. “Rather, in the context of anything sports-related, it refers to only one man—LeBron James.”

The lawsuit describes the campaign as an effort to create the false impression that James was affiliated with the app, which offers sports betting research tools—including bet tracking and odds comparisons. The complaint is seeking an injunction preventing the defendants from using James’ name and likeness, repayment of profits generated through the alleged infringement, and compensatory and punitive damages.

The complaint accuses the appmakers of violating James’ right of publicity under a 1903 New York law, stemming from a woman whose portrait appeared without her consent on 25,000 posters of Franklin Mills flour—and led to New York State requiring written consent to use a person’s likeness in ads. It also leans on a far newer law: New York’s first-in-the-nation rule signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul in Dec. 2025 that requires ads to disclose when they use an AI-generated “synthetic performer.”

The Bron ad carried no such disclosure, the complaint says.

“The integrity of NBA competition—and the public’s confidence that players are not betting on the games they play—is of paramount importance to the league, its players and its fans,” the complaint stated.

Gupta posted the ad to his X account on Nov. 2 with the caption “Where is Bron?”—and the AI figure, shown mostly from behind, copies James’ build and tattoos. It speaks in what the suit says is a synthesized version of his voice. Another scene shows a rider in a Bron cap on a New York City subway car stopped at 14 Street.

The complaint says James’ betting deals, first with DraftKings and now with Polymarket, have focused on football, not basketball, because the NBA bars players from betting on NBA games. By showing him scrolling NBA player props and naming Kalshi, the suit argues, the ad “falsely communicates that Mr. James wagers, or considers wagering, on NBA games and NBA player performance.”

“The Ad catapulted the Bron App from obscurity to controversy, with the Ad gaining a million views within a day—exactly as Defendants intended,” the complaint read. “But Mr. James has no affiliation with Defendants or their product. Defendants’ intentional use of artificial intelligence to steal Mr. James’s name and likeness was instead an unlawful effort to trade on Mr. James’s identity to enrich Defendants.”

The suit alleges the founders built the ad to provoke James. “Defendants calculated that the value of that attention would exceed the cost of any legal consequences, and they treated the violation of Mr. James’s rights as a marketing expense,” it reads.

PlayVision, a California-based company founded in 2025 by Gupta and Zoghby, initially developed AI software designed to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans. Describing itself as “AI moneyball for sports,” the company later launched Bron as an app that marketed itself as a sports analytics and betting research platform—but by spring 2026, it pivoted to consumer betting. The Bron app pulls recommended wagers from more than 150 sportsbooks and prediction markets. It is free to download: Bron Pro costs $29.99 a month or $249.99 a year.

PlayVision and the Bron app did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune.

And according to the complaint, Gupta responded to a cease and desist letter from James’ team on Nov. 5 by suggesting the app would adopt a new name. However, the company had not announced a replacement name when James filed the suit. On Nov. 16, he wrote on X: “We found Bron. Apparently, the lawyers found it too. Find out our new name Wednesday. 10 AM PT.”

At 10:02 AM PT on Wednesday, Gupta posted another video on X showing they had renamed the app to Evie.

The filing, however, still said that’s too little, too late.

“They continue to use the Bron name to this day, prolonging the controversy for as long as it continues to generate attention for the Bron App and violating Mr. James’s rights to serve their marketing goals,” the filing read. “And even a belated name change now would not remedy the exploitation of Mr. James’s brand and goodwill that allowed Defendants to garner these millions of views and attention in the first place.”

The suit also identifies fellow NBA star and former James’ teammate Luka Doncic as another player whose likeness appeared in the app’s campaign. Doncic separately sent the company a cease-and-desist letter, according to the filing.

But that hasn’t intruded on the app’s stride. In response to the suits sent their way, Gupta posted on X—this time, an AI image of the two cofounders sitting in an empty courtroom with the caption: “Taking this to another court. We ain’t done yet.”

Joshua Hong is a News Fellow at Fortune covering data, AI, cybersecurity, energy, and retail.

#5358. Satya Nadella kicks off Microsoft Ignite with an Outlook outage mea culpa: ‘We have work to do’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:38 pm

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella opened his Ignite keynote Tuesday in San Francisco by addressing the elephant in the room: the global Outlook outage that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries last week.

Before getting to Copilot, agents or any of the event’s news, Nadella said the outage was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure has become as “the dial tone for the world.”

“We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” he said. “And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve.”

The line drew applause from the crowd, interrupting Nadella as he moved to thank the IT pros in the audience who kept their own organizations running through the outage.

It was a brief acknowledgment, and he didn’t go into what went wrong. Microsoft’s preliminary report blamed a bug in a fix it began rolling out in July, which its own automatic rerouting spread until most of the servers in a key Microsoft 365 gateway stopped responding. A final report is due Nov. 20.

From there, Nadella moved on to the main show. Watch the keynote below, and see updates here.

#5357. The speaker of the House holds the gavel, but the job covers much more

Free daily briefing on global business news.

What the speaker of the House does goes well beyond holding the gavel — 10 duties, from shaping floor votes to standing second in line for the presidency

The speaker of the House is best known as the person holding the gavel on the House floor. That image covers only a small share of the job. The speaker helps decide which bills reach a vote, shapes who sits on key committees and leads the majority party. The speaker also stands second in line for the presidency, behind only the vice president.

Any account of what the speaker of the House does starts with a split at the heart of the role. The speaker is an officer of the whole chamber, chosen by a vote of the full House. The speaker is also a party leader, the top-ranking member of whichever party holds the majority. Those two jobs sit side by side. One involves running the institution for every member. The other involves advancing a party's agenda and holding its majority together.

The powers attached to the office are real, but they are not unlimited. The speaker shares control of the floor with the majority leader and the Rules Committee. Rank-and-file members have tools of their own. A discharge petition can push a bill to a vote over leadership objections. A motion to vacate the chair can remove a sitting speaker.

The office's formal outline comes from a single clause in the Constitution. Much of its practical weight comes from House rules, precedent and party custom built up over more than two centuries. Sam Rayburn held the post longer than anyone else, a little over 17 years spread across several stretches between 1940 and 1961.

The 10 slides that follow break the job into its main parts. They cover how the Constitution creates the post, how members elect a speaker and how the speaker runs floor debate. They also explain the influence over scheduling and committees, the party leadership role and the place in presidential succession. The remaining slides cover administrative and ceremonial duties, along with the process for removing a speaker.

The speaker of the House exists because Article I, Section 2 of the Constitution says the House chooses its own speaker and other officers. That short provision is the legal footing for the office.

The power to choose belongs to the House alone. The clause gives the president and the Senate no role in the selection.

That arrangement makes the speaker an officer of the chamber itself. The person in the post owes the job to House members, not to another branch of government.

The same provision reaches beyond the speaker. It also lets the House pick the other officers who help run the institution, not only the person who presides over it.

Nothing in the text says the speaker must be a sitting member of the House. On paper, the chamber could elect someone from outside its ranks. It has never done so. Every speaker so far has been a member.

That unbroken pattern began with Frederick Muhlenberg, who became the first speaker in 1789.

The full House of Representatives elects its speaker at the opening of every new Congress. To win, a candidate needs a majority of the members who vote for a named person. Winning the most votes is not enough on its own.

That threshold depends on who casts a vote for someone. A member who answers "present" or is absent does not count toward the total. With all 435 seats filled and every member naming a candidate, the winning mark is 218 votes. Each "present" vote or absence lowers that mark. The number needed to win can then fall below half of the full chamber.

The first stage takes place before the floor vote. The majority party picks its nominee first, usually in a closed-door vote of its own conference. That private step is meant to line up the party behind one candidate before the whole chamber weighs in. The minority party usually nominates its own candidate as well.

The system relies on party unity. A nominee who loses even a few colleagues on the floor can fall short of a majority. The smaller the majority party's edge, the fewer defections it takes to stall the vote.

Kevin McCarthy's election in January 2023 showed what that looks like in practice. He won the speakership only on the 15th ballot. Every failed round sent the House back to vote again, because no candidate had yet cleared the majority mark.

Because the election takes place at the start of each Congress, the post is never held indefinitely. A sitting speaker who wants to stay in the job has to win the vote again when the next Congress convenes.

The process splits the choice between a party and the full chamber. The majority party chooses the nominee in private. The formal decision still belongs to every member who votes on the House floor.

The speaker of the House is the chamber's presiding officer. The speaker opens each session, recognizes members who want to speak and rules on points of order raised during floor proceedings.

Recognition is the starting point of the floor job. A member who wants to address the House does not simply begin talking. The member first needs recognition from the chair. Granting or withholding it is one of the speaker's presiding powers.

A point of order is an objection that the House is breaking one of its own rules. The presiding officer rules on each one, usually on the advice of the House parliamentarian. Those rulings become precedents that later presiding officers consult.

A ruling from the chair is not always final. Any member can appeal it to the full House, which then decides the question by majority vote. The majority often moves to table such an appeal. If that motion passes, the ruling stands.

The speaker does not have to sit in the chair for every hour of debate. Under House rules, the speaker can name another member to act as speaker pro tempore. That designation can last up to three legislative days without the House's approval. The handoff happens often during routine debate. The member holding the gavel on a given afternoon is frequently someone other than the speaker.

The speaker also steps aside when the House sits as the Committee of the Whole House on the state of the Union. That is the procedural form the House often uses to debate and amend bills. The speaker appoints a different member to chair it.

The speaker keeps the right to vote as a member of the House. In practice, the speaker usually does not cast a vote. House rules do not require the speaker to vote in ordinary proceedings.

There are two main exceptions to that habit. The speaker may vote on major questions. The speaker may also vote when a single ballot would break a tie.

The speaker of the House, working with the majority leader and the Rules Committee, largely decides which bills reach a vote on the House floor. That control over the agenda is one of the job's main sources of power. It is shared, though, not held by the speaker alone.

A bill that clears a House committee has no guaranteed path to the floor. Thousands of bills are introduced in each Congress, and most never receive a floor vote.

The majority leader manages the day-to-day floor schedule and announces the coming week's business. The speaker sets the broader priorities that the schedule follows. Decisions on major legislation are usually made by the two leaders together, in consultation with committee chairs and the majority party's members.

For most significant bills, the route to the floor runs through the Rules Committee. The committee writes a resolution, known as a special rule, that sets the terms of debate. The rule specifies how long members may debate a bill and which amendments, if any, may be offered. The full House must adopt that rule by majority vote before it takes up the bill itself.

A second route covers less contested measures. Under a procedure called suspension of the rules, a bill comes up with 40 minutes of debate and no floor amendments. Passage then requires a two-thirds vote of the members present and voting. Under House rules, the speaker has discretion over whether to recognize members to offer suspension motions.

The majority party also follows informal practices about what it brings forward. The best known is the Hastert rule, named for former Speaker Dennis Hastert. It describes a practice of bringing up only bills backed by a majority of the majority party. It is a custom rather than a written House rule, and speakers have set it aside on some votes.

Members who want to get around the leadership have one main formal tool: the discharge petition. A petition can be filed once a bill has sat in committee for 30 legislative days. If 218 members sign it, the bill can be forced to the floor over the leadership's objections.

That threshold equals a majority of the full 435-member House. When the minority party holds fewer than 218 seats, its members cannot complete a petition on their own. They need signatures from at least some members of the majority party.

The speaker of the House shapes several House committees by choosing who sits on them. In practice, the speaker names the majority-party members of the Rules Committee, along with the House members of conference committees and some select committees.

The Rules Committee writes the resolutions, known as rules, that govern how a bill is handled on the floor. A rule sets how long debate runs and which amendments members may offer. A rule that blocks amendments can keep a bill's text intact all the way to the final vote.

The speaker once ran that panel directly. Until the 1910 revolt against Speaker Joseph Cannon, the speaker chaired the Rules Committee.

Today the speaker does not hold the chairmanship. The speaker still picks the panel's majority-party members, however. Through those picks, the speaker keeps a direct tie to the committee that sets the terms of floor debate.

Conference committees are temporary panels of House and Senate negotiators. They resolve differences between the two chambers' versions of the same bill. The speaker chooses the House side of those teams. Those appointees represent the chamber while a final text is worked out. The compromise they reach then returns to both chambers for a vote.

Select committees are created for a set purpose, often an investigation, instead of serving as permanent standing panels. The speaker names the members of some of these committees. Those choices shape who conducts an investigation and how it proceeds.

Speaker Nancy Pelosi used that authority in 2021. She appointed the members of the House select committee on the Jan. 6 attack. Pelosi had become the first woman to serve as speaker in 2007.

These appointment powers have limits. Choosing committee members does not give the speaker sole control of the House. The majority leader and the wider majority party also influence how the Rules Committee's work reaches the floor.

The speaker of the House is the highest-ranking member of the majority party in the chamber. The speaker is also that party's public face, the person most closely identified with what the House majority wants to do.

That party post sits inside the same office that runs the chamber. The speaker presides over the House on behalf of all its members. The same person also leads one side of it.

The party side of the job centers on holding the majority together. That task grows harder when the margin is narrow. A slim majority leaves little room for members of the speaker's own party to break ranks on a vote.

The arithmetic of a close House shows why. If the minority party votes as a bloc against a measure, a small group of defectors from the majority can be enough to defeat it. That gives a handful of members leverage over the speaker. They can ask for changes to a bill as the price of their support.

The party role also explains why the speaker draws so much public attention. As the majority's most visible figure, the speaker stands in for the party in the House. No rank-and-file member carries that role. When the majority's agenda moves forward or stalls, the speaker is usually the person asked to account for it.

The political weight of the office has deep roots. In the early 1800s, Henry Clay built the speakership into a post that drove policy. Under Clay, the office became a seat of political leadership as well as the chair of the chamber. The modern speakership still carries both parts: chairing the House and pushing the majority's agenda.

The speaker of the House is second in line to the presidency. Under the Presidential Succession Act of 1947, only the vice president stands ahead of the speaker.

The 1947 law also sets the order behind the speaker. The president pro tempore of the Senate comes next. Members of the Cabinet follow after that.

The result places two officers of Congress ahead of every Cabinet member. The speaker and the Senate president pro tempore both outrank the executive branch's department heads in the line of succession.

The arrangement ties the presidency to a post the House fills by its own vote. The officer second in line is the person the House has chosen to run its chamber.

The speaker of the House swears in members at the start of each new Congress and signs enrolled bills before they go to the president. Both duties are formal steps that the chamber's business depends on.

The oath itself comes from the Constitution. Article VI requires members of Congress to be bound by an oath or affirmation to support the Constitution. The oath is the step that turns a member-elect into a sworn member of the House.

On opening day, the newly elected speaker first takes the oath from the dean of the House, the longest continuously serving member. The speaker then administers the oath to the other members together. They raise their right hands and take it as a group, returning members alongside first-term ones.

The House also elects its own officers at the start of each Congress. They include the Clerk, the Sergeant at Arms, the Chief Administrative Officer and the Chaplain. The full chamber chooses them, and the speaker does not appoint them alone. Once in place, they answer to the House leadership. Between them, the Clerk, the Sergeant at Arms and the Chief Administrative Officer keep the chamber's records, security and day-to-day operations running.

Signing enrolled bills happens at the other end of the legislative process. An enrolled bill is the final official copy of a measure that both chambers have passed in identical form. It is printed on parchment by the chamber where the bill began.

The speaker signs that copy. The Senate's presiding officer signs it as well. The signatures attest that the text is the version Congress approved. They do not change any of its contents. House rules also let the speaker designate another member to sign enrolled bills in the speaker's place.

Only after both signatures can the bill be presented to the president. Article I, Section 7 gives the president 10 days, Sundays excepted, to sign or veto it once it arrives. A delay in signing at the Capitol pushes back when that clock starts.

The speaker presides over joint sessions of Congress together with the Senate's presiding officer. The speaker also invites the president to deliver the State of the Union address.

A joint session brings the House and the Senate together for a single proceeding. Neither chamber's officer runs it alone. The speaker shares the rostrum with the Senate's presiding officer, so each chamber has its top officer at the front of the room.

That shared arrangement sets joint sessions apart from ordinary House business. On a normal legislative day, only House members take part, and the Senate conducts its own proceedings separately.

The State of the Union starts with the speaker's invitation. The speaker sends it to the president. The president then appears before both chambers to deliver the address.

The invitation runs from the legislative branch to the executive. The address takes place at the speaker's invitation rather than on the president's own initiative.

During the speech, the speaker sits behind the president. The vice president sits beside the speaker. The arrangement places the officers tied to the House and the Senate side by side for the length of the address.

The speaker comes from the party that holds the House majority. That party is not always the president's party. When the two differ, a leader of the opposing party sits behind the president for the full address.

A motion to vacate the chair is the procedure the House uses to remove a sitting speaker. The House first voted a speaker out on Oct. 3, 2023, when members removed Speaker Kevin McCarthy by a vote of 216 to 210.

If the motion passes, the speaker's chair becomes vacant. The House then has no elected speaker until it chooses a new one.

The McCarthy vote was decided by a margin of six votes. It came in the same Congress that had elected him to the post only months earlier. A switch by a handful of members would have changed the result.

The vacancy lasted 22 days. During that stretch, Patrick McHenry served as speaker pro tempore. He held the chair on a temporary basis and was not elected speaker. McHenry treated the role as limited mainly to overseeing the election of a successor. The House passed no legislation while the chair stayed empty. Floor business effectively waited on the outcome of the speaker race. The vacancy ended on Oct. 25, 2023, when the House elected Mike Johnson.

The rules that govern the motion are set by the House itself. They can change from one Congress to the next. In the 119th Congress, House rules require nine members of the majority party to back a motion to vacate before it is privileged.

A privileged motion takes precedence over ordinary business on the floor. Under the 119th Congress rule, that status depends on support from members of the speaker's own party. Members of the minority party cannot make the motion privileged by themselves. As a result, the most direct threat of removal comes from inside the majority conference rather than from the opposing party.

The motion gives the full House a check on the person it elected to run the chamber. The same body that chooses a speaker can also take the job away.

#5356. Washington convinces 4 AI chatbots to plan terror attacks as flawed patches across the internet breaks banks and airlines

Government investigators posing as would-be attackers got ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok to produce workable plans for a bombing and an attack on the power grid, each in less than 12 hours, according to a Government Accountability Office report released Wednesday.

The report landed at the end of a week in which AI has already been tied to real damage, though nobody has blamed a terrorist. On Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton linked an outage on the NSA’s classified network to patching, saying institutions are patching “because these vulnerabilities have been identified,” on Fox Business. “That is what has happened at the NSA today,” he said. Fox Business reported the flaws in question were in PHP, which AI-assisted researchers found over the summer. Testifying before the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday, Clayton called the week’s breakdowns at Microsoft, the FAA, banks and the NSA “separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes,” according to The Washington Post.

“If Congress does not act, it is a question of when—not if—a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, the New Hampshire Democrat who requested the report, said, per Nextgov. She plans to hold at least one hearing on AI safety early next year.

Every chatbot’s safeguards were triggered, and testers got around them “by using common safeguard-bypassing techniques,” GAO wrote. Two of the chatbots produced plans for an improvised explosive device meant to cause mass casualties, aimed at a hotel parking garage and a convention center. The other two gave instructions for attacking electrical substations, naming specific drone and firearm models and how to buy them.

“We got the nefarious information that we were after. So, in this case, those safeguards didn’t work,” said Kevin Walsh, GAO’s director of IT and cybersecurity. The report cites a June statement in which Anthropic said every safeguard used in the industry is vulnerable to jailbreaks.

The caveats matter. Each platform was tested on a single scenario, and Walsh said the testing doesn’t represent “a statistically significant sample.” GAO won’t say which chatbot produced which plan. It defines “viable” as meaning a person “would likely be able to carry out the actions,” and it didn’t test every step. GAO found some details were wrong: in one case, a chatbot’s map put roads in the wrong places. OpenAI told ABC the testing “took place months ago on an older version of ChatGPT,” and Google said it used “earlier models.” Anthropic wrote that it doesn’t dispute “a determined tester can get harmful content” from its system.

GAO made no recommendations. The report doesn’t address AI’s role in finding software flaws, or patching.

Bug hunters have logged 100,222 software vulnerabilities so far this year, more than double 2025’s total, according to a VulnCheck count that crossed 100,000 on Nov. 13, The Register reported. “There’s no denying the fact that vulnerability hunting with AI is driving a majority of what we’re seeing,” VulnCheck’s Josh Bressers said. Microsoft fixed 1,094 flaws on its Nov. 10 Patch Tuesday, after 1,474 in October.

Each one is a patch someone has to install. “Emergency patches go into core infrastructure within hours, often without the full testing cycle,” Yuval Itzchakov, CTO and co-founder of the offensive security company A Security, told Reuters. “That speed and scale of change is itself a source of failure.”

The PHP flaws show the squeeze. AI-assisted teams at OpenAI, Wiz and Calif found bugs affecting every PHP version released in the last decade, Fortune reported when they were disclosed Oct. 21. PHP runs 70% of websites, according to Wiz. The PHP Foundation told sites to patch immediately or go offline until they could.

Sen. Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, extended the patching explanation to the rest of the week. “If you’re trying to patch 10 or 12 in a single week, you have these kind of outages,” he said on CNN, per a transcript.

The companies, the NSA and the FAA blamed AI on the record. The NSA said its outage came during “scheduled routine maintenance,” per Politico. The FAA blamed legacy equipment, and asked whether its upgrades caused the ground stop, it said “No.” Microsoft blamed its outage in part on a bug introduced in a July update, and Chase blamed a software bug.

Most of the flaws AI is finding will never be used in an attack. Only about 1.4% of this year’s vulnerabilities are in VulnCheck’s catalog of known exploited flaws. They still have to be patched.

Chris Krebs, former director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, said on NBC’s TODAY that the outages weren’t attacks but companies finding vulnerabilities with AI and patching them. “The patching is not done. The vulnerability discovery is not done,” he said. “The next 12 to 18 months are going to be a bumpy ride.”

#5355. Seattle tech vet and Sounders FC minority owner Chee Chew joins front office to lead AI push

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am

Chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a new job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI.

Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club announced Tuesday.

“His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer said in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.”

Chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation company toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment.

He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the company’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live.

Chew said his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams.

“In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.”

Chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he said. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids.

The couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry. Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others.

A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew said.

The job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he said.

Talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew said.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years. It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”

Chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help?

On the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with Anthropic’s Claude. “By the time I landed, I sent it to them and said, ‘OK, give this a try,’” he said. The club used it in an experiment to scale up performance marketing before a match.

It’s the kind of hands-on building Chew says he’s been doing a lot of lately.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years,” he said. “It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”

He recently ran an AI analysis of one player’s game, based on stats such as touches, expected goals and distance run. It pointed out strengths and areas to improve. The player was “very hungry for it,” Chew said, and asked if they could do it every game.

The club’s performance analytics group, led by data analyst Tyler Cox, was already ahead of much of the organization, and Chew said he’s helping speed up that work with AI.

The bigger challenge is getting people to change how they work, Chew said. At Zapier, he saw many companies struggle to get results from AI, with some spending “massive token budgets” without a big win. He said the answer is blending AI with traditional automation and fitting it into how people already work.

“It has to be approachable for folks,” he said. “You can’t go in and just throw everything up and start from scratch.”

The Sounders host Real Salt Lake in the wild-card round of the MLS Cup Playoffs on Thursday at Lumen Field. Asked whether AI could help figure out a win, Chew passed.

“I don’t want to get involved and interfere with our coaching staff,” he said.
