#5354. Why a House speaker needs a majority of votes cast, not always 218

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How the House elects a speaker, from private party nomination votes to the Clerk-run roll call, the majority threshold, repeated ballots, the oath and the motion to vacate

The top job in the House of Representatives is filled by a vote the Constitution barely describes. The founding document says the House shall choose its Speaker. It says nothing about nominations, ballots, majorities or what happens when no one wins. Those details come from party custom and House precedent.

Understanding how the House elects a speaker starts with a simple point: the process happens in two stages. The first is private. After a November election, each party's House members gather behind closed doors to pick a nominee. The second is public. On the opening day of a new Congress, the full House votes by roll call, with each voting member answering aloud. Only that second vote makes someone Speaker.

The stakes are practical as well as political. Until a Speaker is chosen, the House does not swear in its members or adopt the rules that govern its work. A smooth vote takes one ballot. A divided majority can turn opening day into a days-long standoff.

Recent history shows both ends of that range. In January 2023, Kevin McCarthy needed 15 ballots to win the gavel. That was the most for a Speaker election since before the Civil War. Mike Johnson won on the first ballot on Jan. 3, 2025. The same rules produced both results.

The process does not end with the vote. A sitting Speaker can be removed through a motion to vacate the chair. Once in office, the Speaker presides over the House floor and stands second in the line of presidential succession, behind the vice president.

This guide walks through each step in order. It starts with the constitutional text and the party nomination votes. It then covers the opening-day roll call run by the Clerk of the House, the majority a candidate needs and what happens when ballots fail. It closes with the oath, the rules for removal and the powers that come with the office.

The Constitution gives the House of Representatives the power to choose its own Speaker, and it says very little else about the job. Article I, Section 2, Clause 5 states that the House "shall chuse their Speaker and other Officers."

The spelling "chuse" was a common 18th-century form of "choose." That short clause settles one question: who makes the choice. The House picks its presiding officer. No other branch of government has a role in the selection.

The same clause gives the House one more power. It closes by granting the chamber "the sole Power of Impeachment."

The Senate works under a different arrangement. Article I, Section 3 makes the vice president the President of the Senate. Senators choose their other officers, including a president pro tempore to preside when the vice president is absent. The House has no outside presiding officer of that kind. Its leader comes from its own vote.

The text also leaves gaps. It does not name anyone to lead the chamber before a Speaker takes the chair.

The "other Officers" are left undefined as well. The Constitution does not list who they must be or what duties they carry. Today, House Rule II provides for the election of a Clerk, a Sergeant at Arms, a Chief Administrative Officer and a Chaplain.

The text sets no membership requirement for the Speaker. Nothing in the Constitution says the person chosen must hold a House seat. Under the plain wording, the House could elect someone from outside the chamber.

The House has never done so. Every Speaker has been a member of the House at the time of election. The House elected its first Speaker, Frederick Muhlenberg of Pennsylvania, on April 1, 1789, during the First Congress.

The constitutional basis for the office is a single line. Everything else about the Speaker election, from party nominations to the floor roll call, was built by the House itself.

Each party picks its candidate for Speaker in a private vote of its own House members, held after the November election. That nomination is only a first step. It does not make anyone Speaker. The post is filled by a vote of the full House on the floor.

The two parties run this step through separate organizations. House Republicans meet as the House Republican Conference. House Democrats meet as the House Democratic Caucus. The names differ, but the job at this stage is the same: settle on one person the party will back when the new Congress opens.

These meetings happen behind closed doors. The public learns the outcome, not the internal debate that produced it. The floor vote that follows is different. On opening day, each member's choice becomes part of the public record.

The November 2022 Republican race shows how a party nomination works in practice. Kevin McCarthy, then the House Republican leader, faced a challenge from Andy Biggs of Arizona. Biggs was a former chairman of the House Freedom Caucus. McCarthy won the conference nomination 188 to 31.

That margin gave McCarthy his party's nomination. It did not settle who would hold the gavel. A conference vote measures support inside one party. The floor vote measures support across the entire chamber. The two results do not always match.

The gap matters most when the majority party holds a narrow edge. A nominee in that position has little room to lose votes from within the party. Members who oppose their party's pick in a private meeting are free to carry that opposition into the public roll call.

For the minority party, the private vote serves a different purpose. Its nominee cannot win the speakership while the majority party stays united behind its own candidate. The vote instead settles whose name the party will place in nomination when the House convenes.

A new Congress convenes at noon on Jan. 3, the date set by the 20th Amendment, unless Congress passes a law choosing another day. Until the House elects a Speaker, the Clerk of the House runs the chamber and confirms a quorum before any vote begins.

The Jan. 3 start date goes back to 1933, when the 20th Amendment was ratified. Before then, the Constitution directed Congress to assemble on the first Monday in December. Under that schedule, a newly elected House often did not hold its first regular session until more than a year after its members won their seats.

The amendment's exception clause gets regular use. Congress has used it to set a different opening day by law. The 112th Congress convened on Jan. 5, 2011, and the 114th Congress convened on Jan. 6, 2015.

An officer who is not a member of Congress presides over the opening session. The Clerk is an officer elected by the House to keep its records and manage much of its legislative and administrative work.

Federal law keeps the Clerk from the previous Congress on the job when the new House assembles. That continuity fills the gap before the new House has chosen any officers of its own.

The same law assigns the Clerk a first task. The Clerk prepares the roll of members-elect from the certificates of election that states send after the November vote. That roll is the official list of people who may answer when the House is called to order.

Before the Speaker election starts, the Clerk confirms that a quorum is present. Members-elect record their presence, and the Clerk announces whether enough have responded for the House to proceed. Only then does the chamber move to nominations.

The Clerk's job on opening day is limited to keeping order and conducting the election. If the voting stretches over several days, the Clerk stays in the chair for each session until a Speaker is chosen.

Speaker candidates enter the House contest through formal nominations made on the floor. The chair of each party's conference or caucus rises to place the party's nominee in nomination. The minority party nominates a candidate too, usually its own leader.

Nominations come at the start of the opening-day proceedings, before any member casts a vote. The Clerk of the House recognizes each nominating member in turn. Each name usually comes with a short nominating speech that lays out the party's case for its candidate.

Republicans give the task to the chair of the House Republican Conference. Democrats give it to the chair of the House Democratic Caucus. Each chair is a party officer elected by the party's own House members. A nomination from that officer presents the nominee as the choice of the party as a body, not of a single ally.

The minority party goes through the same formal step. Its nominee is typically the party's top leader in the House. At the opening of the new Congress on Jan. 3, 2023, Hakeem Jeffries was the Democratic nominee.

The minority holds fewer seats than the majority, so its nominee usually lacks the votes to win. The nomination still gives the party's members a named candidate to support when their names are called. It also puts the party's leader on the record as its choice for the chair.

A nomination is not a vote, and it does not close the field. Party chairs make the main nominations, but other members may also rise to place a name before the House. Members can even answer the roll call with the name of someone who was never nominated. Those answers are recorded like any other vote for a named person.

The nominations frame the contest without deciding it. They tell members and the public which candidates the parties are formally backing before balloting begins. Once the names are in, the Clerk moves to the roll call that settles the result.

The House elects its Speaker through a spoken roll call. The Clerk of the House calls each member's name in alphabetical order, and each member answers aloud with the name of the person they want as Speaker.

That spoken format sets the Speaker election apart from most House business. Most recorded votes in the chamber are cast electronically, with members using voting cards at stations on the floor. The Speaker vote does not use that system. Every choice is said out loud, one member at a time.

The call runs through members' surnames from A to Z. Party and seniority do not affect the order. A Republican and a Democrat with neighboring last names answer one after the other.

Members answer with a name rather than "yea" or "nay." The vote is therefore not a simple up-or-down decision on one nominee. A member can name the majority party's candidate or the minority party's candidate. A member can also name someone who was never formally placed in nomination. Whatever name a member gives is recorded as a vote for that person. A member may also answer "present," which records attendance without backing any candidate.

Tellers keep the count as the names are called. These tellers are House members, typically drawn from both parties. A bipartisan count gives each side a direct view of the tally as it builds.

Once the call is complete, the Clerk announces the result. The announcement lists each person who received votes and the number each received. It also states whether any candidate reached the majority needed to win.

The spoken format also leaves a full public record. Every member's choice is heard in the chamber and captured in the official roll call. The Congressional Record prints each member's name alongside the candidate that member supported. Constituents, party leaders and reporters can see exactly how each member voted.

A candidate for Speaker wins by taking a majority of the votes cast for a named person, not a fixed number of seats. The figure of 218 applies only when all 435 members vote and each one names a candidate.

That makes 218 a figure tied to one set of conditions rather than a permanent requirement. The real target can sit below it.

The base of the calculation is the group of members who actually vote for someone by name. When the 435-member House has every member naming a candidate, a majority of that group is 218.

Absences change the math. A member who is not on the floor during the roll call casts no vote. That member drops out of the total that the majority is measured against, and the number required falls with it.

A "present" vote has the same effect on the count. A member who answers "present" takes part in the roll call but backs no named candidate. That answer does not name a person. It is left out of the base used to set the majority. The bar drops again.

This gives a reluctant member a choice beyond backing the nominee or voting for someone else. A lawmaker who will not support the leading candidate can answer "present" or stay away instead of naming a rival. Either step lowers the number the leading candidate needs. It does not add a vote to that candidate's total.

Votes for other named candidates work differently. A member who names someone other than the front-runner stays in the base. That vote keeps the threshold where it is.

The exact number a Speaker needs is set by the votes actually cast. It can be confirmed only once the roll call is complete and every response has been counted. A candidate can therefore win with fewer than 218 votes when absences or "present" answers shrink the base.

If no candidate wins a majority on the first ballot, the House votes again. It keeps holding new roll calls until one candidate wins a majority, and no rule caps the number of ballots.

Each new ballot starts from scratch. The House does not drop the last-place candidate. It does not hold a runoff between the top two finishers or hand the job to whoever leads. The same majority rule applies on every round.

Members are free to change their votes between rounds. A member can stay with an earlier choice, move to another candidate or name a person who drew no support on the previous ballot. Candidates can also be placed in nomination again before a later roll call.

The Clerk of the House stays in the chair through every round. The House can adjourn between ballots and return later. That pause can give party leaders time to negotiate with holdouts away from the floor.

Kevin McCarthy's election at the start of 2023 shows how long the process can run. The California Republican became Speaker on the 15th ballot, on Jan. 7, 2023. Fourteen roll calls had ended without a winner before that one.

A century earlier, the House faced a similar deadlock. Frederick Gillett won the speakership on the ninth ballot in 1923. Eight rounds had failed to produce a majority before members settled on him.

A first-ballot win remains the usual result. Repeated ballots typically arise when the majority party's own members do not unite behind its nominee.

With a narrow majority, a small group of dissenters can withhold enough votes to block their own party's nominee. That can happen even after the nominee has won the private party vote. A dissenter can vote for another person, vote "present" or skip a ballot. Each of those choices changes the count on that round. The number of votes a candidate needs can therefore shift from one ballot to the next.

The Dean of the House, the chamber's longest-serving member, administers the oath of office to a newly elected Speaker. The Speaker then swears in the rest of the members, and the House turns to adopting its rules package.

Before taking the oath, the Speaker-elect is escorted to the chair. By custom, the leader of the other party introduces the winner and hands over the gavel.

The Speaker goes first in this sequence. Until the Speaker vote ends, the people seated in the chamber are members-elect, not sworn members. The new Speaker becomes the first of them to take the oath.

The oath itself traces to Article VI of the Constitution. It requires senators and representatives to be bound by oath or affirmation to support the Constitution. A member-elect becomes a sworn member only after taking it.

The Dean's part in the ceremony rests on seniority, not party. The title goes to whichever member has the longest continuous service in the House. The member who swears in the Speaker can therefore come from the party that lost the gavel.

Once sworn, the Speaker administers the oath to the other members-elect. They take it together as a group on the floor, not one at a time. That single oath turns the members-elect into a sworn House.

With its members sworn, the House also elects its officers, including the Clerk, the Sergeant at Arms and the Chaplain. Those posts are usually filled by adopting a single resolution rather than by separate roll calls.

The rules package comes next. It sets the procedures the chamber will follow for the two-year Congress that has just begun. Adopting it is a separate vote of the full House.

That vote is needed at the start of every Congress. Unlike the Senate, the House is not treated as a continuing body. Its rules do not carry over on their own. Each new House adopts a set, usually building on the previous Congress's rules with changes.

A motion to vacate the chair is the House's way to remove a sitting Speaker. Under the House rules in force in 2023, any member could offer one. On Oct. 3, 2023, the House voted 216 to 210 to remove Kevin McCarthy. He was the first Speaker removed this way.

The motion puts one question to the full chamber: should the office of Speaker be declared vacant? It does not name a replacement. A successful vote ends the sitting Speaker's tenure. Choosing a successor is a separate step.

That split shapes how a removal vote comes together. Members who back a removal do not have to agree on who should hold the gavel next. They only have to agree that the current Speaker should go. A small group of majority-party members can join with the opposing party to reach a majority. Neither side needs a shared plan for what follows.

Six votes separated the 216 members who backed the motion against McCarthy from the 210 who opposed it. The vote came about nine months into his tenure. The motion needs only a simple majority of the members voting. A narrow margin is enough to carry it.

Removing McCarthy left the chair without an elected Speaker. A Speaker pro tempore, drawn from a list McCarthy had filed in advance, presided in the meantime. The House had to run the full election process again, starting with new party nominations. Mike Johnson won the office on Oct. 25, 2023, by a vote of 220 to 209. His election came 22 days after the removal vote.

The two tallies measured different things. The first showed a majority willing to end a speakership. The second showed a majority able to agree on a replacement. Assembling that second majority took more than three weeks.

Under the 2023 rule, a Speaker could face a removal vote at any point in a Congress, not only on the day of the election. The possibility of removal stayed open for the full term.

The Speaker of the House presides over floor proceedings, decides which members are recognized and sets the floor schedule. The office also ranks second in the line of presidential succession, behind only the vice president, under the Presidential Succession Act of 1947.

Each of the three floor powers covers a different part of the chamber's work. Presiding means the Speaker runs House sessions from the chair. Recognition decides which member gets the floor at a given moment.

Control of the floor schedule decides which measures come up for consideration and when. A bill that never reaches the floor cannot get a vote of the full House. The person who sets the calendar shapes what the chamber takes up at all.

These powers put order in the chamber and the flow of its business in the same hands. The member who wins the opening-day roll call gains control over what the House debates, not only a title.

The succession role reaches beyond the House. If both the presidency and the vice presidency were vacant, the Speaker would be next in line. That ranking links a post filled by a vote of House members to the executive branch.

The Speaker's place in the order comes from a statute, the 1947 act, rather than from the Constitution's text. The place in line belongs to the office, not to any individual. Whoever holds the Speaker's chair occupies that position in the succession order. When a new Speaker is elected, including after a removal, the place in line passes to that person.

#5353. ‘70% chance’ we’re already in an AI bubble: The economist who said ‘not yet’ in January now sees all four horsemen of the bubble apocalypse

Owen Lamont told Fortune in January that the stock market wasn’t in an AI bubble. Now he’s mostly convinced.

“I think there is a 70% chance that as of November 2026 we are already in an AI bubble in the U.S. stock market,” Lamont, a portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management and a former University of Chicago finance professor, told Fortune in an email. “I think a lot has changed this year.”

What changed is the one signal he used to say was missing. Lamont tracks what he calls the “four horsemen of the bubble apocalypse”: overvaluation, bubble beliefs, issuance and inflows of new money. At the time, he said three were present. The holdout was issuance, meaning companies selling new stock to the public. Back then, U.S. firms had bought back roughly $1 trillion of their own shares over the past year, and Lamont treats corporate executives as the “smart money.” They weren’t selling.

They are now. U.S. companies issued a net $2.4 trillion of stock over the 12 months to Nov. 12, by Lamont’s count. In the 12 months to November 2025, they bought back a net $69 billion, and a year before that, $397 billion. In his latest Owenomics blog post, he walks back his January headline: “Today, I would no longer write those words.”

“I think we basically have all four horsemen now,” he told Fortune.

The big number has a big asterisk. Of the $2.4 trillion issuance, $2.2 trillion comes from SpaceX’s June IPO, which Lamont’s method counts at its full market value. Strip it out and net issuance is $192 billion.

That’s still a reversal from net buybacks a year earlier, and the turn includes the biggest names: the Magnificent Seven went from net buybacks of $144 billion in the year to November 2024 to net issuance of $276 billion now, according to Lamont. He writes that Alphabet and Meta switched from buying back shares to issuing them, Tesla sharply increased issuance, and Meta announced plans to raise nearly $98 billion in equity to fund its AI spending.

Lamont admits the SpaceX question is “tough.” “I think one company is not enough to constitute a ‘wave of issuance,’” he said. “On the other hand, we live in a world of concentrated stock markets where a handful of companies have huge market cap, so maybe we should expect waves of issuance that are also concentrated.”

Professional investors are moving the other way: fund managers just cut their net overweight in tech to 12% from 37%, the biggest one-month drop since June 2006, according to Bank of America’s November survey.

Why companies are selling is the open question. In his note, Lamont laid out two explanations: “the smart money is selling because the market is overpriced,” or firms “need to fund the AI buildout.” Asked which he leans toward, he said: “I’m not sure. Could be both.”

Either way, the shares are going to someone. TD Securities’ rates strategists flagged the same shift from the bond side this week, noting that Meta and Oracle have issued equity and that more AI capex funded with stock could ease pressure on long-term Treasury yields.

He also thinks the case for overvaluation got stronger this year because real long-term interest rates rose about 100 basis points. But he isn’t calling a top. “It is not a slam dunk case: the market might be overvalued, but it is not absurdly overvalued,” he said. “Net issuance has turned positive, but it’s not strongly positive.”

By his measure, net issuance is running at 3.1% of total market value, still below the peaks of the 1999–2000 tech bubble and the 2021 COVID boom.

Lamont gave Fortune three conditions that would take him from 70% to a flat call.

“First, the Anthropic IPO occurs and is a success. Second, we see a wave of smaller IPOs, similar to what we saw in 2021: hundreds of IPOs, say five IPOs a week, many of them doubling on the first day. Third, CAPE ratio or other valuation ratios blow through prior records.”

The second one is far off. The U.S. had 90 IPOs in 2025, against 311 in 2021 and 677 in 1996, according to Jay Ritter’s data cited in Lamont’s March note. In January, he told Fortune the shortage of IPOs was “baffling,” and that a full bubble could look like the Nasdaq 100 doubling in a year with the Shiller CAPE ratio near 80. It was around 40 then.

The first condition is about a day away. Anthropic is set to price its IPO Wednesday and begin trading on Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT. Lamont writes that the deal, if it goes ahead, would push issuance above its 2021 peak. Asked if that’s the moment to watch, he said yes, and pointed back to his three conditions.

#5352. Seattle police unleash dog-like robot whose best trick is bomb dispoal

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:43 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:43 am

Seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech. Now they’ve got a piece of tech that looks like a dog.

It’s a big upgrade for the squad, which has handled more than 600 calls so far this year. SPD’s main bomb robot is nearly 20 years old, weighs more than 100 pounds and rolls on tracks, and it can only be hauled around in the squad’s mobile workshop. Spot weighs under 100 pounds, climbs stairs and rides in a pickup truck that bomb techs drive daily.

The robot will only be used for explosive threats in the city and at the port, and it won’t carry a weapon. SPD said a weapon would go against Boston Dynamics’ rules for its robots. Spot’s 360-degree camera sends an encrypted live feed to the operator but doesn’t record or use facial recognition.

The only thing the robot does on its own is open a door, after an operator lines it up. As one bomb technician put it in SPD’s post, Spot will “be as dumb in 10 years as it is today.”

It’s not the first time SPD has turned to a four-legged partner for tech-related work.

Nala, an electronic storage detection K9 — profiled by GeekWire in 2024 — is trained to smell a chemical compound used in making electronics. The Labrador retriever helps SPD’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force find hidden phones, hard drives and micro SD cards during warrant searches. Her handler, Det. Daljit Gill, told GeekWire at the time that Nala turns up a device human searchers missed about 30% of the time.

Boston Dynamics, maker of backflipping Atlas humanoids and other viral-video robots, first unveiled the robodog in 2015. A smaller, all-electric version followed a year later.

The machines have long stirred dystopian unease. A 2017 “Black Mirror” episode featured killer robot dogs inspired by the company’s designs. Still, Spot has turned up in friendlier settings: then-Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos walked one at the company’s MARS conference in 2018 — a scene described by GeekWire’s Alan Boyle as featuring the “anxiety-inducing” robot.

Police departments have embraced the robots, too. More than 60 bomb squads and SWAT teams in the U.S. and Canada use Spot, Bloomberg reported last year, including a regional bomb unit in Portland. New York police returned one in 2021 after public backlash, then brought the robots back two years later.

Back in Seattle, SPD’s bomb technicians see more potential uses down the road, according to the department’s post, including communicating and observing from a distance as part of de-escalation. For now, Spot’s job is limited to explosives.

And the robot won’t be getting a new name, SPD said, “because it is not a toy, or a dog, even though it kind of looks like both.”

#5351. My Business Was Thriving. Then One Question Made Me Restructure the Entire Thing.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

How to get clear on your story and turn it into your biggest business advantage.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I spent more than two decades asking questions for a living as a TV news anchor and reporter. But it took a room full of women casually discussing $20 million and $200 million exits for me to ask myself the one question I never had.

Last year, I gave the opening keynote at Entreprenista’s Founders Weekend in Palm Beach. All weekend, I was surrounded by women who had built and sold companies and were already planning what to build next. It got me thinking about my own business, Jett Communications. We were growing fast, but sitting thousands of miles from my daily routine, I finally asked myself:

Am I building the business I actually want?

After years of interviewing other people, I realized it was time to interview myself.

A business can look successful from the outside and still not fit the life you want to live. On paper, mine looked great.

I didn’t have a traditional business background, but my years in TV news gave me the instincts that became the foundation of my company. Today, I work with executives, founders, athletes, celebrities, family offices and even members of a royal family, along with leaders at Amazon, Meta, Apple, Netflix and Uber. My private clients lead companies with $5 million to $6 billion in annual revenue.

What that doesn’t show is everything else competing for my time. My clients know they can reach me before their high-stakes moments, and at home, I’m the mom who will happily get up at dawn to take my kids NeeDoh hunting at Target (if you know, you know). I love my work, but I was so busy keeping up with all of it that I never stopped to ask whether I wanted to do things differently.

When the pandemic hit, my keynotes and media appearances disappeared within weeks, so I did what I had always done as a reporter: I focused on the story in front of me. My media training business evolved into offering PR services, an online course, a boot camp and a mastermind group, and once the world reopened, I was managing all of that while getting back on corporate stages.

I’m proud of what I built, especially because I did it while raising a toddler during lockdown and navigating infertility, including a miscarriage and multiple procedures.

But in hindsight, I was in survival mode at work and at home. Don’t get me wrong, survival mode can be productive, but when you’re constantly reacting, you stop designing and you never step back to ask whether the business you’re running still fits your goals.

When I got home from Florida, I started to explore my options. Then two companies approached me about acquiring my business, and those conversations forced me to think about what someone would actually be buying and what I wanted to spend my time doing.

The answer wasn’t another course, program or a larger team. It was to double down on the work I love, which is to sit across from someone, ask the questions other people don’t think to ask, find the story beneath their accomplishments and help them show up with clarity and confidence, whether they’re stepping into a boardroom, onto a keynote stage or under the arena lights.

The one thing that has helped me build my business more than anything else is knowing my own story and being able to tell it. It’s also what I see accomplished leaders struggle with most, because they can build incredible companies and still not know how to explain what makes them different.

Once clients get clear on their story, I’ve watched it change the trajectory of their businesses and careers. One client, a life sciences executive navigating a global reorganization, wasn’t sure what her next step would be. We built a platform around her expertise in women’s healthcare, and she went on to land keynote invitations, a new role and a board seat.

Fourteen years in, those were the moments I kept coming back to, so I rebuilt my business around them. I created a bespoke one-day experience for individuals who don’t have weeks or months to get clear on their story, and our Leadership Lab, which helps teams communicate with the same clarity. Once I knew what I wanted my business to be, my LinkedIn profile was the first place I went to share it.

My clients taught me how much business happens before anyone gets in a room together, because investors, partners and future hires form impressions long before the first meeting.

Here are five things I’d tell any entrepreneur ready for their next step.

It’s tempting to only post the wins, but the decisions and challenges behind them tell people so much more about you. Share the thing that didn’t go as planned or the lesson you learned the hard way. People want to know what you know, but they also want to understand how you think.

If your visibility hasn’t kept up with your growth, people may still know an older version of you, so use your profile and posts to write the headline yourself. It’s wonderful when people say your name in rooms you’re not in, but only if they’re describing who you are today.

Some of my best business relationships started with a thoughtful reply, not a pitch. Congratulate people, share work you think deserves attention and comment when you actually have something to add.

Once I got clear on exactly who I wanted to work with, the right people started recognizing themselves in what I shared and reaching out. Client stories (shared with permission) are one of the best ways to do this, because when someone reads about a situation just like theirs, they can picture what working with you would look like.

To make it even clearer who you serve, I’d point entrepreneurs to LinkedIn Premium Business. Imagine a founder who just sold her company and wants her next chapter to be advising early-stage CEOs. People still know her as the founder of her last company, so a built-out Services section on her profile helps them see what she offers now, and request matching can connect her with people already looking for that kind of help. When a CEO lands on her profile, reviews and testimonials from founders she’s mentored build trust right away, and a custom button takes them straight to her calendar. She can also use InMail to reach out to founders she’d like to work with, and for someone who just needs advice on one big decision, a paid one-on-one advice session is an easy place to start.

When I was on TV, I learned I was never really talking to the thousands of people watching, but to one person sitting at home. LinkedIn works the same way, so instead of announcing what you do, write like you’re talking to that one person. That’s what makes people feel like you understand them, and it’s what makes the right person reach out.

I used to think growth meant adding more: more services, more people, more opportunities. Now I think it’s figuring out what you want to do more of, and having the guts to build around it.

If you take one thing from my story, let it be this: stay in the room a little longer, listen to people playing a bigger game than you are and then interview yourself. Ask whether you’re building the business you actually want, or just getting really good at running the one you already have.

#5350. How a USDA public health alert differs from a recall on meat, poultry and egg products

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A USDA public health alert and a recall both flag potentially unsafe meat, poultry or processed egg products, but they differ in whether the product is still sold

The same package of frozen chicken in a home freezer could end up named in a federal recall or in a public health alert. The label on that notice is not a matter of wording. It tells consumers something specific about where the product is likely to be.

Both kinds of notices come from the Food Safety and Inspection Service, known as FSIS, which is part of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. FSIS regulates meat, poultry and processed egg products. The Food and Drug Administration regulates most other foods, including fresh produce and dairy. That split defines what a USDA notice can cover. A USDA notice applies only to the three product categories FSIS oversees. A warning about a bag of spinach comes from the FDA instead.

The core of the USDA public health alert vs. recall question is availability. A recall removes product that is still in commerce, meaning it may still be on store shelves or moving through distribution. A public health alert warns consumers about product that is likely no longer available for purchase but may still be in homes. FSIS also uses alerts when it lacks enough information to request a recall. An alert does not mean the product is safe to eat.

Recalls carry another layer of information. Each one is assigned to Class I, Class II or Class III according to the health risk involved. Public health alerts carry no class at all. USDA recalls are also voluntary actions taken by the company. FSIS does not have mandatory recall authority, though it has other tools to keep unsafe product away from consumers. The FDA, by contrast, holds mandatory recall authority for most foods under the Food Safety Modernization Act.

The 10 slides below cover how each type of notice works and what separates them. They also explain the problems that commonly prompt a notice, from Listeria monocytogenes to undeclared allergens. One slide shows how to match a package to a notice using the establishment number in the USDA mark of inspection. The last two slides cover what to do with an affected product and where to find current notices.

USDA food safety notices come from the Food Safety and Inspection Service, or FSIS. FSIS regulates meat, poultry and processed egg products. The Food and Drug Administration regulates most other foods.

FSIS is an agency of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. A food safety notice that carries the USDA name is an FSIS notice.

The agency's scope is limited to three product categories: meat, poultry and processed egg products. A USDA notice can only involve a product from one of those groups.

That limit makes the issuing agency a useful clue. A notice from FSIS signals that the product involved is meat, poultry or a processed egg product. A USDA notice will not cover a bag of salad or a box of cereal. Those foods fall outside the FSIS categories.

The FDA oversees most of the remaining food supply. A warning about a food outside the three FSIS categories generally comes from the FDA rather than the USDA.

The split also points readers to the right place to check. Someone trying to confirm whether a packaged meat or poultry item is affected should start with FSIS notices. Someone checking on a food outside those categories should look to the FDA instead.

A USDA recall is a company's action to remove meat, poultry or processed egg products from commerce because they may be unsafe or mislabeled. The Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), the USDA agency that oversees those products, publishes the notice that tells the public what is affected.

The key word is commerce. A recall targets product that is still moving through distribution or still available to buyers. The point is to pull that product back before more of it is sold or eaten.

Two kinds of problems can lead to a recall. One is safety, meaning the food itself may pose a hazard to the people who eat it. The other is labeling, meaning the package does not accurately describe what is inside. A labeling problem alone can be enough to prompt a recall.

A USDA recall applies when a meat, poultry or processed egg product is still in commerce, and a public health alert applies when it probably is not. That availability question is the main factor separating the two notices issued by the Food Safety and Inspection Service, or FSIS.

When product is still in commerce, a recall has work to do in the marketplace. Product may be sitting in warehouses, in distribution centers or in store display cases. The company responsible for it has to get it back. The FSIS notice tells the public about a removal that is under way.

A public health alert fits a different situation. The window for taking the product off sale has largely closed. Stores may have sold through their stock, or the item may no longer be offered. A removal from commerce would find little or nothing left to collect. The remaining concern sits in kitchens, refrigerators and home freezers.

Every meat, poultry or processed egg product recall announced through the U.S. Department of Agriculture is a voluntary action by the company responsible for the product. The Food Safety and Inspection Service, the USDA agency that oversees those foods, does not have mandatory recall authority.

That means FSIS cannot order a company to pull its product. What it can do is request a recall. When FSIS makes that request, the decision to remove the product from commerce still formally rests with the company.

The agency has other tools if a company does not act. FSIS can detain product, which keeps it from moving further through commerce. It can also seize product. And it can withdraw inspection services from the establishment involved.

The establishment number is the plant code printed inside the round USDA mark of inspection on meat, poultry and processed egg product packaging. It usually appears as "EST." followed by a number. FSIS notices list this code to identify the plant behind an affected product.

The number points to the facility where the food was produced or processed under federal inspection. It does not identify the brand. A single plant can pack products for several different labels. A single brand can also come from more than one plant. Two packages with the same name on the front can therefore carry different establishment numbers.

The mark itself is a small circle printed on the label. It can sit on the front, the back or the side, depending on the package design.

The FSIS recalls and public health alerts page is the official place to read USDA notices about meat, poultry and processed egg products. Questions can go by phone to the USDA Meat and Poultry Hotline at 1-888-MPHotline (1-888-674-6854).

The Food Safety and Inspection Service, the USDA agency that regulates those three product categories, publishes the page. Recalls and public health alerts are both posted there. A reader can check either kind of action in one place, without looking up a separate source for each.

Each notice spells out how to identify the affected packages. It names the products and gives their package sizes and dates. It also lists the establishment number, which appears inside the USDA mark of inspection as "EST." followed by a number. The full notice, rather than a shortened summary of it, shows every affected item at once.

The package itself offers a second clue. Meat, poultry and processed egg products inspected by FSIS carry the round USDA mark of inspection. That mark ties the product to FSIS oversight. A package bearing it is the kind of item a USDA notice can cover.

Egg items need a closer look. FSIS jurisdiction names processed egg products specifically. The wording of a notice, together with the agency that issued it, shows which category an egg item falls into.

For anyone reading a food safety headline, the issuing agency is the first detail to check. A USDA notice points to meat, poultry or processed egg products. Any other food is most likely an FDA matter.

The scope is narrow. A USDA recall applies only to the three product categories FSIS regulates: meat, poultry and processed egg products.

The FSIS notice serves as the public record of the recall. It names the company involved, describes the affected products and states the reason for the action. It also gives the recall class, which reflects the level of health risk.

Each notice is specific. It lists the product names, package sizes and dates that define which items are covered. It also includes the establishment number from the USDA mark of inspection, which ties the product to the inspected establishment that produced it.

That precision limits the recall's reach. Only the items matching the details in the notice are part of the recall. Other products from the same company, or the same type of food sold under different labels, are not covered unless the notice lists them.

Responsibility for the removal sits with the company. The business that made or distributed the product takes it back from the market, and FSIS makes the action public through its notice.

A public health alert is a consumer warning from the Food Safety and Inspection Service about meat, poultry or processed egg products. It covers products that are likely no longer available for purchase but may still be in people's homes.

FSIS is the agency within the U.S. Department of Agriculture that oversees those three product categories. It turns to an alert in two distinct situations. Each one answers a different question about a potentially unsafe product.

The first question is where the product is. Food bought before a problem came to light can stay in a refrigerator, freezer or pantry after it has disappeared from store shelves. In that case, the people at risk are the households that already took it home, not the stores that once sold it. An alert is written for those households.

The second question is what the agency knows. FSIS issues an alert when it does not have enough information to request a recall. The alert lets the agency tell the public about a concern without having the basis it would need to ask a company to act.

An alert is a different kind of action from a recall. A recall is a company removing product from commerce. An alert is a public warning from FSIS itself, directed at consumers rather than at the supply chain.

FSIS posts its public health alerts on the same web page as its recall notices. Each notice identifies the affected items by product name, package size and dates. Readers can compare those details against what they have at home.

An alert does not declare a product safe. It reflects only that the item is likely no longer for sale. Anyone holding a product named in an alert should follow the instructions in the notice itself. Those instructions may tell consumers to throw the product away or return it as the notice directs.

That is why an alert speaks directly to consumers. Its aim is to reach people who bought the product earlier and may still have it, not to direct a company to clear shelves.

Availability is not the only branch in the decision. FSIS also turns to a public health alert when the information it holds is not sufficient to request a recall. Either way, the alert warns the public without a company removal action attached.

For a shopper reading the headline, the notice type works as a quick signal. A recall points to an item that may still be on sale and could be bought today. An alert points to an item that is likely no longer available for purchase.

An alert is not a sign that the product is safe to eat. It means only that the product is likely gone from stores. Some of it may still be sitting in homes.

FSIS assigns every meat, poultry or processed egg product recall to one of three classes based on the health risk of eating the product. Class I signals the most serious risk, and Class III the least.

Class I covers cases where there is a reasonable probability that eating the product will cause serious health consequences or death. The definition sets two bars at once. One is how likely harm is. The other is how severe that harm would be. A Class I recall involves a product that clears both.

Class II applies when there is a remote probability of adverse health consequences from eating the product. Both measures fall below the Class I standard. The chance of harm is described as remote rather than reasonable. The harm is described as adverse rather than serious or fatal. A remote probability is still a probability of harm.

Class III applies when eating the product will not cause adverse health consequences. It is the only class whose definition rules out adverse health consequences from eating. A recall can cover product that may be mislabeled as well as product that may be unsafe. A Class III recall removes product from commerce for a reason other than a risk from eating it. A labeling error that poses no health risk to the person eating the product fits this class.

The class measures the health risk of eating the product and nothing else. It does not show whether the product is still on store shelves. Other parts of the recall notice describe the affected product itself.

Public health alerts sit outside this three-tier system. FSIS does not assign a class to an alert. The missing class does not mean the product is safe to eat. It reflects that an alert is a different kind of notice from a recall, with no classification step attached.

A request from FSIS therefore comes with those options in reserve. If a company declines, the agency can still act against the product itself or against the plant's inspection.

The FDA works under a different rule. It has mandatory recall authority for most foods under the Food Safety Modernization Act. FDA jurisdiction covers most foods other than meat, poultry and processed egg products. Its mandatory power reaches most of the food supply outside FSIS oversight.

The split means two products in the same grocery cart can fall under different rules. A recalled bag of salad greens or jar of peanut butter falls under the FDA, which can compel a recall. A recalled package of ground beef or chicken sausage falls under FSIS, which can only request one.

For shoppers, the voluntary nature of a USDA recall does not signal a lower level of risk. The word "voluntary" describes how the recall began. The recall class assigned to it describes the health hazard. A Class I recall is still voluntary, even though it covers products with a reasonable probability of serious health consequences or death.

Many USDA recalls and public health alerts trace back to a short list of problems: the bacteria Listeria monocytogenes, Salmonella and E. coli O157:H7, undeclared allergens, foreign material and misbranding. The cause named in a notice tells a consumer what kind of risk the product carries.

Listeria monocytogenes is a frequent concern in ready-to-eat foods such as deli meats, hot dogs and cooked sausages. People often eat those products without cooking them again. Any contamination that happens after processing can therefore reach the consumer directly. Listeria can also grow at refrigerator temperatures. Many other foodborne bacteria cannot. The illness it causes, listeriosis, poses the greatest danger to pregnant people, newborns, older adults and people with weakened immune systems.

Salmonella is most closely associated with raw poultry. It causes salmonellosis, an illness that typically brings diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps. Thorough cooking kills the bacteria. Cross-contamination from raw meat to cutting boards, hands or other foods can still spread it.

E. coli O157:H7 is a Shiga toxin-producing strain of the bacterium most often linked to ground beef. Grinding can move bacteria from the surface of the meat into the interior. Undercooking may then leave them alive. Some infections lead to hemolytic uremic syndrome, a condition that can cause kidney failure. Young children and older adults face the highest risk of that complication.

Undeclared allergens appear when a product contains an ingredient such as milk, eggs, wheat or soy that its label does not list. This can happen when a package ends up with the wrong label. It can also happen when a recipe changes and the label is not updated. For a person with a food allergy, eating the product can trigger a serious reaction.

Foreign material covers physical objects that should not be in food, such as pieces of plastic, metal, glass or rubber. These can cause choking, cuts to the mouth or dental injuries.

Misbranding is a labeling problem. It can mean the label misstates what is in the package or leaves out required information. An undeclared allergen is one form of misbranding. The category also covers errors that carry no allergy risk, such as an incorrect product name or missing label details.

FSIS notices list the establishment number alongside other identifying details. Those usually include the exact product name as it appears on the label, the package size or weight, and one or more dates. The dates can be a packing or production date, or a use-by or best-by date.

A match on the establishment number alone does not settle the question. The product name, package size and date also need to line up with the notice. A package from the named plant with a date outside the listed range may not be covered. A package with the right product name but a different plant number may not be covered either. A package with a matching name and plant number but a different package size may also fall outside the notice.

Food moved out of its original packaging loses these identifiers. Ground meat repackaged into freezer bags or deli meat moved into storage containers no longer carries the establishment number, the dates or the package size. In that case, the label cannot confirm a match with the notice.

Do not eat a meat, poultry or processed egg product named in a USDA recall or public health alert. Check the refrigerator and the freezer, then throw the product away or return it as the notice directs.

Those steps are identical for both kinds of notice. The difference between a recall and an alert concerns store shelves, not kitchens. Once a product is in a home, the label on the notice does not change what the household should do with it.

Start with the freezer. Frozen meat and poultry can sit at home for a long time after purchase. A product that left stores before any notice appeared may still be in a freezer drawer. That is the situation a public health alert is meant to reach.

Then move to the refrigerator, where fresh and ready-to-eat meat and poultry are usually kept. A notice can name refrigerated products as well as frozen ones.

Hold the package next to the notice before deciding anything. The notice names specific products, package sizes and dates, and only a package that matches those details is affected. A similar item with different details may fall outside the notice.

Check each package separately. Two packages of the same product can carry different sizes or dates, and a notice may cover one without covering the other.

Read the instructions in that particular notice once a package matches. Some notices tell consumers to throw the product away. Others say it may also be returned to the place of purchase. One notice's instructions do not necessarily carry over to the next.

Keep a matched product out of every meal. Do not cook it into a larger dish. Do not give it to someone else. Do not set it aside to decide about later. A matched product has two destinations: the trash or the store, as the notice directs.

A recall notice on the page states its class, from Class I through Class III. A public health alert posted there carries no class. Checking for that label is a quick way to tell which kind of action a listing describes. On a recall, the class also shows how FSIS rated the health risk.

The page lists only USDA-regulated foods. A notice about a product outside meat, poultry and processed egg products will not appear there. Those notices come from the FDA, which regulates most other foods.

The hotline offers a direct phone line to USDA for questions about meat, poultry and processed egg products. Its number is published in two forms. One spells part of it in letters as 1-888-MPHotline. The other gives the digits, 1-888-674-6854. Both versions dial the same line.

Keeping the package nearby during a call makes it possible to read out the product name, package size, dates and establishment number. Those are the same details FSIS uses in a notice to define which products it covers.

#5349. Skilled trades leaders admit ‘nothing is future-proof’—but AI can’t replace America’s growing demand for blue-collar workers like auto technicians

As AI forces office workers to rethink how tasks get done, skilled trades jobs have largely been seen as a more insulated, safer path to a six-figure career. However, hands-on roles like plumbers, electricians, and auto technicians aren’t exactly immune to the changes sweeping the workforce, either.

“Nothing is future-proof,” Mary Culler, president of Ford Philanthropy, said at the Fortune 500 Innovation Summit on Tuesday. “But I do think that a lot of the skilled trades are just those jobs that are going to be required to have a human there.”

Auto technicians—who are in short supply, for example —could increasingly use AI to help diagnose vehicle problems, she said, but still need a human to do the actual manual labor.

Carhartt CEO Linda Hubbard echoed that AI-powered efficiency will change how skilled trades workers do their jobs—but she said that the industry’s labor needs—fueled by the data center boom and broader infrastructure investments—will continue to outpace any productivity gains from the technology.

“No matter how good we get at encouraging people, I think we’re always going to be challenged to get the number of people that we need into the trades to just rebuild the infrastructure of the country,” Hubbard said on stage in an interview with Fortune’s Kristin Stoller.

Employers are expected to fill approximately 1.7 million skilled trades openings annually between now and 2034—but roughly a quarter of the industry’s existing 18 million workers are over 55 and nearing retirement.

Skilled trades work isn’t for everyone. The jobs can be physically demanding, require working outdoors in difficult conditions, and sometimes depend on project availability. But they can also offer something increasingly attractive to workers: relatively strong job security, salaries that can reach six figures, and even a pathway to owning a business.

Getting more people to recognize those opportunities, however, has been a challenge.

“We’re seeing pushback both on the cost of college, what jobs really require college degrees,” said Maria Flynn, CEO of Jobs for the Future. But decades of trade policies and other economic shifts have also left some communities with fewer skilled trades opportunities than they once had, she said.

“We’re having to rebuild trust, rebuild that awareness, and helping parents, young people, school counselors really understand what these 124 different skilled trades occupations offer and what the paths are into those roles,” Flynn said.

That perception gap is particularly evident among the people responsible for advising students on their next steps. While 95% of counselors agree trade school is a valuable and credible post-high school option, just 54% say they often recommend vocational or trade school, and only 28% often recommend an apprenticeship, according to a report released earlier this year by the Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades.

“We need to change the perception and get the guidance counselors to start talking about the opportunities,” Culler said.

Even after convincing someone that a skilled trades career might be right for them, the industry still has to get them through the training process and into a job.

The Alliance’s September report found that among every 100 who start an apprenticeship, just 48 complete the program, and only 29 enter a skilled trade occupation within five years of leaving it. The numbers are similarly challenging for related postsecondary programs: Of every 100 entrants, 48 complete their programs and just 34 go on to work in a skilled trade.

Flynn described the problem as “pipeline leakiness,” which can often come down to a lack of support for workers navigating training programs. That includes seemingly basic but consequential barriers like transportation and childcare.

“We really need to be working on this together,” she said.

Preston Fore is a reporter on Fortune's Success team.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:57 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:33 pm

Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the company’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor.

“Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” said Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the company’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.

Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he said.

The full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou said.

Microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude.

For “advanced” users of each company’s agent tools, it showed $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat.

The numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude.

Partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The company is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects.

The companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks.

The product has less than a tenth as many weekly users as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report said.

New MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella announced that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry.

The lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft says it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose.

Microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it says matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other new models cover image editing, live speech and transcription.

The other new business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Company consulting arm. AT&T used an earlier version of the program, Custom Models, to build a MAI model for 5G network analytics.

It’s the latest step in Microsoft’s push for what Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called “long term self-sufficiency,” which started with seven homegrown models at Build in June.

Keeping costs in check: The cost theme ran through the keynote. In a demo, Althoff showed Copilot building a keynote outline, a slide deck and a customer tracker for a retail conference, plus an agent he named Amelia to keep the work going.

The cost of his two-hour Sunday session: about 10,000 credits, or roughly $100. Althoff presented that as a bargain compared with the staff time it would have taken: “my team hits the ground running for NRF without me bothering them,” he said.

Microsoft is also selling tools to keep that bill in check. A new Agent 365 Business Analytics feature shows business leaders what’s driving their AI spending and what they’re getting for it, and a companion Cost Management tool lets IT set spending policies and get alerts. Microsoft cited a McKinsey survey in which 93% of respondents reported exceeding their AI budgets.

In another notable announcement, Microsoft and Salesforce unveiled “Copilotforce,” bringing Salesforce customer data and actions into Copilot, Teams and Fabric. The Copilot plugin is available in preview.

Earlier, Nadella opened the keynote by addressing last week’s global Outlook outage.

#5347. A No-Layoff Promise Isn’t About Compassion. It’s About Discipline.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Most leaders who promise “no layoffs” drop the idea when revenue falls.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

That’s how Paul Gund described his position on job cuts. His son Steve, now the third-generation CEO of The Gund Co., still runs the St. Louis composite materials manufacturer by it. It’s a great line. It’s also the least interesting part of the story.

Plenty of leaders say something similar during good years. Few still mean it when revenue falls. The difference isn’t conviction, but what happens long before the downturn arrives.

The results are hard to argue with. As The Wall Street Journal’s Allison Pohle reported, Gund has averaged 18% annual growth for a decade, with about 1,300 employees and roughly $400 million in annual sales, and has never laid anyone off. Hundreds of family-business leaders have visited to study the model and most struggle to copy it.

That’s not surprising. They’re studying the promise when they should be studying the plumbing.

When Pohle was asked how the company avoids layoffs, the first answer wasn’t about values. It was operational: the company staffs conservatively and relies on employees picking up overtime.

A no-layoff policy doesn’t survive on willpower. It survives because hiring decisions made in a strong quarter are made as if a weak quarter is coming. Every open role gets weighed against a promise that can’t be broken later. Headcount isn’t a reward for growth. It’s a long-term obligation the company has to be able to keep.

Almost all companies run the opposite way. They hire ahead of demand when times are good, then cut when the forecast turns. Then they issue a statement about “difficult decisions” and “the long-term health of the business.” The value they claimed – that people matter – was never connected to how they staffed, budgeted, or planned. It was a sentiment, not an operating rule.

This is what I call the Translation Gap. Organizations are good at stating what they believe. They’re good at executing tasks. What they rarely build is the bridge in between: the specific, repeatable behaviors that make a belief true in everyday decisions.

At Gund, their commitment to bridging the gap shows up in at least four places:

None of these is inspiring or special on its own. But together, they’re what make the promise real.

That’s what’s worth stealing. Every principle, value or cultural belief you want to hold under pressure needs a short list of supporting actions that anyone in the organization can point to and apply to their own role. If you can’t name them, each concept will fold the first time things get expensive.

The Gund Company is candid that no layoffs doesn’t mean no one leaves. People get coached out. Not everyone buys into the culture, and when the company finds out someone isn’t a fit, they have the hard conversations.

But that’s the most essential point. A culture that protects people fiercely has to be selective about who is in it. If you promise employees their jobs are safe from the business cycle, you’d better be sure the people you’re protecting are carrying the culture forward. Otherwise the promise becomes a shield for the wrong behaviors, and employees who do buy in start to resent it.

Most leaders tend to treat kindness and rigor as opposites. But the kindest thing you can do for a team committed to a shared way of working is refuse to let that way of working erode.

Gund also admits the no-layoff commitment creates strain. Because hiring is so intentional and the business is growing fast, it’s hard to develop leaders quickly enough. Overtime has its limits. Lean staffing has its limits.

But culture and values don’t die because things get hard. Rather, they die because of the bait-and-switch. Leaders who adopt a principle because it sounds good and never discuss the cost will turn around and abandon it when the bill arrives. The cost was always coming, they just hadn’t planned for it, and employees know it.

A principle worth keeping is one whose trade-offs you’ve already accepted. Gund accepted slower leadership development, heavier reliance on its existing people and harder conversations about fit. That’s the price of the promise. And because they named it, they can manage it instead of being ambushed by it.

Pick any value or commitment your company claims. “Customer-first.” “Integrity.” “Innovation.” “Our people matter.” Then ask three questions:

Paul’s line works because his company built the cultural operating discipline to back it up, and has sustained it across generations. The idea gets the attention, but the staffing model, hiring rigor and willingness to coach people out do the work.

Your values, principles and commitments don’t need better phrasing, but rather consequences.

That’s how Paul Gund described his position on job cuts. His son Steve, now the third-generation CEO of The Gund Co., still runs the St. Louis composite materials manufacturer by it. It’s a great line. It’s also the least interesting part of the story.

Plenty of leaders say something similar during good years. Few still mean it when revenue falls. The difference isn’t conviction, but what happens long before the downturn arrives.
