#5346. What happens when the House flips: 10 powers that shape bills and markets

Free daily briefing on global business news.

What happens when the House flips: how a new majority reshapes bills, spending deadlines, debt-limit fights and oversight, and where investors see policy risk

A House majority controls only one chamber of Congress. Yet that control decides which bills reach the floor, which spending fights hit a deadline and which investigations go public. House members serve two-year terms. A single election can shift that control and change the direction of Washington until the next vote.

The House has 435 voting members, and the party that holds a majority runs the chamber. It picks the Speaker, names the chair of every committee and sets the rules under which bills are debated and amended. The Constitution also requires bills that raise revenue to originate in the House. That gives the majority the first move on federal tax legislation.

Those powers have firm limits. A House majority cannot pass a law on its own. Every bill must also clear the Senate and win the president's signature, or survive a veto through an override. When the House changes hands while the other party holds the White House or the Senate, the result is divided government. Under divided government, the bar for new legislation rises.

Understanding what happens when the House flips means looking past the seat count on election night. A House majority change reshapes the legislative calendar and the leverage each side brings to funding bills and the debt limit. Oversight of the executive branch shifts as well. A flip can also close off budget tools that a party holding the House, Senate and White House might otherwise use.

Markets pay attention for practical reasons. Tax rates, federal spending levels, the timing of debt-limit votes and the risk of a government shutdown all run through Congress. A change in House control does not dictate where stock prices go. It does change who sets deadlines and who must agree before bills pass. That shapes the policy uncertainty that investors weigh around taxes, budgets and federal borrowing.

The 10 slides that follow walk through the mechanics, from the 218-seat threshold and the Speaker's gavel to committee control and the power of the purse. They also cover shutdowns, debt-ceiling standoffs, impeachment and budget reconciliation. The final slide sets out what a House majority cannot do on its own and which policy risks draw investor attention.

A party needs 218 of the House's 435 voting seats to hold a majority when every seat is filled. That majority gives a party control of the chamber's agenda. It does not give that party control of the Senate or the White House.

The 435 figure is set by statute, not by the Constitution. Congress fixed the size of the House through the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929. Seats are divided among the states by population after each census. A state can therefore gain or lose seats every 10 years.

The 435 voting members are not the whole chamber. The House also seats six nonvoting members. Five are delegates, from Washington, D.C., Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands. The sixth is a resident commissioner from Puerto Rico. These members can serve on committees but cannot vote on final passage of legislation. They do not count toward the 218 threshold.

Every seat is contested at each general election in an even-numbered year. Control can therefore change in a midterm year as well as in a presidential election year.

The 218 figure is a starting point, not a fixed rule. Members die, resign or leave for other jobs during a term. Each departure leaves a vacancy. The Constitution requires House vacancies to be filled by election rather than appointment. Until a special election takes place, the chamber operates with fewer than 435 members. That lowers the number of votes needed for a majority on the floor.

Vacancies matter most when margins are thin. A party holding only a few seats more than the threshold can see its working margin shrink with a single resignation from its own ranks. The same logic applies to individual votes. Bills generally pass with a majority of members present and voting. That means absences can shift close outcomes.

Seat control is also different from vote control. The majority party does not need every member to agree with leadership on every issue. It does need enough of them to stay together when the minority votes as a bloc. In a narrow majority, a handful of defectors can sink a bill their own leaders support.

The majority party effectively chooses the Speaker of the House. The Speaker presides over the chamber and is second in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president. When the House flips, a new Speaker and new priorities at the top of the chamber almost always follow.

Article I, Section 2 of the Constitution gives the House the power to choose its own Speaker. The full chamber votes. A candidate needs a majority of the members who vote for a named person. In practice, each party nominates its own leader. The majority party's nominee wins when its members hold together.

The Presidential Succession Act of 1947 sets the order that puts the Speaker directly behind the vice president. That makes the post one of the most senior offices in the federal government, not only a legislative job.

Day to day, the Speaker shapes what the House does. The office controls the floor schedule and refers bills to committees. The Speaker also acts as the public face of the majority's agenda. A Speaker from the party opposed to the president can decide which White House priorities ever reach a vote.

A narrow majority limits that power. When a party holds only a few more seats than it needs, a small bloc of its own members can block a candidate or a bill. Kevin McCarthy's election in January 2023 showed how this works. He needed 15 ballots to win the gavel. It was the first Speaker election to go past a single ballot since 1923.

McCarthy won the job partly through concessions to holdouts in his own party. One was a rule change that let a single member force a vote to remove the Speaker. On Oct. 3, 2023, the House voted him out through a motion to vacate. It was the first time the House had removed a Speaker in U.S. history.

The chamber then went 22 days without an elected Speaker. Mike Johnson won the post on Oct. 25, 2023. During that gap, the House did not pass ordinary legislation. The episode showed how a Speaker's hold on the job depends on the votes of the majority's own members.

The party holding the House majority names the chair of every committee and holds the majority of seats on each panel. It also runs the Rules Committee, which sets the terms for debating and amending most bills that reach the floor.

Together, those two levers decide which proposals get a hearing and which never come up for a vote. When control of the chamber changes hands, the gatekeepers change with it.

Committee chairs control the calendar. A chair decides which bills get hearings, which witnesses testify and when a markup takes place. A markup is the session where committee members debate, amend and vote on legislation before sending it to the full House. A bill that a chair declines to schedule usually goes nowhere.

That structure matters to business because committees divide policy by subject. The Financial Services Committee handles banking, securities and housing finance. The Energy and Commerce Committee covers health care, telecommunications and energy, among other areas. A new majority puts its own members in charge of each of those portfolios.

Committee ratios reinforce that control. The majority party holds more seats than the minority on every panel. That lets it win most committee votes on party lines. The minority can offer amendments and make its case, but it rarely has the votes to force an outcome.

The Rules Committee is the last checkpoint before the floor. For most significant bills, it writes a resolution, known as a rule, that sets how long debate lasts and which amendments can be offered. The full House votes to adopt that rule before taking up the bill itself.

A closed rule bars floor amendments entirely. A structured rule allows only the amendments the committee selects. Those choices let the majority shape a bill's final form and keep unwanted proposals off the floor.

The panel has long been weighted toward the majority, traditionally with nine majority members and four from the minority. That margin is wider than the split on most other committees.

The main route around this system is a discharge petition. If a majority of the full House signs one, a bill can be pulled out of committee and brought to the floor without leadership's backing. Discharge petitions rarely succeed.

For companies and investors tracking legislation, the chairs a new majority installs determine which proposals get hearings in each policy area, from bank regulation to health care.

The Constitution requires every bill that raises revenue to start in the House, and annual spending bills begin there too by long-standing practice. A new House majority therefore writes the opening version of federal tax and spending legislation.

The party in control decides which tax changes get written into legislation and which never leave committee. It also sets the opening numbers for how much each federal agency receives.

The revenue rule comes from Article I, Section 7 of the Constitution. Its first clause says all bills for raising revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives. The same clause lets the Senate propose or concur with amendments, as it does on other bills.

Tax legislation in the House runs through the Ways and Means Committee. Its chair, chosen by the majority party, shapes bills on income taxes, tariffs and other revenue measures. The Senate's counterpart is the Finance Committee.

Spending follows a separate track. Article I, Section 9 bars money from leaving the Treasury except through appropriations made by law. The House Appropriations Committee usually drafts those bills first. That sequence is custom, not a constitutional command.

The Appropriations Committee divides its work among 12 subcommittees, each responsible for one annual funding bill. Those bills cover defense, agriculture, homeland security and the rest of discretionary spending. The federal fiscal year starts on Oct. 1, which sets the calendar for that work.

Annual appropriations do not cover everything. Social Security and Medicare benefits are mandatory spending, set by permanent law rather than yearly bills. A new majority cannot change them through the appropriations process alone.

The House's head start has limits. The Senate can amend a House revenue bill heavily. It sometimes takes a House-passed bill and replaces its text entirely. The House, in turn, can return a Senate-originated revenue bill through a procedure known as a blue slip.

Neither chamber can finish the job alone. Every tax or spending bill must pass the Senate in identical form and then go to the president for a signature. A new House majority can redirect budget priorities, but it needs the Senate and the White House to turn them into law.

A House flip often produces divided government, in which one party runs the House while the other holds the White House, the Senate or both. Under split control, no party can turn a bill into law without cooperation from the other side or enough votes to override a veto.

The constitutional path for a bill stays the same when the majority changes. A measure must clear the House and the Senate in identical form before it goes to the president. The president then has 10 days, not counting Sundays, to sign it or return it with objections.

A veto raises the bar sharply. Overriding one takes a two-thirds vote in each chamber, counted among members present and voting. If all 435 House members vote, an override needs 290 of them. That threshold sits far above a simple majority.

The practical result is that a new House majority gains the power to block more readily than the power to enact. It can decline to take up the president's priorities. It can also pass its own bills while knowing the Senate or the president may stop them. Measures that do become law under split control generally require votes from lawmakers in both parties.

The 2010 midterms show the pattern. Republicans won control of the House that November. Democrats kept the Senate, and Barack Obama remained president. The following year brought a standoff over raising the federal debt limit.

That fight ended with the Budget Control Act of 2011, which Obama signed on Aug. 2, 2011. The law paired a debt-limit increase with caps on discretionary spending. It also created a joint congressional committee charged with finding further deficit reduction.

The committee did not agree on a plan. That outcome triggered automatic across-the-board spending cuts, known as sequestration, which began taking effect in March 2013. The sequence shows how split control pushed a major fiscal decision into a negotiated deal struck under deadline pressure.

For businesses and investors, divided government changes the odds on policy. Large shifts in tax rules, regulation or federal programs need support from both parties to pass. Without that support, existing law generally remains in force.

A government shutdown begins when Congress lets appropriations lapse without passing new funding. Spending bills need House approval. That gives the House majority's position real weight in whether a deadline passes quietly or turns into a standoff.

The federal fiscal year starts on Oct. 1. Congress is supposed to pass 12 regular appropriations bills by then to fund agencies for the year. It rarely finishes on time. Lawmakers often pass a continuing resolution instead. That stopgap measure keeps agencies running at existing levels until a new deadline.

Each stopgap sets up another cliff. A new House majority that wants deeper cuts, or that wants to attach policy demands to funding, can refuse to pass a clean extension. The Senate and the president can reject the House's version in turn. When no bill is signed before the deadline, money stops flowing to the affected agencies.

The Antideficiency Act bars agencies from spending money Congress has not appropriated. Agencies without funding must furlough workers whose jobs are not deemed essential. Employees whose work protects life and property, such as air traffic controllers, keep working without pay until funding resumes.

Not everything stops. Social Security and Medicare benefits continue. Both programs run on mandatory spending rather than annual appropriations. A shutdown can also be partial. If Congress has already passed some of the 12 bills, the agencies those bills cover stay open.

That is what happened in the shutdown that began on Dec. 22, 2018. Several departments had already received full-year funding, while others had not. The dispute centered on money for a wall on the U.S.-Mexico border. The partial shutdown lasted 35 days, the longest on record at that time, and ended on Jan. 25, 2019.

The sequence of events in that episode is easy to misread. The shutdown started while Republicans still held the House. Democrats took control of the chamber in January 2019, partway through the standoff. The flip changed who sat at the negotiating table, but it did not cause the lapse.

An earlier case shows how split control can produce the same result. In October 2013, a Republican House clashed with a Democratic Senate and White House over the Affordable Care Act. Funding lapsed for 16 days before Congress passed a deal to reopen the government.

For investors, shutdowns add a layer of uncertainty around each funding deadline. Federal contractors can face delayed payments while agencies are closed. Agencies that publish economic data may also suspend their releases until funding returns. That leaves markets with fewer official numbers to work from.

Raising the federal debt limit requires an act of Congress, which gives a House majority direct leverage over U.S. borrowing. After a standoff over that vote in 2011, Standard & Poor's cut the U.S. credit rating from AAA to AA+ on Aug. 5 of that year.

The debt ceiling is a legal cap on how much the Treasury can borrow. It does not approve new spending. Congress authorizes spending and sets tax levels through separate laws. Borrowing covers the gap between the two.

The limit decides whether the Treasury can keep issuing debt to pay for obligations lawmakers have already approved. A vote on the ceiling concerns paying existing bills, not adding new ones.

Only legislation can lift or suspend the limit. The House must pass a bill, the Senate must pass the same bill, and the president must sign it. A House majority from the party opposite the White House can withhold its votes until it wins concessions on spending or other priorities.

When borrowing reaches the cap, the Treasury Department turns to accounting steps known as extraordinary measures. These let it keep paying bills for a limited time. Once they run out, the government risks being unable to meet all of its obligations on schedule.

The projected date when that could happen is often called the X $TWTR-date. It becomes the working deadline for negotiators in Congress and the White House.

The 2011 standoff showed that a debt-limit fight can reach financial markets even without a default. Lawmakers passed a deal before the borrowing deadline, yet S&P lowered its rating days later. It was the first time S&P had rated the U.S. below its top grade.

Treasury securities serve as a benchmark for borrowing costs around the world. Banks, pension funds and foreign central banks hold them in large amounts. Any doubt about timely payment on that debt reaches portfolios far beyond Washington.

For anyone tracking a House majority change, the debt limit is a recurring pressure point rather than a one-time event. A new majority inherits whatever borrowing deadline comes next on the calendar. Investors treat the timing and handling of that deadline as a source of policy uncertainty.

A House majority directs the chamber's investigations, including which subpoenas committees issue and which officials are called to testify. The House also holds the sole power to impeach under the Constitution, while the Senate decides whether to convict.

Oversight is one of the first things to change after a flip. Committee chairs decide which agencies, programs and decisions get a closer look. A new majority facing a president of the other party often turns that machinery toward the executive branch.

Subpoenas are the main enforcement tool. Under House rules, committees can compel documents and testimony from government officials, companies and private individuals. When a witness refuses, the full House can vote to hold that person in contempt of Congress. A criminal contempt citation goes to the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, who decides whether to bring charges.

An investigation does not need a bill to pass in order to have an effect. Hearings can produce document releases, public testimony and committee reports. They can also lay the groundwork for legislation in later sessions. For businesses, a hearing on one industry can put that sector's practices under public scrutiny even when no law follows.

Impeachment runs on a separate track. That power comes from Article I, Section 2. Articles of impeachment pass with a simple majority vote. Impeachment is a formal charge, not a removal from office.

Article I, Section 3 gives the Senate the sole power to try impeachments. Conviction requires two-thirds of the senators present. When the president is on trial, the chief justice of the U.S. presides. A conviction removes the official from office. The Senate may also vote to bar that person from holding federal office again.

The Constitution limits the grounds to treason, bribery or other high crimes and misdemeanors. It applies to the president, the vice president and all civil officers of the U.S. Federal judges fall within that group.

The House has impeached three presidents: Andrew Johnson in 1868, Bill Clinton in 1998 and Donald Trump in 2019 and again in 2021. The Senate did not convict any of them. A House majority can bring charges on its own. Removal depends on a Senate supermajority that a House flip does not deliver.

Budget reconciliation lets certain tax and spending measures pass the Senate by a simple majority, bypassing the filibuster. The process begins only after the House and the Senate both adopt a budget resolution. That requirement gives the House majority a say over whether the route opens at all.

The filibuster explains why the tool matters. Most legislation in the Senate needs 60 votes to end debate through a cloture motion. Parties rarely hold that many seats. A reconciliation bill avoids that hurdle. Senate debate on it is also capped at 20 hours.

Congress created the procedure in the Congressional Budget Act of 1974. It works in stages. First, both chambers agree on a budget resolution. That resolution can carry instructions directing specific committees to produce changes in revenue, spending or the debt limit. The committees then draft the legislation, which moves as a single package.

The route has limits. The Senate's Byrd rule bars provisions considered extraneous to the budget. That includes measures whose budgetary effect is merely incidental to their policy aims. Any senator can raise a point of order against such a provision. Waiving the rule takes 60 votes. As a result, reconciliation suits tax and spending changes far better than broad regulatory overhauls.

The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 shows how a party with unified control can use the tool. Republicans held the House, the Senate and the White House at the time. They adopted a budget resolution with reconciliation instructions. The tax overhaul then passed the Senate without a single Democratic vote.

Democrats used the same procedure under their own unified control. The American Rescue Plan Act passed through reconciliation in 2021. The Inflation Reduction Act followed the same path in 2022.

A House flip changes the calculation. A budget resolution needs majority support in both chambers. If the opposing party controls the House, the president's party can no longer count on adopting one. Without that resolution, no reconciliation bill can reach the Senate floor.

For businesses and investors, the shift narrows the range of likely fiscal outcomes. Large party-line tax cuts or tax increases become much harder to enact. Tax and spending changes that do pass after a flip generally require agreement from both parties.

A new House majority cannot ratify treaties or confirm cabinet officials, judges and most other nominees. Those powers belong to the Senate, so a flip shifts the policy risks investors weigh rather than setting the market's direction.

Treaty approval sits with the Senate alone. Article II, Section 2 of the Constitution requires two-thirds of senators present to consent before a treaty takes effect. A House majority, however large, gets no vote in that process.

Trade agreements can work differently. Many have been carried out through implementing legislation, which must pass both chambers like any other bill. In those cases, the House does have a say.

Nominations follow the treaty pattern. Supreme Court justices, federal judges, cabinet secretaries, ambassadors and the chair of the Federal Reserve all need Senate confirmation. A change in House control leaves those votes entirely with senators.

There is one exception. Under the 25th Amendment, ratified in 1967, a president fills a vacancy in the vice presidency by nominating a replacement. That nominee needs a majority vote in both the House and the Senate. Gerald Ford $F was confirmed this way in 1973, and Nelson Rockefeller followed in 1974.

The House also cannot erase a federal regulation on its own. Agencies write rules under authority Congress has already granted. When Congress wants to overturn a rule directly, it must pass a measure through both chambers, and the president can veto it.

Interest rates sit outside the chamber's reach as well. The Federal Open Market Committee sets monetary policy independently of Congress. The Fed chair does testify twice a year before the House Financial Services Committee, and the committee's majority-party chair runs those hearings.

Investors tend to focus on four areas after a House majority change. The first is tax policy, including whether expiring provisions get extended and whether new tax proposals ever reach a floor vote. The second is spending deadlines tied to the federal fiscal year, which begins Oct. 1.

The third is debt-limit timing, meaning when the Treasury approaches its borrowing cap and how long Congress takes to act. The fourth is regulatory oversight. Hearings, document requests and subpoenas can put a spotlight on specific industries and companies.

None of these factors determines a market outcome on its own. Each one adds a decision point to the calendar. Each also widens the range of possible policy results that businesses and investors have to plan around.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The charter creating the new class takes effect Jan. 19 under the filing, and a proposed schedule sets a trial for April

Photo by Laurent Hou/Hans Lucas /AFP via Getty Images

Meta $META Platforms said it will not issue any Class C stock, through a dividend or otherwise, while shareholder lawsuits over its reclassification plan are pending in Delaware. The company made the commitment in a stipulation filed Wednesday in the Delaware Court of Chancery.

The stipulation needs approval from Chancellor Kathaleen St. Jude McCormick. It sets trial for April 19-23, 2027, in Wilmington, and Meta's response to the consolidated complaint is due Nov. 24. Defendants say they do not expect the trial to need all five days.

The court consolidated the shareholder cases on Nov. 6 and named California State Teachers' Retirement System and PFA Pension forsikringsaktieselskab as lead plaintiffs, according to the filing. The 10 lawsuits allege that CEO Mark Zuckerberg and other board members breached their fiduciary duties, according to Bloomberg.

The filing says nothing in the order prevents the amended charter that creates the new class from taking effect Jan. 19, 2027. If a final, non-appealable order declares the charter invalid, Meta must file certificates of correction with the Delaware Secretary of State stating that it has been rescinded. The same step would apply to the certificate of designations for Meta's 6.50% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock, the filing says.

"In the best interest of our shareholders, we are seeking a final determination as quickly as the court will allow, and we will vigorously defend against these claims," Meta said in a statement, according to Bloomberg.

Meta had sought a fast-tracked trial, while the plaintiffs wanted McCormick to allow more time before the case is heard, according to Bloomberg. Meta has said it needs the new class to fund its AI infrastructure buildout and must act quickly, citing companies' loss of access to the bond market.

Meta's board approved the new non-voting class in October after a special committee made up of independent directors with no stake in the deal unanimously recommended it. The board declared a one-time dividend of one Class C share for each Class A and Class B share, contingent on the charter taking effect. The board will set the record and payment dates by later action, the company said.

Under an agreement with Meta, 20% of the Class C stock Zuckerberg receives would be freely saleable, and the other 80% would carry sale restrictions, according to the company's filing.

Seattle startup Aarden AI on Tuesday announced $8 million in new funding to grow its team and accelerate its work helping landowners evaluate potential uses for their properties and navigate deals with developers building data centers, clean energy projects, housing and other developments.

Founded last year, the company says its clients collectively own or manage approximately 14 million acres worldwide — nearly the land area of West Virginia. Aarden’s team said it has evaluated more than $500 million worth of land deals.

“But land markets remain opaque and manual with far too much friction. Finding the right site, and building trust with the right partners quickly, is more important than ever for our economy and our environment,” founder and CEO Danan Margason said in a statement.

The company combines data on hundreds of land attributes with historical market data and proprietary models to assess development suitability, valuation trends, ownership and community sentiment. Its tools and services also help developers identify sites and connect with landowners.

Aarden generates revenue through subscriptions to its technology, which includes AI-native data, models and investment tools, and through fees for services tied to specific deals or analyses.

The new round brings Aarden’s total funding to $12 million. Overture Ventures led the round, with participation from Madrona and Propeller Ventures. “Diligence that used to take months now produces investment-grade answers we can act on, and that is shaping how we manage value across our portfolio,” said Alex Hinson, president and CEO of Resource Management Service.

Other companies offering property research and analysis tools include Acres, which provides land data, valuations and due diligence tools, and Land id, which offers property insights and mapping tools.

Ben Eidelson, a partner at Stepchange Ventures, which participated in the startup’s first funding round, said the company is already having an impact.

#5342. Chipotle, Macy’s, and Ally CEOs on why loyalty perks matter more as shoppers balk at high prices

When Chipotle overhauled its rewards program in April, it made perks like free chips and guac easier to snag and added half-off entrées, as diners started to balk at high prices.

For the burrito chain, the program helps it weather inflation and keep customers in the Chipotle habit. It now counts more than 24 million active members, and they drove a third of sales in the third quarter, the highest share Chipotle has reported.

“I think in this modern world, you have to be really up to speed on what’s going on with your loyalty consumer because arguably it’s the most valuable consumer within your ecosystem,” Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright said Tuesday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, on a panel moderated by this reporter.

Loyalty programs have become a front line in the fight for market share. The freebies get people in the door, but the bigger prize is the data: a detailed record of what customers buy and when, which lets brands tailor offers and makes it harder for shoppers to stray. Boatwright, Macy’s CEO Tony Spring, and Ally Financial CEO Michael Rhodes run very different businesses: Macy’s is No. 192 on the 2026 Fortune 500, Ally is No. 275, and Chipotle is No. 351. All three are leaning on that math.

Boatwright said the pull to trim perks is real. As a rewards database grows and inflation squeezes margins, he said, “The gravity pulls brands toward, ‘ How do I capture some margin here.” His own team brought him ideas for cutting rewards.

“We are unwilling as a brand to do that,” he said. “I said, come back to me with 10 ideas on how to increase value for the consumer and let’s have a conversation.”

That stance tracks with Chipotle’s refusal to chase traffic with deep discounts. In February, Boatwright said he didn’t want to “devalue our core offering” with McDonald’s-style deals and planned price increases below the rate of inflation. Loyalty perks let the chain hand its most frequent diners more value without cutting menu prices for everyone.

The same logic shaped Chipotle’s answer to GLP-1 weight-loss drugs: a high-protein menu with low-priced add-ons rather than markdowns. “You’ve got to have innovation that doesn’t discount the core offering, but meets a consumer need state,” Boatwright said.

Spring, who took over as CEO of Macy’s Inc. in February 2024, has been steering the 168-year-old department store operator’s turnaround. He said a loyalty program only works if shoppers believe it does.

“Loyalty is integral, I think, to the relationships people have with brands,” Spring said. “And we are constantly striving at Macy’s, Bloomingdale’s, and Bluemercury to make sure that the loyalty program has value in the eyes of the consumer, not in our eyes.”

The payoff comes when a shopper decides where to look first, at the mall or online. “If the Macy’s app or the Bloomingdale’s app is there and I already have rewards in my wallet, it’s going to encourage me to go there maybe and complete my activity,” he said.

Macy’s program is built to be easy to join, Spring said, with rewards that don’t depend on how a customer pays and bigger ones for Macy’s credit card holders. The most committed shoppers can earn perks like free merchandise, free delivery, and after-hours shopping. “If you are more committed to us, we want to provide that value to you,” he said.

Spring is also thinking about what happens to those perks when an AI agent does the shopping. Macy’s has started working with Google’s Gemini on agentic commerce, he said, and the priority is making sure reward points, gift cards, and delivery promises still work when a bot places the order.

Food, clothes, and home goods offer sensory experiences that financial services can’t match, and few people feel much affection for their bank. Ally Financial, which bills itself as the largest all-digital bank in the U.S., is trying anyway. In May, it rolled out Loyally, a fee-free rewards program open to customers regardless of their account balance.

“The question really is how can we add some real value for customers that gives them reasons they want to keep on coming back to our site and engaging with us,” Rhodes said. “We’ve literally had it for like six months now, but the early results are really encouraging.”

Ally is starting from a strong base, by Rhodes’ account. He said customer retention runs well over 90%, about 15% of new account volume comes through referrals, and 70% of customers are Gen Z or millennials.

Rhodes argued that AI search is raising the stakes on every customer interaction, because what customers and employees say about a brand feeds the engines that make recommendations. “There are people who spend 10 times what we spend,” he said of Ally’s marketing budget. “Yet in the AI search engines and unbranded inquiries in consumer banking, we show up number one.”

The harder balance is rewarding regulars while still persuading new customers to try a brand. Spring said that’s where a retailer’s customer data comes in: breaking shoppers into cohorts and targeting each one, both to drive new traffic and to “create extraordinary value for your highest, most loyal consumers.”

“It’s not a one-size-fits-all approach,” Spring said. “It needs to be very bespoke. And you have to leverage tools like, dare I say, AI.”

Boatwright said every change to Chipotle’s program aims to draw more users in at the top of the funnel, then “make it much more sticky within the funnel and get those consumers coming back more often.”

The next test may come when the customer isn’t the one searching. Boatwright said agentic AI ordering is coming whether brands are ready or not, and Chipotle has to make sure it shows up “when you ask your agent, tell me the best burrito in town.”

Phil Wahba is a senior writer at Fortune primarily focused on leadership coverage, with a prior focus on retail.

#5338. ‘Do not search Amazon’: Meta’s Muse now shops elsewhere by default

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 2:36 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:45 am

Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking.

The shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked. The instructions include a template brief for Muse’s browser that says, “Do not search Amazon.”

The change was spotted last week by Juozas Kaziukenas, founder of the e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, who asked Muse for the text of its shopping skill and compared it with the version from the day before. He posted the before-and-after on Friday. GeekWire asked Muse for its shopping skill and got the same language.

“Amazon blocked Muse, so now Muse blocked Amazon,” Kaziukenas wrote on X.

Muse is also told not to name Amazon as a site to search in that browser brief, “even as an example,” unless the user asked for Amazon. The skill steers the agent to Walmart and Target for general goods, Best Buy for electronics, and Home Depot or Lowe’s for home improvement.

For Muse users, not much changes in practice. Amazon began blocking Muse in September, less than two weeks after Meta launched the agent, showing anyone who tried to shop through it a message saying continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use. Kaziukenas said any Amazon search would fail anyway because of the block.

What’s new is that Meta appears to be going along with what Amazon asked for. When it began blocking Muse, Amazon said it had asked Meta to “remove Amazon from the experience.” Meta hadn’t said publicly how it would respond.

Meta didn’t respond to an inquiry about the change. An Amazon spokesperson said the company had nothing to share.

Amazon objected that Muse didn’t identify itself when it browsed the site and appeared to capture and store customer credentials. Meta has said Muse has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods. The standoff set off a broader debate over who owns the customer relationship when an AI agent does the buying.

Since then, both sides have kept moving. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada signed up for Muse in its first six weeks, Forbes reported, and Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora and Wayfair are among the retailers working with Meta on it.

The business stakes are high for Amazon. It generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, including sponsored products that appear as people browse its pages — ads a shopper might never see if an outside agent does the searching. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said Muse will take a small cut of the transactions it handles.

Amazon has fought this battle before, suing Perplexity last November over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. It’s now pressing that case in part on the same Conditions of Use it cited in blocking Muse.

On Amazon’s earnings call last month, CEO Andy Jassy said outside shopping agents aren’t making a meaningful dent in Amazon’s advertising business. “Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet,” he said, adding that the experience still isn’t great or more convenient than going straight to a retailer.

Jassy said Amazon expects to work with “horizontal agents,” general-purpose assistants like Muse, but believes its own Alexa for Shopping will be the main agent people use to shop Amazon. Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, combining its Rufus shopping chatbot with the Alexa+ assistant.

It has since started letting some customers text Alexa to shop, much as people do with Muse.

#5337. Oklahoma’s governor sees universities as ‘stuck in their ways.’ His fix, a 3-year bachelor’s degree, is already spreading fast

Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt has a problem with the four-year degree, and he brought it to a room full of the people who hire its graduates.

“The academic community are kind of stuck in their ways. They don’t like to change,” Stitt said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, on a panel with U.S. Steel CEO David Burritt. He said when he digs into the degree programs at the University of Oklahoma and Oklahoma State, “there’s a book this thick and then you’ve got like three people graduating from these different things.”

He added: “I’m not saying that degree is not important, but you can’t be all things [to] all people.”

His fix is a 90-credit bachelor’s degree, 30 credits short of the standard 120, or roughly a year less of tuition. In-state tuition and fees at public four-year colleges averaged $11,950 in the 2024-25 school year, according to the College Board. Stitt said the idea is to keep the rigor of the requirements, trim some electives, and “get kids ready for the workforce quicker.”

RAND counted 119 reduced-credit bachelor’s programs publicly announced across the U.S. as of May 2026, most of them in “applied and workforce-facing fields.” Only five were announced in 2024. In 2026 alone, RAND counted 50 through May, when its data collection ended, and Jason Lee, a senior policy researcher at RAND and the report’s lead author, told Fortune he has seen roughly 100 more announcements since. That puts this year at about 150, though Lee said the newer count hasn’t been through RAND’s quality-assurance review and should be treated as approximate.

Stitt signed an executive order in February ordering a 90-day study of 90-credit “accelerated” degrees, and the Legislature followed with HB 3315, which required the State Regents to study feasibility. In June, the regents took action to create a framework for the degrees.

“A three-year degree speeds up workforce entry and makes so much sense for students who are ready to work and support a family, right here in Oklahoma,” Stitt said in a statement at the time.

On Sept. 3, the regents approved four reduced-credit degrees ranging from 90 to 103 credit hours, according to the Oklahoma Council of Public Affairs: social work at the University of Oklahoma, two at Oklahoma State, in artificial intelligence and in business, and workforce development at Rogers State University.

“A college degree doesn’t have to take four years just because it always has,” Stitt posted on X.

The University of Oklahoma told Fortune that it sees itself “at the forefront of rethinking traditional approaches to higher education to better serve students and meet Oklahoma’s workforce needs,” leading the way in developing three-year bachelor’s degrees, while ensuring traditional degree programs are structured to avoid unnecessary credit hours that can delay graduation.

Other states are moving, too. Tennessee’s higher education commission approved a policy in July allowing bachelor’s degrees of as few as 90 credit hours. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott directed the state’s coordinating board to develop pathways in August. The University of North Carolina system approved a pilot in April, and 11 campuses have submitted proposals, according to the James G. Martin Center.

Through May, most of the growth came from individual colleges, especially private ones, Lee told Fortune, though states and accreditors shaped it too, since both have a hand in approving new programs. Since then, he said, “it seems to have become much more common for state actors to encourage these programs at their public universities,” as in Oklahoma, Tennessee, and Texas. Ohio and Indiana have gone further, he said, and required their public universities to adopt them.

The three-year degree tests an old question in economics: how much of a degree’s value comes from what students learn, and how much from what it tells employers. Michael Spence shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in economics, in part, for showing how education can work as a signal, costly proof of ability that employers can’t see directly. A shorter degree is cheaper to get. Nobody knows yet whether it signals as much. Much of Europe has run three-year bachelor’s degrees since the Bologna reforms began in 1999.

RAND found that business, information technology, and cybersecurity look most workable for shorter degrees, while fields with clinical or licensing requirements are less adaptable. How graduate schools, employers, and licensing boards will treat the degrees remains uncertain, RAND found.

“These programs are too nascent to follow graduates into the workforce,” Lee told Fortune.

“We don’t have employers who said, ‘Gee, we’ve had three-year graduates,’” Madeleine Green, executive director of the College-in-3 Exchange, told Inside Higher Ed this month.

The programs are still small. Johnson & Wales University has 135 students across four three-year programs, and Weber State has 30 across three, according to Inside Higher Ed.

Faculty groups have pushed back. The American Association of University Professors and the American Federation of Teachers objected to Massachusetts’ approvals on grounds of “academic integrity.”

“This is not innovation. This is just cutting corners,” AAUP president Todd Wolfson told the Associated Press in August. A year less of tuition is also a year less of revenue for the schools.

Stitt’s other pitch to the CEOs was apprenticeships. He said he had visited Switzerland and Germany, where compulsory education stops after the first year of high school and students start working inside companies, and that Oklahoma made liability insurance fixes so companies could take on high school students. He told the room about a 19-year-old in Switzerland who wanted to be an architect. After three years at an architecture firm, she could work as a draftsperson, and university was still open to her.

“We’ve got to rethink that in our workforce needs here in the U.S.,” Stitt said.

[This report has been updated with comments from Rand’s Jason Lee.]

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5336. AI Search Is Tipping The Balance In Favor Of Big-Box Stores. Here’s How Small Retailers Can Fight Back

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI search overwhelmingly favors major retailers. Small merchants can take these three steps to get noticed by chatbots.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

This fall, my company took an important message to the heart of New York City.

The call to action: “Prompt Local.” At our pop-up storefront in the East Village, we showed how shoppers can tweak AI search to make it recommend independent retailers. Across the front window, scenes of people searching online were paired with specific prompts designed to steer AI agents toward local businesses.

From working with tens of thousands of merchants, we knew it was time to take a stand. There’s a lot at stake for small retailers, and we’ve got the receipts to prove it. As AI search quickly becomes the norm, those stores are getting lost in the shuffle.

A new study we commissioned shows that nine times out of 10, AI directs shoppers to major retailers. Looking to buy a new road bike in New York? Chances are, ChatGPT will provide a list of national chains, even when there’s a great independent store just around the corner. The buyer didn’t ask for that kind of list. The model decided for them.

For the past two decades, being discoverable online revolved around SEO. The basic question was: Are you showing up in Google results? Search engines learned shoppers’ locations and surfaced nearby businesses.

Those priorities shouldn’t disappear just because answers now come from chatbots. If AI platforms are becoming the new front door to commerce, they share responsibility for which businesses get found.

But small retailers can’t afford to wait for these companies to refine their search results. AI is changing the rules, and stores need to keep up. They have to think not only about whether search engines can find them, but whether AI understands who they are, what they sell, and why they’re worth recommending.

One place to start is by educating customers. Our study found that adding words like “independent” or “locally owned” to AI searches reduced big chains’ share of recommendations to as little as one in 10 on Google’s platforms.

Retailers can spread the word by sharing simple search tips with shoppers in-store, on their websites, and across social media. The more consumers make independent businesses a priority in their searches, the stronger the signal to AI companies that local options deserve greater visibility.

Beyond educating shoppers, here are three more things merchants can do to raise their profile in AI search.

To get AI’s attention, small retailers also need to give them something to find. And the closer a shopper gets to making a purchase, the tougher the competition becomes. Our study showed that when someone names a specific product, a small store’s odds of being the top recommendation fall from roughly one in three to one in 10.

Big retailers also have an advantage when it comes to how much information about them is readily available online. Their catalogs, inventory, product descriptions, reviews, and locations are already highly visible. Small merchants may have deeper expertise and better curation, but AI can’t recommend what it can’t see.

That makes it even more important for retailers to put their inventory online. AI agents increasingly fetch product information directly, which means retail websites may effectively become showrooms for both AI and human shoppers.Here, AI is part of the solution. New tools let retailers showcase their entire product catalog so agents can find what they’re looking for. Besides syncing that inventory with your POS, they write descriptions that make those products easier for AI to discover.

Making a retail website simple for AI to read is critical, too. Behind the scenes, a merchant can clearly label product details like price, brand, and whether an item is in stock, while also giving search and AI crawlers a map of the pages it wants them to find.

When shoppers use an AI chatbot to search, they ask a lot of questions. What jacket styles are hot this fall? Which supportive running shoes are best for beginners? What are the top ergonomic office chairs for working from home?

For independent retailers, that creates another opportunity to get noticed. The key is to establish yourself as an expert by building authority around what you sell.

Useful, substantive content can help. For example, a bike shop could create TikTok or YouTube videos showing how to set up tubeless tires or replace a worn chain. Those clips may look educational, but what they’re really doing is showing the expertise behind the business.

Of all the social platforms, YouTube could be an independent merchant’s best friend. Just ask the small luxury watch dealers who use long-form informational videos to build trust — by exploring topics like how to avoid buying a fake.

YouTube’s connection to Google makes it an even more powerful tool for independent retailers. Gemini regularly surfaces videos from the site, giving merchants another way to get their expertise (and products) in front of shoppers using AI search.

A steady stream of blog posts can do the same thing. By posting weekly about fashion trends, for instance, a women’s clothing boutique gives AI systems more proof that it knows its category inside and out.

If that sounds like a heavy lift, it doesn’t need to be. AI assistants can help write, publish, and manage blog content, while built-in SEO tools help optimize each post for traditional search and make it easier for search engines to crawl and AI systems to understand.

To stand out in AI search, small retailers also need to rethink what social media is for.

Platforms like Reddit, Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube still help stores reach shoppers. But they now do a second job: showing AI what a business sells, what it knows, and what it specializes in.

AI tools are paying attention. Social posts appear in almost 70% of Google’s AI Overview responses. And in Google’s AI mode, they show up in almost half of responses to searches that don’t name a brand — the ones shoppers type before they know your store exists.Meta’s new Muse agent takes this further. Muse works inside Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp, which reach 3.6 billion people a day. With a shopper’s permission, it can learn their taste from what they follow, like, save, and share. Every customer who engages with a store’s posts is teaching their agent that the store belongs on their shortlist. Retailers with active, engaged communities are more likely to be recommended.

That’s the real opening for local retailers: AI remembers what shoppers like. Once a customer shows their agent they value a certain kind of store, like a neighborhood bookshop or an independent boutique, it can keep recommending similar places.

For their part, retailers should show up consistently where both shoppers and AI are paying attention. By embracing this new reality, they can turn a potential threat into a reason for customers to make the trip.

This fall, my company took an important message to the heart of New York City.

The call to action: “Prompt Local.” At our pop-up storefront in the East Village, we showed how shoppers can tweak AI search to make it recommend independent retailers. Across the front window, scenes of people searching online were paired with specific prompts designed to steer AI agents toward local businesses.

From working with tens of thousands of merchants, we knew it was time to take a stand. There’s a lot at stake for small retailers, and we’ve got the receipts to prove it. As AI search quickly becomes the norm, those stores are getting lost in the shuffle.
