#5335. 12 Speaker of the House firsts, from Frederick Muhlenberg to Kevin McCarthy

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These Speaker of the House firsts, from Frederick Muhlenberg in 1789 to Kevin McCarthy's 2023 removal, trace how the office gained, lost and reshaped its power

The U.S. Constitution names only one officer of the House of Representatives. Article I says the House shall choose its Speaker and other officers. It says nothing more about the job. Everything else that defines the speakership has been settled by the House itself since 1789. That includes how much power the office carries, how a member wins it and how a Speaker can lose it.

As a result, the office's history reads as a record of improvisation. Practices that look fixed today often began as a single Speaker's ruling, a floor fight or an election result without precedent. Many of these firsts mark a moment when the balance of power inside the chamber shifted. Sometimes it moved toward the Speaker, and sometimes away.

The Speaker presides over the House and controls much of its agenda, including which bills reach the floor and when. The office also stands second in the presidential line of succession, behind the vice president. That placement comes from the Presidential Succession Act of 1947.

This timeline gathers 12 Speaker of the House firsts in chronological order. It is a selection, not a complete record of every precedent the office has set. It begins in April 1789, when the 1st Congress reached a quorum and elected Frederick Muhlenberg of Pennsylvania. It ends in October 2023, when the House removed a sitting Speaker through a motion to vacate for the first time.

In between are the entries that trace the job's reach. One Speaker won the post on his first day as a member. Another later moved to the White House. One changed what counts as a quorum. A later Speaker saw his powers cut by insurgents in his own party working with the opposition. The list also covers the longest total tenure and the longest unbroken run. It includes a party's return to the majority after decades in the minority. It also marks the first woman to hold the gavel and her return to the post years later.

Each entry stands on its own. Readers can start with the founding-era Speakers or jump to the 2023 fight over the gavel, which took 15 ballots to settle. The entries show how the House has expanded, limited and contested the Speaker's authority over time.

Frederick Muhlenberg, a Pennsylvania representative, became the first Speaker of the House in April 1789. Members chose him once the chamber gathered a quorum during the 1st Congress.

The new Congress was due to open in March 1789 in New York, then the seat of the federal government. Too few representatives had arrived to conduct business. The House could not organize itself or elect officers until enough members reached the city. Once a quorum assembled in April, choosing a presiding officer was among its first acts.

Muhlenberg brought prior experience in running a legislature to the post. He had served in the Continental Congress and had presided over the Pennsylvania Assembly. He was also president of the Pennsylvania convention that ratified the Constitution in 1787.

Muhlenberg was born in 1750 in Trappe, Pennsylvania. He was ordained as a Lutheran minister before turning to public office. His father, Henry Melchior Muhlenberg, organized the first Lutheran synod in North America. His brother Peter Muhlenberg served as a general in the Continental Army.

Henry Clay, a Kentucky representative, was elected Speaker of the House in 1811 on his first day as a House member. He held the post in three separate stretches, the last ending in 1825.

The vote came on Nov. 4, 1811, when the 12th Congress convened. Clay was not new to national politics. He had already served two short stints in the U.S. Senate, filling unexpired terms. The House was a different setting. Members chose a newcomer to lead them before he had cast a single vote in the chamber.

Clay arrived as a leader of the War Hawks. This group of mostly Southern and Western members pressed for a harder line against Britain. As Speaker, he used his authority to advance that agenda. Congress declared war on Britain in June 1812, starting the War of 1812.

Thomas Brackett Reed, a Maine Republican, was Speaker of the House from 1889 to 1891. In January 1890, he ruled that members sitting in the chamber but not voting would count toward a quorum. The ruling ended the minority's ability to stall the House by staying silent.

The tactic Reed confronted was known as the "disappearing quorum." The Constitution requires a majority of the House to be present to do business. Minority members could attend a session and simply decline to answer the roll call. They were then recorded as absent.

If enough of them stayed quiet, the count fell short of a majority. The House could not act, even with most of its members physically in the room. When the majority party held a narrow edge, a determined minority could freeze the legislative calendar this way.

Sam Rayburn, a Texas Democrat, holds the record for the most total time as Speaker of the House. Across three separate stretches between 1940 and 1961, he held the gavel for about 17 years. No one else has served longer in the office.

His first stretch began in September 1940. Rayburn, then the House majority leader, was elected Speaker after the death of Speaker William Bankhead of Alabama. He kept the post until 1947.

The breaks in his tenure came from elections, not from any challenge inside his own party. Republicans won control of the House for two Congresses during his career. The first ran from 1947 to 1949, and the second from 1953 to 1955. Each time, Rayburn led House Democrats as minority leader.

His second stretch as Speaker ran from 1949 to 1953. His third began in 1955 and lasted until his death from cancer in November 1961. He was still Speaker when he died.

Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, became Speaker of the House in January 1995. His party had won control of the chamber in the 1994 midterm elections, ending a run of Democratic majorities that dated to the 1950s.

Across those decades, every Speaker was a Democrat. Democrats also chaired every standing committee and set the floor schedule.

Gingrich first won his seat in 1978 and took office in January 1979. Through the 1980s, he built a reputation as a combative critic of the Democratic leadership. House Republicans elected him minority whip in 1989, making him the party's second-ranking leader in the chamber.

In September 1994, House Republicans unveiled the Contract with America, a campaign platform Gingrich helped shape. More than 300 Republican House candidates signed it. The document promised votes on 10 bills within the first 100 days of a Republican-led Congress. Its proposals included a balanced budget amendment, a line-item veto and changes to welfare.

Nancy Pelosi was elected Speaker of the House again on Jan. 3, 2019. The vote made her the first former Speaker to win back the gavel after a break since Sam Rayburn did so in 1955.

Her return came eight years after she lost the post. Pelosi first held the speakership from 2007 until January 2011. Republicans won control of the House in the 2010 midterm elections, and she became minority leader.

Two Republicans held the gavel during her years out of the office. John Boehner of Ohio served as Speaker from 2011 until he resigned in 2015. Paul Ryan of Wisconsin followed him and served until the end of the 115th Congress in January 2019.

Democrats regained a House majority in the 2018 midterm elections. That result set up Pelosi's second election as Speaker on the opening day of the 116th Congress.

Kevin McCarthy became the first Speaker of the House removed from office by a vote of the full chamber. On Oct. 3, 2023, the House ousted the California Republican through a motion to vacate the chair. He had held the gavel for less than nine months.

A motion to vacate is a resolution that declares the Speaker's office empty. If a majority of members voting approves it, the Speaker loses the post immediately.

Rep. Matt Gaetz, a Florida Republican, filed the motion on Oct. 2, 2023. It came two days after the House, under McCarthy, passed a stopgap spending bill with Democratic votes. That measure kept the federal government open and averted a shutdown.

The path to the vote ran through the rules McCarthy accepted to win the speakership that January. Those rules let any single House member force a vote on removing the Speaker. Under the previous Congress, a motion to vacate needed the backing of a party caucus or conference.

The 1st Congress had a heavy agenda. It created the departments of State, War and the Treasury. It set up the federal court system through the Judiciary Act of 1789. It also approved 12 proposed constitutional amendments. As Speaker, Muhlenberg signed the enrolled resolution that sent them to the states in 1789. Vice President John Adams signed it as well, as president of the Senate. The states ratified 10 of the amendments, which became the Bill of Rights.

Muhlenberg did not hold the gavel in the 2nd Congress, which met from 1791 to 1793. Jonathan Trumbull Jr. of Connecticut served as Speaker instead. Muhlenberg then returned to the chair, serving a second stretch from 1793 to 1795. That return made him the first person to hold the speakership on two nonconsecutive occasions.

The early speakership was mainly a presiding role. The Speaker kept order, recognized members during debate and ruled on procedure. Muhlenberg stayed in the House until 1797. He died in 1801 in Lancaster, Pennsylvania.

His main tool was committee assignments. House rules at the time let the Speaker appoint committee members. Clay placed allies on the committees that handled foreign affairs and military matters. That gave the Speaker a direct hand in shaping which bills moved and how.

Clay's approach turned the speakership into a center of political power. Earlier Speakers had acted mostly as presiding officers. Clay used the chair to steer legislation and policy as well as to run debate.

His first stretch ended in January 1814. He resigned the speakership to join the U.S. delegation that negotiated peace with Britain. That delegation produced the Treaty of Ghent, signed in December 1814.

Clay returned to the House and was elected Speaker again in 1815. During his second stretch, Congress took up the dispute over Missouri's admission as a state. Clay played a central role in the Missouri Compromise of 1820. He left the chair later that year.

His third stretch began in 1823. It ended in 1825, when Clay left the House to become secretary of state under President John Quincy Adams. He later returned to the Senate and ran for president three times without winning.

James K. Polk is the only Speaker of the House who went on to become president. The Tennessee Democrat held the gavel from 1835 to 1839, then served in the White House from 1845 to 1849.

Polk was born in North Carolina in 1795 and built his political career in Tennessee. He entered the House in 1825. He was a close ally of Andrew Jackson. Supporters called him "Young Hickory," a nod to Jackson's nickname, "Old Hickory."

His speakership covered the 24th and 25th Congresses. Polk won the post in 1835 by defeating John Bell, a fellow Tennessean. The chamber he led was split between Jacksonian Democrats and the new Whig Party, which had formed in opposition to Jackson.

Those divisions made the job contentious. Whig members challenged his rulings and pressed him on procedure. In 1836 the House also adopted the "gag rule," which tabled antislavery petitions without debate. Fights over that rule ran through his time in the chair.

Polk left the House in 1839 to become governor of Tennessee. He then lost races for that office in 1841 and 1843. Those defeats left him without a public post as the 1844 presidential contest approached.

The Democratic National Convention met in Baltimore in 1844. Martin Van Buren arrived as the front-runner but could not secure the nomination. Delegates turned to Polk, a compromise candidate, on the ninth ballot.

In the general election, Polk defeated the Whig nominee, Henry Clay. He pledged to serve a single term and kept that promise.

His presidency expanded U.S. territory. The 1846 Oregon Treaty with Britain set the northwestern boundary at the 49th parallel. The Mexican-American War ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848. That treaty brought California and much of the Southwest under U.S. control.

At home, Polk restored the Independent Treasury system. He also signed the Walker Tariff, which lowered import duties.

Polk left office in March 1849. His successor was Zachary Taylor, a Whig. Polk died of cholera in Nashville that June.

Reed stopped relying on roll-call responses alone. He directed the clerk to record the names of members who were present but refusing to vote. Those members were then counted toward the quorum. Democrats protested loudly from the floor, but the ruling stood.

The House then wrote the principle into its rules for that Congress. The package became known as the Reed Rules. It also gave the Speaker more room to rule out motions offered only to delay business.

The new method was tested in court. In United States v. Ballin, decided in 1892, the Supreme Court upheld the House's power to set its own way of determining whether a quorum was present.

The episode is tied to Reed's nickname, "Czar Reed." Critics used the label to describe the control he exercised over the floor. The ruling shifted power away from the minority and toward the Speaker and the majority party.

Democrats dropped the counting rule after they took control of the House following Reed's first speakership. They adopted their own version of it in 1894. Reed later returned to the chair, serving as Speaker again from 1895 to 1899.

In March 1910, a coalition of insurgent Republicans and Democrats removed Speaker Joseph G. Cannon from the House Rules Committee. The vote broke the Speaker's control over which bills reached the floor and how they were debated.

Cannon, an Illinois Republican, held the speakership from 1903 to 1911. Colleagues and the press knew him as "Uncle Joe." In that era, the Speaker appointed members to House committees and also chaired the Rules Committee.

Those two powers worked together. Committee assignments let Cannon reward allies and sideline critics. Control of the Rules Committee let him decide when legislation came up for a vote and under what terms.

Cannon used that leverage to slow measures he opposed, including proposals backed by progressive members of his own party. Republicans from the Midwest and West who wanted reform found their bills stalled. They became known as insurgents.

The decisive challenge came from George Norris, a Republican representative from Nebraska. He introduced a resolution to change how the Rules Committee was chosen. Cannon's supporters argued that the resolution was out of order. The dispute carried through several days of floor debate.

Norris's measure passed when Democrats joined the insurgents. It expanded the Rules Committee, gave the full House the power to elect the committee's members and barred the Speaker from sitting on it.

Cannon answered the defeat by inviting a motion to declare the chair vacant. Albert Burleson, a Texas Democrat, offered it. The motion failed. Many insurgents who had voted to curb Cannon's powers would not vote to remove him from office.

Cannon remained Speaker until the end of that Congress. Democrats then won control of the House in the 1910 midterm elections. Missouri Democrat Champ Clark became Speaker in 1911. The new majority also moved committee assignment power away from the Speaker.

The Speaker has not served on the Rules Committee since the 1910 vote. Later Speakers shaped the panel through their party's leadership rather than by holding a seat on it.

Cannon's name remains on Capitol Hill. The Cannon House Office Building, completed in 1908, is the oldest of the House office buildings.

That span put him in the chair under four presidents: Franklin D. Roosevelt, Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John F. Kennedy. Eisenhower was a Republican. Rayburn spent much of the late 1950s as a Democratic Speaker working with a president from the other party.

Rayburn worked through personal relationships with members. He hosted lawmakers in a private room in the Capitol known as the "Board of Education," where they gathered after hours. Truman, then vice president, was in that room on April 12, 1945. There he received a call summoning him to the White House. At the White House, he learned that Roosevelt had died.

Rayburn also served as a mentor to Lyndon B. Johnson, a fellow Texan. Johnson began his House career in the 1930s before moving on to the Senate.

Rayburn first entered the House in 1913. He represented a district in northeast Texas that included his hometown of Bonham. Before Congress, he had served as speaker of the Texas House of Representatives.

John McCormack of Massachusetts succeeded him as Speaker in January 1962. The Rayburn House Office Building, which houses congressional offices on Capitol Hill, carries his name.

Thomas P. "Tip" O'Neill, a Massachusetts Democrat, served as Speaker of the House from 1977 to 1987. His 10 years in the chair are the longest continuous tenure in the office's history.

O'Neill took the gavel in January 1977, at the opening of the 95th Congress. He succeeded Carl Albert of Oklahoma, who had retired. O'Neill had already moved up through the Democratic leadership. He served as majority whip and then as majority leader under Albert.

O'Neill was born in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1912. Before reaching Congress, he served in the Massachusetts House of Representatives and rose to become its speaker. He then won the U.S. House seat that John F. Kennedy gave up to run for the Senate. O'Neill took that seat in 1953.

His speakership spanned five consecutive Congresses, the 95th through the 99th. Sam Rayburn of Texas holds the record for total time as Speaker. Rayburn's service, though, was broken into separate stretches by periods of Republican control. O'Neill held the gavel without interruption from his first election as Speaker until his departure.

O'Neill's decade as Speaker overlapped two presidents. His first four years came under Jimmy Carter, a fellow Democrat. The remaining six came under Ronald Reagan, a Republican. Reagan drew on votes from conservative Democrats to pass his 1981 tax and budget plans over O'Neill's opposition.

The two men also reached agreements. In 1983, O'Neill and Reagan backed a bipartisan package of Social Security changes. The package built on recommendations from a commission chaired by Alan Greenspan.

Live television coverage of the House began during his speakership. C-SPAN started carrying House floor proceedings in March 1979, early in the 96th Congress.

O'Neill did not run for reelection in 1986. He left Congress when his term ended in January 1987. Jim Wright of Texas, the majority leader, succeeded him as Speaker. O'Neill died in Boston in January 1994.

His memoir, Man of the House, written with William Novak, came out in 1987. The phrase "All politics is local" became the saying most closely associated with him. It also became the title of a book he wrote with Gary Hymel, published in 1994.

The 1994 losses extended to the Democratic leadership. Speaker Tom Foley, a Democrat from Washington state, lost his own seat. He was the first sitting Speaker defeated for reelection since 1862.

Once in charge, the new majority rewrote House rules. Committee chairs became subject to a limit of three consecutive terms. The Speaker's own tenure was capped at four consecutive terms. The House also abolished three committees and cut committee staff by about a third. The eliminated panels were the District of Columbia, Merchant Marine and Fisheries, and Post Office and Civil Service committees.

Gingrich's speakership also brought clashes with President Bill Clinton over the federal budget. Two government shutdowns followed. The first lasted from Nov. 14 to Nov. 19, 1995. The longer one ran from Dec. 16, 1995, to Jan. 6, 1996.

In January 1997, the House reprimanded Gingrich over an ethics case and assessed him a $300,000 penalty. After Republicans lost House seats in the 1998 midterms, he announced he would step down as Speaker. He left Congress in January 1999.

Nancy Pelosi became the first woman to serve as Speaker of the House on Jan. 4, 2007. The California Democrat won the post on the opening day of the 110th Congress, more than two centuries after the first Speaker took the chair in 1789.

Her election followed the 2006 midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of the House. Pelosi took the gavel from Dennis Hastert, an Illinois Republican who had held it since 1999.

Pelosi reached the speakership by rising through her party's House leadership. Her Democratic colleagues elected her whip in 2001. She became the party's top leader in the House in January 2003. That made her the first woman to lead a major party in either chamber of Congress.

Her congressional career began in San Francisco. She won her House seat in a 1987 special election and represented a San Francisco district for decades afterward. She also became the first Italian American to serve as Speaker.

Her roots are in Baltimore, where she was born. Her father, Thomas D'Alesandro Jr., represented a Maryland district in the House and later served as mayor of Baltimore.

The 2007 vote also changed the presidential line of succession. No woman had ever stood as high in that line as Pelosi did once she took the gavel.

The milestone closed a long gap for women in the House. Jeannette Rankin, a Montana Republican, became the first woman elected to Congress in 1916. She took her seat the following year. Women served in the House for about nine decades before one held its top post.

Pelosi's first stretch as Speaker covered four years and two Congresses. During that time, the House passed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, which President Barack Obama signed in February 2009. The House also passed the Affordable Care Act, and Obama signed the health care law in March 2010.

That stretch ended after the 2010 midterm elections, when Republicans won back the House majority. John Boehner, an Ohio Republican, succeeded her as Speaker in January 2011.

Her return required support from critics inside her own party. A group of House Democrats pushed for new leadership after the midterms. Pelosi won over enough of them in part by agreeing to limit how long she would serve as Speaker. Several Democrats still voted for other candidates when the full House chose its Speaker.

The gap between the two comebacks spans more than six decades. Rayburn regained the office in 1955 after Republicans controlled the House for two years. Pelosi's absence lasted four times as long as his.

Pelosi held the gavel for two more Congresses, the 116th and the 117th. During that stretch she presided over the House as it impeached President Donald Trump twice. The first impeachment came in December 2019 and the second in January 2021. After the 2020 elections, she led a narrow Democratic majority.

Republicans won the House in the 2022 midterm elections. Pelosi then announced she would not seek a leadership post in the next Congress. Hakeem Jeffries of New York succeeded her as leader of House Democrats.

Her second stretch as Speaker ended in January 2023. Across her two stints, she spent eight years in the office.

Kevin McCarthy, a California Republican, became Speaker of the House in the early hours of Jan. 7, 2023, on the 15th ballot. He reached the gavel only after 14 earlier rounds of voting failed to produce a winner.

The contest opened on Jan. 3, 2023, the first day of the 118th Congress. Electing a Speaker is the first order of business in a new House. Until that vote is settled, members-elect cannot take the oath of office. The chamber also cannot adopt its rules, form committees or pass legislation.

Republicans had won a narrow House majority in the 2022 midterm elections. McCarthy had led the House Republican conference since 2019, and he was the party's nominee for Speaker. To win, a candidate needs a majority of the members who vote for a named person. With so few seats to spare, a small bloc of Republicans could keep him below that line.

That bloc formed on the opening day. A group of conservative Republicans withheld their support and cast votes for other names instead. Democrats backed their own leader, Hakeem Jeffries of New York, on every ballot. Neither candidate could reach a majority, and the House kept voting.

The standoff stretched across several days of roll calls. McCarthy and his allies negotiated with the holdouts between votes. Several of those members moved into his column on Jan. 6. The rest did not switch outright.

On the 15th ballot, the final holdouts voted present rather than naming another candidate. A present vote does not count toward the total of members voting for a named person. That lowered the number McCarthy needed, and he cleared it shortly after midnight.

Rep. Hal Rogers of Kentucky, the dean of the House, administered the Speaker's oath to McCarthy. McCarthy then swore in the other members-elect as a group. With that step done, the House could adopt its rules and begin its formal work for the new Congress.

An earlier attempt to remove a Speaker this way never reached the floor. In 2015, Rep. Mark Meadows of North Carolina filed a motion to vacate against Speaker John Boehner. The House never voted on it. Boehner announced his resignation later that year.

McCarthy's removal left the chamber without an elected Speaker. Patrick McHenry, a North Carolina Republican, stepped in as Speaker pro tempore. His name sat at the top of a confidential list of successors McCarthy had filed with the House Clerk. A House rule adopted after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks requires each new Speaker to submit such a list.

House Republicans put forward several nominees for the job over the following weeks. The search ended on Oct. 25, 2023, when the House elected Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, as Speaker.

McCarthy did not run to reclaim the post. He left Congress at the end of 2023.

#5334. Jeff Bezos has some advice for Nvidia’s board on its CEO search

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 5:05 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:50 am

Jeff Bezos says Nvidia should look inside the company for its next CEO, and he doesn’t give an outsider much chance of success. The Amazon founder, now co-CEO of AI engineering startup Prometheus, made the comments Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event.

“If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated,” Bezos said. Outside CEOs at complex companies, he added, “have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding,” and he would consider hiring one “a last resort.”

Nvidia’s board says it has no plans to bring Huang back. Harvey Jones, the longtime director named the company’s first board chair last week, opened Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

Jones said the search will include internal and external candidates, and that the board wants a permanent CEO in place quickly but won’t rush the pick.

Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and CEO for 33 years, had posted a statement on X that morning offering to return. He said he had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life and would cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation last Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman who U.S. officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, according to the Wall Street Journal.

CFO Colette Kress, who spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, is interim CEO.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to leave open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Sunday that talk of a Huang comeback is “ridiculous.”

The Amazon precedent (not really): Bezos has been through a founder handoff of his own. He turned over the Amazon CEO job in 2021 to Andy Jassy, a longtime insider who built AWS. When Semafor raised the comparison, Bezos called it a poor one, saying there has never been a more carefully planned transition.

He said he didn’t know enough about what happened in Nvidia’s board meetings to say whether Huang should return. But he called Huang a remarkable founder who deserves “admiration and respect no matter what.”

Huang himself said in a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14 that he hoped his successor was already inside the company.

The Nvidia comments came in a wide-ranging interview. Bezos also said Blue Origin is using Prometheus tools on two projects, called President Trump by far the most communicative of the presidents he has worked with, and said Robert Pattinson was the clear choice to play the next James Bond after screen tests of five finalists.

Business as usual, officially: Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, including $107.6 billion from its data center business. On the call, it raised its forecast for next fiscal year’s revenue growth to about 75%, from 70%.

Kress didn’t mention Huang by name on the call. Asked about the leadership transition, she said customers, suppliers and employees remain behind the company, calling it “business as usual.” She ended the call with a short pep talk that finished, “We’ve got this.”

In case the board was wondering about one outsider in particular, Bezos is spoken for. During the Semafor interview, he described running Prometheus as “Nirvana.”

#5333. This 54-Year-Old Left Her Full-Time Therapist Job to Focus on a Flavorful Side Hustle Making $10K a Month on Amazon: ‘I Used ChatGPT’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Lana Wimmer wanted to bring a different kind of beverage to market.

This Side Hustle Spotlight Q&A features Lana Wimmer, 54, of St. George, Utah. She started her side hustle Öl Brew (pronounced “cool” without the “c”), a nonalcoholic sparkling fruit malt beverage, while working about 40 hours a week as a mental health therapist. Once she caught herself sitting in a therapy session thinking about Öl Brew, she knew she had to focus on the business full-time. The brand generates about $10,000 a month in revenue on Amazon.  Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

When did you launch the side hustle, and what specific consumer pain point did you want to address? We launched Öl Brew in 2026, about six months ago, but the idea had been with me for eight years. For most of that time, I kept hoping someone else would make these drinks. I had absolutely no ambition to enter the beverage industry.

My husband and I had lived in Europe and the Middle East, where we’d discovered nonalcoholic fruit malt beverages with this wonderful depth, body and flavor. They were nothing like the sodas we had back home. When we returned to the U.S., I couldn’t find anything that compared. The options felt uninspired: soda, sparkling water or a mocktail trying awfully hard to replace alcohol. I didn’t want an imitation of something else. I wanted a genuinely different drinking experience.

How did you validate that people would actually pay for your solution before investing serious money?One evening, I finally shared my idea over dinner with friends. The response was immediate. Everyone wanted better nonalcoholic options; this wasn’t just my personal preference.

I was also watching a shift in consumer behavior, particularly among my own adult children and their friends. They weren’t gathering around alcohol. They were cold plunging, working out and training for HYROX competitions. Their social lives looked different, and so did their beverage choices. Having spent decades as a therapist, I was especially interested in what was driving that shift. People were becoming more intentional about how they spent their time, what they consumed and how they connected.

Those early conversations gave me the conviction to invest although they weren’t proof of purchase. That came later when we got the product onto shelves and watched customers respond. Sometimes you recognize a gap in the market because you’ve been standing in it for years.

Which two or three essential tools, apps or pieces of gear did you buy in your first week, and which ones did you skip to save money?My first tools were a notebook, my computer and ChatGPT. I started writing down everything I wanted to build, followed by a much longer list of everything I didn’t know.

I used ChatGPT to research flavor houses, co-packers, brand management companies, distributors and how the beverage industry actually works. It helped me learn the terminology, understand the process and figure out whom I needed to talk to. But the real education came when I started taking those questions to people with experience. AI gave me a starting point. Industry professionals gave me context, perspective and occasionally some very expensive lessons.

I also listened constantly to business and beverage podcasts, particularly The Game with Alex Hormozi, Tim Bush’s On the Shelf and Joey Pedone’s Sippin’ & Selling. I didn’t spend money on elaborate software systems or expensive subscriptions in the beginning. My priority was understanding the business well enough to make informed decisions. I learned quickly that information is relatively easy to find. Knowing what to do with it is another matter entirely.

What were the first three steps you took in your first 30 days?My first 30 days were focused on three things: Developing a go-to-market plan, identifying our target consumer and first four flavors, and finding the people who could help bring the product to life.

I used AI to help research the industry and build an initial strategy. Then I settled on apple, lemon, peach and pomegranate as our first flavors. I wanted something familiar enough that people would be curious to try it, but different enough that they’d immediately recognize this wasn’t ordinary soda.

Then came the investment. I spent $50,000 hiring a beverage development company to help formulate the drinks and connect us with a co-packer. I also hired a branding company to develop our can designs and brand book. Altogether, the initial upfront cost, including the pilot run and production run, was about $200,000.

Here’s what I learned later: The formulation work could have been arranged without that fee. I didn’t know that at the time. That was an expensive introduction to an industry where relationships, experience and knowing the right questions to ask can save you a tremendous amount of money.

How did you land your first paying customer?Our first paying customer came after our pilot run and initial production, and there was nothing sophisticated about the sales strategy. We walked into a local grocery store, sat down with the manager, introduced ourselves and told him what we were building. He agreed to carry Öl Brew.

Another local farmers market retailer followed, and suddenly our drinks were on shelves, where actual customers could decide if our idea had merit. Those first accounts gave us more than revenue. They gave us feedback, credibility and the opportunity to start building a business in the real world.

After all the planning, design, and money we’d spent, our first sale came from sitting across a table and having a conversation. I rather love that.

Nowadays, which specific tools or platforms help you bring in customers, and what is one feature inside those tools that saves you the most time?We’re using Instagram, TikTok Shop, Amazon, Walmart.com and our Shopify website to introduce consumers to Öl Brew and drive sales. Because we’re bringing an entirely new beverage experience to the American market, our marketing has to do more than create awareness. We have to give people a reason to be curious. Most consumers understand soda. They understand sparkling water. But sparkling fruit malt soda? That’s a conversation starter.

On the operational side, Klaviyo has been particularly useful for automating customer communication through Shopify. We can capture email addresses, create welcome sequences, share promotions and maintain relationships without manually managing every interaction. That kind of automation matters when you’re running lean.

What was the single biggest bottleneck that almost stalled your business, and what exact change or process fixed it?Distribution has been our biggest challenge. The beverage industry has a complicated relationship between retailers and distributors. Retailers want to know who’s distributing your product. Distributors increasingly want retail authorizations before they’ll take on a new brand. Which leaves emerging brands trying to convince both sides to move first.

We would attend trade shows and return with interest from eight distributors across the country. The conversations were promising, the enthusiasm was real, and then everything would stall because we didn’t yet have the retail commitments to support distribution. It was frustrating and forced us to reconsider our approach.

We realized we needed to focus less on how many distributors were interested and more on securing actual retail placements. That meant targeting independent stores and smaller retailers more willing to take a chance on something new. We also brought on an experienced VP of sales to help sharpen our strategy, prioritize accounts and build a more disciplined approach to retail expansion. It’s a significant shift, and we’re beginning to see a clearer path forward.

How many months did it take to reach consistent monthly revenue, and what was your average monthly profit during your first six months?We’re still working toward consistent monthly revenue. We’re only a few months into launch, and building a beverage brand requires significant capital long before the revenue catches up. But we’ve had encouraging early traction.

During Sober October, Öl Brew reached No. 14 in a nonalcoholic beverage ranking on Amazon. We also generated approximately $10,000 in Amazon revenue during October, just months after launching on the platform.

We’re not yet consistently profitable. We’re investing in inventory, marketing, distribution and the team we need to support growth. There’s a part of entrepreneurship that rarely makes it into the success stories: the period when you’re spending money, making adjustments and trying to determine which investments will actually produce results. That’s where we are.

What is your current monthly revenue and profit margin? We’re about six months into launch, with Amazon generating approximately $10,000 in monthly revenue, plus additional sales through retail and other ecommerce channels. We’re still investing heavily in growth, so we haven’t established a consistent net profit margin.

What part of the work do you still handle yourself, and which tasks have you outsourced?As for my time, I spend roughly 10 hours a day on Öl Brew, often more. My work falls into three main areas: brand awareness, retail and distribution, and manufacturing and operations. We’ve outsourced Amazon optimization and SEO, TikTok Shop management and creator partnerships, and much of our branding, marketing and social media execution.

If someone is starting from scratch today, what are common beginner mistakes they should avoid?Don’t rush into hiring. I made the mistake of trusting people who promised far more than they could deliver. Some were convincing, experienced and very good at selling their services. I was excited about building the brand, and that excitement sometimes made me move faster than I should have.

Now, I recommend interviewing at least three to five people or companies before making a significant hire. The interview process itself is an education. You’ll hear different strategies, cost structures and perspectives on what’s possible. Eventually, you’ll begin to recognize who understands the work and who simply knows how to sell it.

And don’t confuse confidence with having all the answers. I started a beverage company at 54 after a career in mental health. I knew a great deal about people and relationships. I knew very little about beverage manufacturing, distribution or retail. That experience has been both humbling and energizing. What I brought into this business wasn’t industry expertise. It was curiosity, conviction and a willingness to learn. I still believe those are some of the most valuable things an entrepreneur can have.

Be ambitious about what you want to build. Just be equally discerning about who you trust to help you build it.

#5332. Squeezed by rising costs, Gen Z is still buying wellness and lip gloss

Gen Z is still spending. It’s just far more deliberate about where the money goes, and beauty and wellness keep making the cut, executives from Ulta Beauty, Pacsun, and Upstart said at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Tuesday.

The squeeze on young consumers is real. Upstart cofounder and CEO Paul Gu told Fortune‘s Ellie Austin that the economy looks strong on paper, with record retail sales, a solid job market, and stocks near all-time highs. The catch for people in their twenties, he said, is simple: “Stuff costs too much money.”

That pressure shows up in the data. Deloitte’s 2026 Gen Z and Millennial Survey found that 55% of Gen Z are delaying major life decisions, such as starting a family or launching a business, because of their finances.

Credit is part of the problem. “We see that something like nearly 60% of all Gen Z consumers just don’t even bother to apply for credit because they assume they’re going to be rejected,” said Gu, who took over as CEO of the AI lending company in May. “I think they’re basically right. You can’t really go to a bank without a long credit history and expect to get approved for a meaningful amount of credit when you need it… That number, by the way, is almost three times as high as what you would see for older Americans.”

For retailers, that squeeze hasn’t meant cheaper baskets. Ulta Beauty president and CEO Kecia Steelman, No. 39 on Fortune‘s 2026 Most Powerful Women list, said young shoppers aren’t choosing between feeling secure and treating themselves. “It’s a little bit of a mix of both,” she said.

“We don’t see the consumer trading down, and we don’t see this segment of the consumer demographic trading down either,” Steelman said. “Value is the perception of: Is it worth my investment in the dollars that I have?… They’re being a lot more conservative, but I just happen to be in a great category that they’re choosing. They’re prioritizing beauty and wellness.”

The numbers back her up. Ulta, a Fortune 500 company with $12.4 billion in revenue last fiscal year, raised its full-year guidance in August after second-quarter comparable sales rose 3.8%. That tracks with what Bank of America has called Gen Z’s “treat culture”: small, frequent purchases that many young people see as necessities.

Pacsun CEO Brieane Olson sees the same discipline. Young shoppers put “a lot more intentionality behind purchase than we’ve seen in the past,” she said, calling their decisions “purposeful and intentional.”

Olson pointed to Pacsun’s annual youth research, which found that wellness “ranks at the very highest in terms of what they are trying to achieve.” In the 2026 edition, conducted with GlobalData and published in September, 59% of more than 6,000 respondents aged 11 to 24 named being mentally healthy as a top goal by age 35.

Social media may spark interest, but both CEOs said purchases still tend to happen in person. Ulta has 47 million loyalty members, and 75% of its sales come from people who shop only in stores, Steelman said. Just 5% come from shoppers who buy only online. Gen Z also makes up 65% of Ulta’s store associates.

“TikTok has definitely changed the way that things can go viral in a very short period of time. But it’s not the thing that’s really driving the Gen Z consumer,” Steelman said. “I think that’s where they have the discovery. But human connection is still what makes them make the decision.”

Olson said Pacsun is seeing “a large return to in-person shopping” among 16- to 24-year-olds. The retailer also gives young customers a direct say through its youth advisory council. A 13-year-old member recently suggested an after-hours shopping event for friends, Olson said, and it grossed close to what Pacsun’s stores bring in per hour on Black Friday.

For companies that want Gen Z’s business, Gu said the starting point is to stop turning them away. Young people apply for credit and get rejected, he said. “This is like the daily experience of young consumers, and that is no way to build a relationship with them.”

Allie Garfinkle is a senior writer and editor at Fortune, where she runs Term Sheet; leads coverage of private capital, investors, and startups; and co-chairs the Brainstorm conference series.

#5331. U.S. charges Russian man with stalking Palantir workers over Ukraine work

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Prosecutors say Igor D'iu was recruited over Telegram to surveil employees of a Palo Alto company because of its help to Ukraine

The Justice Department announced charges on Wednesday against Russian national Igor D'iu, accusing him of acting as an agent of Russia and stalking employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company. A federal grand jury indicted him on four counts: conspiracy to act as a foreign agent, acting as a foreign agent without notice to the Attorney General, interstate stalking and fraud in connection with identification documents.

The department did not name the company, which has an office in Palo Alto, California. The company was Palantir $PLTR Technologies, Bloomberg revealed. According to CBS News, context in the charging documents hints that the company may be Palantir. Palantir did not immediately respond to requests for comment, according to both outlets.

"The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian of the Northern District of California said in a statement.

According to the indictment and a supporting affidavit, co-conspirators recruited D'iu through Telegram in 2026. They told him the work was for "the Motherland" and tasked him with collecting intelligence on the company, citing its supply of weapons used against Russia in Ukraine. He traveled from Istanbul to Mexico City in June, where he was connected with a person who helped him cross the U.S. border, prosecutors say.

The co-conspirators told him to buy laptops, phones, networking equipment and remote access software, the affidavit says. They directed him to photograph employees' laptop screens at a coffee shop near the Palo Alto office and to place a laptop near the company so they could access it remotely.

Prosecutors say D'iu searched for employees' home addresses, including that of a senior executive. On or about Sept. 3, he followed a female employee for close to 30 miles from Palo Alto toward San Francisco, running a red light to stay behind her. She called 911 and drove to a San Francisco police station, and D'iu ended the pursuit, according to the Justice Department.

Investigators intercepted two packages from overseas containing a falsified California ID card, an altered U.S. passport and a Social Security card in the name "Hugo Landry Johns," the affidavit says. FBI agents searched D'iu and his East Palo Alto residence in October. They recovered about $18,000 in cash, two laptops, two iPhones, two Russian passports and a notebook of 10 addresses, many matching employees' residences. The notebook also held profiles of at least three employees.

The FBI also uncovered exchanges in which co-conspirators shared pictures and addresses for at least four employees and instructed D'iu to pretend to be a food courier, according to CBS News.

The U.S. Attorney's Office said D'iu was arrested on Oct. 30. He first appeared in court on Nov. 2 and is still being held by federal authorities. His next appearance is scheduled for Nov. 24.

If convicted, D'iu faces up to 10 years in prison on the foreign-agent count without notice to the Attorney General, up to five years each on the conspiracy and stalking counts, and up to one year on the fraud count. An indictment alleges crimes, and defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

#5330. ‘You said spicy, right?’ Panel takes on Washington’s economic blind spots — and what needs to change

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:15 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 11:49 am

Washington’s biggest economic threat may be the conviction that it’s already doing everything right.

That was the pointed warning from a Technology Alliance panel Tuesday, where a conversation about talent and economic growth became a challenge to the state’s self-image as an innovation leader.

“You said spicy, right?” Rob Ogburn asked, taking up the invitation to speak bluntly.

“The economy is very strong. The economy is not competitive at all,” said Ogburn, executive director of Business and Community Services at Central Washington University.

While tech giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and sectors including aerospace and biotech are powering today’s economy, that doesn’t mean Washington is positioned to win tomorrow’s investment, develop its workforce or spread opportunity beyond its major employment centers.

Amelia Ransom, former vice president at Smartsheet and past Nordstrom leader, questioned the definition of success, arguing that future growth also depends on investing in people and businesses outside the corporate spotlight.

“Who do we mean when we say winning? Who is it? Who are we talking about, and who are we leaving out?” Ransom said, later adding, “We have to close the daylight between who we say we are and who we actually are.”

The panel was held in downtown Seattle and moderated by Jolenta Coleman-Bush, director of Microsoft Philanthropies. It also included Rachel Smith, president of Washington Roundtable.

Rather than simply calling for more talent and innovation, panelists examined how Washington develops the people already here, whose perspectives inform its decisions and how effectively its institutions and stakeholders work together.

Unification is essential. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., led the passage of the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022 to bolster semiconductor manufacturing and innovation in AI and energy. But her home state has received just 0.3% of the funding awarded so far, Ogburn said.

He argued that other states and regions were more effective at uniting to make their case for investment, showing their collective resources and the problems they could solve.

“We showed up and said, ‘We’re competing with our neighbor, and we’re better than them.’ No investor is going to look at that and say you’re going to make the best use of my money,” Ogburn said.

Cultivate talent, don’t just recruit it. Ransom compared workforce development to a restaurant, a grocery store and a garden: recruiting ready-made workers, developing the talent already here and growing the long-term pipeline.

“The middle is where we probably need to spend more time, which is at the grocery store, which means you’ve got to learn to cook,” she said. Her point: Invest in Washington’s existing employees, students, and businesses.

Smith wants employers to identify the high-wage, high-skill jobs they need filled so educators and businesses can coordinate strategies to prepare workers for those roles.

Fill essential information gaps. Panelists called for a clearer picture of community skills and barriers to opportunity, more voices to challenge prevailing assumptions, and closer examination of how regulations affect businesses.

“We’ve gotten in this war of the rankings where everybody’s like, “No, we’re the best. No, we’re the worst.” And we we’ve got to stop doing that,” Smith said.

The region needs data-backed insights into the reasons behind the rankings, she said. Smith pointed to the recently formed Economic Development Council and its planned statewide strategy as a step toward a more coordinated approach.

Whether these efforts succeed, Ogburn said, should be judged by the communities themselves.

“And then, if you want to measure success, go back to those communities and ask them if they feel successful,” he said. “Do they have agency and self-determination?”

#5329. Your Business Is Saving Hours With AI. So Why Are Customers Still Waiting?

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Before investing in another automation tool, ask whether the time you’re saving is actually improving your customers’ experience.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recently, while working on a healthcare client’s project, my team encountered a problem that had nothing to do with our ability to do the work.

We needed access to the client’s digital platforms. What should have been a straightforward process became a series of emails, permission issues, authentication problems and confusion over which accounts controlled what.

The actual work wasn’t the obstacle. Getting everything in place so we could do the work was.

I’ve encountered different versions of this problem throughout my consulting career. Teams have the expertise. The technology exists. Everyone wants to move forward. Yet progress stalls because the underlying process is more complicated than anyone realized.

It made me think about how businesses are approaching artificial intelligence. We’re investing in tools that promise to make work faster, but how often do we stop to examine what’s slowing the business down in the first place?

When entrepreneurs think about productivity, they naturally focus on the time employees spend completing tasks. How quickly can we produce a report? How much time can we save creating content? Can AI respond to routine inquiries? Those are reasonable questions.

But consider what happened in the healthcare project. Automating another task wouldn’t have resolved who owned the account, who could authorize access or how the team should handle authentication. Those were process and accountability problems.

This is why I believe every business should examine its workflows before investing heavily in automation.

I’ve previously written about why entrepreneurs should examine workflows before hiring more employees. The same principle applies to technology.

If responsibilities are unclear and information is scattered, automation may simply help a flawed process move faster.

A business owner might celebrate saving 20 hours a week. The customer is asking a different question: Why am I still waiting?

That gap is easy to overlook because internal performance metrics don’t always reflect the customer experience.

Imagine improving the speed of customer service responses while leaving the underlying resolution process unchanged. Customers might receive answers sooner but still wait days for their problems to be addressed.

The business reports an efficiency improvement. Customers experience little difference. I see a similar disconnect in marketing. Companies sometimes invest in generating more leads without examining what happens after those leads arrive.

As I explored in my article about why businesses can spend more on marketing while attracting fewer customers, more activity doesn’t automatically translate into better commercial results. The lesson applies to AI as well.

Measure the outcome, not just the activity that produced it.

One thing I’ve learned from managing complex projects is that technology cannot replace clear ownership. Someone still needs to make decisions, resolve exceptions and take responsibility when something goes wrong.

Before automating a process, I ask three questions:

If those answers aren’t clear, technology isn’t the first thing I would fix.

For example, automated appointment reminders can reduce administrative effort. But if patients cannot easily reschedule or reach someone when they need help, the experience remains frustrating.

The same is true for sales, onboarding and service delivery. Customers appreciate convenience, but they also want confidence that someone is paying attention.

This may be the most important question entrepreneurs should ask about AI.

Saving time is only valuable when businesses put that time to better use. This is the AI productivity trap: Faster work doesn’t necessarily mean faster growth. The real opportunity lies in using that efficiency to improve customer relationships, solve problems and create measurable business value.

Suppose a new system saves your team 10 hours every week. What do you do with that time? Do you reinvest it in customer relationships? Improve service quality? Reduce expenses? Give employees more opportunities to solve problems that technology cannot handle?

Or does that time simply disappear into additional meetings and administrative work? The answer matters.

In my earlier Entrepreneur article about why business growth doesn’t always improve profitability, I discussed the importance of looking beyond top-line results. Productivity deserves the same scrutiny.

An efficient business isn’t necessarily a profitable one, and a productive team isn’t automatically delivering a better customer experience.

Entrepreneurs need to decide how efficiency gains will create value before assuming they will.

My advice is simple: Choose one process that repeatedly creates problems. It might be customer onboarding, appointment scheduling, account access, proposal approvals or resolving support requests. Follow that process from beginning to end.

Talk to the people involved. Identify where information gets lost, approvals stall or responsibilities become unclear. Then ask whether the problem requires automation at all.

Sometimes the answer is a better system. Sometimes it’s eliminating an unnecessary approval. Sometimes it’s giving one person clear responsibility for following through.

Make one change, measure what happens, and expand what works. You may discover that the most valuable improvement costs considerably less than another software subscription.

I’m enthusiastic about what AI can do for entrepreneurs, especially smaller businesses competing with organizations that have significantly greater resources. But I don’t believe adopting more technology automatically makes a company more competitive.

The healthcare project reinforced something I’ve seen repeatedly: Even capable teams with good technology can struggle when the underlying process isn’t working.

Your customers don’t see how many hours you save internally. They notice whether you deliver what you promised, respond when they need you and make their lives easier.

Before celebrating how much faster your business has become, make sure your customers can feel the difference.

Recently, while working on a healthcare client’s project, my team encountered a problem that had nothing to do with our ability to do the work.

We needed access to the client’s digital platforms. What should have been a straightforward process became a series of emails, permission issues, authentication problems and confusion over which accounts controlled what.

The actual work wasn’t the obstacle. Getting everything in place so we could do the work was.

#5328. AI's one-model era is over

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Businesses stopped picking one AI. That’s a problem for the companies selling them, a threat that comes even as Anthropic is about to IPO

Photo Illustration by Cheng Xin/Getty Images

A version of this article originally appeared in Quartz’s AI & Tech newsletter. Sign up here to get the latest AI & tech news, analysis and insights straight to your inbox.

Anthropic is days away from asking the public to buy in. Investors are weighing a pitch that values the Claude maker at up to $1.4 trillion, and Thursday is the expected first day of trading.

Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz.

That price assumes customers who picked Claude will keep picking Claude. But by the time the IPO roadshow started, many of them were already shopping around.

AT&T $T was one of them. In May, open models handled about a fifth of the telecom company’s AI work. By September, the share had doubled to 40%, and its AI costs had fallen by as much as 80% since earlier in the year.

The company did not drop Claude or ChatGPT. Instead, a router scored each request for difficulty, sent the easy ones to open models from Meta $META, Google $GOOGL, and Nvidia $NVDA, and saved the expensive models for the hard problems.

Revolut went further. The British fintech rolled out Claude Code in early 2026, and watched some engineers burn through up to $10,000 a month before capping their budgets.

Then it moved roughly 2,000 engineers onto GLM, an open-weight model from the Chinese developer Z.ai, running on 56 Nvidia chips operated in-house. The switch cut coding costs by about 90% in under a year.

They are not the only ones being a little promiscuous. On Vercel’s AI Gateway, a service that lets developers access models from many providers through one connection, almost a third of teams changed their most-used provider in September alone.

Open-weight models handled 71.5% of traffic that month and captured almost a quarter of spending, up from about one-twentieth in June.

The growing competition put pressure on prices, even as more tokens are used. Spending through the gateway ran about 13 times higher than in December 2025, while the average price per token dropped 47%.

The consumer data offered another warning for the model makers. As providers' capabilities expanded, consumers became less likely to pay for multiple services at once. They were switching between providers, but increasingly saw little reason to pay for more than one. People were dating around, one subscription at a time.

For the giants, this is an awkward moment to discover how little loyalty their customers owed them. Anthropic has committed close to $900 billion to data center capacity, much of it through long-term agreements that would be difficult to unwind. Its third-quarter operating loss was $567 million. The economics depend on keeping customers willing to pay a premium for its models.

Fortunately for Anthropic, it still led where the money was. Claude Opus 5.5 took 11% of September spending on Vercel’s gateway, more than double the share of OpenAI’s top model, which came in second. A Chinese model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, ranked third.

The shift also created opportunities for the middlemen, as it tends to in a gold rush. Gateways and routers were becoming the point where customers chose between models, while American hosting providers collected more than two-thirds of the September spending on Chinese models.

None of it should have come as a surprise. A Google researcher had laid out the whole problem in an internal memo that escaped onto a public Discord server in 2023. They argued that neither their employer nor OpenAI had a moat, and that customers would stop paying for a model once a free one was nearly as good.

Anthropic’s prospectus ran to more than 400 pages. While it never used the word moat, its risk factors warned that customers might drift toward “smaller, cheaper, or open-source alternatives.”

#5327. Big Sean and Jalen Rose made it big. Now they’re making sure they keep showing up for the city that raised them

For the 13th draft pick Jalen Rose, loving Detroit means showing up for the city on the good days, the bad days, and all the ordinary ones in between. The former NBA star—whose mother created the name Jalen—has spent years giving back to the place that raised him. And along the way, he’s learned what separates those who lift Detroit from those who only show up during election time.

“You show up during a holiday or election, that type of thing, but you’re not here on a Wednesday when it’s the middle of January and it’s freezing outside,” Rose said Tuesday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.

Sitting beside him was multi-platinum rapper Big Sean, whose real name is Sean Michael Leonard Anderson, who also grew up in Detroit and has turned his success into opportunities for young people back home. Between Rose’s tuition-free high school, Big Sean’s recording studios, and their growing entertainment ventures, the two are investing in Detroit’s next generation while trying to make the city a place where young talent can build careers of their own.

Rose understands firsthand what it means to grow up without much. Some days, his family didn’t have heat or hot water, so they relied on kerosene heaters and boiled water to wash.

“My motivation was growing up poor and watching, you know, my mother go to work,” he said.

As a kid, he promised his mother he’d make it to the NBA and get their family out of poverty. He even started writing “Dr. J” on his school papers, borrowing the nickname of the basketball legend Julius Erving.

“I’m going to the league. You know, I’m gonna get us out the hood,” he recalled telling her. He kept that promise, playing 13 seasons in the NBA and never forgetting the people who helped him get there.

Now, his Jalen Rose Leadership Academy is completing its 16th school year, serving 460 high school students and supporting roughly 1,100 graduates pursuing education after high school, Rose said. And the work is paying off, as Rose noted that the school has Detroit’s highest student index, a distinction he takes immense pride in.

And Big Sean has been in Rose’s corner since long before they shared a stage Tuesday, attending the academy’s first graduation back in 2015. More than a decade later, the students keep Rose motivated.

“You know, our young people, the way they receive it just makes me want to work harder for them because they deserve the opportunities,” Rose said.

Giving back started long before Big Sean went platinum with hits like “Blessings” and “Bounce Back.”

His grandmother served as a captain in the Six Triple Eight, the all-Black, all-female Army unit that sorted military mail during World War II. Growing up, he watched her make helping others a family tradition, no matter how much the family had.

“No matter how good or bad the years were,” Big Sean recalled, his grandmother made sure the family donated clothes and supported people in need—a lesson that stayed with him as his music career took him around the world.

The Sean Anderson Foundation is run by his mother, who was backstage Tuesday while his father and brother cheered from the audience. Through it, he has built recording studios at Boys & Girls Clubs, giving young people a chance to learn not only how to perform but also how to become sound engineers and work behind the scenes.

The first of those studios opened at his alma mater, Cass Technical High School, where Big Sean once risked suspension for selling his own CDs. Years later, he had his own kind of “Bounce Back” moment, returning to the school not to sell music, but to help the next generation make it.

“It was cool to see a full-circle 180 moment,” he said.

The work has since expanded to the new Boys & Girls Club at Detroit’s restored Michigan Central Station, where he and Usher backed the $1 million Detroit Entertainment Innovation Incubator, which opened in February, to give young Detroiters access to creative and technical training.

There, young people can explore everything from engineering and film makeup to sneaker resale and tech. Big Sean said seeing young people from those programs land jobs has been one of the most rewarding experiences of his career.

“It’s the first time that I’ve seen all the hard work of giving back starting to pay off,” he said.

Both men are also thinking beyond philanthropy, working to make Detroit a place where creative talent can build careers—not just a place artists leave once they get noticed.

Rose launched Same Page Entertainment in February with Detroit Pistons owner Tom Gores, aiming to produce films, documentaries, television shows, and other media from Detroit.

He said the goal is to create the kind of entertainment hub Tyler Perry built in Atlanta, giving Detroiters opportunities both in front of and behind the camera. For years, Rose said, pursuing a media career meant leaving Detroit for Los Angeles or New York. He wants to change that.

Big Sean, who also sees some NBA crossover serving as the Pistons’ creative director of global experience, has been using the team’s platform to spotlight local artists. He even teased a major entertainment project that he said Michigan Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson knows about and wants to support, though he wasn’t ready to announce details just yet.

“Detroit has something magical here, and it’s up to us to activate the magic,” Big Sean said.

And even as his career has taken him around the world, he hasn’t forgotten where it all started. He sees his success as a chance to make the road a little easier for those coming after him.

“Wherever we go, you always leave breadcrumbs behind,” he said, explaining that those breadcrumbs aren’t just for finding his own way home, but for helping someone else follow the path.

#5326. Bezos and Bond: Amazon founder played a big role in casting new 007

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:36 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 6:36 pm

Jeff Bezos has a space company, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder said he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios announced Monday.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos said a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The New York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos said the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos said. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

“We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he said. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”

#5325. Battery startup Sila lands potential $1B Panasonic deal, plans Central Wash. expansion adding 500 jobs

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the company plans to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

“This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky said. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

The company has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round announced in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced plans for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky said.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he said.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

“None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5324. Anthropic prices IPO at $83 per share, giving it a $1.5 trillion valuation

Anthropic priced shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday at $83 per share, above its initially guided ranged of $70 to $78 per share, and likely valuing the AI company at $1.5 trillion.

Anthropic’s stock will begin trading Thursday on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker ANT, marking one of the most highly anticipated IPOs in years as well as one of the largest ever.

The San Francisco-based AI company said it increased the number of shares sold in the offering to 980 million, instead of the 825 million shares it initially planned to sell. The expanded float means Anthropic will raise roughly $80 billion in the IPO—and as much as $92 billion if the underwriters choose to exercise an over-allotment option.

The offering will provide Anthropic with a critical infusion of capital as it seeks to stay ahead in the AI race and to invest in the computing infrastructure to train its models. The IPO will also make instant billionaires out of numerous Anthropic employees and early investors, particularly the seven cofounders who created Anthropic in San Francisco just five years ago.

Anthropic is the first pure-play maker of frontier AI models to go public (SpaceX also does rockets, and Google and Meta both have massive businesses in search and social media), and its Wall Street debut is being closely watched as a barometer for the health of the broader AI industry. The IPO comes as the AI boom is in a period of uncertainty following a leadership shake up at AI chipmaker Nvidia and growing public backlash to AI data centers.

At a $1.5 trillion valuation, Anthropic would be the second most valuable IPO of all time, behind SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO in June. Measured by capital raised however, Anthropic’s $80 billion would top the $75 billon raised by SpaceX.

Seven strategic partners, including Google and Nvidia, have also agreed to buy $26 billion of non-voting Anthropic stock at the IPO price.

Anthropic’s revenue has soared thanks to strong demand from business customers. In the nine months ending September 30, Anthropic generated $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. The company posted a $104 billion net loss in its most recent nine-month period, though the bulk of the red ink is because of the way it accounted for its convertible notes.
