#5323. ‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting new software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”

The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy said there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The new products take that approach further:

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said.

AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The new products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Plenty of company: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy said. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy said.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the company’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

The business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy said. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy said Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the company, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

About 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building new products.

Despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the company, Duffy said Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy said Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”

#5322. Your Best Employees May Be the Ones Nobody Hears From

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The people who speak most confidently in meetings aren’t always the people with the best ideas. Here’s how leaders can stop overlooking valuable talent.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Every workplace has someone who seems to have an answer for everything. They’re quick to contribute in meetings, comfortable challenging colleagues and rarely hesitate when an executive asks for an opinion.

Then there’s the employee who listens carefully, takes notes and says very little.

Which one gets noticed? Too often, it’s the person who speaks first.

I’ve led and worked with teams across consulting, technology and marketing, and I’ve learned to be careful about equating confidence with capability. People communicate differently. Some think through problems by talking. Others need time to consider the information before forming an opinion.

Neither approach automatically produces better judgment. But many workplaces reward one more visibly than the other.

Think about how most brainstorming sessions operate. A leader presents a problem and asks for ideas. Someone immediately offers a suggestion. Another person agrees, adds something, and the conversation moves forward.

Within minutes, a direction begins to emerge. The session appears productive. People are engaged, ideas are flowing, and decisions are being made.

If the first confident suggestion becomes the foundation for the discussion, everyone else may spend the meeting reacting to that idea instead of considering alternatives.

This is especially problematic when the most senior person speaks first. Employees may hesitate to challenge an executive, even when they recognize a weakness in the proposed approach.

That’s why I prefer giving people the problem to think about before asking them to solve it together. Even a short explanation sent ahead of a meeting can change the conversation. People arrive with their own observations rather than immediately responding to whoever speaks first.

Some employees contribute best through discussion. Others communicate more effectively in writing or smaller groups. A leader who relies exclusively on group meetings may never hear valuable insights from people who dislike competing for attention.

I would build more than one opportunity for participation into important decisions. Ask employees to submit their observations before a meeting. Invite questions afterward. Create smaller working groups when a topic requires deeper thinking.

And when someone who rarely speaks contributes an idea, give it the same consideration you would give a suggestion from your most outspoken colleague.

The objective isn’t to force quiet employees to become more extroverted. It’s to make sure communication style doesn’t determine whose judgment matters.

A leader can repeatedly tell employees that every idea is welcome. Those words mean very little if people watch a colleague get embarrassed for disagreeing.

Employees notice how leaders respond to criticism, particularly when the criticism is valid. In my earlier Entrepreneur article about transparent decision-making, I discussed why explaining how decisions are made is essential to building organizational trust.

That principle extends to brainstorming. You don’t need to accept every suggestion. But people should understand why an idea was adopted, rejected or deferred.

If you ask for different perspectives and then consistently reward agreement, employees will eventually stop offering them.

There is another dimension to this problem. Even when quiet employees perform exceptionally well, their contributions can remain invisible beyond their immediate managers.

They receive positive feedback, but the opportunities that lead to career advancement go elsewhere. I previously explored this distinction between receiving advice and gaining access to opportunity, and it raises a useful question for business owners: Are you developing capable employees, or are you also making sure their capabilities are recognized?

When someone does excellent work, bring that contribution into conversations where decisions about responsibility, promotions and opportunities are being made. Don’t reserve high-visibility assignments for the people who are already comfortable promoting themselves.

Here’s something I would encourage every founder to try.

Think about your last five important team decisions. Who contributed most of the ideas? Whose recommendations shaped the final outcome? Were the same three or four people consistently heard?

Now look at who wasn’t part of those conversations. Were they excluded because they lacked relevant expertise, or because nobody created an opportunity for them to contribute?

You may find that the organization has more insight available than its meetings suggest.

Try rotating who leads discussions. Ask people to share independent recommendations before opening the floor. Review whether important assignments are distributed according to capability or visibility.

These changes don’t require a new leadership program or expensive technology. They require awareness of how influence operates inside your business.

I’m not suggesting that confident employees should speak less or that every idea deserves equal weight. Organizations need people who can articulate their thinking, make decisions and move work forward.

But confidence should never become a substitute for sound reasoning. The strongest leaders create conditions in which employees can question assumptions without worrying about how that will affect their standing. They also recognize that sometimes the person who speaks last has been thinking about the problem longer than anyone else.

Before your next brainstorming session, consider whether you’re hearing from the people with the most to contribute or simply the people most comfortable contributing.

Your best idea may already be sitting in the room. You might just need to make space for it.

Every workplace has someone who seems to have an answer for everything. They’re quick to contribute in meetings, comfortable challenging colleagues and rarely hesitate when an executive asks for an opinion.

Then there’s the employee who listens carefully, takes notes and says very little.

Which one gets noticed? Too often, it’s the person who speaks first.

#5321. JPMorgan taps 20-year company veteran Bregje de Best as its next CFO

JPMorgan Chase has named Bregje de Best, who has spent two decades at the company, as its next chief financial officer.

The 43-year-old will lead the finance organization at JPMorgan Chase, No. 12 on the Fortune 500. The company had $5.1 trillion in assets and $372 billion in stockholders’ equity as of Sept. 30. She will succeed Jeremy Barnum following the company’s first-quarter 2027 financial reporting, JPMorgan announced Tuesday.

At that time, she will join the firm-wide operating committee, and Barnum will become a vice chairman. Barnum informed the company of his intention to conclude his tenure as CFO after six years in the role.

The appointment will make de Best the latest woman to serve as JPMorgan’s CFO. Her predecessors include Marianne Lake, who held the role from 2013 to 2019, and Jennifer Piepszak, now chief operating officer, who served as CFO from 2019 to 2021.

Since June 2025, de Best has served as CFO of JPMorgan’s commercial and investment bank (CIB). The Dutch banker joined the company in 2006 and previously served as co-head of global corporate banking. DeBest has also held senior roles in investment banking and markets in the United Kingdom and Asia.

JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon described de Best in the announcement as an “extraordinary leader,” citing her experience in finance and across the CIB’s businesses. “She has a deep understanding of how our company operates,” Dimon said.

Her investment banking background is shared by a notable number of current CFOs. According to executive search firm Crist Kolder Associates’ 2026 midyear Volatility Report, 22% of sitting CFOs at companies in its combined Fortune 500 and S&P 500 sample have investment banking experience. Of those with that background, 20% work in the financial industry.

Research also finds that companies increasingly want CFOs with operational experience. De Best’s experience extends to the operational side of the business: As CIB CFO, she oversees business management and controls across JPMorgan’s global banking, markets, payments and securities services businesses.

In a LinkedIn post earlier this year, de Best described attending a firm-wide senior leadership conference focused on resilience, global growth and the rapid pace of innovation. “It’s clear that AI and digital assets are transforming every aspect of our business, and I’m energized by our commitment to building for the future and leading the industry forward,” she wrote.

Barnum and de Best will work closely during the transition. He will lead the January and April earnings announcements and the company’s Investor Day in February, according to JPMorgan. After becoming a vice chairman following first-quarter reporting, he will remain at the company until early 2028, working with Dimon and other senior leaders on firm-wide initiatives.

The company will announce de Best’s successor as CFO of the CIB early next year.

Sheryl Estrada is a senior writer at Fortune, where she covers the corporate finance industry, Wall Street, and corporate leadership. She also authors CFO Daily.

#5318. I’ve Built and Sold Several Tech Companies. Here’s What I Know About Building a Business That People Trust

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

I used to think a great product would sell itself, but building several companies taught me customers need more proof than that.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’ve been building technology companies for more than two decades.

When I started my first business at 18, selling computers in Romania, my “brand” was nonexistent. Like any entrepreneur starting out, I had to convince people to take a chance on a company they didn’t know. That’s far from easy.

In 2003, I founded Hertza Telecom, an internet service provider. Later, I founded a national telecommunications company. Today, I run ZeroBounce, an email validation and deliverability company I launched in a market already crowded with established competitors.

Every time I’ve started a new business, I’ve faced the same challenge: Why should anyone trust a company they’ve never heard of?

You can tout the quality of your product and its reliability all you want. You can use words like “leading” or “best-in-class” on your social media and website. But as it’s commonly said: talk is cheap. You may know your claims are true, but how do you get someone else to believe them?

It starts with a product that keeps its promises, so well that customers are willing to vouch for you. To reach the next level, you need credible third parties to back you up, too. Once you have all this, you have to raise your visibility.

None of this is easy, and you can’t skip any steps. Here’s what’s worked for me, from building a product people recommend to earning the kind of credibility you can’t buy.

Advertising can buy you short-term attention, but a product won’t last long if customers don’t like it or find it useful. If what you offer has serious flaws, word will spread fast.

Here’s the thing: Most founders get this backward. We think about the launch, the website, advertising, PR and growth long before the product lives up to its promises.

At ZeroBounce, accuracy was the promise everything else depended on. Before we launched, I wanted our email list validation service to reach at least 98% accuracy. It took a lot of testing and plenty of frustrating moments to get there.

When we launched, the website wasn’t pretty, and the back end left a lot to be desired. But the product was something we could stand behind. We’ve kept raising the bar since then. Today, we guarantee 99.6% email verification accuracy on most email domains, and we’ve published terms for what happens if we fall short. Your most important claims should be specific, because they need to be measurable.

Reviews have never been more valuable. We read them before booking a hotel room, ordering virtually any product under the sun and choosing software. Your customers are doing the same research on you. Don’t fear reviews. Embrace them and make them part of your marketing.

A good review can answer questions your website can’t. Did the product work well? Was support helpful? Did the customer say that they’d choose the product again?

But here’s what takes many founders a long time to learn: Handling praise is easy. Negative reviews are where you have a chance to shine.

That surprises some people. But how you respond when something goes wrong can say more than the review itself. We’ve had upset customers update a one-star review to five stars after seeing our genuine efforts to fix the problem.

Give your satisfied customers a frictionless way to share their experience, and do this early. Pay close attention to what people are saying, especially when the feedback is uncomfortable. Take your ego out of the equation. It isn’t easy, but that feedback is the most valuable information you have for improving your product. You’re also building a public record of how your company treats people.

Some customers will be unfair. That’s okay. You and your team can show true integrity.

Any company with a budget can throw money at advertising. PR is a different game. To make the news, an editor or producer has to decide you’re newsworthy and that their audience would care. You can’t pay for that. You have to earn it.

ZeroBounce has invested heavily in marketing over the years, but PR builds our credibility in a different way. When a renowned media organization features your company, the message packs a powerful punch because you can’t pay for it.

The same goes for industry awards and certifications. Security is a big deal for data companies like ours, so we complete annual SOC 2 Type 2 audits and hold ISO/IEC 27001 certification. We’ve also been recognized on national lists of the most successful companies in the U.S.

The point isn’t to collect media and award logos. It’s that there’s tremendous value when a credible organization examines part of your business and puts its own reputation on the line by praising your work.

You can’t assume a great product will find its market on its own.

We’ve tested various marketing channels at ZeroBounce because I wanted potential customers to find us wherever they were looking for a solution to their email marketing problems.

Say a prospect first reads an article about your company. Next, they see your name in search results. Then they visit your website, read customer reviews and look at your social media profiles. People rarely make an important business decision or a significant purchase after one exposure to a company. They research, compare and check the temperature before they decide.

What they’re looking for is consistency across all of those signals. They want to see satisfied customers and signs of trustworthy leadership. You’d be surprised how many online companies don’t have a single person’s name attached to them. You need an active presence and consistent information. Every box you check removes a little more uncertainty and earns a little more trust.

If someone hears about your company today, they may check out your company’s LinkedIn before they ever speak with your sales team. They’ll notice the language you use to describe the business, the kind of people who work there and what you publish. They’ll also notice whether customers engage with you and whether the company seems active. Have you ever visited a company’s LinkedIn page and found that its last post was a year and a half ago? What impression does that leave with you?

For B2B businesses especially, founders should give that presence the attention it deserves. We’ve built ZeroBounce’s presence across all major social media platforms. But two to three years ago, we looked closer at our metrics and we realized LinkedIn is where we should put most of our focus.

Putting our time and attention into LinkedIn has paid off: our community and engagement began to grow, and now we’re exploring new ways to reach more people. Our next step is to upgrade to a Premium Company Page.

The credibility features caught my attention. A LinkedIn Premium Company Page would let us feature a customer testimonial prominently and showcase our awards, right where prospects are already checking us out. When people like or comment on our posts, we could automatically invite them to follow the page. We’d also get deeper insight into how people engage with our content and how our page compares with competitors’.

That last part especially interests me — I want to know what catches people’s attention and where we stand against other companies in our space.

At a certain point, your company may pursue a higher-tier customer, enter into a new market, seek investors or become part of an acquisition. When that happens, the scrutiny is dialed up even more.

Decision makers will examine your product, customers and revenue. Everything will get a close look: your leadership, security, reviews, press coverage and how you’ve presented yourself through the years. Many companies try to polish these things right when they need them, when, in reality, their reputation should have been years in the making.

Start with building a product or service that’s worth trusting. Take the very best care of your customers. And let those customers speak. Give credible third parties plenty of reasons to talk about you. Market the business enough that the right people know it exists. And take care with every place a customer might go to look you up.

Trust takes time to build, but you don’t have to figure it out alone. LinkedIn’s new Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build credibility and reach customers, and LinkedIn’s small business tools can help you strengthen every place prospects look you up.

You don’t need everyone to trust your company. You just need to give the right people enough good reasons to decide that they can.

I’ve been building technology companies for more than two decades.

When I started my first business at 18, selling computers in Romania, my “brand” was nonexistent. Like any entrepreneur starting out, I had to convince people to take a chance on a company they didn’t know. That’s far from easy.

In 2003, I founded Hertza Telecom, an internet service provider. Later, I founded a national telecommunications company. Today, I run ZeroBounce, an email validation and deliverability company I launched in a market already crowded with established competitors.

#5317. Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest update on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the company looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn launches reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

#5316. How to Spot Employee Burnout Before the Holiday Rush Takes Its Toll

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Here’s how small businesses can use workforce technology to prevent employee burnout and keep operations running smoothly.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For a small business owner, a perfectly planned holiday schedule can bring a sigh of relief. Every shift is covered, employees are picking up extra hours, and the team is poised to keep pace with demand. But a schedule that works on paper can hide a business that is leaning too heavily on the same people.

Your most dependable employee may be covering their third extra shift this week. A manager may be staying late every day to finish work that customer demands pushed aside. Those efforts keep the business moving today, but relying on them week after week, especially at a small or growing business, leaves little room for employees to recover or for the business to handle another absence.

That is why burnout prevention belongs in holiday business planning and workforce strategy. Burnout is often treated as an employee well-being issue, but for small businesses it is also an operational challenge. When fatigue, overtime, absenteeism and scheduling pressure build across a workforce, they create risks that affect service levels, productivity and the ability to meet customer demand.

The right workforce technology helps owners see that pressure building. Connecting scheduling, timekeeping and payroll information makes it possible to spot recurring workload problems, understand who is affected and adjust coverage before another request to stay late becomes the only solution.

UKG’s 2025 Retail Workforce Report found that only 18% of retailers anticipated employee burnout as a major challenge. Meanwhile, UKG’s 2025 global study of frontline workers found that 76% of frontline employees reported feeling burned out at work.

Underestimating that strain can lead an owner to plan for holiday sales the team cannot sustainably support. If the staffing plan assumes everyone can keep adding hours, a single absence can leave the business struggling to serve customers and put even more pressure on the people who remain. Earlier visibility into workload gives owners time to arrange coverage before that cycle begins.

Small business leaders often work alongside their employees and know them well. Yet familiarity can make a staffing problem harder to recognize. The person who always volunteers becomes the first person asked, and a supervisor’s willingness to stay late gradually becomes part of the plan.

Disconnected systems make that pattern easier to miss. A schedule shows a filled shift, while payroll records the extra hours after they have been worked. Bringing those records together gives owners a clearer view of how often the business depends on the same employees to close its staffing gaps.

Overtime is one of the most important workforce operations signals because it shows where demand and workforce capacity are no longer aligned. Occasional extra hours may be welcome for some, but repeated overtime concentrated among a few employees warrants a closer look, especially when their schedules also leave little time between shifts.

Imagine a small retailer whose most experienced associate regularly stays an hour past her scheduled finish. Each request seems reasonable in isolation. Over three weeks, however, she also covers two absences and works several closing shifts followed by early openings. The owner sees someone dependable; the combined records reveal the true cost of how much additional work she is carrying.

Connected timekeeping and scheduling tools can make that cumulative demand visible without requiring the owner to reconstruct it from old schedules and messages. Alerts about approaching overtime or short intervals between shifts give a manager a chance to discuss coverage before publishing the next schedule.

Attendance changes add another piece of context. If absences rise on a team that has been working extra hours, the combination is worth exploring. While data alone does not establish that someone is burned out, it helps managers ask better questions about workload and support.

This is where workforce analytics earns its value for a lean business: It helps owners manage workforce operations proactively rather than reactively. Effective workforce operations requires connecting labor demand, staffing levels, scheduling, attendance, timekeeping and employee experience data to create a complete picture of how work gets done. When leaders can see those connections, they can intervene before a staffing challenge becomes an operational disruption.

Holiday staffing decisions often start with last year’s sales, but sales alone cannot explain why a team keeps falling behind. A store may have enough labor hours for the week and still depend on employees staying late because coverage does not line up with the work. That mismatch can turn an otherwise manageable holiday workload into a recurring source of exhaustion.

Consider a shop where afternoon pickup orders regularly arrive while employees are unloading a delivery. Associates leave stocking unfinished to help customers, then spend the end of their shifts catching up. To an owner reviewing weekly totals, the overtime may suggest the store simply needs more hours overall. Connecting order activity, labor demand, scheduling and timekeeping data can reveal a workforce operations problem that would otherwise remain hidden.

With demand forecasting and scheduling technology, that pattern can inform the next schedule. If the overlap is likely to recur, the manager can plan for stockroom coverage while keeping associates available to serve customers. AI-assisted scheduling can help identify an employee with the right skills and availability, reducing the time the manager spends working through possible changes.

The benefit is that the closing team no longer has to absorb the same unfinished work night after night. Addressing the bottleneck earlier can make finishing on time more predictable, giving employees greater confidence in their schedules. For the owner, it also creates a clearer basis for deciding whether to move existing coverage or invest in additional hours.

Better data also makes employee conversations more useful. A manager who can see repeated extra shifts can ask how that arrangement is working and what would make the coming weeks manageable. The answer may be a consistent day off, a different start time or continued access to additional hours.

That distinction matters during a season when employees may be balancing holiday expenses with family responsibilities. An automatic reduction in hours could create a different source of stress. Current availability and employee preferences help managers respond to what people actually need.

In UKG’s 2025 retail survey, 86% of retailers said frontline employees wanted more flexibility than their organizations provided. For small businesses, delivering that flexibility can be difficult when every change requires phone calls, group texts and a manager to coordinate the exchange.

Mobile self-service scheduling reduces that friction by letting employees view schedules, request time off and arrange shift swaps in one place. Scheduling rules can help check that replacement coverage meets role requirements and flag potential overtime. Employees gain a practical way to manage a conflict, while managers spend less time chasing responses.

The benefit goes beyond convenience. Someone who can resolve a scheduling conflict has more control over how work fits into life outside it. When employees see that technology makes those adjustments easier, they have a concrete reason to trust its role in the workplace.

Small businesses rarely have someone available to spend hours analyzing workforce reports. Technology is more useful when it brings a developing problem to the manager’s attention and makes the next decision easier, such as highlighting an open shift alongside qualified employees who are available to work.

Timing determines how many options remain. A coverage gap identified before next week’s schedule is published may be addressed through a voluntary shift change or additional staffing. The same gap discovered during a rush is more likely to land on whoever is already there.

Managers need that support themselves. UKG’s retail report found that 31% of retailers said managers worked additional shifts when understaffed. A supervisor covering the floor has less time to plan coverage or help a new employee learn the job, which can leave the team dependent on the same experienced people again.

Keeping demand forecasts and schedules connected also matters after peak sales pass. Returns and inventory work can continue into January, and a smaller team may still face a substantial workload. Visibility into that work gives owners a better basis for deciding when staffing can ease.

A successful holiday season depends on having a workforce that can sustain the work and the operational visibility to support it. Burnout, absenteeism, overtime, scheduling conflicts and staffing shortages are often treated as separate challenges, but they are all connected workforce operations signals.

When small businesses bring those signals together, they gain a clearer understanding of how work gets done across the organization. Workforce operations technology provides the visibility needed to identify strain early, align staffing with demand and respond before employee pressure becomes an operational problem.

Ultimately, organizations that manage workforce operations effectively are better positioned to support their people, serve customers consistently and perform through the busiest times of the year.

For a small business owner, a perfectly planned holiday schedule can bring a sigh of relief. Every shift is covered, employees are picking up extra hours, and the team is poised to keep pace with demand. But a schedule that works on paper can hide a business that is leaning too heavily on the same people.

Your most dependable employee may be covering their third extra shift this week. A manager may be staying late every day to finish work that customer demands pushed aside. Those efforts keep the business moving today, but relying on them week after week, especially at a small or growing business, leaves little room for employees to recover or for the business to handle another absence.

That is why burnout prevention belongs in holiday business planning and workforce strategy. Burnout is often treated as an employee well-being issue, but for small businesses it is also an operational challenge. When fatigue, overtime, absenteeism and scheduling pressure build across a workforce, they create risks that affect service levels, productivity and the ability to meet customer demand.

#5315. Crunchbase Data: Nvidia’s Startup Funding Deals Hit A Record. What’s Next After Huang?

Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026.

The chipmaker and its NVentures arm have participated in more than 120 startup funding deals so far this year, according to Crunchbase data, already topping last year’s record-setting pace and marking its most prolific year yet as a private-company investor.

With co-founder Jensen Huang’s sudden departure this week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs including with employees and a woman U.S. intelligence experts suspect of spying for China, we took a fresh look at where Nvidia and NVentures have been investing and what the future could hold.

Nvidia is the most active corporate investor so far in 2026, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. It and NVentures together are also among the top 20 most active investors in startups this year overall.

Nvidia’s startup investments this year total 121 and span AI model developers, data center operators, robotics startups and healthcare companies. That continues the broad approach we examined last year, when the company and its venture arm participated in 91 known startup financings, up from 54 the year prior.

The largest Nvidia-backed deals in 2026 include OpenAI’s Series G, which closed at $122 billion in March, and Anthropic’s $30 billion Series G in February. (Those figures represent the entire rounds, including other investors’ contributions, rather than Nvidia’s individual checks.)

The company also participated in a $3.9 billion September Series F for AI infrastructure provider Crusoe and a roughly $3.5 billion September Series D for model developer Mistral AI.

Of course, large as those deals are, Nvidia’s startup bets represent a small fraction of the company’s incredible market capitalization. Even as its share price tumbled this week with Huang’s departure and the surrounding news, Nvidia’s valuation remains close to $4 trillion.

NVentures’ activity shows how far that investment footprint extends beyond the best-known model developers.

The venture arm’s larger bets this year include robot intelligence developer Skild AI’s $1.4 billion January Series C, and autonomous driving startup Waabi’s $750 million Series C in the same month. It also backed two rounds for Bedrock Robotics, which develops technology to automate construction equipment: a $270 million Series B in February and a $600 million Series C in October. Its healthcare investments included a $150 million April Series E for medical imaging AI company Aidoc.

As in years past, Nvidia and NVentures usually participate alongside other investors. The company or its venture arm are listed as lead or co-lead investors in about 1 in 5 of its deals this year, per Crunchbase data.

For startups, Nvidia’s value as an investor also extends beyond its deep pockets. NVentures describes its offering as access to technical teams, technology integrations and help reaching customers.

Nvidia’s new leadership could bring a different approach to risk. Before this week’s news, CFO and now interim CEO Collette Kress had pushed back on Huang’s increasingly large AI investments, Reuters reported this week, citing two people familiar with the matter.

Nvidia’s board has said it expects operations, customer commitments and its product roadmap to continue without interruption. That assurance leaves the pace of future investments an open question. With earnings scheduled for Nov. 17, founders and investors will be watching for signs of how much of Huang’s investment playbook continues under new leadership.

#5314. Tech Moves: Microsoft names 2 leaders, loses 1; DoorDash VP departs; BluePill, Glacis get execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 18, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:36 pm

— Weiwei Yang has left Microsoft after more than a decade to co-found a startup that is “building the power grid for the AI age,” according to her LinkedIn profile.

Yang was most recently a senior director with Microsoft Research, working on grid technology. Her team built a grid dataset and released small foundation models to help users operate and expand electrical infrastructure.

Yang thanked her community at the tech giant, adding, “I hope the relationships and collaborations we’ve built continue well beyond Microsoft, and that we find many new ways to work together.”

— Allie Mellen has joined Microsoft as principal director for security research and threat intelligence. Mellen was previously a principal analyst at Forrester. She also wrote “Code War,” a book that explores cyberattacks as a powerful geopolitical weapon.

In her new role, Mellen said she will lead strategy for protection and threat intelligence, “helping shape what intelligence we produce, how AI can improve its speed and quality, and how we turn that knowledge into better protection for customers.”

— Agility Robotics, the Salem, Ore., company that had its Nasdaq debut earlier this month, has announced three leadership changes:

— Former tech executive Drew Sheriff has been named CEO and president of the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass. Sheriff was previously a vice president at DoorDash and has held leadership roles at Amazon, Starbucks and Parachute Home. His roles focused on customer experience, product growth, strategy and marketing.

“His skill set is the ideal background for charting how we attract customers and how we delight customers in this new age,” Jeff Seely, board chair for the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass, told the Seattle Times.

— Microsoft has named Caroline King as director of its Washington state community and philanthropy team, with a focus on advocacy work across housing, affordability and other priority issues.

King is the founder and past CEO of Washington STEM, an organization that coordinates research, advocacy, policy, philanthropy and partnerships to support science, technology, engineering and math education in the state. She most recently served as a leader on the governing body of an international school in Luxembourg.

— Longtime Amazon and Microsoft tech exec Scott Wiltamuth has retired — mostly.

Wiltamuth joined Amazon in 2011 as an AWS vice president overseeing a large organization building developer and management tools. In 2018, he took a seven-month leave for colon cancer treatment. After returning, he sought a director-level position and thanked company leaders for helping him find a better fit. “Their flexibility and creativity enabled me to extend my AWS career,” he said.

Wiltamuth launched his tech career at Microsoft in 1993 and left nearly 19 years later as director of program management for Visual Studio Pro.

He now spends time with his wife and family, traveling, golfing, swimming and reading. “I don’t plan to pursue another full-time operational role,” Wiltamuth said, “but may do some part-time work.”

— Adam Nygate has exited Palo Alto Networks to co-found and lead a stealth startup based in Seattle. He was founder and CEO of Huntr, a platform launched in 2019 where security researchers could submit information on AI and machine learning vulnerabilities. Protect AI acquired Huntr, and Palo Alto Networks later acquired Protect AI.

“Huntr was a bet that open source gets safer when vulnerabilities are visible to the people who can fix them, even when that made life uncomfortable for vendors who’d rather keep things quiet,” Nygate said in a post announcing his career change and impending new baby.

— BluePill, a Seattle-based marketing startup that helps brands predict consumer behavior, has named Mike Weis as chief revenue officer and head of sales.

Weis has 40 years of experience in consumer packaged goods, retail and commerce, beginning his career as a Pacific Northwest leader at Unilever and holding executive positions at Catalina and Quotient Technologies. Recent roles include adviser at Contento2, eGateway Capital and And1 Advisors.

“Beyond the incredible résumé, Mike is one of the kindest, most genuine, and most passionate people I’ve met. Someone who has accomplished so much, yet brings so much humility, curiosity, and energy to every conversation,” said Ankit Dhawan, CEO and founder of BluePill.

— Glacis, a Seattle startup that builds tamper-proof records of AI behavior, has named Caer Mistral Sanders as a technical co-founder. Sanders has launched startups and joins Glacis from Thoughtworks. Before that, she held leadership roles at Wayfair and Onshape. As a teenager, she published a book on mixed-reality control systems and won a world robotics championship.

In a post announcing the new role, Sanders said she has designed medical record systems, researched robot communication, patented cryptographic technology and built widely used AI platforms. “This is the first time in my career I get to bring all of those skills to bear on one problem, and I couldn’t be more excited!” she added.

— The PNW Battery Collaborative has welcomed Jason Demeny as its director of communications. Demeny is a marketing leader whose past employers include Crusoe, Patch, Qualtrics and Apptio. Earlier in his career, he spent more than a decade at Microsoft over two stints, most recently leading teams that served the Azure Partner Experience group.

The nonprofit PNW Battery Collaborative brings together startups, innovators and researchers focused on energy storage.

— Tom Wheeler, former chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, has joined the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based company building accountability infrastructure for autonomous AI. Wheeler led the FCC from 2013 to 2017.

Known, previously called Identity Digital Innovation Labs, spun out of Identity Digital in September.

— Versium has promoted Matthew Baumgartner to vice president of engineering. The Redmond, Wash.-based company provides data and software that help businesses identify potential customers, fill in missing contact information and target their marketing. Baumgartner has been with Versium since 2018.

— Charlie Trillingham has been named communications manager for University of Washington programs in AI and machine learning. He previously served as a marketing and communications lead for the UW Foster School of Business.

#5313. ‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”

#5312. Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

#5311. VC Firm Plural Closes On $1.1B To Invest In European Startups With Potential For ‘GDP-Level Impact’

Early-stage startup investor Plural says it has closed on its largest fund to date — just over $1.1 billion, or 1 billion euros — to lead early-stage investments across Europe.

With the announcement, Plural joins a select group of European venture firms that have raised funds of a billion dollars or more in recent years. Others include Balderton Capital, Atomico and Index Ventures, which is co-headquartered in London and San Francisco. It also follows a Q3 that marked Europe’s strongest venture funding quarter in years.

“Our common theme is ambition. We go after the founders that are building the most ambitious things we can humanly find,” Sten Tamkivi, a co-founder of the firm, said in an interview with Crunchbase News. “Our stated objective remains to have a GDP-level impact on Europe with the companies that we back.”

Plural’s portfolio is a mix of energy, compute, defense, robotics, health and software. The firm first backed fusion energy company Proxima Fusion in its 2023 pre-seed round and has also invested in energy storage company Ore Energy. In defense and aerospace, its investments include European defense tech company Helsing and hypersonic flight and missile company Hypersonica, whose Series A it led in 2026. Plural also led the 2024 Series B for The Exploration Co., which develops space transportation.

In robotics and manufacturing, Plural has backed Monumental, which develops bricklaying robots; Sunrise Robotics, which builds robots for manufacturing; CircuitHub, which manufactures circuit board assemblies; and Upside Robotics, which develops agricultural robots. In compute, its investments include optical AI accelerator company Olix and photonic networking company Oriole Networks. More recently, Plural led the pre-seed round for Callosum, which is building a routing layer for heterogeneous compute.

Its investments have shifted year to year and fund to fund based on where the most ambitious founders are pulling the firm, said Tamkivi.

“Europe has agonized maybe a little bit too much about, ‘Hey, we missed this wave in the models, and the big labs are in the U.S. and China,’  and so forth. But if you look at the rest of the pyramid, we’re doing well,” he said.

The latest fund is the firm’s third and is double the size of its fund 2, raised in 2024, and 4x its first fund, closed in 2022.

Plural’s portfolio companies have had a breakout year, raising more than $3 billion in follow-on capital so far in 2026.

The team has six equal partners, all prior founders and operators based in London, Tallinn and Paris. Plural was founded by Taavet Hinrikus, co-founder of Wise, and Tamkivi co-founder of Teleport, both early employees at Skype, as well as Ian Hogarth, co-founder of Songkick, and Khaled Helioui, former CEO of Bigpoint.

The team has two other partners: Carina Namih, co-founder of HelixNano, and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty, a former Uber executive.

Each partner aims to make one to three new investments per year, leaving  bandwidth to work hands-on with founders.

The firm’s entry point is seed and Series A, where it likes to lead. “We’re still early-stage investors, so two-thirds of this money that we raise goes into early stage. What we’ve tagged on top is that now we have more capital to follow through in our winners, and  double down and triple down,” Tamkivi said, adding: “there’s more reserves to do that.”

Thanks so very much to NextWorld Capital for generously hosting us; to the boutique PR and strategy firm KCPR for its early support of the program; and to Carta — the platform for investors, founders, and employees to manage their cap tables, valuations, investments, and equity plans — for joining us as our newest partner in the evening.

P.S. We’re also headed to Berlin soon, including to interview Klarna’s Sebastian Siemiatkowski, who we last sat down with at a tiny coffee shop in San Francisco (before his company became Europe’s most highly valued private company). Hope to see some of you there, too.

Mark Hurd, who until last month was one of two CEOs leading the database software giant Oracle, passed away this morning at age 62, one month after telling employees in a letter that he was taking a leave of absence owing to health reasons. TechCrunch has more here.

SoftBank Group is assembling a rescue financing plan for WeWork that may value the office-sharing company below $8 billion, according to Bloomberg. The new figure is a fraction of the $47 billion valuation the startup commanded as recently as January, and yet it *still* seems a little high when compared with its bigger, profitable, publicly traded rival IWG, whose valuation is roughy half that amount.

Fun fact: Amazon went public in 1997 with $16 million in revenue and a market cap of $438 million. #ThoseWereTheDays. Unless you can write a $1 million check, it’s almost impossible to get exposure to early stage tech. Enter EquityZen. EquityZen allows accredited investors to access proven pre-IPO tech firms like Impossible Foods, SpaceX, Stripe, Rivian Automotive and Epic Games through its pooled funds. Explore EquityZen’s secondary market today.

WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann didn’t plan for his family’s control of WeWork to end at his death but instead expected to pass that control to future generations of Neumanns, too, says Business Insider.

The outlet reports that in a speech Neumann gave to employees in January of this year, footage of which it says it has viewed, Neumann is seen saying that WeWork isn’t “just controlled — we’re generationally controlled.” He reportedly goes on to say that while the five children he shares with wife Rebekah Neumann “don’t have to run the company,” they “do have to stay the moral compass of the company.”

According to BI, Neumann even invoked his future grandchildren, telling those gathered: “It’s important that one day, maybe in 100 years, maybe in 300 years, a great-great-granddaughter of mine will walk into that room and say, ‘Hey, you don’t know me; I actually control the place. The way you’re acting is not how we built it,’” he said.

These may sound like more outlandish proclamations from Neumann, who has a flair for the dramatic. (Talking to Fast Company earlier this year, he compared WeWork to a rare jewel, asking, “Do you know how long it takes a diamond to be created?”)

But before WeWork began coming apart at the seams, Neumann had every reason to believe that he could pass power down to his heirs.

ArsenalBio, a year-old, South San Francisco-based biotech outfit that hopes to improve the ability of T cell therapies to better fight a broader range of cancers, has raised $85 million in Series A funding. Investors include Westlake Village BioPartners, the Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, Kleiner Perkins, the University of California, San Francisco Foundation Investment Company, Euclidean Capital and Osage Venture Partners. Madbox, a 4.5-year-old, France-based mobile games studio, has raised $16.5 million in Series A funding from Alven. TechCrunch has more here.

Tenfold, a four-year-old, Austin, Tex.-based maker of customer service software, has raised $7.5 million in Series C funding led by Next Coast Ventures, with participation from earlier backers Andreessen Horowitz, Geekdom Fund, and Salesforce Ventures. Pulse 2.0 has more here.

Bloomberg Beta, the six-year-old, San Francisco-based outfit that uses Bloomberg LP’s money to make bets on startups, has closed its third fund with $75 million, according to Roy Bahat, who’d previously run the online media company IGN and who operates the fund as an equal partnership with Karin Klein and James Chan. (Klein formerly ran Bloomberg’s new initiatives; Chan was formerly a principal with Trinity Ventures.) We talked with Bahat briefly last night about the new vehicle to ask how its capital will be deployed.

The Kik messaging platform has been bought by MediaLab, a holding company which operates Whisper and a number of other apps, the company announced earlier today. CoinDesk has more here.

Di-Ann Eisnor, a WeWork exec, has left the company, says The Information. Eisnor reported to Adam Neumann and had “hired a group of designers, researchers and engineers focused on urban problems such as housing affordability and constructing buildings with sustainable material,” says the outlet, adding that her team of about 30 employees have left the company or are planning to depart.

#5309. In The AI Era, Keep Hiring New College Grads — And Make Them Managers From Day One

A few months ago, I was sitting lakeside with a neighbor. He is the head of AI for a pharmaceutical company, and he mentioned the truly incredible productivity his senior team is receiving from AI.

Then he paused and turned to me and said: “You know, I may never hire another junior engineer again. Which is great for the business right now, but who’s the next generation that is going to run this when we retire?”

The concern over what will happen to young people just entering the workforce is one many of us are grappling with right now, and it has a human dimension. Not just what happens to employment rates, but what happens to my students or my children?

College graduates typically do the individual contributor knowledge work that AI is evermore capable of delivering. To cite one statistic, a recent Stanford study found employment of 22 to 25 year olds in occupations most exposed to AI is running 19% below rates for their peers in less AI-impacted sectors, and that gap has been widening.

What role will new graduates play in the age of AI? And how will we develop the generation of managers who will supervise AI? Fortunately, we have thriving examples with 200 years of history on how to teach 22 year olds to do exactly that.

Our claim is that the reason senior folks get more out of AI today is not primarily because they have greater subject knowledge, but rather because they are good managers. They have to trust folks who work for them without completely trusting them, they have to divide tasks, delegate clearly, check results and patiently correct, coach, and sometimes shift personnel on their teams.

The future for new graduates is to become great managers now, at the very beginning of their career, and not after a long period of individual contribution.

The nature of the innovation of AI is that it delivers knowledge work. We know a lot about human knowledge workers and the analogy to AI knowledge workers is strong.

Knowledge workers know much more about their individual sphere of expertise than their managers do. Good managers routinely organize and lead knowledge workers who are just flat-out much smarter than they are. They do this through the craft of management.

These same qualities, as AI behaves more like AI executives, naturally give good managers the skills to manage AI agents, who become the individual contributor knowledge workers.

It is no secret that the investment industry culture values most highly the brilliance of the individual contributor who delivers the incisive observation, makes the correct investment call, and closes the one-on-one negotiation with a win.

I have lived this culture for a long time. Calling an investor a “great people manager” is a backhanded compliment at best. In the investment industry, the jump from individual contributor to manager usually arrives midcareer or later, and typically with little to no formal training in the craft of management.

The analyst, associate and vice president are primarily acting as individual contributors (though of course they may mentor a few junior folks), and are not shifting to acting primarily as managers of other knowledge workers until principal or perhaps partner.

When I was an analyst at Morgan Stanley many years ago, the hierarchy ran from analyst to managing director. Analysts were the ultimate individual contributors, and whenever an analyst would attempt to delegate some work to others, we had a name for that: “managing analyst.” This clever put-down reflected the cultural belief that real credit goes to those who do, not those who deliver through the work of those they manage.

This blind spot on the importance of management is not limited to the investment industry. As another salient recent example, let’s look at the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Much has been written about this event, where OpenAI agents hacked into Hugging Face.

In OpenAI’s own report on the incident, its proposed long list of fixes, including stronger security, alerts on breaches and post-incident remediation, does not address directly training its employees to be better managers of these agents. That’s even as the company acknowledges that members of an internal team at OpenAI knew of many of the concerning behaviors (including message board and unauthorized internet access) in late May, and did not act until July.

This may be an unfair analogy, but imagine if we hired 1,200 workers to operate a warehouse complex, gave each of them detailed written instructions, and then had all the line managers and senior managers leave for a week. If we came back to find that someone had stolen a delivery van, the problem wouldn’t be that these weren’t the right workers or that the instructions weren’t clear enough. The problem is lack of management.

As I was wrestling with this problem, I talked with my business school classmate Michael Quoia, who attended the U.S. Naval Academy and served as an officer, and then built a career in executive leadership development. He recalled:

“When I met my division of 25 sailors in Yokosuka, Japan at the young age of 22 years old, I was greeted by my senior chief petty officer, who already served for nearly 20 years. Behind him, we had several organizational levels including the first line sailors who conducted maintenance on the fire control systems. This was actually a harder problem than we are facing with AI. This was about supervising at least three levels without experience. I was expected to provide character, judgment, problem solving and leadership, despite not having come up through the ranks. How did the Navy develop these qualities in me so that I could bypass time in the seat as a frontline worker?”

Like companies facing the AI dilemma we have been exploring, the military needs to develop capable leaders who lack entry-level experience. And while the military is a very relevant example, it is not the only one. The Home Depot’s store management program and General Electric’s Crotonville are two examples of corporations who recruit high-potential talent and put them through an accelerated leadership development program to prepare them to lead people in jobs they have not done.

Let’s look, though, at how the Naval Academy provided Michael’s training, and what that may mean whether you are 22 years old or hiring 22-year-olds.

First, the foundation of developing future officers is the development of moral leadership. The mission of the United States Naval Academy begins with the phrase “To develop midshipmen morally, mentally, and physically … .” In an age of AI, first-line managers of AI agents will need integrity and a moral compass, because AI does not come with that reliably pre-installed. It is no overstatement to suggest that moral leadership of AI could have societal implications and needs to be developed.

Second, the service academies are intentionally designed as leadership laboratories. From plebe summer to commissioning, midshipmen progress from learning how to be a good subordinate to true manager. What is most relevant to the age of AI is that simulated leadership learning is possible and proven if designed with care.

Third, the service academies build high-pressure situations into their leadership laboratory. While most companies are not placing their first-line managers in life or death situations, the ability to lead in high stakes situations, for instance to take personal responsibility for an AI agent swarm you launched which is now “going rogue,” requires composure and decisiveness under stress and pressure.

If a 22-year-old ensign can manage 25 sailors on a Yokosuka destroyer, albeit with support from senior officers and enlisted, our 22-year-old college graduate can certainly be trained to manage 25 super-intelligent agents. The moment for practicing the craft of management will shift from 32 years old to 22 years old, across the businesses of knowledge work.

In short: We need to bring back the “managing analyst.” We need to recognize that AI agents behave like knowledge workers and therefore need to be managed. We should reset the culture in knowledge work industries that management is a valued skill, beginning at the start of one’s career and not midcareer.

These entry-level workers are smart, motivated, learn quickly and work hard. There is a huge unmet need for the craft of management in corralling this new generation of AI agents. We have the proof points across nearly 200 years from our service academies that these skills can be taught to the young, and the young can deliver them with distinction. The future for college graduates is a redefinition of their jobs away from being individual-contributor knowledge workers and toward being effective managers and leaders from the very beginning of their careers.

Bob Morse co-founded Strattam Capital in 2014 and is managing partner. He has served on numerous private and public technology company boards, and currently is a director of CloudHesive, Contegix, Daxtra Technologies, Green Security, Resource Navigation and Trax Group. Previously, he was a partner and member of the investment committee at Oak Hill Capital Partners. He also worked at GCC Investments and Morgan Stanley. Morse serves on the board of directors of Austin PBS and as member of the advisory board for the HMTF Center for Private Equity Finance at The University of Texas at Austin McCombs School of Business. He attended Princeton University, graduating summa cum laude with a BSE, and Stanford Graduate School of Business, where he earned his MBA and was an Arjay Miller Scholar. Morse lives in Austin.

Michael Quoia is co-founder and partner at KSE Leadership, which assesses and develops leaders and teams. A 25-year leadership advisory veteran with partner-level roles at Heidrick & Struggles and Russell Reynolds Associates, he began his career as a U.S. Navy  surface warfare officer. He is a graduate of the U.S. Naval Academy and holds an MBA from the Stanford Graduate School of Business.
